articles.title: Online threats put Eastern Samar, Samar schools on heightened alert
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — Two schools in Eastern Visayas have tightened security measures and coordinated with authorities after separate threats circulated online, underscoring continuing concerns over school…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — Two schools in Eastern Visayas have tightened security measures and coordinated with authorities after separate threats circulated online, underscoring continuing concerns over school safety following the deadly shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City in June.

Samar Colleges, Inc. in Catbalogan City and Llorente National High School in Llorente, Eastern Samar, issued separate statements on Friday, August 28, assuring students, faculty, employees and parents that authorities were responding to the reported threats.

At Samar Colleges, the school said it had learned of a social media threat allegedly made by a person identified as “Jeonard Obing” who supposedly intended to take revenge against the school for giving a failing grade.

The school said it found no record of the individual in its database of past and present students but nonetheless treated the threat as serious, particularly in light of recent incidents of violence in schools.
Samar Colleges said it immediately reported the threat to police through a blotter and coordinated with law enforcement authorities and the Catbalogan City government.

It also heightened security controls at all campus entrances, including mandatory body and bag checks, and deployed metal detectors to prevent firearms and other weapons from being brought onto school premises.

The school’s guidance counselors, faculty members and discipline officers were likewise instructed to monitor students exhibiting violent tendencies, unusual behavior or other warning signs that could potentially lead to violence.
“We shall prevail,” Samar Colleges board chair and president Rhea Cea Piazon said in the school’s Aug. 28 statement, while urging stakeholders to remain vigilant.
In Llorente, the Schools Division of Eastern Samar also issued an official statement on a reported threat involving Llorente National High School.
The Department of Education said it immediately addressed the reported threat and coordinated closely with the Philippine National Police and local authorities.
The division said it continues to enforce its zero-tolerance policy against bullying, harassment and security threats, whether these occur within school grounds or in the digital space.
It also cited strengthened protection protocols, including heightened inter-agency security, active child protection committees and strengthened cyber-safety advocacy.
The DepEd statement urged parents, learners and community stakeholders to remain calm and vigilant, while warning against spreading unverified information online.

The Llorente statement’s subject line refers to a reported “bomb threat,” while its body describes the incident as an alleged shooting threat. Authorities have not publicly confirmed that an actual explosive device was found at the school.

The latest incidents come more than two months after the June 22 shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, where two students, aged 14 and 15, allegedly opened fire on their classmates. Three students were killed and at least 20 others were injured.

The shooting, one of the country’s rare deadly school attacks, prompted calls for tighter security in schools and greater attention to threats and warning signs involving students. The suspects, who are both minors, are under the custody of the Department of Social Welfare and Development though the 15-year-old was charged for murder counts and multiple serious injuries.

Since then, reports of threats circulated through social media have heightened anxiety among schools, parents and students in Eastern Visayas, with school officials increasingly turning to police coordination, access controls, threat assessment and cyber-safety measures.

The incidents also highlight the challenge faced by schools in distinguishing between idle or malicious online posts and credible threats. Both Samar Colleges and DepEd-Eastern Samar stressed that threats must be taken seriously while authorities determine their credibility.
Samar Colleges said its security measures were intended not only to respond to the latest threat but also to deter anyone from attempting to carry out an attack.
The school emphasized that the safety and well-being of its students, faculty and employees remain its paramount concern.
Meanwhile, DepEd-Eastern Samar appealed to the public to rely on verified information from school authorities and designated emergency channels rather than spreading unverified reports online. /das

articles.title: Lacson flags 4 ‘fraudulently’ titled parcels of reclaimed land in Taguig
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Four parcels of alleged illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City have been identified with “fraudulently” issued titles that will be turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Four parcels of alleged illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City have been identified with “fraudulently” issued titles that will be turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman for investigation, Sen. Panfilo Lacson disclosed on Saturday.

In a post on X, formerly Twitter, the senator shared an update regarding the investigation of infrastructure and reclamation projects in Taguig City, saying at least four parcels of illegally reclaimed land have been discovered to date.
According to Lacson, the parcels covered areas ranging from 5,000 to 193,027 square meters. All four were processed through various patent and land registration procedures, namely:
“(a) via Administrative Patent issued to… (name withheld at the moment) covering an area of 9,204 sq meters under OCT No. (xxx);
(b) through Judicial/Ordinary Land Registration Processing covering an area of 5,000 sq meters issued to… (xxx) under OCT No. (xxx);
(c) via Homestead Patent issued to… (xxx) involving 181,077 square meters under TCT No (xxx);
(d) 193,027 sq meters issued to… (xxx) under TCT No. (xxx)”
Lacson, moreover, disclosed that there are four other parcels with no plotted titled lots in the Land Registration Authority’s (LRA) digital records.
He said documents related to the properties will be turned over to the Ombudsman’s “fact-finding team” for appropriate action.

The senator had earlier said the Ombudsman has issued subpoenas to the LRA, Taguig Registry of Deeds, the Department of Public Works and Highways, and the Philippine Reclamation Authority amid the ongoing probe into Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano’s bailiwick.
“Since [Senator] Cayetano keeps publicly asking for evidence, I’ll give it to him, in the spirit of public interest,” he said in the same thread.

Cayeto has consistently maintained that to his knowledge, there are no “ghost” projects in Taguig City. However, the senator said he was prepared to respond to the allegations once Lacson specified the projects and evidence linking the anomalies to him.
The feud between the two senators began in July after Lacson said Cayetano had crossed the line by questioning the increase in his personal net worth.
Lacson later alleged that there were irregularities in the flood control projects and reclamation works in Taguig City, which prompted the investigation. /das

articles.title: JBC opens applications for next chief justice
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) on Saturday opened applications and nominations for the next Supreme Court chief justice ahead of Alexander Gesmundo’s compulsory…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) on Saturday opened applications and nominations for the next Supreme Court chief justice ahead of Alexander Gesmundo’s compulsory retirement on November 6.
In a notice issued on Saturday, the JBC said the deadline for the submission of applications, along with the necessary documentary requirements, is on October 13, at 4:30 p.m.
The JBC is a constitutional body that screens and vets nominees to the president for vacant posts in the judiciary, the Office of the Ombudsman, and members of the Legal Education Board.
Aspirants may refer to the 2020 Revised JBC Rules, as amended, on the official website of the JBC for the qualification requirements and evaluative criteria.
Among the requirements are sworn Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth, accompanied by an explanation in case of an unusual, appreciable or sudden increase or decrease in net worth.

Affidavit of Waiver of Confidentiality and Secrecy of Bank Deposits must also be submitted, as well as certifications issued by banks or other financial institutions, medical records, and necessary clearances, among others.
The qualifications of applicants shall be formally reckoned by the Council as of the date of nomination, according to the JBC.
Applicants found to have deliberately made “false statements, misrepresentations, or concealments” on any documents submitted shall be disqualified from being nominated or may be subject to perjury.
Gesmundo is the fourth magistrate appointed by then-President Rodrigo Duterte in 2021 and the country’s 27th chief justice.
His successor will be the first Chief Justice to be appointed by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. /gsg

articles.title: Bodies of 2 missing Aeta children retrieved from Zambales lake
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — The bodies of two Aeta children who went missing after a boat carrying 13 passengers capsized in Mapanuepe Lake near San Marcelino town were recovered Saturday, Aug. 29, three…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — The bodies of two Aeta children who went missing after a boat carrying 13 passengers capsized in Mapanuepe Lake near San Marcelino town were recovered Saturday, Aug. 29, three days after the incident.
The two were identified as Chandnea Serrano dela Cruz, 3, and Anqelito Serrano Liwanag, 8, according to the Philippine Coast Guard.

In a phone interview, Police Maj. Exodus Rodriguez, chief of the San Marcelino police, said a resident traveling toward Barangay Buhawen spotted the body of the 3-year-old girl while passing through the lake.
The resident retrieved the child and brought her to authorities, where her father confirmed her identity, Rodriguez said.
After the girl’s body was recovered, police asked a boatman to accompany them back to the area where she was found, according to Rodriguez.
They then spotted the body of Anqelito nearby and recovered it.
Rodriguez said weather conditions had been unpredictable during the search, with rain and strong winds easing at times before suddenly intensifying.
Despite the conditions, search operations continued for the remaining missing passenger, a 26-year-old pregnant woman.
On Thursday, Aug. 27, the 13 Aeta passengers were aboard a motor banca that capsized near the Sunken Church in Barangay Buhawen while they were returning to their community in Sitio Lumibao.
With the recovery of the two children, eight Aetas have now died in the incident, including five children, while four others survived. /das

articles.title: Over 1,000 Olongapo City folk forced to evacuate due flooding
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — Over 1,000 Olongapo City residents were forced to seek shelter in safer, higher areas on Saturday as widespread flooding hounded the city amid persistent monsoon rains. Data…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — Over 1,000 Olongapo City residents were forced to seek shelter in safer, higher areas on Saturday as widespread flooding hounded the city amid persistent monsoon rains.
Data from the Olongapo City Information Center showed that 1,395 individuals from 452 families were staying in evacuation centers as of 9:30 a.m. Saturday.
Some affected residents were forced to stay outside designated evacuation centers, according to city authorities.
Flooding also left residents stranded in several parts of the city on Friday night as water levels in rivers continued to rise and eventually reached spilling levels.
The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said the southwest monsoon or “habagat”, continued to affect Luzon, including Olongapo City.
Pagasa is also monitoring a low-pressure area located 520 kilometers north-northeast of Itbayat, Batanes as of Saturday.
Zambales was among areas forecast to receive 100 to 200 millimeters of rainfall from Saturday to Monday, according to Pagasa.
Photos provided by Olongapo City Mayor Rolen Paulino Jr. showed residents stranded by floodwaters in several parts of the city on Friday night.

articles.title: Zambales floods displace over 6,000 residents
articles.summary: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — Over 6,000 residents were forced to evacuate in several towns in this province as floodwaters rose amid persistent heavy rains. Data from the Provincial Disaster Risk…

blocks.text: SAN ANTONIO, Zambales — Over 6,000 residents were forced to evacuate in several towns in this province as floodwaters rose amid persistent heavy rains.
Data from the Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office showed that 2,241 families or 6,399 residents are staying in evacuation centers across the province as of 10 p.m. Friday.
Botolan recorded the highest number of evacuees at 2,721, as rescue teams continued to assist residents in flood-hit communities.
Floodwaters rose in several areas as rivers and waterways swelled following sustained rains, prompting local authorities to deploy rescue teams to affected and hard-to-reach communities.
The flooding also further damaged flood-control structures that had already been affected by previous flooding.

articles.title: Dinagat Islands rolls out measures vs water crisis
articles.summary: SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur — The Dinagat Islands provincial government is pursuing groundwater drilling, desalination and continued water rationing as emergency measures to ease a worsening water…

blocks.text: SAN FRANCISCO, Agusan del Sur — The Dinagat Islands provincial government is pursuing groundwater drilling, desalination and continued water rationing as emergency measures to ease a worsening water shortage that prompted the province to declare a state of calamity.

Gov. Nilo Demerey Jr. said the declaration was made early so the provincial government could respond before the effects of the prolonged dry spell further worsened, particularly in communities already experiencing a water shortage.
“Unsaon pa ang sagbot kung patay na ang kabayo” (“What good is the grass if the horse is already dead?”), Demerey said in an interview on Aug. 26.
The governor said the provincial government prepared several short-term measures, including drilling in areas believed to have underground water sources.
Solar-powered pumps are being considered for identified sites that could be developed as alternative water sources.

Demerey also said the province has three reverse osmosis machines that may be used for desalination, a process that removes salt and other impurities from seawater so it can be treated for potable use.

The Public Information Office said another reason for the early declaration of a state of calamity was to allow municipal and barangay governments to access available Quick Response Funds for urgent interventions in communities affected by the water crisis.

Demerey said the provincial government is also seeking additional assistance from national government agencies and line agencies for programs and other interventions that could help ease the shortage.
Water rationing, meanwhile, is continuing in areas identified as critically affected.
Residents have been urged to conserve water and prioritize its use for drinking, cooking, personal hygiene and other essential household needs.

Demerey appealed to Dinagat residents to cooperate in managing the province’s limited water supply while the provincial government, local government units and barangays continue looking for immediate and practical solutions. /gsg

articles.title: 2 Bulacan dams release water, 200 families in Marilao evacuated
articles.summary: CITY OF MALOLOS — Two dams in Bulacan resumed releasing water on Friday as heavy rains brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon pushed their water levels closer to, and in one case beyond, their…

blocks.text: CITY OF MALOLOS — Two dams in Bulacan resumed releasing water on Friday as heavy rains brought by the enhanced southwest monsoon pushed their water levels closer to, and in one case beyond, their spilling levels, according to the Bulacan Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO).
Bustos Dam was releasing 294 cubic meters per second (cms) of water on Saturday morning after it began discharging 261 cms at 8 and 9 p.m. Friday.
Its water elevation rose to 16.33 meters at 8 p.m. and 16.42 meters at 9 p.m., nearing its 17-meter spilling level.
Ipo Dam also began releasing water at 9 p.m. Friday, discharging 35.50 cms, which increased to 70.10 cms at 11 p.m. as its water elevation climbed to 101.40 and 101.65 meters, respectively.
Ipo Dam’s spilling level is 101 meters. On Saturday morning, it continued to release 68.10 cms, with its water elevation at 101.17 meters.

Angat Dam, meanwhile, had a water elevation of 194.62 meters above sea level (masl) on Saturday. Its level has risen by nearly 44 meters from 150.55 masl on July 26 but remained 15.38 meters below its 210-meter normal high-water level.

Residents in low-lying areas and communities near the Angat River system that could be affected by water releases had already been evacuated during previous releases triggered by the southwest monsoon and Tropical Cyclones Luis and Maymay, said Manuel Lukban Jr., head of the Bulacan PDRRMO.
In Marilao town, an initial 200 families in NorthVille, Barangay Lambakin, were placed under preemptive evacuation after floodwaters rose to more than 3 feet.
Lukban said the Marilao River had begun overflowing as floodwaters cascaded from rain-soaked mountainous areas of Bulacan, particularly Norzagaray.
High tide on Saturday was forecast at 3.71 feet, or 1.13 meters, at 10:48 a.m.
Meanwhile, several waterways in the Pampanga River Basin, a major contributor to flooding in parts of Bulacan, particularly Calumpit, were at critical, alarm or alert levels.

articles.title: Pinatubo, Taal lahar flow warning issued as monsoon rains persist
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) on Saturday warned of possible lahar flows in Pinatubo and Taal volcanoes amid continuous rains. Phivolcs…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (Phivolcs) on Saturday warned of possible lahar flows in Pinatubo and Taal volcanoes amid continuous rains.

Phivolcs warned that prolonged heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon or “habagat” may generate lahar, or volcanic sediment flows, and muddy streamflow in rivers and drainage areas near the volcanoes.

“Prolonged and intense rainfall may generate non-eruption lahars on major rivers draining western Pinatubo Volcano where significant deposits of the 1991 PDCs remain on the watershed,” Phivolcs said in an advisory.
It added that the lahar from Pinatubo may occur on the upper to middle reaches of Sto. Tomas-Marella and Bucao river systems.
Meanwhile, the muddy stream flows may affect the lower reaches and communities of Zambales, including San Marcelino, San Narciso, San Felipe, and Botolan.
The volcanic sediments may also occur along the O’Donnell and Pasig-Potrero River systems and affect downstream communities in Tarlac and Pampanga Provinces.
Heavy rainfall may also cause muddy streamflow and even volcanic debris around Taal volcano, primarily on the west and north slopes of the lake.
These can affect parts of Batangas provinces, particularly Agoncillo, Laurel and Talisay.
Phivolcs advised the affected communities to continuously monitor weather conditions and to take precautionary measures when necessary. /gsg

articles.title: Groups press DENR to suspend mangrove earth-balling
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Environmental groups are urging the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to suspend the earth-balling and relocation of mangroves, warning that the practice…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Environmental groups are urging the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to suspend the earth-balling and relocation of mangroves, warning that the practice could result in the death of up to 80% of trees removed, as a House resolution calls for an examination of the agency’s policy.

The call was made by the Global Mangrove Alliance Philippines (GMAP), international ocean conservation organization Oceana and mangrove scientist Dr. Jurgenne Primavera of the Zoological Society of London (ZSL), amid a congressional inquiry into the DENR’s guidelines allowing mangrove earth-balling in exceptional circumstances.

The DENR memorandum, dated Oct. 8, 2025, is titled Interim Operational Guidance and Conditions on the Earth-balling and Relocation of Mangroves in Exceptional Circumstances. It provides guidance for processing requests to earth-ball and relocate mangroves pending the completion of a study by the agency’s Ecosystems Research and Development Bureau.

Under the memorandum, mangroves “shall not be removed or disturbed” as a rule. Earth-balling and relocation may be considered only in specified exceptional cases, including when mangrove trees pose a danger or when the activity involves an infrastructure flagship project endorsed by the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development, provided that mitigation measures to avoid impacts on mangroves have been exhausted.
The guidelines also prohibit the DENR from accepting or processing requests for earth-balling and relocation for commercial, recreational or other private purposes.
Survival of transplanted mangroves
The environmental groups, however, said available scientific evidence raises concerns about whether mangroves removed through earth-balling can survive after transplantation.
“Repeal the DENR Guidelines now. Congress must investigate to stop this threat to our remaining mangroves,” Primavera, ZSL’s chief mangroves scientific adviser, said.
The groups cited several studies they said had been presented to the DENR as early as March 2025.

These included a China-based study that recorded only 20% to 25% survival of two mangrove species 10 months after earth-balling; an Australia-based study that found mortality after 2.5 years among mangroves with an average trunk diameter of more than 5 centimeters; and Philippine data showing adult mangroves in five barangays in Ibajay, Aklan, had average trunk diameters of 9 to 16 centimeters.

The House resolution filed by Mamamayang Liberal Party-list Rep. Leila de Lima cites additional research indicating that successful earth-balling is ecologically and physiologically limited to trees with stem widths of less than approximately 8 centimeters.
It also says mangroves in coastal areas typically targeted for infrastructure development in the Philippines have mature stems ranging from 10 to 30 centimeters in diameter or more.
Earth-balling involves digging up a tree together with surrounding soil to form a compact mass, which is then secured and transferred using equipment such as a crane or bladed tree spade.

“[S]tudies have shown that mangrove earth-balling and transplantation establish that the practice fundamentally disrupts the integrated soil-water-vegetation connections upon which mangrove ecosystems depend, resulting in losses of ecosystem function,” the House resolution stated.
DENR guidelines impose safeguards
The DENR memorandum, meanwhile, states that the survival of earth-balled mangroves must be the “paramount consideration” in all cases.

It requires proponents to follow established methodologies for selecting transplanting and replacement sites, preserving the root system and soil ball, timing the operation according to tidal and seasonal conditions, and using appropriate equipment and transport techniques.
Proponents must also submit a Mangrove Rehabilitation and Monitoring Plan before any permit is issued.

The memorandum further requires transplanting and replacement sites to meet ecological standards involving tidal elevation, hydrological conditions, salinity and soil conditions, slope and wave protection, and proximity to existing mangrove stands.

For projects covered by the Philippine Environmental Impact Statement System, proposed earth-balling and relocation activities must also be included in the applicable environmental assessment documents.
Actual earth-balling, transplanting and replacement planting must be conducted under the direct monitoring and supervision of the concerned DENR field office, according to the memorandum.
Pending applications for mangrove earth-balling and relocation, meanwhile, will be evaluated under the safeguards in the memorandum.

“Proponents with incomplete requirements or pending submissions shall be directed to update their applications in compliance with these provisions prior to further evaluation. No permit shall be issued unless full compliance with this Memorandum is observed,” the agency said.
The memorandum also says existing guidelines and requirements for the issuance of cutting or earth-balling permits will remain in effect and will apply alongside the new provisions.

It also provides that unauthorized cutting, earth-balling or relocation of mangroves may be subject to penalties under Presidential Decree No. 705, as amended, the Fisheries Code and other applicable laws.
House questions legal basis of policy
Beyond the scientific concerns, the House resolution questions whether the DENR memorandum is consistent with existing laws and international commitments on mangrove protection.
It cites Section 99 of Republic Act No. 8550, as amended by RA 10654, or the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998, which prohibits the conversion of mangroves for other purposes.

The resolution also points to Presidential Proclamation No. 2152, which declares the entire province of Palawan and certain other areas as mangrove swamp forest reserves, and the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act, or RA 8371, when mangrove areas fall within ancestral domains.

The resolution argues that the DENR’s issuance could conflict with these protections, describing the “unilateral issuance of administrative guidance” as a “grave overreach of executive regulatory authority.”
It also asks House committees to examine the memorandum’s legal validity and determine whether it should be revoked or amended.

Specifically, the resolution calls for the inquiry to “review the legal validity of the administrative issuance in light of existing mangrove protection laws, recommend its immediate revocation or amendment as may be warranted, and call for the conduct of a comprehensive, independent scientific review.”

The proposed inquiry would also look beyond the current memorandum. De Lima’s resolution asks lawmakers to review and consolidate existing legislation and explore a new mangrove conservation and protection law establishing “clear, enforceable standards for mangrove preservation, rehabilitation, and sustainable management.”
Mangrove loss raises stakes for coastal communities

The Philippines is home to at least 50% of the roughly 65 mangrove species found worldwide, but its mangrove cover has declined from about 500,000 hectares in the early 20th century to roughly 285,000 to 311,400 hectares in 2020, according to Oceana.
The House resolution puts the remaining cover at about 284,798 hectares and says the country has lost more than 64% of its mangroves since 1918.

The resolution notes that mangroves help protect coastal communities from storm surges, flooding and erosion while also serving as nurseries for marine species, supporting fisherfolk livelihoods and contributing to climate change mitigation.
For Oceana Vice President Von Hernandez, allowing earth-balling could put those natural defenses at further risk.
“By allowing earth-balling, the DENR is sacrificing proven nature-based solutions for short-term economic gain,” Hernandez said.

“Shouldn’t the DENR be held accountable for reneging on its mandate to protect mangroves and uphold nature-based safeguards especially at a time when every coastal community in the country is under siege from flooding and storm surges?” he added.
Concern over Cancabato Bay

Oceana also pointed to Cancabato Bay in Tacloban City, Leyte — known as “ground zero” of Supertyphoon Yolanda (Haiyan) in 2013, one of the deadliest typhoons in recorded history, which killed at least 6,300 people — as a potential site for further mangrove removal.

The organization said operators of Daniel Z. Romualdez Airport announced on July 29 that “mangroves in the airport’s vicinity will have to be removed to make way for shore protection infrastructure, a new perimeter road, and to prevent bird strikes.”
According to GMAP, many coastal areas with mangroves targeted for cutting were declared no-build zones after Supertyphoon Haiyan.
Stronger mangrove protection
GMAP has called for a halt to earth-balling while Congress examines the policy.
“In the spirit of precaution, all earth-balling of mangroves must stop while Congress examines the scientific, legal, and governance questions surrounding the policy,” the group said.
The groups also cited the 40-hectare Floodway Project in Jaro, Iloilo, as an example of infrastructure being integrated into a natural mangrove environment.
They are urging the passage of the proposed National Coastal Greenbelt Bill, which seeks to strengthen mangrove restoration and nature-based solutions for vulnerable coastal communities.
Oceana said it supports De Lima’s investigation and the proposed legislation.
“With climate impacts intensifying, we appeal to President Marcos Jr. to certify the passage of this bill as urgent,” Hernandez said. /dm

articles.title: Number of missing in Nepal, China floods soars to nearly 3,000
articles.summary: NUWAKOT, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan…

blocks.text: NUWAKOT, Nepal — Rescuers in Nepal and China were still battling Saturday to locate thousands of people missing days after a deadly, tsunami-like wall of water and debris swept through the Himalayan region, engulfing villages.

The number of missing soared to nearly 3,000 Saturday, according to the latest figures from both countries, with 633 bodies recovered and reports that some of the dead may have been swept downstream as far away as India.

In an area home to vast energy infrastructure projects, Nepal’s disaster authority added 933 hydropower workers to a missing persons list that already included trekkers and pilgrims to Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash.
Those who made it out say they have lost everything and now face an agonizing wait to discover the fate of missing loved ones and the prospect of rebuilding their lives from nothing.
“All the settlements near the river were swept away. There is nothing left,” survivor Buddhi Ram Dangol told AFP.
Samjhana Thing said she had been waiting three days for news of her missing brother.
“We don’t know anything. Hopefully he is in a safe place,” she said.
‘Enormous’ trauma
The trauma of Wednesday’s catastrophe has been “enormous,” and as many as 93,000 people may have been affected, the Red Cross said, with the death toll expected to rise.
Emergency teams had been racing to retrieve survivors from affected zones, where the widespread devastation meant food and water supplies were running out.
Compounding the search for the missing are fears of further flooding in affected areas.
The deluge of ice and mud caused huge lakes to form, and one of these formations has become a direct threat to emergency workers scouring the region for survivors.
Nepali police urged all rescuers to “immediately move to a safe location,” saying they had received information that “a water dam has burst again on the Tibetan side.”

In Tibet, where Chinese authorities are the only source of information, Beijing suspended its rescue operation in the hardest-hit area of Gyirong over the risk of renewed flooding before saying the threat had eased.
State news agency Xinhua reported early Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the area.
‘All swept away’
On the Nepali side of the border, the military located people trapped in the tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project, where they were working to find a way in to extract the survivors.
“Two helicopters have been dispatched, but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel,” army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet told AFP.
Some 350 workers and residents have been brought to safety from the site, he added, but efforts were ongoing to rescue more than 100 people trapped in the same area.
Workers rescued from other dam projects along the Trishuli valley described a disaster that unfolded with terrifying speed.
Buddha Tamang told AFP he survived only because he was inside a tunnel at the dam where he worked when the flood struck.
“The senior officers working on the other side, they were all swept away,” Tamang, who was airlifted on Thursday after being marooned for more than 24 hours, told AFP.
Nepal reported a death toll of 626 people on Saturday.
There are 2,426 people, including hundreds of foreigners, who are out of contact in Nepal.
Across the border in Tibet, which is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, seven people died and 554 remain missing, state news agency Xinhua reported early Saturday.
Authorities also said they had evacuated 555 stranded tourists and 499 Chinese residents from Tibet.
In India, authorities said they had recovered seven bodies from rivers flowing from Nepal, believed to be flood victims.
Pilgrimage route
Scores of Hindu devotees from across the world are among those missing on the border, as many were on a pilgrimage to Tibet’s Mount Kailash.
Sivaranjani Muthunathan was traveling by bus with 56 others toward the Chinese border when they became stuck in what they thought was a traffic jam.
“Then there was fog, smoke, something that seemed to suddenly engulf us,” Muthunathan, 46, told AFP on Friday, showing a phone video she recorded of a torrent surging toward her.
Around them, vehicles were swept away or buried under mud.
“One by one, we also climbed out through the driver’s side,” then scrambled up a hill, she said. /das

AfD youth wing: Germany shouldn't leave euro

blocks.caption: The AfD's youth wing, Generation Deutschland, has around 2,500 membersImage: Markus Scholz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The youth wing of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has broken ranks with party leadership and called for Germany not to leave the euro currency.

"We do not want Germany to leave the euro, but to address the existing structural flaws in the euro system," Jean-Pascal Hohm, head of the Generation Deutschland (GD) youth organization, told the Bild newspaper.
The GD is due to adopt a position on the issue at a conference in the city of Magdeburg on Saturday.
A draft statement says the euro has strengthened the European single market but has "structural flaws," and calls for reforms that would improve stability without giving up Europe's economic unity.
In its 2025 election manifesto, the euroskeptic AfD has called for Germany to leave the euro, the single currency of 21 EU member states.

The GD was established last year as the AfD's new youth organization after the party dissolved its previous youth wing, the Junge Alternative (JA), after it was labeled right-wing extremist by intelligence officials.

articles.title: Brgy officials in Tigbauan, Iloilo resign over foul odor, mosquitoes emanating from farm
articles.summary: ILOILO CITY— All nine officials of a barangay (village) in Tigbauan town of Iloilo province are going to resign over a problem with a poultry farm. Barangay Captain of Rene Taño Linobayan led the…

blocks.text: Barangay officials of Linobayan, Tigbauan town, Iloilo province. (Photo from Barangay's Facebook page)
ILOILO CITY— All nine officials of a barangay (village) in Tigbauan town of Iloilo province are going to resign over a problem with a poultry farm.
Barangay Captain of Rene Taño Linobayan led the submission of their mass resignation to Tigbauan Mayor Virgilio Teruel this week.

The resignation of Taño as well as Barangay Kagawads Joesa Mae Mendez, Mary Rose Agapay-Sagala, Leticia Trespecios, Leticia Tasic, Rico Taño, Johnny Vale, and Efren Tayag; and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) chairperson Ejelyn Claire Casio are set to take effect on September 10.
According to Taño, the mass resignation is a protest over the problem that escalated with a poultry farm in neighboring Barangay Sipitan.
It was last year that Linobayan residents started complaining of the foul odor and the presence of mosquitoes.
Barangay officials led by Taño reported it to the local government unit (LGU), which sent an inspection team that found that the odor was "minimal".
This did not sit well with residents while Taño and other barangay officials are facing a civil damages case filed by the new owner of the poultry farm.
On his part, Teruel urged the barangay officials to reconsider their decision to resign as it would impact the services in Barangay Linobayan.
The Local Government Code stipulates that resignations of barangay officials only can take effect if it's accepted by the municipal mayor.
Teruel also denied that the LGU of Tigbauan under his administration did not properly take action against the problems caused by the poultry farm.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet floods: rescuers work through night at hydropower tunnel as number of missing climbs to almost 3,000 – latest updates
articles.summary: Nepali army digs through thick mud that has filled tunnel at plant in Rasuwa, as death toll from flash floods rises to 626 with seven confirmed dead in Tibet

blocks.text: Search and rescue efforts intensify to locate people trapped inside mud-filled tunnel
The Nepalese government said the army is digging through the thick mud that has filled a hydropower tunnel where people are believed to be trapped inside.
“The work to open the tunnel’s entrance has been intensified since early on Saturday morning,” the Nepalese prime minister’s office said in a post on Facebook.
A team of 82 personnel from the Nepalese army and police “has been continuously working since last night to excavate the tunnel entrance and accelerate the search operation”, it added.
“The rescue efforts, however, have been made extremely challenging by the persistently adverse weather in the area.”

blocks.caption: A handout photo made available by the Nepal army shows personnel rescuing survivors from a hydropower tunnel following flash floods in Rasuwa district, Nepal. Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPA
A rescuer pulls a survivor through the thick mud to safety. Photograph: Nepal Army Handout/EPA

blocks.text: It was not immediately clear how many people remain trapped inside the tunnel. The Nepalese government said two people were pulled from the mud yesterday, with footage of the dramatic rescue operation shared on social media. You can watch that here:
Key events

items: 52m agoSearch and rescue efforts intensify to locate people trapped inside mud-filled tunnel
2h ago‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal
3h agoOpening summary

blocks.text: This is an interesting piece in the Conversation by Dibyesh Anand, professor of international relations and deputy vice-chancellor at the University of Westminster, about how China’s control over Tibet can make it harder for Nepal and other countries downstream to prepare for sudden Himalayan disasters, such as glacial lake outburst floods.

blocks.caption: This screengrab from footage released by the Tibet military command shows an aerial view of the mudslide-affected area near Gyirong border port in Tibet. Photograph: Tibet Military Command/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Tibet is governed by China, which took control of the previously self-governing region by force in the early 1950s. Nepal shares a long, mountainous border with Tibet, and the two regions are closely connected by their geography, rivers and trade, making events on the Tibetan plateau particularly significant for communities downstream in Nepal.
Anand writes:

double quotation markDespite warm relations with Beijing, and the Nepalese government’s assurances that it follows the “One China” principle and permits no support for Tibetans, China’s tight control over Tibet creates complications. The region is administered as a militarised frontier. Access runs on permits and clearances, the area is closely watched by armed police and the military and outsiders – foreign journalists, independent researchers, at times even diplomats – are routinely kept out. Tibet is an information black hole. Beijing’s anxiety extends across the border as Nepal is home to more than 10,000 Tibetan refugees and has long been the main escape route out of Tibet. China pressurises Nepal to police Tibetan activism, seal crossings and fold border management into a security partnership meant to insulate the plateau from the outside world. The glacial and hydrological data from the Tibetan plateau, the information often needed to anticipate flooding, is also treated as strategically sensitive by China and is closely held. Nepal has no mechanism to receive real-time glacial lake and river data from the Chinese side and its officials have sometimes gone further, accusing Beijing of withholding it. When a disaster in the Nepal-Tibet border region demands that rescuers cross quickly or that a warning travel downstream from an upstream lake, it runs into a system built for control rather than speed.

The Guardian’s senior China correspondent Amy Hawkins also writes about how China’s tight control over information and restrictions on journalists in Tibet have made it difficult to independently assess the full extent of the flooding and damage on the Chinese side of the border. You can read her report here:
India said it is increasing surveillance of glaciers and glacial lakes in its Himalayan regions bordering Nepal and China.

The deadly floods on the Nepal-Tibet border were believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse that was detected as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event by geologists. You can read this explainer to find out more about how a collapsing glacier can generate a powerful flood, and whether the climate crisis is contributing to the risk.

blocks.caption: Distant view of the snow capped Indian Himalayas in the Binsar region of Uttarakhand. Photograph: Steve Taylor ARPS/Alamy

blocks.text: Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India’s Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, said: “Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbour, and also have a similar geographic situation … we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region.”

Uttarakhand is one of the most ecologically sensitive regions of India, with 1,266 glacial lakes. As glaciers melt, water can accumulate in lakes held back by natural barriers. If those barriers fail, vast volumes of water can be released suddenly, triggering devastating floods.
“We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state,” Kaushik told AFP.
‘The flood took everything I have’: survivors grieve for relatives and homes swept away in Nepal

The Guardian’s south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen and journalist Gaurav Pokharel report from the Nepalese town of Bidur, where rescue efforts are being coordinated. They spoke to survivors mourning loved ones and confronting the loss of their homes and livelihoods after devastating floods swept through their communities.

blocks.caption: Sangke Dolma Tamang (in red), 61, watched flood waters tear away her husband, her home and almost everything she held dear. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: Among those caught in the floods was Sangke Dolma Tamang, who described the moment she watched her husband being swept away and returned to find her home and village destroyed:

double quotation markSangke Dolma Tamang, 61, had been cheerily cooking snacks in her village of Mailung in the Rasuwa district when the floods came without warning. The whole family ran uphill for safety, but as she grabbed for her husband, he slipped from her grip and was washed into the dark, fast-moving waters. “Others tried to pull him to safety, but the flood swept him away,” she said, tears rolling down her weathered cheeks. There was, she said, nothing left of her village now. She had spent a night sheltering on higher ground, until an army helicopter arrived and brought to her safety at the barracks. Her son too was missing since the disaster, and she waited anxiously for any news. “Now I have nothing left to live for,” said Tamang. “The whole house is gone. We couldn’t salvage anything.”
Nepal’s government has appealed for financial help as it faces the daunting task of recovering from the devastating flash floods and braces for the possibility of more flooding.
Entire communities have been swept away, leaving families homeless or sheltering in temporary facilities.
“Multiple bridges have been washed away and major roads disrupted, leaving some of the worst-affected communities extremely difficult to reach,” the Red Cross says.
At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged, leaving about 10,000 school-age children affected, according to the UN Children’s Fund.
The disaster comes just ahead of the anniversary of last year’s 8-9 September mass anti-corruption protests that toppled the government.

Nepal is now led by prime minister Balendra Shah, a 36-year-old rapper turned politician widely known as “Balen”. The former Kathmandu mayor swept March elections on a wave of euphoria calling for political change.

blocks.caption: Machines clear a road at the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong County, in southwest China’s Xizang Autonomous Region.   Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock
Members of the Nepali Army load relief material into a helicopter to be transported to areas affected by flash floods.  Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/Reuters

Residents watch as an excavator helps people to collect some of their belongings from their house in the aftermath of flash floods at Trishuli, in Nepal’s Nuwakot district.  Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The risk of a lake formed after the glacier collapse bursting near the China-Nepal border where the ⁠devastating flood occurred earlier ⁠this week has decreased, ​Chinese authorities said today, as its size appears to have shrunk.

Satellite images from Thursday this morning suggest water in the lake – straddling the China-Nepal border ⁠at the confluence of two rivers – has been slowly flowing through, decreasing the reservoir gradually, state broadcaster CCTV reported, citing the water resources ministry.

The ministry said satellite imagery of the surface area of the ⁠lake at Purepu Tsangpo river showed it was 99,000 sq metres in size this morning – around the size of ​14 football fields combined – having shrunk by 21,000 sq metres compared ‌with images from Thursday.

blocks.caption: An aerial drone photo shows a view around a barrier lake formed after a mudslide upstream of the Gyirong Port in Tibet. Photograph: Jigme Dorje/Xinhua/AP

blocks.text: Experts and authorities have warned of the extremely high risk of secondary disasters in the valley, especially from the lake that was formed by glacier debris, potentially endangering rescue operations downstream.

State-owned engineering and rescue enterprise China Anneng, which has been monitoring the lake since Thursday, dispatched a 15-member team on Friday with reconnaissance drones, portable satellite stations and mobile surveillance cameras to gather more data about the ‌lake.
An overflow from the lake on Friday temporarily halted rescue work before further assessment deemed the risks manageable.
Opening summary
Thank you for joining us for our continuing coverage of the aftermath of Wednesday’s catastrophic flash floods in the Himalayan mountains near the Nepal-Tibet border.
Poor weather has hampered aerial rescue operations in Nepal as the search for thousands of people missing enters its fourth day.

Nepal’s finance minister says his country will need up to $5bn to rebuild ⁠after the ⁠floods, believed to have been caused by a melting glacier high up in the mountains that set off a deadly cascade of water into the valleys below.
Finance ‌minister Swarnim Wagle told Reuters ‌today those figures are “just an ​estimate” and that “loss and ⁠damage is ​being assessed”.
Here’s a summary of what we know so far:

items: Nearly 3,000 people are missing. Nepal’s disaster agency on Saturday said 2,426 people were missing on its side of the border, while China’s Xinhua news agency reports the total number of missing in Tibet is now 554.
The death toll in Nepal has now risen to 626, while China’s Xinhua news agency earlier today reported seven people confirmed dead in Tibet.
More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far but at least 93,000 people are estimated to have been affected by the disaster, according to the Red Cross.

At least 777 foreigners are missing, with Nepal’s disaster agency on Friday reporting 517 foreigners unaccounted for – which could include tourists and foreign workers – and Chinese officials putting the number of foreigners missing at 260.

articles.title: Missing fisherman found dead after motor banca runs aground in Cagayan
articles.summary: SANTA ANA, Cagayan — The body of a 54-year-old fisherman who went missing after his motor banca was recovered by the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) in Santa Ana, Cagayan on Friday, August 28. The Coast…

blocks.text: SEARCH ENDS IN TRAGEDY: Coast Guard personnel recover the lifeless body of a 54-year-old fisherman who was reported missing after his motor banca was found aground in Barangay Palawig, Santa Ana, Cagayan. (Photo courtesy of Coast Guard via Liezle Inigo)
SANTA ANA, Cagayan — The body of a 54-year-old fisherman who went missing after his motor banca was recovered by the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) in Santa Ana, Cagayan on Friday, August 28.

The Coast Guard District North Eastern Luzon (CGDNELZN), through Coast Guard Station Santa Ana and Coast Guard Sub-Station Palaui, recovered the victim during a search and rescue operation launched after his disappearance was reported.
Authorities said the fisherman was reported missing after his motor banca was found along the shoreline of Barangay Palawig.
Coast Guard personnel immediately coordinated with local authorities and maritime agencies and mobilized search teams.
Nearby Coast Guard units were also directed to conduct search efforts within their respective areas of responsibility.
The search later focused on waters beneath Palawig Bridge, where the SAR team located and recovered the victim’s body.
The remains were positively identified by the victim’s relatives and brought to the Rural Health Unit of Santa Ana for proper disposition and turnover to the family.

articles.title: PNP assisting school security guards to ensure students' safety in Quezon
articles.summary: CAMP NAKAR, Lucena City- The Quezon Provincial Police Office (PPO) is maximizing the deployment of police personnel to assist school security guards, particularly in public schools, and ensure…

blocks.text: Police Col. Romulo Albacea, Quezon police director, interviewed with the media on police assistance to public schools in Quezon. (Danny Estacio)

CAMP NAKAR, Lucena City- The Quezon Provincial Police Office (PPO) is maximizing the deployment of police personnel to assist school security guards, particularly in public schools, and ensure security checks on students coming to the school campuses in Quezon province.

Police Col. Romulo Albacea, Quezon police director, said in an interview with the media here that police chiefs have been directed to assist the security of the school guards in preventing students from bringing unallowed things while attending their classes.
"Police have no authority to intervene in the school's policy; only police primarily duties are to extend assistance," he said.

Albacea encouraged schools’ administration to use their security forces with metal detectors and other instruments for checking bags as fast as possible, most especially those schools with a huge number of students.

He added that the only role of the police is to assist with police visibility within the surroundings of the school to prevent students from unlawfully doing what happened recently, the shooting incidents in Zamboanga and in Tacloban City.
He advised those police personnel who were assigned to the school not to display guns while assisting the school’s security forces.
Albacea added that only they can provide security assistance to public schools, but in the case of private schools, it depends on the request of the school administrators.

articles.title: Dutch institute issues 'red alert' over Trump-shaped ecstasy pills
articles.summary: The drugs have a delayed effect which "increases the risk of overdose", the institute has advised.

blocks.text: A Dutch drug addiction and mental health institute has issued a "red alert" to users about potentially lethal ecstasy pills in the shape of US President Donald Trump's head.
The Utrecht-based Trimbos Institute said several of the pills had been handed in at testing centres in August and were found to contain a "very high" amount of the chemical PMMA.
"Do not use this pill under any circumstance," the institute said in its warning, cautioning that the drug could cause "overheating with potentially fatal consequences".
It issued images of the pills, which feature a depiction of Trump's head on one side and the words "Trump" and "NL" stamped on the other.
PMMA, or para-methoxymethamfetamine, is a substance similar to MDMA – the active ingredient in ecstasy pills.
"However, the effect occurs later, and the stimulating effect is often absent," the institute advised. "This increases the risk of overdose."
Users are being warned they could experience symptoms such as nausea, an increased heart rate and convulsions hours after ingesting the pills.
Trimbos Institute spokesperson Anniek Groothuis told the Associated Press that it had no reported cases of death or serious illness among possible users.
While producing, selling and using ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, a 2024 Dutch government report said the substance was "still quite popular as a party drug".
The report added that, in 2022, a "record 550,000 people" had taken the drug at least once.
This is not the first time Donald Trump's facial features appear to have been used as inspiration for the shape of ecstasy pills.

In 2017, German police confiscated about 5,000 carrot-coloured ecstasy tablets in the shape of the US president's head – which they believed had been promoted on the internet under the slogan "Trump makes partying great again".

articles.title: Nepal-China flood survivors reach safe areas as families await news of nearly 3,000 missing
articles.summary: NUWAKOT, Nepal (AP) — Most arrive with nothing except the clothes they are wearing. As rescue efforts in communities buried by catastrophic flash floods along the border between Nepal and China…

blocks.text: NUWAKOT, Nepal (AP) — Most arrive with nothing except the clothes they are wearing.

As rescue efforts in communities buried by catastrophic flash floods along the border between Nepal and China entered their fourth day Saturday, authorities continued finding survivors and transporting them to safety. At relief centers, as some arrive, families wait anxiously for news of their loved ones as the death toll and the number of people unaccounted for continued to rise.

After Nepali authorities updated their figures Saturday, the combined toll in Nepal and Tibet rose to 633 dead and nearly 3,000 people missing. Chinese authorities have reported seven deaths and more than 550 missing.
In Nuwakot, one of the Nepali districts devastated by the floods, helicopters resumed operations before noon Saturday after poor weather temporarily hampered aerial rescue activities.
Some helicopters were loaded with boxes and bags of aid, including clothes, instant noodles, crackers and rice. Others returned from the flood-hit areas carrying survivors.

An older man was carefully helped off one helicopter, while a soldier carried an older woman on his back to a medical tent. There, medics checked her blood pressure, breathing and heartbeat, as well as her teeth and gums.
About a dozen people emerged from another helicopter. Soldiers carried several babies who had also been evacuated.
The evacuees had been brought from the nearby community of Trishuli.
Villagers return to devastated homes
As people were still evacuating from Trishuli, some village residents were returning to see what could be salvaged from their decimated homes.

One boy walked out of the village carrying muddy sandals from his house. Another woman, Shoba Shretha, returned to find her dog, Sweetie, who she was forced to leave behind when the floods came. Shretha sat on the ground petting her and feeding her water from a bottle.
At some point, relief coordinators cleared villagers, press and volunteers from the entrance to Trishuli, as excavation equipment drove into the flooded village, continuing to dig.
Families begin to lose hope

In Kathmandu, Nepal's capital, relatives and friends gathered outside the main government hospital from early morning, desperately searching for news of loved ones who remain missing after the incident.
Many shuffled between the help desk and the hospital notice board, clutching photographs and scanning injured patients' lists in the hope of finding them.

Dil Maya Lama stood weeping outside the help desk at the hospital, searching for any information about her missing brother. She travelled from Ramechhap district on Saturday in search of her 26-year-old brother, a driver for a hydropower company in Rasuwa.
"I came here with the hope that I might find him," she said. "There is no information about him."
Nelza Moktan anxiously sought information about her missing cousin, who also worked as a driver in Rasuwa.
"I feel hopeless. It has already been four days," she said.

Families covered hospital walls with posters showing missing relatives, displaying photographs and contact numbers in a desperate appeal for any clue that could bring them home. Nearby, officials had also pasted photographs of bodies yet to be identified in hopes they could be recognized by families or friends.

Gajendra Rawat, a security official at the hospital help desk, said families had so far registered around 1,600 missing persons since the disaster struck. "People are coming from all parts of Nepal," he said.
Back in Nuwakot, military personnel taped sheets of paper listing dozens of missing people to a wall at a relief center, prompting families to crowd around and search for their relatives.
Some scanned the lists, took photos and wiped away tears as they looked through the names.
Rajesh Kumar Ram, who is searching for his son, desperately scanned a list of names.
"I'm hopeful, by chance that my son is somewhere," he said, crying as he spoke. "Maybe they find him stuck somewhere. I'm waiting for that moment only."
Outside, people walked along mud-covered streets past signs of the disaster. On one street, a truck was stuck in the mud with its bed raised in the air.
Rescuers battle to find survivors at disaster-hit areas

Search and rescue efforts continued at several locations in Nepal and China's Tibet, including the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project in Nepal's Rasuwa district and the severely damaged Gyirong border crossing on the Chinese side.

Nepali Army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet said rescue efforts would continue at the hydropower construction site, where authorities believe more than 100 people are trapped in a tunnel filled with thick mud.

Basnet said rescuers had used baskets and ropes to reach some people, but the operation remained difficult because of 4 to 5 feet (1.2 to 1.5 meters) of mud and the limited number of places where helicopters could land.
He said rescue teams had also been forced to relocate temporarily when authorities issued warnings about possible further flooding.

Rescuers have been on high alert for more flooding from a new lake that formed high up in the Himalayan mountains after the initial floods Wednesday. Experts warned that the lake, created after a glacier collapse that triggered the floods, was starting to overflow.

Monitoring data from the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources showed late Friday that the lake had dwindled in size. The water level dropped by 10 meters (32 feet) from the high point on Thursday morning, Chinese broadcaster CCTV said.
Aid trucks could be seen traveling from Kathmandu, Nepal's capital, toward the affected areas.
Search continues at devastated China-Nepal border crossing

The broadcaster was showing Saturday images of rescuers getting to Gyirong Port, the hard-hit border crossing with Nepal. Some reached the area by foot and via rafts. Some were dropped down from drones flown to the area. "Anyone, anyone?" rescuers yelled, according to footage by the broadcaster.
It was not immediately known how many people were at the border checkpoint building when the floods hit.

On Saturday, Nepal's disaster agency said the death toll had climbed to 626 with 2,426 people missing in the country. There was little information on survivors on the Chinese side, where the death toll rose to seven Friday as state media showed evacuations of villages and leaders' efforts to direct the relief response.

More than 3,700 people have been rescued in Nepal so far. China's state media said 554 people were missing on the Chinese side. Hundreds of the missing are foreigners who were in the area to work, trek or make a pilgrimage to a sacred peak.

articles.title: 'Fake news pala, ha?': Ping gives details of 4 'fraudulently' titled, illegally reclaimed lands in Taguig
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson has dispelled insinuations that his earlier disclosures on the illegal reclamation activities in Taguig City were “fake news". In an X post on Saturday, Aug. 29, Lacson…

blocks.text: Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson has dispelled insinuations that his earlier disclosures on the illegal reclamation activities in Taguig City were “fake news".

In an X post on Saturday, Aug. 29, Lacson said the four parcels of illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City have been initially identified as covered by "fraudulently" issued land titles, while at least four other parcels have no plotted title lots in the digital file of the Land Registration Authority (LRA).
"Since Sen. (Alan Peter) Cayetano keeps publicly asking for evidence, I’ll give it to him, in the spirit of public interest," he said, referring to the Senate Minority Leader.
Lacson said the details of the four "fraudulently" titled parcels, which he stressed was "NOT FAKE NEWS," include:
(a) one covered by an Administrative Patent, involving 9,204 square meters under an Original Certificate of Title (OCT);
(b) one covered through Judicial/Ordinary Land Registration Processing covering an area of 5,000 square meters under an OCT;
(c) one covered by a Homestead Patent involving 181,077 square meters under a Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT); and
(d) one involving 193,027 square meters under a TCT.
Some details, including the names of those to whom the titles were issued to, as well as the OCT and TCT numbers, were withheld for the time being as the investigation is still ongoing.
"All of these will likewise be turned over to the Ombudsman fact-finding team for their further appropriate action," he added.

Earlier, Lacson bared that the LRA was checking the origin and history of several newly uncovered land titles covering some 38.83 hectares of illegally reclaimed areas on the Taguig City side of Laguna Lake.
The uncovered land titles were based on the materials provided by the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA) to Lacson's office.

“I requested the LRA to backtrack the history of the issued OCTs (original certificates of title) and other modes of titling, so we will find out how they were manipulated with the end in view of filing criminal charges against those responsible,” Lacson said,
He added that these titles may be declared void ab initio (void from the start) once the PRA initiates forfeiture proceedings in accordance with law.

Earlier, Lacson said several crates of documents from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) related to anomalous projects in Taguig City were also set to be turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman.

articles.title: US, Ecuador forces strike alleged drug smuggling boat
articles.summary: Tackling drug trafficking in Latin America is a key priority for Washington. In March, Ecuador joined a US-led coalition to combat the drug trade in the region.

image.caption: The US military said the people on board were escorted to Ecuador before the vessel was destroyedImage: U.S. Southern Command/SOUTHCOM

blocks.text: The US military said on Friday it had destroyed an alleged drug trafficking boat in a coordinated operation with Ecuador.
In a post on X, US Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) said that its forces intercepted a vessel "operating as a floating refueling station" in the Eastern Pacific.

According to SOUTHCOM, the vessel was operating "in support of the Los Choneros violent narco-terrorist organization," referring to one of Ecuador's most powerful criminal gangs, which Washington has designated as a Foreign Terrorist Organization.

"Working together with our Ecuadorian partners, our coalition dealt a decisive blow to a narco-terrorist operation responsible for moving significant amounts of drugs through the region," SOUTHCOM said.
US, Ecuador combat drug cartels
In March, Ecuador joined President Donald Trump's "Shield of the Americas" — a US-led coalition focused on combating drug trafficking across the region.
Ecuador's strategic location between Colombia and Peru — the world's two largest producers of cocaine — makes the country a key transit hub for drug-trafficking gangs.
The US military launched Operation Southern Spear in September 2025 as part of a fight against drug trafficking in the region.
The Trump administration, however, has not presented definitive evidence that the vessels targeted in its operations were carrying or transporting illegal drugs.

articles.title: Michael V. to new grads: ‘Make yourselves impossible to replace’
articles.summary: Michael V. may be one of the country’s most recognizable entertainers, but when he returned to his alma mater as a commencement speaker, he had a very 2026 message for the newest batch of graduates:…

blocks.text: Michael V. may be one of the country’s most recognizable entertainers, but when he returned to his alma mater as a commencement speaker, he had a very 2026 message for the newest batch of graduates: Don’t let AI make you obsolete.
The Kapuso Comedy Genius returned to the Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila (PLM) on Aug. 28, not as a student this time, but as one of the speakers for the university’s 58th Commencement Exercises.

Addressing graduates of the College of Education, College of Humanities, Arts and Social Sciences, and College of Science, Michael V. tackled one of the biggest questions facing young professionals today, the growing presence of artificial intelligence in the workplace and everyday life.
His advice was simple: Use AI, but don't try to become AI.
He challenged the Class of 2026 to develop the qualities that technology cannot replicate, including imagination, compassion, problem-solving, leadership and the ability to create meaningful change.

“Yes, AI will probably be here to stay but remember: machines can never live your life for you. Hindi nito kayang mangarap para sa’yo. Hindi nito kayang magmahal para sa’yo. Hindi nito kayang magdesisyon kung anong klaseng tao ang gusto mong maging dahil ikaw lang ang makakagawa noon,” he said.
“Use technology but don’t lose your humanity,” he added.
Then he left them with a parting message that neatly summed up his point:
“Go out there and make yourselves impossible to replace.”

articles.title: Barbie Forteza draws a hard line on cheating
articles.summary: Barbie Forteza knows exactly where she stands when it comes to infidelity and she isn't leaving much room for negotiation. For the actress, cheating isn't something she would simply brush aside in…

blocks.text: Barbie Forteza knows exactly where she stands when it comes to infidelity and she isn't leaving much room for negotiation.
For the actress, cheating isn't something she would simply brush aside in the name of love or second chances. Once trust is broken, she believes a person has every right to walk away.
That was the thinking behind her now-viral “F–k, no” response when she was asked if she would give a cheating partner another chance during a media conference.
Barbie further explained her position during an appearance on “Fast Talk With Boy Abunda,” Friday.
According to Barbie, her answer has less to do with holding a grudge against cheaters and more to do with how she views herself.
“The way I was raised is that you should value yourself,” Barbie said in Filipino. “I support myself. I treat myself out. In a way, that’s how much I love myself.”
For Barbie, being in a relationship means voluntarily giving someone something she considers precious: her time, attention and affection.
“So loving another person who isn’t related to me, who isn’t my family, to whom I don’t have any obligation to, only for that person to cheat on me? Why? Right?” she said.
“I chose you. I have no obligations toward you, and then you cheat on me? My time is valuable. My attention is valuable,” she added.
And that is why, for Barbie, the problem isn't limited to the act of cheating itself.
She said she would also draw the line at anything in a relationship that makes her feel diminished or undervalued.
“I guess it’s not just cheating. It’s anything that would make me feel like I have been treated as less,” she explained.
Trust, once given, is another matter.
“Because I gave myself to you, my time, my love, most importantly. Then you betrayed my trust,” Barbie said.
She was quick to point out, however, that this is her personal standard and not a rule she expects other couples to follow.
“That’s just for me,” she said.

articles.title: Palanca award-winning authors, editors, and bookworms share favorite Pinoy-authored books
articles.summary: As Buwan ng Wika draws to a close this August, what better way to celebrate the Filipino language than by revisiting stories written by Filipino authors? For this forum, we asked Palanca…

blocks.text: As Buwan ng Wika draws to a close this August, what better way to celebrate the Filipino language than by revisiting stories written by Filipino authors?

For this forum, we asked Palanca award-winning authors as well as some content creators to share the Filipino books that have stayed with them. From gritty fiction and crime novels to coming-of-age stories and horror books, their picks show the range of Filipino literature and the different ways stories can shape how young readers see themselves, their communities, and the world around them.
‘Mapanglaw ang Mukha ng Buwan’ by Efren R. Abueg

‘I became a writer because of Efren R. Abueg’s short story “Mapanglaw ang Mukha ng Buwan,” which is included in the book ‘Mga Agos sa Disyerto,’ alongside works by Dominador B. Mirasol, Rogelio L. Ordoñez, Edgardo M. Reyes, and Rogelio R. Sikat.

This book has had a profound influence on several generations of Filipino short story writers. It also demonstrated the power of words to give strength and support to the oppressed and the disadvantaged, especially those who have no voice in society.’

blocks.caption: Joe Chua

blocks.text: Joe Chua
‘Andong Agimat’ by Arnold Arre, ‘Libing Isa’ by MPAU, ‘Patay Kung Patay (Death be Damned)’ by Mike Alcazaren, Noel Pascual, and AJ Bernardo, and ‘Trese’ by Budjette Tan and Kajo Baldisimo

‘All of these use horror as a way to explore Philippine society. But more than that, they’re fun to read. It’s a hyperviolent comic book that was the right thing for me to read at the right time and was what got me interested in local comics. I don’t know if I can recommend it now in light of all the school violence, though.’

blocks.caption: Yvette Tan

blocks.text: Yvette Tan
‘Sa mga Kuko ng Liwanag’ by Edgardo M. Reyes

‘I love this book not only because Reyes is a writer I admire, but also because of the novel's effective portrayal of the cruel and dangerous face of the city. It realistically presents major social issues, vividly narrates the true condition of the poor, and depicts the complex struggles of ordinary workers. It also highlights the voicelessness of the poor in the face of oppression. And another thing I value most about this novel is that it is not only the story of Julio and Ligaya, but also the story of many Filipinos struggling to survive.’

blocks.caption: Perry Mangilaya

blocks.text: Perry Mangilaya
‘Macarthur’ by Bob Ong

‘Gritty and unapologetic, Bob Ong’s ‘Macarthur’ is a book I read many years ago yet still think about every now and then. It highlights the strength of laughter as a coping mechanism. It introduces moral conundrums. It enrages. It is hard to believe the book is just 98 pages because it manages to do so much.’

blocks.caption: Firas Abbound

blocks.text: Firas Abbound
‘Dekada ’70’ by Lualhati Bautista

‘If I have to answer only one, I’ll go with “Dekada ‘70” by Lualhati Bautista. This changed the way I read (fiction) books from treating them as pure escapism to realizing they hold powerful reflections of our history and society.’

blocks.caption: Veron Cruz

blocks.text: Veron Cruz
‘Kulang na Silya’ by Ricky Lee

‘There are so many books to choose from, but I’ll keep coming back to “Kulang na Silya” by Ricky Lee. There are also so many Ricky Lee books to choose from, but this one, specifically, really feels like medicine for a creative who is about to give up, or for anyone, really, who is going through a difficult time. Truly, a National Artist for a reason.’

blocks.caption: Paula Michaella

blocks.text: Paula Michaella
‘Janus Silang’ by Edgar Calabia Samar

It is a five-book series that follows Janus, a 14-year-old gamer who plays Tala, an online game inspired by Filipino mythology. Everything changes one game night when all the other players suddenly turn to dust, leaving Janus as the only survivor.

Janus follows the chosen-one trope. The series starts with a horror-esque atmosphere and gradually becomes more fantasy as its universe expands. Along the way, readers are introduced to a wide array of creatures from Filipino mythology and folklore, along with exciting and action-packed fight scenes.

Readers who grew up watching ‘Pedro Penduko,’ ‘Wansapanataym,’ and ‘Kakabakaba Adventures’ will surely find something nostalgic in the series. On the other hand, younger generations are in for a treat as they explore the richness of Filipino culture.

blocks.caption: JP Obias

blocks.text: JP Obias

These choices may come from different genres and generations, but they share one thing: each book left a lasting impression on its reader. And as Buwan ng Wika comes to an end, they offer a reminder that Filipino stories are not simply something to celebrate for one month. They are stories worth returning to, especially for a new generation of readers.
