articles.title: Death toll from Nepal-Tibet floods rises to over 600
articles.summary: Heavy rain is complicating an already difficult rescue effort, as hundreds remain missing three days after deadly flash floods hit the Nepal-Tibet border region.

image.caption: More than 2,400 people remain missing following the floods in NepalImage: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

blocks.text: The latest death toll from the devastating flash flood along the Nepal-Tibet border was reported on Saturday to be over 600, as frantic rescue operations to search for hundreds of missing people entered a fourth day.
According to Nepal's disaster agency, the death toll in Nepal now stands at 626, with 2,426 people — including foreigners — still missing.
Across the border in Tibet, China's state news agency, Xinhua, has confirmed seven deaths and reported 554 missing individuals.
A glacial collapse on Wednesday sent rock, ice, mud and debris surging through the Himalayan mountain river systems below.
The flood swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants.
What is the status of rescue efforts in Nepal?
Rainy weather conditions are hindering aerial rescue operations in Nepal.
Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told the media on Saturday that helicopter operations were on hold until the weather improved.
Rescuers are battling thick layers of mud in the affected areas, which is making it difficult for helicopters to land and take off.
Tunnels in the mountainous region are also a challenge, Basnet said.
The army has located people trapped in a tunnel of the Trishuli 3A hydropower project in Nepal's Rasuwa District. Over 100 people are believed to be inside the tunnel filled with mud.

Basnet said that rescuers were struggling to locate the entry points of the tunnel and had made use of baskets and ropes to reach some people. There are also limited places for helicopters to land in the area.

blocks.caption: Members of the Nepal Army load relief material as a helicopter containing relief supplies takes offImage: Athit Perawongmetha/REUTERS

blocks.text: On Friday, Nepal's Army shared visuals of some people being rescued from the tunnel. The survivors were seen stuck in the mud, while officials crawled through the sludge and held out their hands to them.
Nepalese authorities said that the bodies of many flood victims have also been found dozens of kilometers from the disaster zone in Chitwan District in southern Nepal, which borders India.
Meanwhile, Indian authorities said they recovered the bodies of seven people who were swept downstream from Nepal and believe them to be flood victims.
More than 1,000 believed missing after Nepal flash floods
Nepal needs help in technical areas, says foreign minister
Late on Friday, Nepal's Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal told the Reuters news agency that his country needed equipment, along with technical knowledge in tunnel rescue operations.

Khanal also told Reuters that Nepal did not need help with search and rescue operations but needed assistance in opening transport and communication lines in places where bridges were destroyed, identification of dead bodies, DNA testing and storage of bodies for a longer timeframe.
"We have already made requests for such ⁠specialized ​services and technical assistance in areas where we don't have enough expertise and technical know-how," ​Reuters quoted Khanal as saying.
Nepal's Foreign Ministry had on Friday declined foreign involvement in search and rescue.
Nepal's post-flood rebuilding estimated at $4-$5 billion
In another Reuters interview, Nepal's Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said that the Himalayan nation may need $4 billion ⁠to $5 billion ⁠to rebuild after the flood.
The estimate is equivalent ​to nearly a tenth of Nepal's economy.

"The initial estimate is ​between $4-$5 billion. Just an estimate," Wagle told Reuters, adding that the bill would be much less than what was needed in reconstruction after the disastrous 2015 earthquake — Nepal's worst ‌ recorded disaster.
"Loss and damage is being assessed," he said.

blocks.caption: People carry salvaged belongings from damaged houses following the flash floods and mudslideImage: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

blocks.text: What do we know about rescue operations in Tibet?

In Gyirong, one of the hardest-hit areas in Tibet along the China-Nepal border, Beijing had temporarily halted its rescue efforts due to the risk of renewed flooding before announcing that the threat had waned.
China's Xinhua agency reported on Saturday morning that two villagers had been rescued in the Gyirong area.

blocks.caption: Rescue workers operate excavators and loaders to repair a damaged road leading to Gyirong PortImage: China Daily/REUTERS

blocks.text: The glacial collapse on Wednesday led to the formation of a barrier lake upstream due to debris dams. Experts warned that the lake had started to overflow.
On Saturday, Chinese authorities announced that the lake had begun to shrink.

China's state broadcaster, CCTV, cited the Ministry of Water Resources as saying that satellite imagery of the surface area of the lake in the Tsangpo River basin on Saturday morning showed a reduction of around 21,000 square meters compared to images from Thursday.
Authorities have also identified a larger body of water at the bottom of the glacier collapse.

"We estimate its area to be over 120,000 ⁠square ​meters, but its depth is currently unknown," Reuters quoted Chen Hongqi, a senior engineer at ​the Ministry of Natural Resources' Geological Disaster Technical Guidance Center, as saying.
Reuters also reported an official of Nepal's Disaster ​Management Authority as saying that flood risks will remain until the two lakes have fully drained.

articles.title: Palawan junior tennis brings 3-week showcase to Mindanao
articles.summary: The Palawan Pawnshop nationwide junior tennis circuit shifts to Mindanao next week for a three-tournament swing that will take the country’s premier grassroots talent-search to Davao del Sur, Sultan…

blocks.text: The Palawan Pawnshop nationwide junior tennis circuit shifts to Mindanao next week for a three-tournament swing that will take the country’s premier grassroots talent-search to Davao del Sur, Sultan Kudarat and Cotabato, giving the region’s young players another major platform to compete, gain ranking points and valuable experience and showcase their skills.

Following the successful staging of the Palawan Junior Series last March, which featured stops across the Visayas and Luzon, the long-running circuit continues its nationwide trek with a busy Mindanao schedule designed to sustain the momentum of junior tennis while providing more youngsters from the countryside an opportunity to test themselves against the best players in their age groups.

The Mindanao swing kicks off with the MJFC “Araw ng Digos Junior Age-Group Championships” on Sept. 2-8 at the Digos City courts in Davao del Sur, with another strong field expected to vie for honors in the boys’ and girls’ singles in the 12-, 14-, 16- and 18-and-under categories.
Titles in the boys’ and girls’ 14-and-U and 18-and-U doubles will also be disputed in the tournament being held in honor of Digos City Mayor Josef Fortich Cagas.

The series then moves to Sultan Kudarat for the Bagong Pilipinas age-group tournament on Sept. 10-15, with the Capital Indoor and Outdoor courts in Isulan serving as venue. The Mindanao swing wraps up with the Kidapawan Juniors Championship on Sept. 16-22 at the Kidapawan City courts in Cotabato.

Palawan Pawnshop has remained at the forefront of this grassroots movement, sustaining a year-round, nationwide junior circuit that goes beyond simply staging tournaments. The program serves as an extensive talent-identification and development platform, allowing promising players to gain competition experience and potentially earn consideration for future national pools and teams.

Sanctioned by Philta and Universal Tennis Ranking and supported by Dunlop, ICON Golf & Sports and the Palawan Group of Companies, the nationwide talent-search was initiated by Palawan Pawnshop president and CEO Bobby Castro as part of his continuing effort to raise the standard of junior tennis in the country.
And while Mindanao takes center stage for three consecutive weeks, the nationwide circuit remains in full swing elsewhere.

Siquijor will host another junior tournament, the Governor’s Cup, on Sept. 17-22 at the Capitol tennis courts. The event, sponsored by Gov. Jake Villa, will feature the same age-group divisions, adding another venue for young players to compete and sharpen their skills.

articles.title: Jack Logan: Digital creator to novelist
articles.summary: When did books stop being entertainment? There was a time when people found their escape, their stories and their adventures within the pages of a book. Today, with digital media dominating how we…

blocks.text: When did books stop being entertainment?

There was a time when people found their escape, their stories and their adventures within the pages of a book. Today, with digital media dominating how we consume stories, that tradition can sometimes feel like a thing of the past.
But is it really over for books?
Not quite. There are still people who believe in the magic of the printed page and are willing to bring it back to a generation raised on screens.
Jack Logan is one of them.
Better known as a digital creator, filmmaker and storyteller, Logan is now venturing into a decidedly old-school form of entertainment: the novel.
His first book, “The Pabebe Chronicles: The Flower and the Warrior,” is a 300-page Filipino-language fantasy-comedy that mixes romance, politics, magic, war and humor.
For Logan, however, the book is about more than simply telling a story. It is also a way of encouraging people to read.

“Ako kasi personally mahilig ako magbasa. And this book is my way of encouraging others to do the same. Iba rin ang feeling na hawak mo ang libro, naamoy at nararamdaman mo yung texture ng mga pahina...iba e,” he said.
It is an interesting choice for someone who has made much of his name in digital media.

Logan is a filmmaker, writer and digital creator known for “Jack Logan Realtalks” and “The 12 Days Saga” film trilogy. His documentary “Makabagong San Juan” was also nominated for Best Single Digital Programme/Short Film at the Asian Television Awards.
But writing a novel is a different thing.
There is no camera, no actor and no editing room to hide behind.
There are just words and the reader.
Logan has been carrying “The Pabebe Chronicles” around for a while. He first came up with the story in 2015 and shared it with friends. Like many ideas, however, it sat around for years.
In 2025, he picked it up again.
This time, he decided to finish it.
The result is “The Pabebe Chronicles: The Flower and the Warrior,” the first published book in what Logan plans as a trilogy.
“Basically, it's a fantasy story,” he says. “But it's also a love story. It's political. It's funny.”
The story takes place in Erodas, a fictional realm dealing with the aftermath of the War of Golds. There are kingdoms, royal families, warriors, magic and old grudges.
And then there are the people caught in the middle of all that.
One of them is Bianca, a weaver from Lambak whose royal identity has been erased.
There is also Jack, an amnesiac warrior who has a violent past but cannot remember everything about it.
Then there is Pabie, the Kondesa of Amazon, who Logan says brings a very different energy to the story.
Their lives eventually cross as the political problems of Erodas become complicated by prophecy, deception and magic.
But don't expect Logan to suddenly become very serious just because his characters live in a fantasy kingdom.
That was never the point.

“I wanted it to be Filipino,” he says. “Ito kung paano ninyo nakilala si Jack Logan, ganun din ito. Iisa lang ang boses ko as creator so, kung nagugustuhan ninyo ang mga gawa ko before, tiyak magugustuhan ninyo rin ito.”
That includes the humor.
The book has what Logan describes as a Filipino comedic rhythm, with contemporary language, satire and pop-culture references mixed into the fantasy setting.
“It's fantasy, but the way they talk is Filipino,” he says.
That probably explains the title, too.
“The Pabebe Chronicles” doesn't exactly sound like the name of a grim medieval epic. And Logan isn't pretending otherwise.
He wants to have fun with the genre.
“You can have a very serious scene, then suddenly somebody says something funny,” he says.
That sounds very Filipino.
It also sounds very Jack Logan.
There is one other unusual thing about the book.
“The Flower and the Warrior” is the first “Pabebe Chronicles” novel to be published, but it is actually Book II in the story's chronology.
The saga's timeline goes “The War of Golds,” “The Flower and the Warrior” and then “The Last Baruk.”
Logan knows this may sound slightly confusing.
For now, though, he is happy that readers finally get to enter Erodas, one page at a time.
“The Pabebe Chronicles: The Flower and the Warrior” is published by Central Book Supply, Inc. and is available in hardbound and paperback editions.

articles.title: Exeter University approves deal with Saudi Arabia to train military officers and officials
articles.summary:
In move that could generate millions, Exeter academics to deliver MA at National Defense University in Riyadh

The

blocks.text: The University of Exeter has approved plans for a “formal partnership” with Saudi Arabia to train senior military officers and government officials, despite long-held concerns about the Saudi government’s human rights record, the Guardian has learned.

In a deal that could generate millions of pounds for the Russell Group university, Exeter academics will deliver an MA in applied security and strategy (also known as an MStrat) to a cohort at the National Defense University (NDU) in Riyadh.

The MA will form the academic component of the NDU’s global strategy and strategic leadership programme, starting in 2026-27, and will be delivered to about 20 individuals per year, over three years. Until two years ago, the NDU was called the Saudi Armed Forces Command and Staff College.

The Saudi partnership has come to light at a time when the university is under fire from leading writers, broadcasters, academics and other alumni over plans to cut 150 jobs, primarily in the humanities, arts and social sciences, for which the highly ranked university is renowned.
The Exeter branch of the University and College Union (UCU) accused university managers of chasing “dirty money”.

A UCU spokesperson said: “We are horrified but hardly surprised to learn that management at Exeter are more interested in flogging military training to despotic regimes than in defending world-class humanities and social sciences teaching.”

The Exeter deal has not been widely publicised. It was approved by the university council in February this year, then endorsed by its senate the following month. In council minutes, seen by the Guardian, the partnership with the NDU is marked “Strictly confidential and commercial in confidence”.

In its marketing material, the university says the MStrat blends “academic depth with practical application”. It is aimed at working professionals in the armed forces, the government and international organisations and “offers a rigorous yet flexible environment in which to build strategic expertise”.

UK universities often sell consultancy and training to foreign governments via contracts worth millions of pounds. All such proposals have to be vetted first by university authorities to assess the legal, ethical and security risks of any potential collaboration.

Similar concerns were raised earlier this year when the Judge business school at the University of Cambridge put forward proposals to provide “leadership development” and “innovation management” to Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry. Senior academics described it as “horrifying” and a betrayal of the university’s commitments to freedom of expression.

Last month, the UK government announced the formation of a defence universities alliance – with Exeter among the 35 founding members – to “bring together academia and the armed forces” as part of a £182m investment to strengthen defence research and build critical skills.

A spokesperson for Exeter University said: “The MA in applied security and strategy has been taught at Exeter since 2012 through our strategy and security institute. Its students include serving British military personnel sponsored by the Ministry of Defence and Chevening scholars supported by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.

“We are in discussions to deliver this established Exeter programme to a cohort at the National Defense University in Riyadh. Professional military education has formed part of the UK’s defence relationship with Saudi Arabia for many years, including through UK government institutions.
“Partnerships of this kind are assessed on academic and ethical grounds, through a process separate from budget planning.

“Like universities across the sector, Exeter continues to develop external partnerships and educational activity that supports our academic mission and enables our expertise to have impact in the UK and internationally.”

The UCU spokesperson responded: “Rather than chasing dirty money like this, we believe a university should be about protecting freedom of speech, upholding human rights and ensuring a wide range of brilliant courses and a fantastic student experience.”

articles.title: FULL INTERVIEW: Mike Dizon on drumming for 3 bands, love for food
articles.summary: Dizon sits down with Rappler to talk about his beginnings in music, what it's like for him to move from genre to genre as the drummer of TEETH, Sandwich, and Pedicab, and how he discovered his love…

blocks.text: Dizon sits down with Rappler to talk about his beginnings in music, what it's like for him to move from genre to genre as the drummer of TEETH, Sandwich, and Pedicab, and how he discovered his love for documenting the restaurants he comes across
MANILA, Philippines – It’s not every day that an artist finds himself being a part of three of the Philippines’ most influential bands at the same time, until you meet Mike Dizon.

Dizon co-founded the alternative rock and grunge outfit TEETH in 1993. Years later, he also began playing the drums for rock band Sandwich and electronic rock band Pedicab. He is also a prolific songwriter, and is the mind behind hit songs like “Laklak” and “Prinsesa” by TEETH.
Outside of music, though, Dizon runs a successful YouTube channel, where he visits local eateries to try out the best dishes on the menu.

Ahead of TEETH’s reunion concert tour in celebration of their 33 years as a band, Dizon sits down with Rappler to talk about his beginnings in music, what it’s like for him to move from genre to genre, and how he discovered his love for documenting the restaurants he comes across.
Catch the full interview at 7 pm on Saturday, August 29, by bookmarking this page or heading to Rappler’s YouTube! – Rappler.com

articles.title: As insults fly around trade, negotiators for Canada and the U.S. avoid getting personal in public
articles.summary: Politicians from Canada and the United States have thrown varying degrees of personal insults back and forth across the border this week, but the two governments' trade negotiators avoided getting…

image.caption: Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, left, and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer outside Greer's office on Aug. 19, the day after the Trump administration temporarily delayed tariffs on Canada. (Kelly Geraldine Malone/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: World

Politicians from Canada and the United States have thrown varying degrees of personal insults back and forth across the border this week, but the two governments' trade negotiators avoided getting personal — at least in public. Experts believe the two trade leads are striking a different tone because they have a different role to play as the dispute heats up.
Politicial scientists, PR expert say negotiators are staying out of the fray as part of wider strategy

This week, politicians from Canada and the United States have traded personal insults across the border, describing others as weak, nasty, foolish, ridiculous and a loser — the last paired with a curt invitation to "kiss my ass."

The taunts have escalated the feud between the two countries, which has already led to crushing tariffs on tens of billions of dollars worth of cross-border goods. But the two governments' trade negotiators have avoided getting personal, at least in public.

items: The art of inflicting pain: How to select targets for Canada's counter-tariffs

blocks.text: Political scientists and a public relations expert say the trade leads are striking a different tone because, like their predecessors in past negotiations, their bosses have given them a specific role to play in the trade dispute — one that would only be made harder by bad blood.

"What we're seeing is a choreography, a play, if you like, where you've got different people playing different roles to have the overall effect that you want to achieve," said Jaime Watt, founder of the public relations firm Navigator.
Negotiators don't help themselves with 'silly insults': professor
Trade talks between the U.S. and Canada collapsed on Aug. 21, with each side later blaming the ⁠other for spoiling what seemed to be the closest chance at a deal in months.

Neither government has released the text of the scuttled agreement, and negotiators have mostly cited confidentiality when pressed for details, leaving the public to rely largely on politicians' comments to gauge progress — or the lack of it.

On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump further antagonized Canadians when he directed his government to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America, a move quickly dismissed up north as unnecessarily provocative and insulting. He had previously referred to Canadian officials as "clowns" and described Ontario's premier as the "less charismatic, intelligent" version of his late brother.
Does the U.S. rhetoric make trade negotiations harder?
In separate interviews with CBC News, the two countries' respective cabinet members took a different tack. They criticized the other governments' economic policies but didn't make it personal.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said he didn't want spend time dwelling on "who said what about whom" and described his dealings with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer as "always personal and professional."
Two days later, Greer sidestepped a question whether his boss' rhetoric complicates his job.
"I would just say my job is quite narrow, and on trade relations, it's quite narrow," Greer told CBC News on Wednesday, describing his relationship with LeBlanc as "good."
"It's about economics."

Experts said the trade leads are likely avoiding personal insults in public because poisoning the well won't help them achieve their objective: securing the best deal possible for their respective countries.

"They're not going to launch silly insults against one another because it's not good for actually productive conversations," said Aaron Ettinger, a political science professor at Carleton University. "If they can't stand each other, then it's going to be hard to be in the same room with one another."
Canada won't 'rush back to Washington' unless there's a 'viable' deal: LeBlanc
Away from the negotiating table, political leaders have their own goals.

"They're the highest ranking politicians in either jurisdiction and they're both using their space to try to convince people of something," said Lori Turnbull, a political science professor at Dalhousie University.
In a departure from his typical conciliatory tone, Carney used the language of sovereignty and war on Saturday as he called for a generational shift away from an unreliable adversary.
Turnbull, Ettinger and Watt agreed the prime minister was looking to rally Canadians and project strength to global allies as the country enters a costly economic war with the U.S.
They said the prime minister didn't need to mention Trump by name to make the show of defiance, which was later noted by international media.

items: Read Mark Carney's full speech after trade talks with the U.S. collapsed
Canada’s resistance to Trump’s trade demands offers Europe a blueprint. Will the EU take it?

blocks.text: In the days since, Trump has maintained the bombastic, unpredictable and personal approach he has taken toward world leaders throughout his time in the White House. Facing the lowest public approval of his second term, Turnbull said the president is also struggling to resolve the trade war with Canada and the war against Iran as they both drive up the cost of living for Americans.
Trade reps have been 'firm, but friendly' before
Canadian and American trade representatives have a history of tense but cordial relationships during free-trade negotiations.

Nearly a decade ago, while Trump insulted then-prime minister Justin Trudeau in public, Greer and LeBlanc's predecessors were navigating a famously rocky relationship behind closed doors. Meetings between Canada's then-foreign affairs minister Chrystia Freeland and U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer were at points bitter, blunt and loud, but the dynamic evolved.

The relationship improved to the point that Freeland invited Lighthizer to a celebratory dinner at her home in Toronto after they reached a preliminary agreement on the deal that would become the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) in 2018.

Another set of negotiators had a "firm, but friendly" relationship as they negotiated the original North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). When Canadian international trade minister Michael Wilson stormed out on meetings at the Watergate Hotel, his American counterpart arranged tickets to a Friday night Baltimore Orioles baseball game to give the group a breather.
"I said, I've got to take these guys somewhere tonight…. Let's get our mind off trade because it's just getting a little fractious," then-U.S. Trade Representative Carla Hills later recalled.
"We've all stayed close friends," she said of the Canadian team who went to the game. "It really was wonderful. It was a good time."

During the early NAFTA era, George H.W. Bush was in the White House and Brian Mulroney was prime minister. More diplomatic during negotiations, the two leaders continued speaking highly of one another long after leaving office.

"George Bush was fantastic and still is," Mulroney said in 2018, six years before his death. "I tell you, if you want to see a contrast between a civilized, modest, thoughtful, generous leadership and what you're seeing today, there you go."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Rhianna Schmunk is a senior writer covering domestic and international affairs at CBC News. Her work over the past decade has taken her across North America, from the Canadian Rockies to Washington, D.C. She routinely covers the Canadian courts, with a focus on precedent-setting civil cases. You can send story tips to rhianna.schmunk@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Scientists fear Nepal's disaster is just a glimpse of the carnage climate change could cause
articles.summary: Some climate scientists are cautious about prematurely attributing human caused-climate change as the sole cause of the disaster that resulted in the violent flooding of Himalayan villages in Nepal…

image.caption: Nearly 600 people were confirmed dead as of Friday after a flash flood caused by a glacier collapse inundated villages in Nepal's Himalayas. Disaster scientists say human-caused climate change made the collapse all the more likely. (Rajesh Kumar Singh/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Climate

Some climate scientists are cautious about prematurely attributing human caused-climate change as the sole cause of the disaster that resulted in the violent flooding of Himalayan villages in Nepal this week. But other experts say it was the kind of catastrophe they’ve been warning about for years.
Global warming contributes to conditions that make a glacier collapses, floods more likely, experts say
Geoscientist Jakob Steiner says it looks like "someone took a knife," cut a 1,300-metre-wide chunk from the lower part of a glacier on Nepal's Himalayas and "dropped it off the mountain cliff."

The researcher at the University of Graz in Austria says the "blast" of ice, rock and sediment that came crashing down 1.2 km, from a height of 5,000 metres above sea level, temporarily dammed the river below and created a lake.

Once that lake filled with the enormous amount of water released from the glacier, Steiner says the dam breached and unleashed the violent torrent that pummeled downstream villages on either side of the border and buried them in mud.

Additional lakes formed in the aftermath of the initial calamity could soon rupture as well, potentially worsening the death and destruction. So far, at least 579 people have been killed, with about 1,400 others unaccounted for in Nepal, including 32 Canadian citizens and permanent residents.

Indigenous people in the area have long warned climbers that the mountain, Langtang Lirung, is an "angry mountain," Steiner told CBC News Network in an interview from Dhaka, Bangladesh. "They are proven right every year, again and again."
Some climate scientists are cautious about prematurely linking human caused-climate change as the sole trigger of this specific collapse.

But experts who research both glacier hydrology and the effects global warming is having on the frozen parts of the planet known as the cryosphere say this was the kind of catastrophe they've been warning about for years, particularly in the Himalayas.

items: IN PHOTOS | Satellite imagery shows devastation of Nepal flash floods
Nepal flash flood death toll climbs to 579, with 32 Canadians, permanent residents among missing

blocks.text: John Pomeroy, director of the University of Saskatchewan's Centre for Hydrology, says horrific events like this are becoming much more frequent as the effects of climate change are "destroying our natural infrastructure."
"And it's happening in a wink of an eye in Earth's history and too fast for humans to easily adapt," he said.
How climate change set the stage for tragedy
Manjueet Dhakal, a climate scientist in Nepal's capital Kathmandu, had passed through the devastated region on a family trip just days before the collapse.
It was hard for him to see areas he had just visited completely washed away, including the country's largest solar power generation plant.
He says the Himalayas are a "very complicated landmass" that's part of the greater Hindu Kush Himalaya region stretching from Myanmar to Afghanistan and containing more than 63,000 glaciers.
PHOTOS | Aftermath of devastating glacier collapse, flood in Nepal's Himalaya region:
Warmer global temperatures, linked to emissions from the burning of fossil fuels, have "stressed" the mountain region," Dhakal said in an interview with CBC's What On Earth.
That includes altering precipitation patterns, increasing snow melt, triggering more avalanches and drastically accelerating glacier retreat.

"The glaciers are disintegrating," said Pomeroy, explaining that the Himalayas have already lost 21 per cent of their glacier coverage in the first quarter of this century as a result of the planet heating up to the point it's at now.
It's also thawing the permafrost, which he says is what "holds these high mountains together."
"All these things together mean that we'll get events like this every year, somewhere in the world," he said in a separate interview with What On Earth guest host Leisha Grebinski.
The science behind Nepal's violent flash flood
Global concern about glaciers

There was a glacial flash flood in this same Nepal-Tibet border region last year, but it wasn't the result of a massive piece of a glacier breaking off. It was due to what's known as a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), something that happens frequently around the world — including in Canada.
GLOFs happen when water held back at the edge of a glacier by a natural dam made of ice and sediment, called a moraine, overflows or breaches the barrier.

items: A glacial lake in B.C. is at risk of bursting — again. How climate change has raised this risk
What caused the 'shocking' landslide that destroyed a Himalayan village?

blocks.text: Sometimes that's due to sudden and intense downpour, like the one that destroyed a village in India's Himalaya region in August 2025. Other times it can be the result of an avalanche or landslide at a higher elevation that crashes into the pooled water.

They can also happen when pooling meltwater dammed by the glacier itself eventually drains from the bottom of the basin, where the ice meets the bedrock. This happened at the Place Glacier, near Pemberton, B.C., in June.

While GLOFs are naturally occurring, they have become more of a threat, according to research published by Nature in 2023, because global warming is contributing to greater ice loss and subsequently increasing the volume of glacial lakes.

That study estimated some 15 million people are exposed to the risks of GLOFs within 50 kilometres of where they live — largely in the Himalayas, but also the Andes region of South America and the Alps in Europe.

It's a "critical situation" in places like the mountain villages of Nepal, says Slobodan Simonović, director of engineering works with the Institute for Catastrophic Loss Reduction and professor emeritus at Western University in London, Ont.
He says those communities are "nested" very close to the streams and rivers fed by melting water from glaciers, leaving them more exposed.
LISTEN | Why climate scientists say they have been warning about a disaster just like this:
What On Earth26:23The disaster in Nepal as a ‘wake-up call from Mother Nature’
The damage and loss of life these floods can cause is tremendous, Simonović says, noting the effects can be long-lasting and create "a bad situation on so many fronts."

Glaciers are a vital source of water for drinking and irrigation, and he says a collapse like this week's means communities downstream of the initial deluge will have a limited supply in the coming seasons.
Lake formed from glacial debris poses new flood threat at Nepal-Tibet border
Act, don't adapt

Steiner, the geoscientist from the University of Graz, says the disaster in Nepal could have been prevented, but only if governments had "made different decisions 15 years ago on how we use our resources."
Though he says "climate change had a role" in this event, Steiner notes that it's also a matter of being better prepared and having early warning.

items: 10 Toronto residents on a trek in Nepal unaccounted for after deadly flash floods: non-profit group

blocks.text: He says he and either scientists had been working with Nepalese authorities on this front, but it was difficult because of domestic politics and the fact that it's a trans-boundary area, meaning there needs to be co-operation and co-ordination with Chinese agencies on the Tibetan side of the border.
Even with more monitoring and warning systems, the University of Saskatchewan's Pomeroy says we also need to limit further global warming.
He says he hopes the scenes from this catastrophe help to "galvanize the world" to work to reduce greenhouse gases rather than just expecting people to adapt to climate change.
"You cannot adapt to a 20-metre wave of water chasing you down the street that's about to wipe you out."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Nick Logan is a senior writer with CBC based in Vancouver. He is a multi-platform reporter and producer, with a particular focus on international news. You can reach out to him at nick.logan@cbc.ca.
With files from Lauren Pelley, Molly Segal, Jennifer Wilson, Leisha Grebinski, Mark Carcasole and Reuters

articles.title: Cancer survivor fights to axe the U.K.'s sunscreen tax. Should Canada do the same?
articles.summary: A U.K. woman is on a mission to convince her government to scrap its tax on sunscreen. Canadian cancer organizations say this country should consider doing the same.

image.caption: Skin cancer survivor Jessica Zbinden-Webster wants the U.K. government to remove its 20 per cent tax on sunscreen and classify it as a health product rather than a cosmetic one . (Submitted by Jessica Zbinden-Webster)

blocks.text: LISTEN | Interview with skin cancer survivor Jessica Zbinden-Webster :
As It Happens6:31Skin cancer survivor wants the U.K. to axe the tax on sunscreen
When Jessica Zbinden-Webster was diagnosed with skin cancer at the age of 26, it upended everything she thought she knew about sun safety.

"I had always mistakenly assumed that skin cancer was a disease that exclusively affected older people and people who had used sunbeds to excess and who had sun bathed to excess," the West Sussex, U.K., woman told As It Happens guest host Paul Hunter.
"And now, of course, I'm living proof that it can happen to anyone at any time."

Now recovered, Zbinden-Webster is on a mission to convince the U.K. government to scrap its 20 per cent tax on sunscreen. Canadian cancer organizations told CBC this country should also consider making sunscreen tax-free.

"Affordability is particularly important because effective sun protection is not a one-time purchase. Sunscreen needs to be applied generously and reapplied at least every two hours during sun exposure," Falyn Katz, CEO of Melanoma Canada, said in an email.
"For families, outdoor workers and people spending significant time outdoors, the cost can add up quickly. Those costs can create an additional barrier for lower-income Canadians."
An unexpected diagnosis
Zbinden-Webster's cancer journey began in 2018, when she developed what she thought was an unsightly pimple beneath her right eye.
"I had a lot of pimples growing up and that extended into my 20s," she said. "I thought, 'Oh goody, another one to deal with.'"
But several months passed, and the pimple didn't go away.

"One morning, I was sat at my desk and I rubbed the skin on my eye, where the pimple was, and it began to bleed. And that was my red flag. That prompted me to visit my doctor the following day," she said.
"To my surprise, he diagnosed me with skin cancer on the spot."
She had infiltrative basal cell carcinoma, an aggressive, but highly treatable, form of skin cancer that is often hard to detect, but can burrow deep beneath the surface.
The Canadian Skin Cancer Foundation recommends using sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher on any exposed skin any time you're outside.

"I actually only used sunscreen the way most Brits use sunscreen, which is as a seasonal product. I would use it during the summer months and I would also use it more frequently when on holiday," Zbinden-Webster said.
"But I most definitely did not regard it as an everyday essential."
Daily sunscreen is expensive
That's changed. Now that she's cancer-free after a successful surgery, Zbinden-Webster uses sunscreen every day.
It's a healthy habit, she says, but also an expensive one.
Non-prescription sunscreen in the U.K. is classified as a cosmetic product, and subject to a 20 per cent value-added tax (VAT).
"Not only does this send a damaging message about the importance of sun safety to our public health, but it prices the poorest out of skin cancer prevention," Zbinden-Webster said.
Zbinden-Webster's online petition, "Tell the Government to axe VAT on Sunscreen," has garnered more than 100,000 signatures.

She's not alone in her mission. Several U.K. skin health organizations, including Melanoma Focus are also calling for the government to remove VAT from sun protection products with an SPF of 30 or higher.
A 2026 report from the U.K. parliamentary UV Safety Inquiry recommended the same.

CBC was not able to reach the U.K. government for comment, but a spokesperson told the BBC: "As part of our 10-year plan to reform the health service, and through a national cancer plan, we will fight cancer on all fronts, from prevention, to diagnosis, treatment, and research."
What about Canada?
In Canada, sunscreen is regulated as a health product.
However, like many health-care products, it is subject to the five per cent federal Goods and Services Tax, as well as provincial sales taxes, which vary from five to 15 per cent.

"From our perspective, there is therefore a disconnect between recognizing sunscreen as a regulated health product and an important cancer-prevention measure, while continuing to tax it as an ordinary consumer purchase," said Katz of Melanoma Canada.

Lindsay Timm, executive director of the Canadian Cancer Survivor Network, says she welcomes any effort to make sunscreen more accessible, including making it publicly available in parks, outdoor pools and hiking trails.
"We believe that making sunscreen more affordable/accessible is an excellent goal for all countries, including Canada," she said in an email.
Canadians are spending more time in the sun – but many are ditching sunscreen
Health Canada referred questions about the sunscreen tax to the Department of Finance Canada.
"Applying the GST/HST to a broad base of goods and services helps keep the tax more efficient, simpler, and lower," Finance Canada said in an emailed statement.
A handful of basic necessities — including prescription drugs, medical devices, menstrual hygiene products and some groceries — are tax-free in Canada.

Asked whether the government would consider adding sunscreen to that list, the department said: "The government is continually reviewing the tax system to ensure it is both effective and efficient and will continue to do so."

items: Cancer remains top cause of death in Canada as new study shows multiple types rising
Why you shouldn’t count on SPF for all of your sun protection

blocks.text: Zbinden-Webster says it's easy to get bogged down in the bureaucracy.
But then she remembers Australia, where sunscreen with an SPF of 15 or more has long been exempt from the 10 per cent Goods and Services Tax.
"There is hope," she said. "It has been done, and it can be done again."

articles.title: NASA is launching the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. Here are just a few of the wonders it will reveal
articles.summary: If all goes to plan, at 7:26 a.m. Sunday morning, a new space telescope will blast off from Cape Canaveral, Fla., on top of a Falcon Heavy rocket, ready to reveal new wonders about our universe. Here…

image.caption: An illustration is shown of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which is set to launch on Aug. 30 from Cape Canaveral, Fla. (NASA)

blocks.text: Science

If all goes to plan, at 7:26 a.m. Sunday morning, a new space telescope will blast off from Cape Canaveral, Fla., on top of a Falcon Heavy rocket, ready to reveal new wonders about our universe. Here are some things scientists hope to unravel with this new telescope.
'I can't even imagine what we're going to learn,' says one Canadian researcher
If all goes to plan, at 7:26 a.m. Sunday morning, a new space telescope will blast off from Cape Canaveral, Fla., on top of a Falcon Heavy rocket, ready to reveal new wonders about our universe.

The highly anticipated Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is named after NASA's first chief astronomer, also known as the "mother of the Hubble Space Telescope." Once launched, it will orbit 1.5 million kilometres away, at a point called L2 where gravitational forces balance to keep satellites in a steady orbit. It is a five-year mission, with the possibility of extension.
But why bother adding a new telescope to the arsenal of telescopes already in orbit, like the Hubble Space Telescope or the James Webb Space Telescope?

Because each telescope is equipped with different instruments, and Nancy Grace Roman is no different. While it has a mirror that is roughly 2.4 metres across, similar to Hubble, it also has a coronagraph that can block out starlight to reveal planets orbiting distant stars. It also has its Wide Field Instrument that is just as sensitive as Hubble's but has the ability to image an area 100 times larger. It's like going from looking through a pinhole to something the size of a golf ball.
Its camera will be able to resolve billions of stars, allowing for all different types of sky and stellar surveys.
So, what makes Nancy Grace Roman so special? Let's take a look at just some of the highly anticipated discoveries astronomers are hoping this telescope will make.
The search for other planets
While we don't know of any other planets with life, astronomers are continuing to investigate other stellar systems to find out what makes our solar system so unique. Or perhaps it's not that unique.
To date, more than 6,300 exoplanets have been confirmed, mostly from the Kepler Space Telescope.

There are a few ways to look for exoplanets. The most popular is the transit method, where a telescope looks at a star for an extended period of time. If there's a planet that crosses — or transits — in front of it, the light of the star dips ever-so slightly. And that's what Nancy Grace Roman will do as well. But on a much bigger scale.

"It's just going to be crazy how much more we're going to learn because right now you know we've got Kepler, which I guess we looked at, like, 200,000 stars or something like that, and then with Roman we're going to look at 100 million stars and we're going to go from 10,000 planets to 100,000 transiting exoplanets," said Kelsey Hoffman, a co-investigator on one of the observing programs with the telescope and a researcher at Bishop's University in Sherbrooke, Que.
"So that increase in numbers, it's… I can't even imagine what we're going to learn."
But the telescope will also use another method to search for exoplanets — something called microlensing, which allows astronomers to peer even deeper.

items: NASA will no longer attempt to save its aging Swift space telescope
'The Holy Grail of science': Montreal startup's high-tech camera to help NASA search for exoplanets

blocks.text: "If you have a distant star that you like to call a source of light, and then a star with its planets moves precisely right in front of it, that mass of the star and the mass of the planet act as two lenses, and causes the light that's coming from that distant star to bend a little bit, which we observe as a magnification event," explained Jason Rowe, who is also part of a Nancy Grace Roman observing program and is a professor in the department of physics at Bishop's University.
He's particularly excited because this type of observation will allow scientists to look for more Earth-like planets.

"We've discovered previous planets with microlensing, but we're going to kind of blow the doors open and now discover a very large sample of them," he said. "And microlensing is very sensitive to planets at longer periods, including those that have masses about Earth's size, about Earth masses."
Dark matter and dark energy

What we are able see makes up only five per cent of what exists in the universe. Roughly 27 per cent is dark matter, a sort of invisible glue that holds the galaxies and the stars within them together. The other 68 per cent is dark energy, also invisible, and something that is believed to speed up the expansion of our universe.

Astronomers have been trying for decades to figure out exactly what dark matter is, and Nancy Grace Roman will look for dark matter within galaxies and within beautiful globular clusters, a collection of thousands to millions of stars that are all tightly gravitationally bound.
The mission will measure the locations and amount of dark matter, as well as normal matter, in hundreds of millions of galaxies.

"Normally with surveys, you have this trade-off where you decide, am I going to stare out one little patch for a very long time? Or am I gonna scale across the sky?" said Nicole Drakos, an astrophysicist at the University of Hawaii, Hilo, who is also part of a Nancy Grace Roman observational program. "With Roman, you can stare at one patch on the sky, but you still have an enormous area.
"So you can see these distant galaxies, but also see where they live. You can see their environment. You can map out the dark matter structure around them, the gas around them."
The telescope will also investigate dark energy, which, like dark matter, is invisible. But in this case, dark energy is causing our universe to expand rather than slow down.

"I'm, you know, involved with the deep field stuff, so I'm obviously interested in that. But, you know, in my heart, I am a cosmologist; I really love the cosmology," Drakos said. "Getting a better handle of things like the expansion of the universe, I think, is really cool."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Nicole covers all things science for CBC News. As an amateur astronomer, Nicole can be found looking up at the night sky appreciating the marvels of our universe. She is the editor of the Journal of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada and the author of several books. In 2021, she won the Kavli Science Journalism Award from the American Association for the Advancement of Science for a Quirks and Quarks audio special on the history and future of Black people in science. You can send her story ideas at nicole.mortillaro@cbc.ca.

articles.title: 5 Lessons Jasmine Curtis wants every girl to know
articles.summary: With an A-list actress for a sister in Anne Curtis, plus beauty, talent, and wit of her own, most people might think Jasmine Curtis simply has it all. But during World Vision’s #GirlsCan campaign…

blocks.text: Lifestyle | Youth
Through World Vision's #GirlsCan campaign, the actress reflects on the lessons she learned from her mother about finding her voice and claiming her space

With an A-list actress for a sister in Anne Curtis, plus beauty, talent, and wit of her own, most people might think Jasmine Curtis simply has it all. But during World Vision’s #GirlsCan campaign event at Gateway 1 Mall in Cubao last Aug. 22, Jasmine opened up about the barriers she faced and the woman who taught her that breaking them can create more possibilities for the next generation.
As a World Vision ambassador, Jasmine shared how her mother’s experiences shaped the way she and her sister learned to recognize their voices, set boundaries, and pursue their own dreams.
Here are five things to learn from Jasmine’s story.
1. Girls often learn expectations before they learn possibilities
Jasmine pointed out that gender bias can begin at home, sometimes through seemingly simple messages about what girls should or should not do.
“Before a girl learns what she wants, she learns what the world expects of her,” she said.
Repeated expectations can eventually become self-doubt, causing girls to believe that certain dreams, careers, or opportunities are meant for someone else.
2. Her mother became her first example of breaking barriers

For her, the first example of a woman breaking barriers was her mother. Coming from a humble background in Bolinao, Pangasinan, her mother, Carmen had to work early after her own mother became sick. She helped pay for her siblings’ education while putting her own dreams on the back burner.
Her mother also did not finish high school. This made education especially important to Jasmine’s family as she and Anne grew up.
“I learned by watching what my mom did when life didn't make things easy for her,” Jasmine said.
3. One woman’s choices can expand another girl’s possibilities
Jasmine said her mother eventually returned to school and work when she was already in her 40s. She later worked as a nurse aide in a hospital and eventually had her own agency.

Watching her mother make those choices changed how Jasmine viewed her own future. “My mother’s choice has expanded mine,” she said, explaining that her mother’s decision to pursue her own path allowed Jasmine and Anne to imagine more possibilities for themselves.
That example also showed her that a person’s journey does not have to end in one chapter.
4. Speaking up is part of claiming your space
Her mother also taught Jasmine that their voices matter. “We can say no and speak up if we are not treated right,” she said.

Jasmine connected this lesson to her own experience, sharing that she spoke up after receiving disrespectful treatment. For her, claiming space means knowing that girls and women can set boundaries and speak when something does not feel right.
5. Telling girls they can is not enough
The World Vision ambassador then emphasized that empowerment should go beyond simply telling girls to be courageous.
“Girls can’t just mean girls, try harder,” she said. “Because courage isn't enough if the doors were closed.”
She called on parents, teachers, employers, media, men, and women to help create environments where girls have access to education, safety, health information, protection, support, and opportunities.
“Our job isn't only to tell a girl that she can. Our job is to help build a world that doesn't keep telling her she can't,” Jasmine said.
Through World Vision’s #GirlsCan campaign, Jasmine hopes to inspire others to help create that kind of world, where girls can dream, choose, lead, and become who they want to be.

articles.title: ‘Para sa susunod na henerasyon!’ Teodoro urges youth to view West Philippine Sea as fight for future resources
articles.summary: Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto C. Teodoro Jr. called on young Filipinos to recognize the West Philippine Sea (WPS) dispute as a struggle for future sustenance, stressing that…

blocks.text: Department of National Defense (DND) Secretary Gilberto C. Teodoro Jr. called on young Filipinos to recognize the West Philippine Sea (WPS) dispute as a struggle for future sustenance, stressing that maritime resources will be vital for generations to come.

Speaking at the launch of the Bantay Dagat Youth Ambassadors – West Philippine Sea Edition Caravan in San Juan City on Friday, Aug. 28, Teodoro warned that ballooning populations and diminishing global commodities make maritime security an urgent struggle for tomorrow's sustenance.

"Where will you get the fuel to feed yourselves in the future, to run your gadgets in the future, if you do not have the resources under the sea?" Teodoro asked the audience of student advocates and community leaders.
He stressed that the Philippines, as an archipelagic nation, spans 2.4 million square kilometers of maritime domain, contrasted against a land area of only 20 percent.

Therefore, he explained that defending WPS secures vital energy supplies and food sources for upcoming generations, noting that rapid demographic shifts dictate an inevitable competition for raw materials.
"As populations expand in the world, as resources grow more scarce, as needs grow more scarce, there is a temptation to expand and that we cannot allow for your safety in the future," Teodoro noted.

Global expansionist pressures compound these resource demands, and the defense chief pointed to unilateral maritime claims by China that supposedly disregard the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the 2016 Arbitral Award, which invalidated the latter’s claims in the South China Sea.
He emphasized that the Philippines holds a distinct geographical position as the sole ASEAN member possessing both a South China Sea border and a Pacific Ocean maritime frontier.

“You cannot stop the growth of human needs, the growth of society. You can't stop evolution,” Teodoro stated. “What you can stop is somebody else taking what should be yours to support yourself and give it to somebody else, and to me that's how best you should frame the problem set in front of you.”

The forum, organized by the Rotary Club of Chinatown Circle in collaboration with the Philippine Navy, drew key security officials including National Security Adviser Eduardo Oban Jr. and Presidential Anti-Organized Crime Commission Executive Director Benjamin Acorda Jr.
The discussions centered on multidimensional threats ranging from foreign malign influence online to illegal offshore gaming operations.
And to counter foreign maritime encroachment, Teodoro said the national defense apparatus combines internal security operations with broader international deterrence networks.

He detailed the formalization of the country’s Status of Visiting Forces Agreements (SOVFAs) with Canada and New Zealand, while similar pacts await Senate concurrence with France or remain under active negotiation with the United Kingdom.

“You can see that these alliances are for shared interests,” Teodoro said. “And what are these interests? That is to secure the maritime domain for supply chains of like-minded countries who feel threatened by expansionism in their own borders.”

articles.title: Manila opens evacuation centers amid heavy rains, flooding
articles.summary: The Manila City government has opened all evacuation centers and placed key government and health facilities on high alert as heavy rains battered the city on Saturday, Aug. 29. Manila City Social…

blocks.text: Manila Department of Social Welfare (MDSW) accommodates 33 families, or 111 individuals, at evacuation centers across the city on Saturday, Aug. 29. (Photo courtesy of MDSW)
The Manila City government has opened all evacuation centers and placed key government and health facilities on high alert as heavy rains battered the city on Saturday, Aug. 29.
Manila City Social Welfare officer Jay Dela Fuente said all district welfare offices and primary evacuation centers are now operational.
Four centers have begun accommodating 33 families, 111 individuals in total.
AC Herrera Elementary School is sheltering 15 families (45 individuals) from Barangay 197.
The Barangay 199 Multipurpose Hall has taken in seven families (25 individuals) from Estero De Matang Tubig.

Ten families (35 individuals) from San Andres near Tripa de Galina are at District Welfare Office V, while a family of six from Barangay 598 near the flood‑prone San Juan River is staying at Likha Multipurpose Hall.
Hot meals and sleeping mats have been provided to evacuees in District 5.

The Manila City Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (MCDRRM) reported flooding along portions of Taft Avenue, including areas near Quirino Avenue, United Nations Avenue, Kalaw, and the National Bureau of Investigation.
MCCDRRMD chief meteorologist Christian Evangelista said the southwest monsoon (habagat), combined with thunderstorms brought heavy to intense rainfall in the city from 5 a.m. to 1 p.m.

"Sa kasalukuyan ay nakataas pa rin ang Red Rainfall Warning sa NCR at inaasahang magpapatuloy hanggang mamayang 5 p.m. (As of now, the Red Rainfall Warning remains in effect across the NCR and is still expected to last until 5 p.m.)," he added. (Shane Quiachon)

articles.summary: The Muntinlupa City government ordered the removal of billboards due to heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon. The city’s building office issued the directive on Aug. 29 after motorists posted…

blocks.text: A billboard along South Luzon Expressway in Muntinlupa (Photo from Dion Real Rosana on Facebook)
The Muntinlupa City government ordered the removal of billboards due to heavy rains brought by the southwest monsoon.
The city’s building office issued the directive on Aug. 29 after motorists posted videos showing tarpaulins from billboards becoming loose along the South Luzon Expressway (SLEX).
Metro Manila has been placed under a red rainfall warning.

“Accordingly, all advertising materials/commercial billboards must be automatically taken down by billboard operators after the release of a Typhoon Signal No. 1 bulletin or any other significant weather disturbance by the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA),” City Building Official Dynadella Aranda said in the order.
Billboard operators are also required to report to the Office of the Building Official when cracks or spalling are visible in the structures.

articles.title: Tim Cone stands firm on Scottie’s impact for Gilas
articles.summary: Scottie Thompson may have found himself at the center of the online vitriol after his crucial turnover late in the Gilas Pilipinas’ 82-81 victory over Jordan, but head coach Tim Cone remained firm on…

blocks.text: Scottie Thompson may have found himself at the center of the online vitriol after his crucial turnover late in the Gilas Pilipinas’ 82-81 victory over Jordan, but head coach Tim Cone remained firm on the veteran guard’s positive impact to the team.

The national team tactician even praised Thompson for doing most of the blue collar jobs in the contest -- including rebounding and defending against Jordan’s top guards Jalen Harris and Freddy Ybrahim.

Cone said he’s aware of the criticisms towards Thompson, especially when playing for Gilas, but the veteran mentor insisted that the do-it-all guard is bringing a lot to the table not usually seen in the stat sheet.

“People kind of give Scottie a hard time because he was not a great shooter, he’s not a true point guard, he’ll make a turnover here or there but they dismiss all the other stuff that he does,” Cone said of Thompson.
“As we all know in the PBA, he does all the ‘Scottie things. He gets the rebounds, he gets the loose balls. He defends. He knows how to get teams to the execution,” he added.

Thompson, however, got the brunt of fans’ strong opinions after committing a five-second inbound violation with seven seconds left, allowing Jordan to get the final shot of the game. Fortunately, Kai Sotto stepped up and got the game-saving block in the game.

Still, the impact of Thompson was undeniable in the contest, evident in the first quarter when he entered the game for the first time and settled down the team after trailing by as many as 18 points, 26-8.
Thompson also finished with a +13 efficiency.
Gilas team manager and program director Alfrancis Chua also came to the defense of Thompson.
“Defense buong game sa best player ng Jordan, di niyo nakita?,” wrote Chua.
“He will make big shots and get to the rim when he needs to but he really relies on his teammates a lot to make shots,” added Cone.

articles.title: Lacson bares 'fraudulently' titled parcels of reclaimed land in Taguig
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson said Saturday four parcels of illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City were initially identified as covered by "fraudulently" issued land titles, while no less than four other…

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 3:44pm
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.

Senator Panfilo Lacson said Saturday four parcels of illegally reclaimed land in Taguig City were initially identified as covered by "fraudulently" issued land titles, while no less than four other parcels have no plotted title lots in the digital records of the Land Registration Authority (LRA).
In a post on X, Lacson said the details of the four alleged fraudulently titled parcels include:

items: one covered by an Administrative Patent, involving 9,204 square meters under an Original Certificate of Title (OCT);
one covered through Judicial/Ordinary Land Registration Processing covering an area of 5,000 square meters under an OCT;
one covered by a Homestead Patent involving 181,077 square meters under a Transfer Certificate of Title (TCT); and
one involving 193,027 square meters under a TCT.

blocks.text: He said he released the details to supposedly disprove claims that his earlier disclosures on the illegal reclamation activities in Taguig City were "fake news."
"Since Sen. (Alan Peter) Cayetano keeps publicly asking for evidence, I'll give it to him, in the spirit of public interest," Lacson said.
Lacson said certain details, including the names of those to whom the titles were issued to, and also the OCT and TCT numbers, were withheld for the time being while the investigation continues.
"All of these will likewise be turned over to the Ombudsman fact-finding team for their further appropriate action," Lacson said.
GMA News Online has reached out to the camp of Cayetano for comment but has yet to receive a reply as of posting time.

Previously, Lacson said the LRA is investigating the origin and history of several newly uncovered land titles covering some 38.83 hectares of illegally reclaimed areas on the Taguig City side of Laguna Lake.
The uncovered land titles were based on the materials provided by the Philippine Reclamation Authority (PRA) to his office.

"I requested the LRA to backtrack the history of the issued OCTs (original certificates of title) and other modes of titling, so we will find out how they were manipulated with the end in view of filing criminal charges against those responsible," the senator said.
Lacson added that the titles may be declared void ab initio (void from the start) once the PRA starts forfeiture proceedings in accordance with law.

He earlier said several crates of documents from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) related to anomalous projects in Taguig City were also set to be turned over to the Office of the Ombudsman. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: DENR eyes private sector cooperation to curb garbage waste
articles.summary: DENR eyes private sector cooperation to curb garbage waste

blocks.text: Published August 29, 2026 3:41pm
Make this your preferred source to get more updates from this publisher on Google.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) is eyeing private sector cooperation as one of the long-term solutions to address pollution in drainage systems and waterways.
The agency cited the use of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) and the Philippine Ecosystem and Natural Capital Accounting System (PENCAS) in this approach.

Under the Extended Producer Responsibility Act of 2022, large enterprises must take responsibility for the life cycle of their plastic wastes. They are responsible for the recovery of their plastic packaging waste.

“Dati ang solid waste management natin, puro local government lang 'yan, sila ang may mandato diyan. Pero ngayon dito, pinaigting natin 'yung private sector participation. Sila na ngayon ang nag-a-address ng mga plastic waste,” Environment Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna said.

(Before, our solid waste management system, it is all local government, they are the ones with that mandate. But here, we fortify private sector participation. They will now address the plastic waste.)

Meanwhile, the PENCAS creates a framework to account for the true value of natural resources and the ecosystem they serve. This would allow the government to recognize the environmental costs of damage.
The DENR said that it is utilizing 196 trash traps to collect floating waste, while mobilizing 1,500 estero rangers and rover warriors to monitor and clean esteros and rivers in Metro Manila.

“With government, businesses, local governments and the public working together, the Department is working to shift the focus from repeatedly cleaning up garbage to preventing improper waste management from becoming a recurring threat to waterways, communities and the environment,” Cuna said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.summary: Alex Gonzaga and Mikee Morada have welcomed their first child, a baby boy, with the actress-TV host’s own brand publicly celebrating the arrival of their “OG Sizzie.” Alex’s shapewear brand confirmed…

blocks.text: Alex Gonzaga and Mikee Morada have welcomed their first child, a baby boy, with the actress-TV host’s own brand publicly celebrating the arrival of their “OG Sizzie.”
Alex’s shapewear brand confirmed the birth in a social media post on Aug. 27, featuring the couple from their maternity shoot.
“THIS JUST IN? Our Sizzies family just got bigger! Sending the biggest, most heartfelt congratulations to our OG Sizzie,” the brand wrote in the post, tagging Alex.
Alex, whose full name is Catherine Gonzaga-Morada, liked the post.
The brand’s announcement came after Alex shared photos of herself cradling her baby bump, along with a message about saying goodbye to her pregnancy.
“I’ll miss carrying you inside my tummy, my baby. It was like having our own little world,” she wrote.
The post led to speculation that Alex had already given birth.
Her brand’s Aug. 27 message provided another public confirmation of the arrival of the couple’s long-awaited first child.
The milestone comes after Gonzaga and Morada experienced three pregnancy losses.
Gonzaga suffered her first miscarriage in 2021, followed by another in 2023 and a third in 2024.
In May 2026, the couple announced that they were expecting their first child after conceiving naturally.
Gonzaga and Morada have yet to reveal their son’s name or other details about his birth.

articles.title: 6 Filipino fragrance brands putting a local spin on perfumery
articles.summary: The local perfume industry continues to bloom, with homegrown brands creating scents inspired by Filipino stories, memories, and experiences. At a fragrance community event held Aug. 22 to 23 at…

blocks.text: Lifestyle | Fashion and Beauty
From niche creations to nostalgic Filipino-inspired scents, these homegrown brands are worth getting to know
The local perfume industry continues to bloom, with homegrown brands creating scents inspired by Filipino stories, memories, and experiences.

At a fragrance community event held Aug. 22 to 23 at Unbox Promenade, GH Mall in San Juan City, more than 30 local perfume brands from across the Philippines, including Mindanao, Batangas, and Northern regions, showcased their creations. Here are five homegrown perfume brands worth discovering:
Orca Parfums
Founded by entrepreneur and perfumer Gib Osbert Ang, Orca Parfums was born from his desire to revive forgotten fragrance styles while giving them a contemporary touch.
“People’s encouragement, curiosity, and shared love for perfumery have pushed me to refine my craft and explore new possibilities,” he told Manila Bulletin Lifestyle.

Among our favorites are Morning Lust, Sakura et Rose, and Evening Lust, which performed consistently both indoors and outdoors. During our wear test, the fragrances lasted up to six hours, with noticeable projection throughout the day.
Olfaction
Led by cosmetic scientist and perfumer Claire Mavreen,Olfaction creates fragrances designed to transport wearers to people, places, and moments that are either long gone or imagined.

A graduate of Cosmetic Chemistry from Centro Escolar University, Claire draws her scientific background to create distinctive fragrance products. From her latest collection, Two Scoops Please and A Coat of Pastel Purple Clouds stood out among our picks.

Of the fragrances we tested, Olfaction delivered the longest wear time. When applied to pulse points, both scents remained noticeable for around eight hours, making them a strong choice for those who prioritize longevity.

blocks.caption: Artistry

blocks.text: Artistry
Created by 30-year-old Batangas-based engineer Ian Dominique Arano, Artistry treats fragrance as a way to give form to memories, emotions, and imagination.
“As a Filipino niche fragrance start-up, Artistry approaches perfumery as an art form,” Arano said. “Each creation begins with a story.”

The brand currently offers four scents, with Beauty is Terror and Where Everything Meets standing out among our picks. Both developed nicely on the skin and lasted more than six hours when applied to pulse points, making them worth considering for those who prefer longer-wearing scents.
Moonsteria

Headed by singer-songwriter and producer Jessica Rodriguez, also known as Seekada, Moonsteria takes a more personal approach to fragrance. After learning about her rare hearing disorder in 2023, she explored healing and perfumery as new forms of expression. The brand's collections take notes from Philippine folklore, tea rituals, Filipino merienda, nature, music, poetry, and healing.

Sampaguita Polvoron and Midnight Tea are among our favorites. Sampaguita Polvoron offers a playful Filipino gourmand character, while Midnight Tea leans toward a more calming, tea-inspired mood. During our daily-commute wear test, both lasted around four hours, a reasonable performance for their price point.
Blend Labs
Founded by 27-year-olds Ayaka Chikusa and Marc Balaoing, Blend Labs creates fragrances inspired by personal memories, from cocktails and beach trips to family gatherings and love letters.

Our picks are Amaretto and Buko Pandan. The latter is especially memorable, with sweet gourmand quality without becoming overly heaving or cloying. It has the nostalgic feel of the Filipino dessert without smelling like a literal bowl of it. Both scents lasted around four hours during our wear test.
Parfum Astraux

Owned by the 28-year-old security network engineer Rochelle Lubao, Parfum Astraux is behind the now-trending Yosi Break, which turns the familiar idea of a cigarette break into an unconventional wearable scent.
“It started as a creation for consumption only,” she said, adding that they later started to sell it.

For those looking for something playful and unexpected, try Sour Candy and Kwantro Kantos. Both have distinctive scent profiles and lasted around six hours when applied to pulse points during our wear test.
With more Filipino perfumers entering the scene, the local fragrance industry continues to grow. These brands are also giving Filipino creators another way to tell stories through scent.

articles.title: Nine roads remain impassable in Mangatarem amid flooding
articles.summary: MANGATAREM, Pangasinan — Nine roads in this municipality remained impassable to all types of vehicles as of 10 a.m. Saturday, August 29, as flooding continued to affect several areas. The latest road…

blocks.text: MANGATAREM, Pangasinan — Nine roads in this municipality remained impassable to all types of vehicles as of 10 a.m. Saturday, August 29, as flooding continued to affect several areas.

The latest road and flooding situation report was based on monitoring conducted by Municipal Disaster and Risk Reduction Management Office (MDRRMO) and personnel of the Mangatarem Municipal Police Station under the leadership of PMAJ Arturo C. Melchor Jr., chief of police.

blocks.caption: (Photo via Liezle Inigo)

blocks.text: (Photo via Liezle Inigo)

Among the roads reported to be impassable were Bogtong Silag (Sitio Dor. Vergara); Pogon-Aniat going to Dorogan Sawat; Bunlalacao (Sitio Dor. Bunlalacao); Dorongan Punta (Sitio Papalyasen); and Pampano (Mamparan).

Also affected were the routes from Talogtog going to Cabaruan, Suaco, Sapang, and Tococ Barikir; Bogtong Bolo going to Sapang, Suaco, and Cabaruan; Lawak-Langka River to Sitio Ballasiw; Salavante going to Dorongan Sawat; and Dorongan Valerio going to Sitio Dorongan Vergara.

Meanwhile, Bogtong Centro (Highway) was reported passable during the same monitoring period, although motorists were advised to remain cautious due to the prevailing weather conditions and possible changes in road and water conditions.
Melchor and his personnel continue to monitor affected roads and water levels in different areas of Mangatarem.
Authorities appealed to motorists and residents to avoid flooded and impassable routes.
Instead follow local safety advisories, and prioritize their safety amid the continuing threat of flooding.

articles.title: Are our students safe in school? Atom Araullo investigates
articles.summary: A mass shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City on June 22 left three people dead, raising fresh concerns about the safety of students inside schools. Nearly two months later,…

blocks.text: A mass shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City on June 22 left three people dead, raising fresh concerns about the safety of students inside schools.
Nearly two months later, another shooting took place at Ateneo de Zamboanga University on Aug. 18. Two people died in the incident, including the gunman.

The two tragedies have brought difficult questions to the surface: Are the government’s measures enough to protect students? How secure are schools and classrooms? And what more can families, parents and schools do to keep children safe?
These are the questions award-winning journalist Atom Araullo seeks to answer as he takes a deeper look at school safety in “The Atom Araullo Specials: What We Don’t See.”

Rather than stopping at what is immediately visible after a tragedy, Araullo examines the issues and possible threats that may go unnoticed, and the challenges of keeping students safe both inside and outside the classroom.
“What We Don’t See” airs Saturday, Aug. 29, at 9:30 p.m. on GMA Network.
Related Tags
