articles.title: Rescue, evacuation operations continue as flooding affects Mangatarem, Pangasinan
articles.summary: MANGATAREM, Pangasinan — Rescue and evacuation operations continued in several flood-affected barangays in Mangatarem early Saturday as authorities responded to residents displaced by rising…

blocks.text: Rescue and evacuation operations continue in several flood-affected barangays in Mangatarem, Pangasinan, with 55 families or 188 individuals evacuated as of 6 a.m., based on the initial police report. (Photo courtesy of Mangatarem PNP via Liezle Inigo)

MANGATAREM, Pangasinan — Rescue and evacuation operations continued in several flood-affected barangays in Mangatarem early Saturday as authorities responded to residents displaced by rising floodwaters amid persistent rains.
An initial report from the Mangatarem Municipal Police Station showed that 55 families, or 188 individuals, have been evacuated as of 6 a.m. from six barangays.

Affected were 15 families or 45 individuals from Takipan; five families or 45 individuals from Talogtog; nine families or 12 individuals from Cabaruan; three families or nine individuals from Olo Cacamposan; four families or 11 individuals from Bunlalacao; and 19 families or 66 individuals from Dorongan Punta.
Major. Arturo Melchor Jr, chief of police of Mangatarem, said the figures remained subject to consolidation as rescue and evacuation operations are still underway.

The six barangays were those with recorded evacuations at the time of the initial report. Other barangays may have also experienced flooding but had yet to evacuate residents, particularly in communities accustomed to flooding where water levels sometimes recede quickly.
Police, rescuers, and local authorities continued monitoring the situation and responding to calls for assistance as necessary.
Residents in flood-prone areas were urged to remain vigilant, monitor official advisories, and evacuate immediately if ordered by authorities or if conditions become unsafe.
Related Tags

articles.title: Cambodia claims it has wiped out online scam compounds after a sweeping crackdown
articles.summary: PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Cambodia, notorious for being a major center for international online scams, claimed Friday it no longer hosts any of the compounds where the lucrative cybercrime was…

blocks.text: PHNOM PENH, Cambodia (AP) — Cambodia, notorious for being a major center for international online scams, claimed Friday it no longer hosts any of the compounds where the lucrative cybercrime was carried out, although some remain skeptical.

The government’s Ad-Hoc Commission for Combating Online Scams, CCOS, claimed success for its crackdown at a Thursday meeting with about 50 representatives of foreign diplomatic missions and international organizations led by Senior Minister Chhay Sinarith, who heads the anti-scam agency, it said in a statement issued Friday.

“This follows the complete eradication of large-scale online scam operations, strict legal actions against perpetrators, networks and involved officials, alongside the systematic establishment of a cybersecurity legal framework,” it said.

Chhay Sinarith's claims were met with both skepticism and guarded optimism from independent groups that have tracked the scam compounds, which are infamous not only for bilking billions of dollars from people all over the world, but also for carrying out human trafficking.

Thousands of foreign nationals, who are employed to run “romance” and cryptocurrency scams to swindle victims, are often recruited with false job offers and then forced to work in conditions of near-slavery.
Such scams caused estimated combined losses of $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in 2025, said a report in July by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

“The strong confidence placed in the (Cambodian) government’s assertion that all scamming operations in Cambodia have been eradicated is severely misplaced,” Mark Taylor, an independent international anti-trafficking consultant and former head of an anti-trafficking program in Cambodia, told The Associated Press.
“There are credible indicators that significant scamming operations continue and that recruitment of foreign workers into Cambodia for scamming work continues."
Blue Dragon Children’s Foundation, a Vietnam-based anti-human trafficking organization, took more of a wait-and-see attitude.

“There is no doubt that some of Cambodia’s criminal compounds used for online scamming have closed,” said Michael Brosowski, the group’s founder and strategic director, citing a drastic decrease in calls from people who have been trafficked, although the calls have not stopped.
“We hope that the Cambodian government will keep its commitment to close down these compounds and give greater protection to victims of this crime."

Chhay Sinarith said that from July 2025 to Aug. 20, 2026, law enforcement forces investigated 793 suspected scam locations and raided 624 sites, while detaining nearly 30,000 suspects representing 39 nationalities.
Cambodian authorities rescued and deported 58,266 foreign nationals, he said, and 3,477 criminal suspects from 29 nationalities were arrested and placed in pretrial detention.

The crackdown was highlighted by the takedown of two alleged kingpins of the illicit trade, Chen Zhi and Li Xiong, influential Chinese businessmen who had also become Cambodian citizens and were extradited earlier this year after their arrests.

Cambodian lawmakers unanimously adopted a new law in March targeting online scam operations with sentences of up to life in prison, following a government pledge to shut down the centers by the end of April.

articles.title: Remains of two missing children in Mapanuepe Lake tragedy recovered
articles.summary: SAN MARCELINO, Zambales — The bodies of two children reported missing after the drowning incident at Mapanuepe Lake on August 27 were recovered Saturday morning as authorities intensified their…

blocks.text: SAN MARCELINO, Zambales — The bodies of two children reported missing after the drowning incident at Mapanuepe Lake on August 27 were recovered Saturday morning as authorities intensified their search, rescue and retrieval (SRR) operations.

A report from the office of Col. Benjamin Ariola, provincial director of the Zambales Police Provincial Office, said the first body was recovered at around 10:10 a.m. after it was spotted floating on the lake by local resident Marcelo Balario and five neighbors from Barangay Buhawen.
Balario's group, which was traveling by motorized banca from Sitio Lumibao to Buhawen, immediately retrieved the body and brought it to Buhawen Proper.
The victim was later identified by her father, Deolito Pabalan, as Chandrea Dela Cruz Pabalan, one of those reported missing in the August 27 incident.
Less than an hour later, at around 11:05 a.m., rescuers recovered another lifeless body of a child from the lake.
The victim was identified by his father, Palito Liwanag, as Angelito Liwanag.

The recoveries were made during the continuing SRR operation led by responding personnel from the San Marcelino Municipal Police Station and San Marcelino MDRRMO, with assistance from local residents and other responders.
Search and retrieval efforts remain underway as authorities continue to locate and account for the remaining individual reported missing following the incident.
Authorities are also coordinating with the victims' families as the recovery operation continues.

articles.title: Bridging gaps, building dreams
articles.summary: The Biaan Aeta Integrated School in Mariveles, Bataan, turns a new chapter in its inspiring history with the arrival of sustainable power and internet access. This comes courtesy of AuroraPH, an…

blocks.text: The Biaan Aeta Integrated School in Mariveles, Bataan, turns a new chapter in its inspiring history with the arrival of sustainable power and internet access. This comes courtesy of AuroraPH, an initiative that helps bridge the educational and digital divide in the Philippines.

blocks.caption: The power of education. Grade 8 Aeta student Arianne Perio works hard for her education, with a dream to lift her family out of poverty. “Proud ako sa anak ko. Laging nasa honor,” her mom said. (I’m proud of her. She’s always in the honor roll.)

blocks.text: The power of education. Grade 8 Aeta student Arianne Perio works hard for her education, with a dream to lift her family out of poverty. “Proud ako sa anak ko. Laging nasa honor,” her mom said. (I’m proud of her. She’s always in the honor roll.)

Through solar photovoltaic (PV) systems and Wi-Fi, a school that began outdoors under trees with makeshift learning aids is further equipped to address the evolving needs of its students, which include those from the indigenous Aeta Magbukún tribes and the non-indigenous Tagalog.

“Noong na-interview po namin yung mga katutubo, ang isa sa hiniling nila ay magkaroon ng paaralan dito. Halos 99% ng mga katutubo dito noon ay hindi nakakabasa [at] hindi nakakasulat. Kaya noong 2005, nag-start po kami na mag-conduct ng literacy program,” recalled Mariquita A. Banal, Head Teacher and former Principal of Biaan Aeta. (When we interviewed the indigenous people, one of their wishes was to have a school here. Almost 99% of the natives before didn’t know how to read and write. That’s why in 2005, we started a literacy program.)

“Sa tulong ng DepEd (Department of Education) at Mariveles district, naitayo ang Biaan Aeta Integrated School,” she explained. (With the help of DepEd and the Mariveles district, we established the Biaan Aeta Integrated School.)

In its early years, the school dealt with power issues, including gaining access and, eventually, having to pay for the cost. An intermittent internet connection and limited learning tools and instructional materials further compounded its struggles.

“Napakahirap po para sa amin kasi wala po talagang signal. Naaawa ako kasi syempre nahirapan sila, lalo na sa research,” observed Laarnie P. Oliveros, a senior high school teacher at Biaan Aeta. (It’s really difficult for us because there is absolutely no signal. I felt bad for them because they were struggling, especially with their research.)

blocks.caption: The power of empathy. What began as a literacy program to teach the indigenous Aeta Magbukún tribes to read and write is now the Biaan Aeta Integrated School, which Teacher Mariquita A. Banal helped establish with her husband. With today’s growing digital divide, AuroraPH supports Ms. Banal’s lif…

blocks.text: The power of empathy. What began as a literacy program to teach the indigenous Aeta Magbukún tribes to read and write is now the Biaan Aeta Integrated School, which Teacher Mariquita A. Banal helped establish with her husband. With today’s growing digital divide, AuroraPH supports Ms. Banal’s lifelong mission in education.
Still, the school persisted, thanks to the determination of its students and teachers.

“Kitang-kita ko naman po talaga na nahihirapan po sila Mama. Street sweeper po siya sa barangay. Gusto ko po silang maiahon sa hirap,” said Arianne Khaye G. Perio, a Grade 8 Aeta student who wants to be a nurse when she grows up. (I can really see that Mom and the rest of the family are struggling. She’s a street sweeper in the town. I want to lift them out of poverty.)
“Pagdating po sa pag-aaral, masasabi ko pong 100% po akong masipag mag-aral.” (When it comes to studying, I can say that I am 100% hardworking.)

“Isa po sa mga reason ko kung bakit pursigido po akong magturo rito dahil po sa mga bata. Nakikita ko sa kanila yung dedication nila na talagang yung pag-aaral nila gusto nilang makapagtapos,” Oliveros added. (One of the reasons I am so determined to teach here is because of the children. I see their dedication—they truly want to finish their studies.)

Last July 2025, AuroraPH arrived at Biaan Aeta and renewed the hopes of students and teachers alike. It was done in partnership with Aboitiz Power Corporation (AboitizPower) through GNPower Mariveles Energy Center and GNPower Dinginin, together with the non-profit GivePower, the private companies Starlink and Huawei, and DepEd and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority.

AuroraPH is a flagship education and connectivity initiative by Aboitiz Foundation that aims to support 300 off-grid, last-mile schools across the Philippines with solar power, internet systems, digital learning tools, and capacity building.

Biaan Aeta is the first on-grid school to benefit from the effort, enhancing its existing infrastructure to reduce electricity costs and vastly improve online connectivity via Starlink, which uses Low Earth Orbit satellites for internet, thereby bypassing the need for traditional cables or cell towers.

“Napakaswerte natin dito. Napaka-privileged natin dahil may mga katulad ng Aboitiz na handang tumulong sa mga kabataan na nandito,” Oliveros said. (We are very lucky here. We are very privileged because there are companies like Aboitiz who are ready to help the children who are here.)

“Mayroon na silang access sa Wi-Fi. Mas madali para sa mga bata na mag-research, lalo na po iyong mga senior high school students namin. May mga research silang ginagawa na kung saan hindi na sila kailangang bumaba pa sa bayan para lang mag-search,” she further explained. (They now have access to Wi-Fi. It’s easier for the kids to do research, especially for our senior high school students. They can do their research without having to go down to the town just to get information.)

blocks.caption: The power of dedication. When the Biaan Aeta Integrated School began a senior high school program in 2017, Laarnie P. Oliveros was the only full-time teacher. Despite a tiring daily one-hour commute and options to teach closer to home, her invaluable dedication kept her rooted in Biaan Aeta.

blocks.text: The power of dedication. When the Biaan Aeta Integrated School began a senior high school program in 2017, Laarnie P. Oliveros was the only full-time teacher. Despite a tiring daily one-hour commute and options to teach closer to home, her invaluable dedication kept her rooted in Biaan Aeta.
Since AuroraPH and the installation of solar PVs to power 12 classrooms, there has been a 60% reduction in the school’s electricity bill. With its first savings, Biaan Aeta invested in CCTV cameras.

“Malaki ang pasasalamat namin sa Aboitiz Foundation and AboitizPower. Yung tulong nila talagang tuloy-tuloy,” Banal said. (We are deeply grateful to the Aboitiz Foundation and AboitizPower. Their support has been continuous.)

“Natupad nila yung isa sa mga pangarap namin na yung mga bata rito sa paaralan ay maging globally competitive. Na kahit kami ay nasa bundok, hindi kami nahuhuli. Kaya pala mangyari yon sa Biaan Aeta,” she added. (They fulfilled one of our dreams: for the children here at the school to become globally competitive. Even though we are located in the mountains, we are not being left behind. It turns out that this is actually possible for Biaan Aeta.)

AuroraPH has helped over 80 schools across the country, benefiting 9,000+ students. It is aligned with both national developmental goals and the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goal 4, calling for “Quality Education”, or “[ensuring] inclusive and equitable quality education and [promoting] lifelong learning opportunities for all”.

“Ang pinagpapasalamat ko po sa AboitizPower ay binago nila iyong buhay namin bilang estudyante tsaka po mas pinadali po nila iyong pag-aaral namin,” young Arianne said. (What I’m grateful to AboitizPower for is that they transformed our lives as students and made studying much easier).

Police personnel from Pasig, Marikina, and Mandaluyong use their patrol cars to offer free rides to stranded commuters in their respective areas. (Photos from Manggahan Substation Pasig/SubstationFive Marikina CPS/PNP Mandaluyong CPS)

blocks.text: The Eastern Police District (EPD), led by Brig. Gen. Melecio M. Buslig Jr., said the free rides were launched to ease travel woes and help commuters stranded by disrupted public transport.
Its personnel assisted commuters, maintained order, and facilitated the smooth movement of passengers in affected areas.

In Marikina, police stations and substations offered free rides within their areas, including the Parang Substation, which assisted commuters in Barangay Nangka.

The Mandaluyong City Police Station and personnel from its substations also offered free rides to commuters traveling along routes from L. Parada to Barangay Malamig, from Marketplace to Puregold Aglipay, and along Sierra Madre Street in Barangay Highway Hills.
Stranded commuters in Barangays Manggahan and Bagong Ilog in Pasig City were also assisted by personnel from Pasig Substation 2 and the Manggahan Substation.

“Through the leadership of PBGen Buslig, the EPD continues to demonstrate its dedication to responsive and compassionate public service, extending immediate assistance to communities affected by severe weather conditions,” the EPD said.
Authorities said the initiative highlights the EPD’s continuing efforts to ensure the safety, security, and welfare of the public, especially during emergencies and weather-related disruptions.

articles.title: This extremely successful author polarizes German readers
articles.summary: She's young and she says what she thinks: Caroline Wahl is topping Germany's bestseller lists with her novels. But she has also faced public backlash.

image.caption: Author Caroline Wahl, shown here at the 2026 German Film AwardsImage: Sebastian Christoph Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Caroline Wahl, 31, has published three novels to date. All three shot to the top of Germany's fiction bestseller lists.

Now, her fourth book is set to be released on August 28: "1999 Meter über dem Meer" (1999 Meters Above Sea) tells the story of a young woman who takes on a false identity to mingle among the high society in St. Moritz, Switzerland.
It is one of the most anticipated new books of the summer in Germany.
So what is the secret to Caroline Wahl's success?
Debut with a bang
Caroline Wahl's breakthrough came with her first novel, from 2023: "22 Bahnen" (22 Lengths) sold more than a million copies in German-language editions.
The story of the young student Tilda, who has to navigate everyday life alongside her alcoholic mother and her little sister, was praised by critics for its straightforward, modern writing style.
What's more, the novel managed to fascinate readers across generations: It includes references to contemporary pop culture as well as to classic literature.

"The many references make the novels both diverse and ambiguous," says Matthias Schaffrick, a research associate at the Collaborative Research Center "Transformations of the Popular" at the University of Siegen, who recently organized a two-day symposium on Wahl's works.

"What stands out most is how she experiments with different narrative styles and questions them, instead of simply telling a story," Shaffrick tells DW. "This opens up a literary space with multiple possibilities, enabling different interpretations and certainly contributing to the appeal of her novels for many readers."
Polarizing ambition

The success led to the media becoming interested in the young author, and quickly showed that Caroline Wahl does not care much for conventions: She speaks her mind freely and doesn't mind facing backlash. "I enjoy being polarizing," she told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper last weekend. "I like that there's no gray area, people either hate me, and then they really hate me (...). Or they like me."

In the podcast "Hotel Matze," she said she wanted to become one of Germany's most famous authors. Her words quickly created a stir, but Wahl didn't mind: "I'm really not up for false modesty. It's not wrong to state your goals ambitiously," she said on the arts and culture TV show "Twist" on the Arte channel. "For young women in particular, it's more extreme than for men — people get irritated when a young woman says, 'I want to be the best.' I want to change that with my attitude."
A passion for fast cars

Part of that is openly speaking about enjoying her newfound wealth. In an interview with SZ-Magazin, she said: "It's not only the writing that is enjoyable, but also being successful. Financial success is also important." She loves fast cars, drives a convertible and bought a camper van she likes to park somewhere with a view of the sea to work.

On social media, she faced a lot of criticism. She has been accused of making money off the literary depiction of poverty in "22 Bahnen," despite never having lived an impoverished life herself. It's an age-old discussion about whether authors are only allowed to write about things they have experienced themselves. Wahl replied to this criticism on the Deutschlandfunk radio station, explaining that above all, writing to her means "exploring spaces that I don't know and feeling empathy for people who live a different life than mine."

blocks.caption: No fan of false modesty: Caroline WahlImage: Felix Hörhager/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: But even without the debate on her credibility, a young woman who speaks openly about material success still seems to be unsettling for many people in Germany — men and women alike — as the many negative reactions show. To Wahl herself, the debate is misogynist.

On Instagram, she wrote a caption for a photo of her light blue BMW: "I find it weird and don't quite get why it's cool for rappers or other men to show off their AMGs, etc., but when a woman author wants to buy a sports car (and can afford to do so!!!), people advise her not to do it and more importantly, not to show it in public."
Author and influencer

"What happens when something becomes very popular?" asks literary scholar Matthias Schaffrick: "The popularity starts being scrutinized, which you can observe in Caroline Wahl's case. And we can see what it means to be a popular author. It's not only her novels that play a role, but also the persona she creates for herself as an author."

By being active on Instagram, where she has even tested energy drinks, she also taps into the role of an influencer, says Matthias Schaffrick. "It makes her even more popular and offers new topics for conversation. At the same time, the public debate shifts the focus away from her literature, which is what's actually interesting about the Caroline Wahl phenomenon."

Wahl herself admits that the intensity of the backlash and criticism has hurt her. In an interview with the SWR TV channel, she explained that social criticism is not necessarily her intention. "I'm not trying to change anything with my stories. Above all, I want to tell stories."
'22 Lengths' on school curricula

When it comes to best‑sellers, opinions always differ among German literary critics: Is this entertaining literature, or serious literature with high artistic aspirations? The arts and feature sections of numerous newspapers come to different conclusions on whether Caroline Wahl's novels can be classified as part of the latter. In an interview with Spiegel, Wahl said she finds "drawing a line between entertaining and serious simply annoying."

So far, Wahl's novels have not been nominated for the German Book Prize, Germany's highest literature award. In 2024, the writer voiced her disappointment in typical fashion on Instagram: "I'm sad and angry that I have not been included on the longlist, even if I somehow knew this would happen. Too successful, says my agent."
Back then, her debut novel could have been included on the list — a book that was quickly added to school curricula and has now been made into a film.

Likewise, on this year's longlist, Wahl's novel "Die Assistentin" (The Assistant) has not been included. A literature critic from Frankfurter Rundschau had this to say about the decision: "Why is good literature always supposed to hurt before it can be deemed 'valuable'? (...) The fact that an author like Wahl has been ignored, simply because her captivating writing fascinates millions of readers, makes me really angry."
Presumably, Caroline Wahl's fans will ensure that her new novel becomes another bestseller — even without the German Book Prize.

articles.title: Wanted Australian national nabbed in Siargao island tourist hub
articles.summary: CAMP RAFAL C. RODRIGUEZ, Butuan City – Police arrested a 55-year-old Australian national in Siargao island tourist hub, Surigao del Norte, police reported Saturday, Aug. 29. Joint operatives of the…

blocks.text: CAMP RAFAL C. RODRIGUEZ, Butuan City – Police arrested a 55-year-old Australian national in Siargao island tourist hub, Surigao del Norte, police reported Saturday, Aug. 29.

Joint operatives of the General Luna Municipal Police Station (MPS) and the Surigao del Norte Tourist Police Unit (TPU) launched an intensified manhunt operation that led to the arrest of this Australian national male suspect in Sitio Santa Ines, Barangay Catangnan, General Luna town, Siargao Island, Surigao del Norte.

In his flash report to Police Regional Office 13 (PRO 13) Director Police Brig. Gen. Rolindo M. Suguilon late Friday afternoon, Surigao del Norte Police Provincial Office (PPO) Director Police Col. Warren E. Dablo, said the suspect was caught by surprise when the operating team arrived in the targeted area at 11:20 a.m. on Thursday.
The suspect was duly informed of his rights under the Miranda Doctrine and Anti-Torture Warning upon arrest, Col. Dablo said.

Police operatives served and implemented a warrant of arrest against the suspect for five counts of Violation of Republic Act 9262 (Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act of 2004), under Criminal Case Numbers 26-32, 26-33, 26-34, 26-35, and 26-36.

Regional Public Information Office (RPIO) chief of PRO 13 Police Lt. Col. Jennifer S. Ometer said the warrant of arrest was issued by the Regional Trial Court, 10th Judicial Region, Branch 31, Dapa, Surigao del Norte, dated February 13, 2026 and February 18, 2026.
Initial investigation conducted by the General Luna MPS stated that the suspect allegedly committed the offenses against his wife, she said.
The suspect remains in the custody of the General Luna Municipal Police Station for appropriate disposition.

“I guarantee that the Surigao del Norte Police will not tolerate such offenses; no one, foreigner or otherwise, is above the law. We will not rest until all wanted persons are brought before the bar. We stand firm: perpetrators of these crimes shall be held fully accountable," said Col. Dablo, in a statement on Saturday.
Meanwhile, Brig. Gen. Suguilon commended the police force in Siargao Island, Surigao del Norte for their relentless pursuit of justice.

The new PRO 13 chief directed all regional, provincial and city police commanders as well provincial and city police director and municipal chiefs of police to continue without let up the extensive anti-crime operations in all corners in Northern Mindanao region under his close watch.

articles.title: Europe's summer drought threatens fish in rivers, lakes and farms
articles.summary: NOVI SAD, Serbia (AP) — Small boats stand idle on cracked ground in a shriveled side channel of the Danube River in northern Serbia, where the water has receded into a couple of shrinking ponds under…

blocks.text: NOVI SAD, Serbia (AP) — Small boats stand idle on cracked ground in a shriveled side channel of the Danube River in northern Serbia, where the water has receded into a couple of shrinking ponds under pressure from extreme drought and heat. Fish circle in the shallow waters.

“This is all we have, these two little ponds that are full of juvenile fish,” fisherman Dusan Jovanovic said. He said the fish are in danger because there is too little water and its temperature is over 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit).
“If they start to die, they will all die at once,” Jovanovic said.

Persistent drought and scorching heat this summer have ravaged ecosystems and businesses across the region, from a lake in Slovenia and the side channel of the Danube in Serbia, to fish farms in Bosnia, the Czech Republic, Romania and Hungary.

The fish industry has been hit especially hard, with damage estimated in the millions of euros (dollars). This is adding to the already high toll caused by problems with energy and water supplies, devastated crops, losses in river traffic and trade.

Finding themselves unprepared for this year's crisis, countries and businesses are now pondering ways to minimize the effects of future extreme weather events that scientists have tied to human-induced climate change.
Hungary's fish die as entire country faces extreme drought

Around 99% of Hungary’s lands are currently under severe or extreme drought conditions, according to the national meteorological service. Desertification, a process where vegetation recedes because of high heat and low rainfall, threatens much of the Great Hungarian Plain.

Among the most affected are Hungary’s roughly 27,000 hectares (67,000 acres) of fish ponds. The country’s Agriculture and Food Economy Ministry said last week that “persistent heat and water shortages” had led to 1,588 hectares (3,924 acres) of those ponds drying out, causing the deaths of nearly 280 metric tons of fish at 20 farms.

The estimated revenue loss from the damage was 1.3 billion forints ($4.2 million), the ministry said. Producers say replacing lost fish could take years. Sometimes, operators were forced to drain one pond and divert its water to save fish in another, the Hungarian Aquaculture and Fisheries Inter-branch Organization said in early August.
Repeated drought over years hurts Romanian fish farmers

For fish farmers in Romania, especially those cultivating carp, this year’s blistering heatwave follows severe droughts in 2023 and 2024, the effects of which are still being felt, says Catalin Platon, president of ROMFISH National Association of Fish Producers.
In carp production, Platon said, the production cycle is three or four years.

“So what we lost in 2023 has (had an) impact every year since," he explained. Water-use policies that prioritized irrigation for agriculture during the previous droughts, “left us with no water for the fish,” Platon complained.
Czech fish farmers take emergency measures
Fish farmers across the Czech Republic have taken various emergency measures: reducing or suspending feeding to reduce oxygen use, aerating the ponds or draining them when necessary.
The Czech Fishing Association officials say sustained rainfall could ease the immediate crisis, but long-term measures are needed to retain more water in the landscape.
Jan Sokolik, a technician at the Rybarstvi Trebon fishery, explained that “some ponds that were actually low on water have already been fished, but they were all marginal ponds.”
“Now we’re just starting to plan what to do with the big ponds,” he said.
Bosnian trout breeders ‘looking to survive summer’
Veljko Budjen owns a trout farm near Trebinje in southeast Bosnia. He said hot and dry summers have brought serious problems in the mainly mountainous country famous for its trout restaurants.

“Trout is a cold water fish, which requires cold water with a lot of oxygen,” he said. “So during the summer you are forced to reduce trout production and feeding so the business can just barely survive.”
One option, he said, is to add liquid oxygen to the water during summer months. Otherwise, he said, “you wait for the first rain.”
Slovenians pump water into a lake in an attempt to save fish

Emergency teams have been pumping water into Lake Pristava in eastern Slovenia, a favorite spot for fishermen, to try to prevent a mass suffocation of fish from lack of oxygen and water chestnut overgrowing to cover the lake surface.
Firefighters have pumped in 8 million liters (2 million gallons) of water but they still fear it's not enough.
"We are surprised that any fish has survived at all,” Danijel Fras, from the Pesnica Lenart Fishing Association, told public broadcaster RTV Slovenia.
In Serbia, fishermen said the only solution for the endangered fish in the Danube side channel in Novi Sad is to move them to another location.
“The temperatures this year are extreme,” Jovanovic, the Serbian fisherman, said. "No one can remember anything like this.”

articles.title: Ex-White House teleprompter operator ordered to pay $172,000 for Trump speech bets
articles.summary: The staffer was found to have used his prior knowledge of the president's speeches to place lucrative bets.

blocks.text: A former White House teleprompter operator has been ordered to pay more than $172,000 (£127,000) for using inside information to bet on US President Donald Trump's speeches.

Gabriel Perez was found to have made trades on what the president would say during addresses between December 2025 and February 2026 on Kalshi - a prediction markets platform where users can bet on real-world events.
Its regulator, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), said Perez would have to surrender profits of $107,539.02 (£79,452) and pay a civil penalty of $65,000 (£48,000).
The White House has not yet commented. In July, then-press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Perez was on unpaid leave and would not return to his post.
Announcing the settlement on Friday, the CFTC said Perez had "misappropriated" his prior knowledge of Trump's speeches to place bets "in breach of his duty of trust and confidence".
It said his civil penalty had been reduced due to his "exemplary co-operation" with the investigation.
Perez has also been banned from trading for three years.
Writing on X, Kalshi's lead lawyer Bobby DeNault welcomed the decision: "It doesn't matter who you are: violate our rules or federal law and you will face the consequences."

The company previously told the BBC its analysts had noticed unusual betting on "mention markets" – contracts where users predict whether a speaker will use common terms, such as specific countries, campaign slogans or words – in March.
It said it had used account data to find that the user was a federal employee operating White House teleprompters, and had reported the activity to the regulator.
"The words of political leaders like Presidents and Fed chairs cause billions of dollars of movement in FX markets, oil futures, [and] the stock market," it said in a statement in July.
The same month, the White House Management Office had sent a letter to aides telling them not to place bets on prediction markets, administration officials told the BBC's US media partner CBS News.

items: Shanti Dope renews his contract with Universal Records Philippines, continuing a partnership that began when he was 16.

blocks.text: Filipino rapper Shanti Dope has renewed his contract with Universal Records Philippines, extending a partnership that began when he was 16.
Shanti said he decided to stay with the label because it was the first to believe in him when he was starting his career.
“Nag-decide ako to still renew sa UR [Universal Records] since sila naman ang unang naniwala sa akin mula noong 16 years old ako,” he said.
Shanti signed with Universal Records Philippines at 16 and released his breakthrough EP “Materyal,” which included “Nadarang.” The song later appeared on Spotify Philippines’ Top 50 Viral Chart.
He has since released other hits, including “Amatz,” and established himself as one of the notable voices in Filipino hip-hop.
Universal Records Philippines Managing Director Kathleen Dy-Go said the label has seen Shanti develop from a young artist into an established hip-hop act.
“We’ve seen Shanti grow from a young artist with a powerful voice into one of the most distinct voices in Filipino hip-hop,” Dy-Go said.
Shanti’s management, Asintada Management and Production Inc., said it supports his decision to renew with the label.
The renewed partnership comes as Shanti prepares to release new music under Universal Records Philippines, with other projects also in development.

articles.title: Norway’s King Harald V dies at 89 and his son becomes King Haakon VIII
articles.summary: STAVANGER, Norway (AP) — King Harald V of Norway, who went into exile in the United States as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland and refused a string of potential brides from the…

blocks.text: STAVANGER, Norway (AP) — King Harald V of Norway, who went into exile in the United States as a child during the Nazi occupation of his homeland and refused a string of potential brides from the European nobility so he could marry his longtime sweetheart, died Friday. He was 89.
The palace said he died at the National Hospital in Oslo at 6:35 a.m.

Harald was Europe’s oldest monarch. The popular king modernized the royal house but refused to follow in the footsteps of other aging monarchs who have abdicated in recent times. His son automatically became King Haakon VIII.

Like other royal houses in Europe, the Norwegian monarchs serve a largely symbolic role, enjoying celebrity status while real power in the democracy of 5.5 million rests with an elected parliament. Harald was crowned after his British-born father, King Olav V, died in January 1991, and reigned during an oil-and-gas-driven economic boom in his country.

“A whole nation is in mourning and the people of Norway are left with a deep sense of gratitude for a long life in the service of Norway,” Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said in a statement. “For more than three decades as monarch, Harald V demonstrated an unwavering faith in the Norwegian people. He helped us to see the best in ourselves — and in one another.”
Funeral arrangements were not immediately released.
Royal family fled Norway during World War II

Harald was born in 1937 in Asker, near Oslo, becoming the first Norwegian prince to be born in the country since King Olav IV in 1370. In the following centuries, Norway didn't have a king of its own until Harald's grandfather, Haakon VII, was elected king following the 1905 dissolution of the union between Sweden and Norway.

Harald was 3 years old when the Nazis occupied Norway at the start of World War II. To avoid capture, his mother fled with him and his sisters, Ragnhild and Astrid, first to Sweden and then by boat to the U.S., while Harald’s father and grandfather went into exile in Britain with Norway’s government.
Haakon’s refusal to go along with German demands garnered respect among his people.

During their time in the U.S., the Norwegian royals were often guests at the White House. Harald was 6 when he carried out his first official duty, christening new warplanes at a Norwegian air base in Canada.
The family was reunited in Norway in June 1945, shortly after the end of the war in Europe. Harald attended public schools, the Norwegian military college and Oxford University.

Like his father — an Olympic champion sailor in 1928 — Harald loved the sea and sailboats. He represented Norway at several Olympics, and in 1987 he skippered his yacht to gold in the World Championships.
Harald married his longtime sweetheart

As a young man, Harald was urged to find a bride among Europe's noblewomen and princesses. For nine years he shunned a series of prospects, holding out until he finally won his father’s permission to marry his longtime sweetheart, Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a successful businessman.

King Olav had feared the marriage would weaken Norway’s still-young monarchy. Instead, Norwegians greeted the Aug. 29, 1968, wedding with jubilation, and later embraced Sonja as their queen. The couple had two children, Haakon and his older sister, Märtha Louise.

The Norwegian Constitution was altered in 1990 to allow the first born, regardless of gender, to take precedence in the line of succession. However, it was not applied retroactively, meaning that Haakon continued to take precedence over his sister.
When Harald assumed the throne on Jan. 21, 1991, he adopted the same motto his father and grandfather had used: “All for Norway.” He spent the next years trying to modernize the monarchy.

“It has been my experience that the monarchy stands strong,” he once said. “This is not least because my father and grandfather did most things right. That puts me under pressure, but I take it as a challenge.”
Harald won the praise of the country with an emotional speech at a memorial service after a right-wing extremist, Anders Behring Breivik, killed 77 people in bomb and gun attacks in Norway in 2011.

“I remain convinced that the belief in freedom is stronger than fear. I remain convinced in the belief of an open Norwegian democracy and society. I remain convinced in the belief in our ability to live freely and safely in our own country," the king said.

In 2016, Harald gave an unexpected and impassioned speech in support of LGBTQ+ equality, refugees and religious tolerance, saying “Norwegians are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other.” He added that many Norwegians have emigrated from Afghanistan, Pakistan, Poland and other countries and that they “believe in God, Allah, the universe and nothing.”
The public speech extolled the diversity of the Scandinavian nation and was viewed on social media by millions.
Recent scandals have put royal family under scrutiny

Scandal and serious allegations have hung over the Norwegian royal family this year. Harald’s daughter-in-law, now-Queen Mette-Marit, faced renewed scrutiny over her connections with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. That raised questions over her judgment, though she is not accused of any wrongdoing. Mette-Marit apologized for the situation she put the royal family in, part of a broader apology for all those she had “disappointed.”

At around the same time, her eldest son, Marius Borg Høiby, was convicted of rape in a high-profile trial and sentenced to four years in prison. Høiby, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship before she met Haakon, has no royal titles or official duties.

In 2022, Harald’s daughter Princess Märtha Louise gave up royal duties after raising eyebrows by saying she could communicate with angels and becoming engaged to an American man who identifies as a shaman. They married two years later.
In January 2024, after the abdication of Denmark’s Queen Margrethe — his second cousin — Harald said that he stood by the oath he made when ascending the throne: “It lasts for life.”

However, he was hospitalized twice on foreign trips after that, including during a 2024 vacation in Malaysia when he was fitted with a pacemaker and during a February 2026 holiday on the Spanish island of Tenerife when he had a skin infection.

blocks.text: CAMP DANGWA, Benguet -- Police Brigadier General Noel Vallo officially assumed the position of Regional Director of the Police Regional Office Cordillera Administrative Region (PRO CAR) during a Turnover of Command Ceremony held at Camp BGen Rafael T Crame, Quezon City, on August 28.
The ceremony marked the formal transfer of command from PBGen.Ericson Dilag, the outgoing Regional Director of PRO CAR.
The ceremony was presided over Philippine National Police (PNP) Chief Gen Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr., and attended by members of the PNP Command Group and other distinguished guests.

A highlight of the ceremony was the reading and signing of the Assumption of Office, formally installing Vallo as the new Regional Director of PRO CAR. The ceremonial turnover of the Office Symbol and Property Equipment Inventory Book likewise signified the formal transfer of command, accountability, and responsibilities to the new leadership.
In his inaugural address, Vallo outlined his vision for PRO CAR and expressed his commitment to lead the regional police force with professionalism, integrity, and dedication to public service.

A native of Dagupan City, Pangasinan,Vallo is a graduate of the Philippine National Police Academy (PNPA), Class of 1995 “PATNUBAY.” His return to the Cordillera marks a homecoming, having previously served in PRO CAR as Chief of the Regional Logistics and Research Development Division (RLRDD) from 2016 to 2018.

Years after his previous assignment in the region, Vallo returns to PRO CAR in a higher capacity, this time as its Regional Director, bringing with him extensive experience and a renewed commitment to serving the people of the Cordillera.

articles.title: Trump says US has entered deal with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that his administration has entered a sweeping agreement with Venezuela that, if realized, could give the U.S. access to vast amounts of the South…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that his administration has entered a sweeping agreement with Venezuela that, if realized, could give the U.S. access to vast amounts of the South American country’s untapped oil reserves, at cost.
Trump in a social media post announcing the agreement said it was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez.
“The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Trump wrote.

Rodríguez’s government in a statement said the deal involves the development of 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels. It said the agreement could draw $100 billion in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and yield over $209 billion in taxes for Caracas.
Rodríguez in a posting on Telegram predicted the deal “will have a significant impact on our nation’s revival.”

The agreement allows for the United States to partner with an unnamed private operator in Venezuela to create a new private company to take hold of the reserves, according to a U.S. official familiar with the contours of the deal.
The official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, added that Rodríguez granted the company 100-year rights to develop the oil fields.

The deal gives the United States 55% effective output of the new private company -- including an ownership stake and rights to buy oil at cost. The company would be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, according to the official.
Trump is under pressure to show he’s lowering oil costs

The announcement comes nearly nine months after the U.S. military at Trump’s direction carried out an operation to capture Venezuela’s then-President Nicolás Maduro and spirit him to the United States to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.

Trump faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran on Friday reached a six-month milestone with no conclusion in sight. The U.S. has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.
The U.S.-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20% of the world petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.
The average price of gas in the U.S. stood at about $4.09 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. The average price was $3.21 at the same time last year.

A significant drop in U.S. gas prices tied to the agreement should not be expected immediately. Experts have repeatedly warned that a substantial boost in Venezuelan oil production will not happen quickly as repairing and expanding infrastructure takes years and requires billions of dollars.
Persuading big American oil companies to return the region could face headwinds given the political uncertainty and decades of badly damaged infrastructure.

Days after the ouster of Maduro, Trump gathered oil executives at the White House and called on them to rush back into Venezuela. Executives expressed interest in the opportunity but there was also a measure of caution given their past experience in the country.
Darren Woods, CEO of ExxonMobil, the largest U.S. oil company, said at that moment he saw the country as “un-investable.”
But Trump has insisted that his administration has brought a measure of stability to Venezuela.

He has argued that Venezuela stole U.S. oil when former Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez moved decades ago to nationalize hundreds of foreign-owned assets, including those owned by American oil companies.

Rodríguez, in one of her early moves after taking power, signed a law that opens the nation’s oil sector to privatization and reversed a bedrock tenet of the self-proclaimed socialist movement that has ruled the country for more than two decades.
Rubio said on X that the agreement would usher in billions in private investment into Venezuela and lead to lower gas prices in the United States.
“This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people,” Rubio posted.
The oil bought from the new company would go toward filling the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve and toward military use, according to the U.S. official.

Venezuela has one of the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground. That’s about 17% of the world’s supply, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela’s soil are largely mapped and known, experts say. But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1% of the world’s oil.
Maduro remains jailed in the U.S. He has pleaded not guilty.

articles.title: ‘In walked this big bundle of energy’: the day Dolly Parton came to Rotherham
articles.summary:
Country star came to South Yorkshire town in 2007 for UK launch of the Imagination Library, her book donation scheme

Shane Jarman was up a ladder decorating a Christmas tree at the school…

blocks.text: Shane Jarman was up a ladder decorating a Christmas tree at the school where he was deputy headteacher when he got a call asking him to come to Rotherham hospital ASAP. It was December 2007 and Jarman’s wife, Claire, had given birth the previous day to their first child, a girl called Emma, so of course he rushed to the phone. All was well, he was told, but that “everything would become clear” when he got to the hospital.

Once there, his wife told him – somewhat unexpectedly – that they were going to meet Dolly Parton. “And literally within what felt like five minutes,” he recalled, “there were great camera flashes, lots of noise, lots of clicking and in walked this real big bundle of energy.”

blocks.caption: Shane Jarman and his wife, Claire, watch as Dolly Parton holds newborn Emma. Photograph: The Rotherham NHS Foundation Trust

blocks.text: Jarman said that as his wife handed over their tiny 4lb 6oz baby to the country star, “all I remember is seeing Dolly Parton with my little girl’s head in her hand and these great big red nails”.
Was he a little nervous about the nails? “I was very nervous about the nails to be quite honest.”

Parton was in the South Yorkshire former mining and steelworking town – not principally known for its razzle-dazzle – for the British launch of the Imagination Library, the book donation programme the musician had started in her Tennessee home of Sevier County a little over a decade earlier, and which she had been invited to extend to children in Yorkshire.

blocks.caption: Dolly Parton performs at the launch of her children’s literacy scheme in Rotherham. Photograph: Rui Vieira/PA

blocks.text: If Rotherham – or at least a gathering of local dignitaries that assembled later in a disused steelworks – was a little bemused by the singer, Parton knew places like this, and of course knew how to charm.

“I gotta make sure I say your town name right – it’s Rother’m?” she said, flattening the famous southern twang to something approximating flat Yorkshire vowels. “Did I get it right? I’ve been practising because it don’t look like that on paper. In the States, anything that’s h-a-m we have to say Rother-ham.”

Among the torrent of tributes to the entertainer, businesswoman and philanthropist since her death on Monday, Rotherham too has been remembering the impact of a woman who, for all her own glamour, cared deeply about places that had a little less of it.

Parton may have jested when she said she had considered buying a South Yorkshire pied-à-terre (“so you may be walking down the streets of Rotherham and see me coming out of a little cubbyhole somewhere”), but her description of the post-industrialist town as “a heart spot for me” was sincere, thanks to the similarities she saw to her own outsider upbringing.

“I totally related to Rotherham,” she said some years later. “I know that it’s out in an industrial area … When they were making fun of me for going out there, I thought, you know what? Don’t make fun of me.”

The scheme ensured that every child in Rotherham was posted a free book, in their own name, for each month of their life until they were five, funded partly by Parton’s foundation and partly by the local authority and other local funders. Deborah Bullivant, who took over leading the Rotherham Imagination Library shortly after Parton’s visit as part of a wider literacy drive, said that despite some initial scepticism from locals, it “changed the culture” for many.

blocks.caption: Dolly Parton meets young children at the Magna Science Adventure Centre in Rotherham in 2007. Photograph: Getty

blocks.text: “Some people were very suspicious: Why Dolly Parton? What is this thing?” she said. “[But] can you imagine receiving a book, from registering your child’s birth, your baby in their own name receives the book every month through the letterbox? For many families who didn’t really have a background in reading, it changed the culture within their homes to being more of a reading culture and embracing books and using books and sharing books.”

The fact that the literacy drive was so personal to the singer was “the best way to counter any of the suspicion or worries that people had about it”, Bullivant said. “Why is Dolly Parton doing this? Who is she? She doesn’t know about this? Well, she does. She understood she needed to drive her own work herself from scratch. She got the importance of the imagination, of reading, of telling stories.”

Though the Rotherham scheme was wound up in 2015 after the council withdrew support, it would be rolled out to other places in Britain, including Doncaster, North Lincolnshire, the London borough of Southwork (“Hello Suth’rk! This is Dolly!”) and Nottingham (which even coaxed an “Ay up me duck!” from the singer).

blocks.caption: Shane Jarman and his daughter, Emma, now 18, today. Photograph: Family Handout

blocks.text: In total, 6.3m books have been given to children across the four UK nations since one-day-old Emma Jarman received the first one in 2007, a copy of The Tale of Peter Rabbit, which Parton autographed for her. (Globally, the figure is 300m).

Emma, now 18, will shortly be going to university to study biomedical science, “and, if I know Emma, [the book] will go to university with her so that she can show her friends there,” said her father.

articles.title: Parañaque distributes doxycycline to flood-affected residents

The Parañaque City government intensified its health response on Saturday, Aug. 29, as it continued distributing doxycycline to residents in flood-affected areas and evacuation centers.
Mayor Edwin Olivarez ordered the continued deployment of Barangay Health Workers (BHWs) to various communities and evacuation sites to assist residents and facilitate the distribution of doxycycline.
The city government said its health centers in all 16 barangays also remained open to accommodate residents who need the medication.
The continued distribution is part of the city’s efforts to protect residents who may have been exposed to contaminated floodwaters, particularly those in areas affected by flooding.
Residents were reminded to avoid wading through floodwaters whenever possible, as exposure may increase the risk of contracting illnesses.
Olivarez urged residents to prioritize their safety, observe health precautions, and follow advisories issued by city authorities as rains and flooding continue.
The city government also encouraged residents who have concerns about their health after exposure to floodwaters to seek assistance from the nearest barangay health center.

articles.title: Alcaraz returns from four-month injury layoff, ready to be himself at US Open
articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — After sitting out more than four months nursing an injured right wrist that caused him to miss the French Open and Wimbledon, Carlos Alcaraz didn't decide to return for the U.S. Open…

blocks.text: NEW YORK (AP) — After sitting out more than four months nursing an injured right wrist that caused him to miss the French Open and Wimbledon, Carlos Alcaraz didn't decide to return for the U.S. Open to be anything less than his Grand Slam-winning self.
“You’re going to see Carlitos playing the way he always has,” Alcaraz said.

The 23-year-old from Spain is set to play his first competitive singles match Monday, Aug. 31, since getting sidelined by the wrist injury in mid-April. He insists he has not changed anything about his mechanics and expressed confidence about physically feeling great.
"I need competition," Alcaraz said Friday. “We, my team and me, believe that I’m ready. It wasn’t an easy decision. I just did whatever it took to be ready."

Alcaraz is the defending champion and favored to go back-to-back, a year after beating Jannik Sinner and overtaking him for the No. 1 ranking. The field this time does not include Sinner, who withdrew because of a right knee injury.
“We are not going see each other for, like, six months now, seven months,” Alcaraz said. “It’s kind of a weird situation, to be honest.”
Alexander Zverev is the top seed in Sinner's absence. But all eyes are on Alcaraz, who earlier this year won his seventh Grand Slam title by defeating Novak Djokovic in the Australian Open final.

“Everyone is going to be pretty tapped in to see his first match,” 11th-seeded American Frances Tiafoe said. “If he comes back anywhere near his level, it’s tough. Regardless, even if he’s not at his tip-top (shape), you’ve still got to beat him in five (sets).”

Alcaraz opens against Roman Safiullin as he dives right back into best-of-five-set tennis in his return. He did get a chance to shake some rust off by playing a couple of mixed doubles matches with Serena Williams this week, but he knows not getting a full ramp up to the U.S. Open adds another layer of difficulty.
“It’s really challenging,” Alcaraz said. “Probably in terms of preparation and everything, (it) is not the best time.”
But the energy of playing in New York was enough of a draw that he said, “There is no better tournament than the U.S. Open to be back.”
Can he win it off such a long layoff? He knows Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal have done it but does not want to set any expectations.

“I’m not going to set a limit for myself,” Alcaraz said in Spanish. “I don’t want to focus on a specific result. I want to focus on the process we’ve gone through. Just go out there, enjoy it and feel good.”

Zverev, who's now four years removed from tearing ligaments in his right ankle, was reluctant to compare two very different injuries. But he expects Alcaraz to be formidable as the tournament goes on.
“Wrist is never easy,” Zverev said. “I expect him to be maybe a bit rusty the first or second match, but once he gets through that, I think he’s going to be a contender, for sure, here.”

After dealing with intrusive thoughts during his time away from the sport, Alcaraz is still playing a mental game to not worry too much about the injury. His goals are to get through the U.S. Open healthy and stay away from the fear that creeps into his head.
“I just have to go 100%,” Alcaraz said. “I've got to trust my team. I've got to trust my people that tell me that it’s going to be fine.”

articles.title: 8 dead, 123 hit by leptospirosis in Cordillera in first 7 months of 2026
articles.summary: TABUK CITY, Kalinga — Eight people have died while 123 others were stricken by leptospirosis in the Cordillera Administrative Region from January 4 to August 1, 2026, the Department of…

blocks.text: TABUK CITY, Kalinga — Eight people have died while 123 others were stricken by leptospirosis in the Cordillera Administrative Region from January 4 to August 1, 2026, the Department of Health–Cordillera Administrative Region (DOH-CAR) said.
The cases were recorded amid persistent rains and flooding across the region, which increase people’s exposure to water, mud and soil contaminated with the urine of infected animals.
Despite the deaths, the DOH-CAR said the number of cases was 13 percent lower than those recorded during the same period last year.
Farmers were among the most affected, accounting for 39 percent of all recorded cases, according to DOH-CAR Regional Epidemiology and Surveillance Unit Officer IV Dr. Mae Kemeny Manogan.
The median age of patients was 30, indicating that many victims were of working age.
Manogan warned that farmers face increased risks because of their frequent exposure to wet soil, mud and water, particularly during the rainy season.

Leptospirosis is commonly acquired through contact with floodwater, puddles, mud or soil contaminated by the urine of infected animals, particularly rats and other rodents. Farm animals, including cows, carabaos and goats, can also carry the bacteria.
The risk is higher among people with open wounds who come into contact with contaminated water.

Meanwhile, the DOH recorded 3,440 leptospirosis cases and 220 deaths nationwide from January 4 to August 8. While this was 35 percent lower than the 5,318 cases recorded during the same period in 2025, health authorities noted an increase in cases from July 12 to 25.

The DOH-CAR urged residents to avoid unnecessary contact with floodwater and muddy areas and advised those working outdoors to wear boots and protective gear, cover open wounds, and thoroughly wash exposed skin with soap and clean water.
Residents who develop fever and other symptoms after exposure to floodwater or contaminated soil were urged to seek immediate medical attention.
Health authorities said monitoring remains in place as continuing rains could further increase the risk of infection across the Cordillera.

articles.title: EST Cola, Ho Chi Minh ready to shake up PVL Invitational
articles.summary: EST Cola of Thailand and Ho Chi Minh City Volleyball Club of Vietnam may not carry the same household names as the Premier Volleyball League’s top local clubs, but they are coming to the PVL…

blocks.text: EST Cola of Thailand and Ho Chi Minh City Volleyball Club of Vietnam may not carry the same household names as the Premier Volleyball League’s top local clubs, but they are coming to the PVL Invitational with something more important than star billing: the talent, experience and ambition to challenge for the title.

Far from being mere visitors, the two Southeast Asian sides are expected to bring contrasting styles and international experience that could disrupt the established order when the Invitational blasts off Monday, Aug. 31, at the Araneta Coliseum.

Creamline may have the deepest collection of proven stars. PLDT enters with the confidence of a defending champion. Nxled has assembled a star-studded roster capable of making a deep run, while Farm Fresh has the veteran presence and young firepower to cause problems.

But EST Cola and Ho Chi Minh City offer something the local teams cannot easily replicate – a different brand of volleyball forged by competition outside the Philippines, along with players accustomed to the demands of the regional game.

EST Cola, formerly composed of Thailand’s Under-20 national squad, already knows what it takes to compete in the Invitational. It finished fourth in its first appearance in 2024, losing to eventual third-place finisher and 2023 champion Kurashiki Ablaze of Japan in straight sets.
Leading its title charge are hitters Papatchaya Phontham and Nannaphat Moonjakham, middle blocker Waruni Kanram, and liberos Jiratcha Naoprachum and Nichakorn Wansuk.
Ho Chi Minh City, meanwhile, arrives with something to prove.
Vietnam’s new representative will be eager to erase the memory of the country’s sixth-place finish in the 2023 Invitational, when Kinh Bac Bac Ninh failed to win a single match.
The Vietnamese side will bank on the firepower of hitters Thi Kim Thanh Dang, Thi Bich Diep and Thi Nha Phuong Nguyen, backed by middle blockers Thi My Xuyen Le, Thi Nhung Dao and Thi My Duyen Dang.

articles.title: Iceland holds knife-edge referendum on EU membership talks
articles.summary: The Nordic nation shelved earlier plans to join the EU over fishing rights, but geopolitics, including Trump's threat to seize Greenland, has prompted a rethink.

image.caption: Icelanders are voting on whether to restart EU accession talksImage: Leonhard Foeger/REUTERS

blocks.text: Iceland holds a national referendum on Saturday on whether to restart negotiations to join the European Union.
The Nordic nation has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc’s 28th member.
Iceland's left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.
Iceland debates joining EU amid Trump's Greenland interest
What do we know about Iceland's referendum?
As they head to one of hundreds of polling stations, voters will be asked a simple yes/no question:
Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?

The question relates to a previous attempt by the Icelandic government to join the EU in 2009, at the height of the global financial crisis that devastated the local economy. The accession plan was later shelved.

Saturday's vote is described as too close to call, with a Gallup poll on Friday suggesting a narrow majority of Icelanders oppose reopening talks. Other recent polls suggest a narrow lead for the yes vote.
Although Iceland has never been an EU member, it is already closely integrated with the bloc.
It is a member of both the European Economic Area (EEA) — which gives access to the EU's frictionless single market — and the Schengen Area free-travel zone.
Of Iceland's roughly 400,000 population, around 265,000 are eligible to vote.

blocks.caption: Saturday’s referendum is too close to callImage: B. Niehaus/snapshot/IMAGO

blocks.text: What are the deciding factors among voters?
Voters have grown increasingly concerned about geopolitics, including the threat from Russia and US President Donald Trump's threats to seize nearby Greenland from Denmark.
Icelanders, who gained independence from Denmark in 1944, have been asking whether they could be next.
"We can't really trust the US anymore," said Hildur Knutsdottir, a horror fiction writer who plans to vote in favor of EU membership.
Arctic nations sit at the center of a growing contest for the polar north, as the United States, Russia and China jostle for influence over sea routes, natural resources and security.
The left-leaning Icelandic coalition believes EU membership could help counter Trump's ambitions in the North Atlantic.
"The international order that underpinned our security and prosperity for decades is under serious pressure," Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Gunnarsdottir told Reuters last week.
"In times like these, small nations need to ​think carefully about where they stand and who stands with them," she added.
Is the US driving Iceland to join the European Union?
Fishing, interest rates and national identity
The last attempt to join the EU was shelved in 2015 largely over concerns about joining the bloc's common fisheries policy.

Icelanders have been living off hefty cod and haddock catches for centuries and are loath to open the chilled Arctic waters to Spanish, Dutch and other EU trawlers, which is a requirement from Brussels.
The government has said it could try to negotiate a full opt-out from the policy.
Some economists think Icelanders, who have struggled under high inflation and interest rates, could benefit financially from EU membership and possibly the adoption of the euro.
National identity is another driver of voting, with opponents of EU membership noting how Iceland enjoys all the benefits of European integration without being a full member.

"For a country like ours with our small economy, it's very important to maintain our sovereignty and not to transfer more power than we would have to do to the EU," former Prime Minister Katrin Jakobsdottir said at an ​event in Reykjavik ‌on Thursday.
What happens if Iceland votes to restart EU talks?
A yes vote would trigger a negotiating process with the EU's executive branch, the European Commission.
This would involve discussions on 35 areas, from the economy to human rights.
A foreign ministry memo estimates accession talks could start by the end of the year and take 18 to 24 months.

India monitors glaciers after Nepal disaster
Days after deadly flash floods triggered by a glacial collapse swept through the Tibet-Nepal border, India stepped up monitoring of the glaciers in its Himalayan region bordering Nepal and China.
Although the exact cause of the collapse remains unclear, global warming has increased the likelihood of such disasters.

"Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbor, and also have a similar geographic situation... we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region," said Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India's Himalayan state of Uttarakhand.
"We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state," he added.
Kaushik's state is one of India's most ecologically sensitive regions with over 1,266 glacial lakes.

articles.title: Kai Sotto overcomes comeback jitters in Gilas Pilipinas win
articles.summary: Kai Sotto embraces the pressure and steps up when needed the most as he steers Gilas Pilipinas back on track in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers

blocks.text: TOWERING. Kai Sotto in action for Gilas Pilipinas in the FIBA World Cup 2027 Asian Qualifiers.
FIBA
Kai Sotto embraces the pressure and steps up when needed the most as he steers Gilas Pilipinas back on track in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers
MANILA, Philippines – Kai Sotto erupted in a thunderous roar after his block sealed Gilas Pilipinas’ win over Jordan in the FIBA World Cup Asian Qualifiers.
It was the culmination of two years of waiting and pent-up emotions, all released in one defining moment as the 7-foot-3 big man proved to be just what the doctor ordered in his national team return.

“Before the game, I had a lot on my mind. There was a mix of excitement and the realization that it had been such a long time since I last played for the national team,” said Sotto in a mix of Filipino and English.

“I knew I was carrying a lot of pressure, and I’m just really happy that was able to translate into my performance on the court what I had been waiting so long to do — play for the national team again.”

blocks.caption: Kai Sotto overcomes comeback jitters in Gilas Pilipinas win

blocks.text: Sotto finished with team highs of 18 points, 14 rebounds, and 2 blocks as the Philippines escaped with an 82-81 overtime win on Friday, August 28, to get its World Cup bid back on track after losing its last four games in the Asian Qualifiers.

Jordan stayed on the Philippines’ heels until the final second before Sotto swatted away a point-blank layup by Abdullah Olajuwon to secure the victory, much to the delight of a packed crowd at the Mall of Asia Arena.

The block completed the Filipinos’ comeback from 18 points down as they defended their turf even without injured naturalized player Justin Brownlee, with the likes of CJ Perez (16 points), Kevin Quiambao (14 points), and Dwight Ramos (14 points) rising to the occasion.
“I’m really happy that everyone contributed. We had a slow start, but as you saw, we fought our way back. I’m extremely proud of the team,” said Sotto.
Sotto last saw action for the national team in 2024 before an injury in early 2025 sidelined him, but there was little sign of rust as he seamlessly fit back into the squad.
For head coach Tim Cone, that adaptability makes Sotto special.
“He’s really that smart and intelligent. And that makes the people around him better. Everybody’s better when he’s on the floor,” Cone said of Sotto.
“Whether it be passing or screening or rolling, the attention he grabs, he just makes everybody around him better.” – Rappler.com
