articles.title: Venezuelan opposition up in arms over reports US wants big stake in oil and gas
articles.summary:
Critics call move to gain long-term access to country’s massive energy reserves ‘predatory’ and ‘unconstitutional’

Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s…

blocks.text: Reports that the US is preparing to claim a big stake in Venezuela’s massive energy reserves have sparked an outcry, with critics describing the move as “predatory” and a “rapacious” land grab.

Several media outlets this week reported that the Trump administration – which abducted Venezuela’s authoritarian president, Nicolás Maduro, in January and has steered the South American country ever since – hopes to secure long-term access to its oil and gasfields.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn.

On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal said Trump officials were in “advanced talks” with Venezuelan officials to take “a direct stake in more than a dozen oilfields” containing 90bn barrels, nearly a third of Venezuela’s energy reserves.

“This is real and being discussed at the highest levels of the US and Venezuelan governments,” a source told Reuters, which said the fields being negotiated were in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo regions.
Axios claimed the deal would be “a legacy-defining moment for President Trump”, with one unnamed official telling the US outlet: “Calling this deal huge would be an understatement … It is massive.”
Bloomberg, citing sources familiar with the negotiations, said one deal under discussion was a 100-year lease on several oilfields.
The reports caused unease and anger among members of Venezuela’s opposition, who are already up in arms about Trump’s failure to bring about genuine political change after capturing Maduro.

“It’s a land grab – a massive land grab,” said one well-known opposition figure who asked not to be named because of the sensitivities of criticising the US. “It’s revolting because this is not the United States one would have [expected]. This is not the United States of the Marshall plan. This is a rapacious, mafioso United States,” they added.

Since January’s special forces raid on Caracas, Venezuela has been led by an interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president and minister of petroleum. Other key members of Maduro’s regime have also retained positions of power, including the interior minister, Diosdado Cabello, who has been collaborating with Trump officials – despite having a $25m (£18m) US bounty on his head for alleged drug trafficking. Meanwhile, the exiled opposition leader, María Corina Machado, whose movement is believed to have won the 2024 presidential elections, has been sidelined.

Ricardo Hausmann, an exiled former minister and opposition supporter, wrote on X: “An illegitimate interim government with an illegitimate hydrocarbons law has no legitimacy to strike this unconstitutional deal. It will be a fiasco for all involved.”

The economist Francisco Rodríguez urged Venezuela’s national assembly to reject what he called a “predatory deal”. “Handing over Venezuela’s oil wealth to the US contravenes the constitution and is not in the interest of the Venezuelan people – much more when it is done at gunpoint,” Rodríguez said.
Luz Mely Reyes, a prominent journalist and government critic, sarcastically called the “surrender” of Venezuela’s natural riches “the deal of the century”.

Gregory Brew, an energy historian and Eurasia Group analyst, anticipated “quite a lot of suspicion and rejection of any deal that would hand the United States government effective control over Venezuelan resources”.
after newsletter promotion
Brew said the reported deal reminded him of how BP, then the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, controlled the oil resources of Iraq and Iran at the start of the last century.

“Anglo-Persian was given a concession by the shah of Iran in 1901 … in exchange for what was essentially a bribe to the Persian government, and it gave the company sweeping rights. The company was essentially in total control of any oil it found and would be able to retain virtually all the profits of any other oil it found and exploited and exported,” Brew said.

“From Trump’s point of view, the control over oil is something of an end in and of itself,. But if you do try to rationalise it, I think US dominance over Venezuelan oil reserves allows the US to regard Venezuelan reserves as its own reserves: a source of oil from which the United States can draw and that nobody else has access to. I think that’s how the administration is conceiving of this – excluding China, excluding Russia, but I think also excluding other potential customers for Venezuelan oil,” he said. “It sounds colonial, because it is.”

Venezuela’s post-Maduro conversion into what many call a US protectorate is the most dramatic play in Trump’s push to reassert Washington’s influence over Latin America as part of the so-called “Donroe Doctrine”.

That policy is a 21st-century adaptation of the 19th-century Monroe doctrine by which President James Monroe sought to keep European powers out of the Americas. Trump’s version is about countering China’s growing footprint in the region and imposing US will through economic and military pressure.
Maduro’s downfall has brought some change to Venezuela, with hundreds of political prisoners freed under Rodríguez and talks about reforming the regime-controlled supreme court taking place.

But no date has been set for a fresh presidential election and Machado has been unable to return from exile. “Delcy’s been doing a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters last month, claiming Venezuela was “not really ready” for a vote.

articles.title: DFA awaiting confirmation on missing Filipino in Nepal flash floods
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Friday said it is awaiting confirmation from Nepali authorities on a Filipino national reported missing after a glacial collapse…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Friday said it is awaiting confirmation from Nepali authorities on a Filipino national reported missing after a glacial collapse triggered a massive debris flow, sending water, mud, rock and ice surging through communities along the Nepal-Tibet border. on Wednesday.

DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel said the Philippine Embassy in New Delhi and the Philippine Honorary Consulate General in Kathmandu are coordinating with local authorities and are ready to assist Filipinos affected by the disaster.
“They are awaiting confirmation from Nepali authorities on a Filipino national who is reported missing,” Ratonel said in a message to reporters.
The reported missing Filipino appeared in a preliminary record released by the Nepal Tourism Board, which listed one Filipino among travelers unaccounted for in the affected areas.
The Philippine government has yet to independently confirm the report.
Ratonel also said the DFA had forwarded to the concerned office information provided by Chiara Manalo about her brother, Filipino doctor Juan Carlos Manalo.
The DFA has not confirmed that Manalo is the missing Filipino listed in the preliminary record.
Chiara Manalo appealed for help locating her brother, saying he had been out of contact since the disaster struck.
In a Facebook post Friday, she said the family last heard from Manalo at 1:21 p.m. Philippine time on Tuesday.
She said Manalo was traveling with the Isha Sadghuru group on a Kailashyatra tour. The group’s last known location, according to the family, was at the Immigration Office in Gyirong.
“Please help us look for my brother,” Chiara Manalo said.

The family asked anyone with information about Manalo or members of the group to contact them. It also appealed for help in connecting them with agencies that could coordinate with Nepali authorities and ongoing search operations.
The Philippine Embassy in New Delhi and the honorary consulate in Kathmandu remain in coordination with local authorities, according to the DFA. /gsg

articles.title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
articles.summary: Before-and-after images show villages, bridges and a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing washed away by devastating floodwaters.

blocks.text: This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.

Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.

Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.
But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.

Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.

The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.
Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mesut Ersoz and Mike Hill.

articles.title: Thieves steal 600-diamond necklace from Vienna museum in broad daylight
articles.summary: Police are hunting two suspects they believe bought a ticket for the exhibition to get at the jewellery.

blocks.text: Image source, LPD Wien
Vienna police released CCTV images of the suspects
ByBethany Bell
Vienna correspondent

An international manhunt is under way for two men who stole a necklace decorated with more than 600 diamonds from a museum in Vienna after buying a ticket for the exhibition in which it was being displayed.

Police said the two suspects smashed a glass display case at the Vienna Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) on Thursday afternoon and grabbed the platinum and diamond necklace, which is believed to be worth more than $4m (£3m; €3.5m).
The necklace, which was designed for the former Egyptian royal family, was part of an exhibition on the jewellers Van Cleef & Arpels, due to run at MAK until September.
The theft is the latest in a series of spectacular heists of artefacts at European museums.
Vienna police released photos of the two suspects, who were unmasked, captured on security cameras. They are appealing for the public to come forward with information.
The police said in a statement that one of the perpetrators was also believed to have been carrying what was thought to be a real firearm.
After seizing the necklace, they fled "towards the Vienna Stadtpark" just south of the museum, they said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The more than 200-carat necklace was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter to the future Shah of Iran

blocks.text: Image source, Austrian Interior Ministry
The more than 200-carat necklace was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter to the future Shah of Iran
Lilli Hollein, MAK general director, said "the theft of a highly valuable piece of jewellery... has hit us hard".

She said in a statement that MAK had developed a security plan with Van Cleef & Arpels specifically for the exhibition, adding: "Security issues were taken very seriously and all security measures were carefully prepared."
Hollein said staff had reacted calmly and followed the established procedures when the "armed incident" occurred, and that no one had been injured.
She added that MAK had thoroughly reviewed its security measures ahead of the exhibition, "particularly in light of the incidents at major museums in recent years".
Also on Thursday was one of the most important troves of prehistoric jewellery and artefacts was stolen from a Spanish museum.

Four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily earlier this month, while three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth millions of euros were taken from a museum in Parma earlier in the year.
These heists came after the brazen daylight raid on the Louvre in Paris, in which a masked gang stole priceless jewels last October.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The exhibition, minus the stolen necklace, reopened later on Friday

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
The exhibition, minus the stolen necklace, reopened later on Friday
The string of thefts have raised questions about the security of European cultural institutions.
Europol said museum thefts were "becoming increasingly aggressive, with a shift towards violent and forceful methods", adding this "may indicate the involvement of new criminal networks".

The necklace stolen in Vienna on Friday was designed for the former Egyptian royal family and was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter Fawzia to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.
Van Cleef & Arpels describes it as a "triumph of white jewellery". The diamonds on the necklace weigh in excess of 200 carats.
When it was auctioned a decade ago, it had an estimated worth of $3.6m-$4.6m.
Police dog units have been deployed in Vienna and the province of Lower Austria, while forensic experts are analysing evidence and CCTV footage.
The exhibition has now been reopened.

articles.title: Dolly Parton's sister says singer was still thinking of others while battling cancer
articles.summary: Dolly Parton's long history of philanthropy is well-documented, but a touching tribute from her sister reveals how deeply the spirit of giving was entrenched in her.

image.caption: Dolly Parton, seen here at the Grammy Awards in 2019, donated $1 million US toward researching the coronavirus at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. (Jordan Strauss/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Dolly Parton's long history of philanthropy is well-documented, but a touching tribute from her sister reveals how deeply the spirit of giving was entrenched in her.
Stella Parton's emotional post shares Dolly's thoughts near end of life
On Thursday, Stella Parton posted a statement to Instagram describing how she and Dolly used to wake up early and drink coffee together over the phone each Tuesday.

The statement says in one of their final conversations, Dolly told Stella "if there was no hope for her, she would still allow her medical team to try experimental drugs in the hope of helping others in the future."
CBC News asked Dolly Parton's publicist to confirm whether the star was receiving experimental treatment toward the end of her life, but has received no response.
However, Parton's contribution to another recent medical advancement is widely known.

In November 2020, it was revealed she made a $1-million US donation to Nashville's Vanderbilt University Medical Center for COVID-19 research — and part of it went toward the development of the Moderna mRNA coronavirus vaccine.

When it came time for Parton to receive her first dose, she did it on camera while singing alternative lyrics to her song Jolene. "Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging you please don't hesitate."
The doctor seen administering her dose in that video is Dr. Naji Abumrad, who she first met at Vanderbilt University Medical Center in October 2013, after Parton was in a minor car accident.

The pair struck up a long and enduring friendship. According to an opinion piece this week in the New York Times by his son, Jad Abumrad, creator of the podcast Dolly Parton's America, his father was with Parton in her last moments.
Stella Parton said she believes the world saw the famous singer for who she really was.
"My sister was one of the most generous, thoughtful and kind people I've ever known," wrote Stella in her tribute. "She left the world a better place by being in it, so let's follow her example."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Iran war hits 6-month milestone with Trump's attention largely elsewhere
articles.summary: A number of U.S. lawmakers called on Donald Trump to end the war with Iran as it reached its six-month mark on Friday, while the U.S. president has given mixed signals regarding the state of the…

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump is shown Thursday at Ellington Airport in Houston, Texas. Trump expressed ambivalence this week over talks with Iran, after insisting it was imperative to get the country to the negotiating table to prevent them from producing a nuclear weapon. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Asso

blocks.text: World

A number of U.S. lawmakers called on Donald Trump to end the war with Iran as it reached its six-month mark on Friday, while the U.S. president has given mixed signals regarding the state of the conflict.
Trump posts 'mission accomplished,' administration focuses on Iran's economic troubles

Trump has said that the combined effects of the military's offensive strikes and blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have helped the U.S. achieve its objectives. On social media Wednesday, he shared a post declaring "MISSION ACCOMPLISHED 2026," alongside AI-generated images that included the face of Iranian supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed on Feb. 28 as the U.S. and Israel launched airstrikes to begin the war.

Tehran and Washington have exchanged little more than bellicose statements in recent weeks, leaving the diplomacy to third parties, and Trump has been more preoccupied this week, at least publicly, with his anger over Canada calling off trade talks.

It is expected that the U.S. president will increasingly turn his attention to the Nov. 3 midterms, where he has been engaged in efforts to influence how votes are cast, while preparing for a unique, midterm Republican mini-convention in two weeks' time.

Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives' armed service committees, released a statement Friday raising a number of outstanding issues the war has caused, but leading with the toll to those serving in the military.

"Losses continue to accumulate, including 19 American service members killed and over 750 wounded, while thousands of innocent civilians have been killed across the region," said Smith. "Tens of billions of dollars of taxpayers' money is being wasted while driving up the cost of gas, utilities, and groceries at home and throttling economies around the world."
'More costly and more unstable'

The U.S. and Israel have killed a number of Iran's top religious, military and political officials and Khamenei's successor, his son Mojtaba, hasn't been seen in public amid reports he was seriously injured early in the war.

As well, it has been estimated that the price of rice is up some 60 per cent since the war began and beef 150 per cent higher for Iranians, who have also dealt with long lines to fill up vehicles. The International Monetary Fund forecasts that Iran's gross domestic product will contract more than 5 per cent this year.

But costs have also been incurred on the U.S. side beyond the literal price tag for Operation Epic Fury, from the approval rating for Trump in multiple polls to higher prices at gas pumps for many Americans due to the disruption in oil markets. The war has also strained relations between the White House and allies in Europe, the Middle East and Asia, as Trump has expressed anger that they haven't supported the U.S. in the war.

items: Trump orders joint military exercises with South Korea to be scaled back
Trump threatens to bomb Oman if it 'gets in the way' with Iran

blocks.text: Trump "has made the world more costly and more unstable," Brett Bruen, a former U.S. diplomat now at the D.C.-area public affairs agency Global Situation Room, told CBC News on Friday.

Iran found leverage after the initial shock and awe of the U.S. strikes through its own drone attacks and mining in the critical Strait of Hormuz. That dissuaded commercial vessels from countries not friendly to the regime from transiting the passage where substantial amounts of oil and liquefied natural gas typically were moved.

The U.S. eventually responded with its own naval blockade to prevent the movement of ships to Iranian ports. Trump has repeatedly said the strait is open, including this week, but ship-tracking services have estimated activity at roughly 5 per cent to 15 per cent of pre-war volumes.

Democrats earlier this week called for more transparency on the cost of the war. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth told a congressional committee in July that the war had cost the military $37.5 billion US, but the opposition and some think-tanks believe that total underestimates the cost, given the missile systems and munitions the U.S. has expended this year, diminishing stockpiles.
"Pete Hegseth should be fired, the war must end and taxpayer dollars should be spent to make life more affordable," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York posted on social media on Friday.

Few Republicans have expressed opposition to the war itself, though some have criticized military tactics. Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who generally opposes U.S. military interventions abroad, is an exception.

"The 1973 War Powers Act required Trump to withdraw forces within 90 days absent authorization from Congress," he posted on Friday. "[The administration] ridiculously claimed to stop the war & restart new hostilities @ 91 days. We are past 180 days. End the War."
LISTEN | Author, Iran-U.S. historian Trita Parsi (July 23):
Front Burner27:28Is Iran becoming a 'forever war'?
Some embassy staff in region reportedly set to return

Trump said this week he's "not in a hurry" to get Iran back to the negotiating table. It was a striking contrast to his messaging for much of the summer, where he said it was imperative to reach a deal with Iran to prevent it from obtaining a nuclear weapon.
There are no talks, but also no sense that a renewed military offensive is on the horizon.

The administration said it is focused on choking Iran economically, even as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's "Operation Economic Outcast," announced on Monday, was heavy on warnings and lighter on details.
The U.S. threatens Iran with ‘economic D-Day’ | About That

As well, Reuters reported this week that the Trump administration will soon start sending diplomatic personnel back to some missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized due to the fighting. Posts in Lebanon, Israel, Saudi Arabia and Iraq are among those where staff will return, albeit at less than full capacity, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.

Bruen told CBC News that the administration squandered an opportunity to affect change in Iran that would have been less costly, given the unusual level of domestic strife and protest seen there in January as demonstrators railed against perceived corruption of the regime and economic conditions.
Trump at the time promised Iranian protesters that "help is on the way," but by the next month the U.S. launched its military campaign with Israel.
Bruen, a former member of Barack Obama's administration, was pessimistic about what comes next after the six-month mark.
"It drags on indefinitely. I don't see an easy ending to this around the corner," he said. "I don't think the dynamic in the region changes very much."
With files from Reuters and the Associated Press

articles.title: Russia ‘losing 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit’
articles.summary:
Moscow recruits an estimated 1,000 people a day but western officials say it cannot keep up with casualty level

Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can…

blocks.text: Russia is losing about 6,000 more troops in Ukraine each month than it can recruit, western officials have said.
While Russia is still acquiring new battlefield recruits at speed, with an estimated rate of 1,000 a day, in the last two months even this has not been sufficient to replace those killed or injured.
“We estimate that the gap between the number of people Russia is losing to casualties and the number they’re being able to recruit is around 6,000 a month at the moment,” one western official said.

“Putin’s response to this has been to escalate himself and to target civilian infrastructure and civilians in Ukraine, firing over 360 missiles since early July and exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of defence against ballistic missiles. It’s clear that Moscow intends to try and break Ukrainian morale by destroying its energy infrastructure this winter.”
Such tactics are in part because Putin has limited options for overcoming the huge losses on the battlefield with more recruitment.

Western officials believe further mobilisation would be a big risk both politically and economically, saying the last such event, in autumn 2022, saw about a million – often highly skilled – Russians leave the country, with less than half returning.
It is also unclear whether the Russian military could absorb the several hundred thousand new recruits which would result, given a lack of equipment and officers.
Ukraine has repeatedly attacked Russian targets connected to oil, creating fuel shortages, but has appealed repeatedly for more help from allies, both with offensive missiles and defence systems.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham has told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK will share information about Storm Shadow missile components with Kyiv. Photograph: Ukrainian presidency/Sipa/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Andy Burnham visited Kyiv on his first overseas trip as prime minister this week. He told Volodymyr Zelenskyy that the UK would give Ukraine previously classified information on the British-manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles.

Burnham has also urged the international community to do more to protect Ukraine against Russian attacks, particularly with more US-made Patriot interceptor missiles. He is expected to make this argument at next month’s UN general assembly in New York.
In response, Russia has made repeated threats of retaliation, including talk of attacks on UK military targets both inside and outside Ukraine.

The western officials said that while the threat from Russia remained very real, the situation had not changed, and the assessment was that “Putin absolutely wants to avoid a direct confrontation with Nato”.

One official said: “We are seeing a continuation of hostile rhetoric and various accusations against the UK. This is absolutely consistent with longstanding Russian military doctrine, which is to use rhetoric to both exploit fears in adversaries and to influence decision-making. So this is not a new phenomenon.”

Officials say Russia still has the capability to target the UK, with cyberattacks or physical attacks on civilian targets by proxies, for example on factories or warehouses. Last year, six men were jailed for their involvement in an attack ordered by Russia against a warehouse in east London housing aid to Ukraine.
But officials said their assessment was that Putin would limit any such action to avoid more direct conflict with Nato.

Putin’s overall aim in Ukraine, western officials believe, is to maintain a campaign of attrition, hoping that support from Ukraine’s allies will ebb away, particularly if governments are spooked by public alarm over Russian threats.
Such threats should be seen, one official said, as attempts to create a “fractured and more vulnerable Europe”.

Another said: “It’s important to keep in mind that this is not new. Russia has invoked the threat of the possible use of nuclear weapons numerous times in recent years to try to scare us into ending support for Ukraine.”

articles.title: What next? Kurds say yes, Druze still say no to united Syria
articles.summary: The Druze minority in Sweida, Syria, is now the only group that hasn't accepted central government authority. How does the end of an independent Kurdish area impact Druze plans for a different,…

image.caption: Druze militias and Israeli threats have kept Syrian government forces out of the Druze-majority province of SweidaImage: Izettin Kasim/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: This week, Syria's Kurdish minority agreed to dissolve what had been their almost 14-year-long experiment in independent rule.

During the Syrian civil war, which began in 2011, the Kurds consolidated their authority over a large part of northeastern Syria, and wanted to maintain that after the civil war ended. But as Kurdish leader Mazloum Abdi said this week, "circumstances have changed."

Kurdish fighting forces, which go by the name of the Syrian Democratic Forces, or SDF, will now be integrated into the general Syrian military, and the oil-rich area they ruled will come under the authority of the central government.
All this means that Sweida province, home to much of Syria's Druze minority, is now the only area not to have accepted the authority of the central government.

blocks.caption: The Druze are ethnically Arab and one of Syria's many religious minorities, making up around 3% of the populationImage: Fahd Kiwan/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: End of idea of 'decentralized Syria'
There is no doubt that the change in the situation with Syria's Kurdish community will affect what is happening in Sweida, experts say.

When Omer Ozkizilcik, a nonresident senior fellow at US think tank, the Atlantic Council's Syria Project, met with Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri in early 2025, the Druze leader said he was in daily phone contact with Abdi.

"He said that they were coordinating all their efforts and that they had a similar political vision for Syria — that is, decentralized with autonomous regions," said Ozkizilcik. "He basically repeated the Israeli approach, where they believe Syria should be divided, with an autonomous zone on the coast for the Alawite [minority], for the SDF in the northeast, and then in the south for the Druze. That shows that al-Hijiri's political vision was highly dependent on his alliance with the SDF."
That idea is no longer feasible. "Basically it puts an end to this vision of a fragmented, weak and decentralized Syria," the Ankara-based analyst argued.
That is also probably the reason why, earlier this week, al-Hijri again emphasized the Druze ties to Israel, Ozkizilcik suggested.
On Monday in Sweida, al-Hijiri declared the Druze an "inseparable part of the state of Israel."
"Even in terms of our beliefs, we share common ground," he said.

blocks.caption: Observers have pointed out while al-Hijiri (pictured) has said the Druze have common interests with Israel, it's not the same as linking religionsImage: Ali Haj Suleiman/Getty Images

blocks.text: ​​​​​​But it's clear that having Israel annex Sweida would be very difficult for a number of reasons, including geography and demographics. Sweida is also still dependent on the central Syrian government. Despite it being impossible for government forces to enter the area, Sweida still receives public services, salaries, pensions, power and water from Damascus.
What caused the rift?

The exclusion of government forces began after intercommunal violence in Sweida in July 2025. Fighting started between Druze and Bedouin locals. Government forces arrived, ostensibly to quell the violence, but they too were then accused of attacking Druze communities.
A report by the United Nations found over 1,700 people died as a result of the clashes.

The event resulted in deep Druze mistrust of the new Syrian government. Even locals who had been in favor of a united Syria began to question whether it might not be better to have a semi-autonomous Druze state.

"There has been a complete erosion of trust," Lubna al-Basit, a Sweida activist, told DW. "Before discussing solutions, the reality today is that the government must be held accountable for the massacres committed in Sweida."
Another Druze, now based in the US but who wished to remain anonymous for security reasons, believes the new Syrian government is more radical than it looks.

"They're trying to behave in way that appeases the West," he told DW. "But you know, we have this joke. They're indicating to go left when they're turning right. For the Druze, the priority would be security, dignity and a chance for prosperity. I don't think many people see that as attainable under the current Syrian government."

blocks.caption: The UN report also said that Druze, Bedouin and government-allied forces may all have committed war crimes in July 2025Image: Izettin Kasim/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: In September, a road map to repair relations was formulated with Jordanian and American negotiators. But Druze allied with al-Hijiri rejected the plan, and the central government hasn't done much to bring July 2025 perpetrators to justice. In June, the UN's special envoy to Syria said no progress had been made on the road map.

Since last year, Syria's central government "has dealt with the [Sweida] issue on the premise that a large-scale military confrontation would not resolve the crisis," researchers at the Syrian Center for Security and Defense Studies, or MISDAD, wrote in a paper this month.

Any such confrontation "would have deepened the rift with the local community and given external actors greater room to intervene or exploit the tension. Therefore, the Syrian government opted for a more cautious approach, based on calming the situation on one hand, and utilizing the state's security, administrative, and economic tools on the other."

Basically, the researchers at MISDAD continued, the Syrian government is waiting it out, hoping that increasing prosperity elsewhere in the country and the problems al-Hijiri's factions already have running the province's public services, will bring Sweida back to the fold.

blocks.caption: A memorial service in Sweida: The crisis of Druze trust in the Syrian central government is severe after last year's violenceImage: Shadi Al Dubaisi/JNA/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 'small authoritarian regime in Sweida'
What isn't likely to happen is any kind of revolution, Ozkizilcik explained.

"The issue here is that al-Hijiri has the guns, Israeli financial support and Israeli military advisers from the Israeli-Druze community," he continued. "There is basically a small authoritarian regime in Sweida that's controlled by al-Hijiri, so it would be very difficult for the Druze community to rise up against him."

Opponents of al-Hijiri have been forced out of the province, abducted or killed, there's been fighting between different Druze militias, and there have even been some small civilian protests. Reports say al-Hijiri loyalists have also stopped Druze civil servants from working with ministries in Damascus.
Ozkizilcik and other observers believe a resolution to the situation in Sweida won't come down to what al-Hijiri wants anyway.

Just as American military support — or rather, its withdrawal — for Kurdish forces was integral to the new resolution between the central government and Syrian Kurdish forces, what happens with the Druze community next is also likely to come down to external forces.

Some have argued that the situation in Sweida was a way for Israel to pressure Syria as the two governments tried to negotiate a new security agreement. Throughout 2025, senior Syrian and Israeli politicians were involved in talks, with mediation from the US, to potentially reactivate a 1974 disengagement agreement. However, these fell apart late last year.

Since the overthrow of the dictatorial Assad regime in Syria in late December 2024, the US has said it is in favor of a unified Syria. Israel appears to want the opposite, arguing that a divided Syria won't pose a threat.

"The real decision maker [on Sweida] will be Israel, not al-Hijiri," said Ozkizilcik. "Once — or if — there is a potential security deal between Syria and Israel, then I believe we will also see a political solution to Sweida and the Druze."
What needs to happen for the Druze to feel secure in Syria?

articles.title: Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues
articles.summary: A group of migrants is accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, while some locals set fire to their camps on the beach.

blocks.text: A month after tens of thousands of migrants entered the city of Ceuta, a Spanish exclave in North Africa, there have been outbreaks of violence as tensions mount between locals and foreign arrivals.
The Spanish government has been accused by opposition parties of struggling to manage the crisis effectively.
Ceuta's residents have complained of feeling unsafe on the streets, as well as expressing concerns about the burden being placed on public services.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the mass crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.
The vast majority of the migrants returned to Morocco within hours of their arrival, but several thousand remain in Ceuta, many of them children, and most are sleeping rough on beaches or streets.
Anti-migrant demonstrations earlier this month were largely peaceful, but in recent days they have become increasingly violent.

On Thursday, several dozen locals prevented Red Cross personnel from distributing food and water to the migrants. Afterwards, some set fire to migrant camps on Trampolín beach, the main site where they have been sleeping, and there were also clashes with the police.

Those incidents came hours after the arrest of 12 migrants who were accused of throwing stones at a military vehicle, breaking its windows and injuring the four men inside. That same morning there were reports of vigilante groups pursuing migrants through the streets.
Journalists and film crews have also reported being threatened.
"This is a city which has been under pressure, […] which has the right to normality," the mayor of the exclave, the conservative Juan Jesús Vivas, told Antena 3 television.
"The dignity of Spain is a stake right now in Ceuta," he said.
The socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has appealed for calm and accused Vivas's People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox of stoking the tensions.
José María Figaredo, a member of Congress for Vox, is being investigated for a possible hate crime after saying, soon after the migrants' arrival, that they should be "hunted down, one by one".

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told a congressional committee: "We have heard during these weeks rhetoric and comments that contribute to the stigmatisation of immigrants and which feed social division at a moment when what we need is responsibility and statesmanship."
Javier Celaya, who represents Ceuta in Congress for the PP, accused the government of treating "the invaders as victims when the real victims are us, the people of Ceuta".
On Friday, all the parties in the Ceuta local assembly signed a declaration condemning violence.
Earlier this week, the government centralised management of the situation, overriding the local authority, after criticism that it had been slow to respond.

Defence Minister Margarita Robles also apologised to those in Ceuta who "may have felt, or who even still feel, abandoned or not sufficiently cared", as the government unveiled plans to overhaul the country's immigration laws.

Much of the recent ill-feeling in the city appears to be driven by government plans to move migrants into existing public buildings, such as sports centres, in order to be able to process their legal status in an orderly way and return those not eligible for asylum to Morocco.
Many local people, and Vivas, oppose this initiative, due to concerns that it will move the migrants closer to residential areas.
The government is also facing questions about who was behind the mass migrant crossing.
Politicians on the right and the far left have accused Morocco of involvement, pointing to its alleged use of the border with Spain in the past to exert political pressure.
Sánchez and his Socialist Party instead blame people traffickers, insisting that Rabat is a reliable partner which facilitated the immediate return of most of the arrivals.
Nonetheless, the crisis has placed the sovereignty of Ceuta, and its fellow autonomous city Melilla, under the spotlight.
Morocco has maintained a longstanding claim to the territories, which it has reiterated in recent weeks.
Spain's Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he "roundly rejected" such comments by Morocco.
"I don't speak about, nor have I spoken about, nor are we going to speak about Spain's territorial integrity with Morocco or with anyone else," he told the congressional committee.

articles.title: Poa, AFP witnesses to testify on DepEd funds misuse
articles.summary: Three officials of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and defense lawyer Michael Poa are expected to testify on the alleged misuse of the Department of Education (DepEd)’s confidential…

blocks.text: Defense spokesperson Atty. Michael Poa urged both sides to be cautious in using terms such as "scam" that could influence public perception as the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte continues on August 26, 2026.

MANILA, Philippines — Three officials of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) and defense lawyer Michael Poa are expected to testify on the alleged misuse of the Department of Education (DepEd)’s confidential funds next week.

The prosecution panel said one of the witnesses, Col. Manaros Boransing II, will testify how an annual military event received no reward money or financial assistance from DepEd, even though the agency used the military activities in explaining its use of confidential funds.

Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong, a spokesman for the panel, also said the prosecution intends to revisit certifications involving the AFP and the Youth Leadership Summit, after DepEd used the activities in explaining confidential fund expenditures questioned by state auditors.

During the House inquiry in 2024, military officers whose certifications were later used in DepEd’s response to Commission on Audit findings testified that the Youth Leadership Summits were funded by the military and participating local governments and that their units received no DepEd confidential funds for those activities.
Adiong said Boransing’s testimony will be weighed together with the audit records and other evidence for the appreciation of the Senate impeachment court.
The testimony of Col. Magtangol Panopio will also focus on the issue, particularly on the AFP certification used by DepEd, even though the signatories previously said they did not know that purpose.

Prosecution adviser and spokesman Ace Barbers said the hearing should also protect the military’s institutional neutrality, as the officials’ testimonies will show whether military officers knowingly took part in the funding process or whether their signatures were used without a full explanation of the documents’ purpose.
He said the certifications matter because they may have been used to answer an audit question and support a public fund liquidation.
Meanwhile, Poa’s testimony could fill important gaps from his previous appearance before the House inquiry about the DepEd’s confidential funds, the prosecution said.
Poa served as DepEd chief of staff and spokesman while Vice President Sara Duterte was education secretary. He is now part of Duterte’s defense team and serves as defense spokesman.
The House prosecution plans to call him as a hostile witness in connection with the alleged misuse of P112.5 million in DepEd confidential funds.
Barbers said Poa’s former position placed him close to documents and official responses that the senator-judges need to understand.

articles.title: Leptospirosis deaths climb to 23 in Manila
articles.summary: The number of deaths in Manila due to leptospirosis this year has climbed to 23 following two more fatalities recorded yesterday, the city government said.

blocks.text: Commuters use an elevated walkway to cross a flooded section of a street triggered by heavy monsoon rains in Manila on August 17, 2026.
AFP / Ted Aljibe
MANILA, Philippines — The number of deaths in Manila due to leptospirosis this year has climbed to 23 following two more fatalities recorded yesterday, the city government said.

An additional 45 new cases brought the total number of leptospirosis cases in the city to 455 from Jan. 1 to Aug. 28, according to data from the Manila Health Department and City Epidemiology and Surveillance Unit.
Of the 455 cases, 155 were from San Lazaro Hospital alone. Thirteen of the 23 deaths were also from the hospital.
Ten of the 13 fatalities were male, while three were female. San Lazaro medical chief David Suplico said the age range of the deceased was between 22 and 59 years.
As of yesterday, the hospital had 157 patients with leptospirosis following 38 new admissions.

Mayor Isko Moreno previously said the surge of leptospirosis in the city is expected to rise further, citing the disease’s two-week incubation period following the severe flooding that hit Manila a week ago.
Other Department of Health (DOH) hospitals and the Philippine Red Cross are assisting San Lazaro Hospital by deploying additional manpower and bed capacity, Suplico said.

The hospital has written Moreno and the Department of Public Works and Highways to address the flooding in the hospital during heavy rains. Suplico warned that rising rainwater would force the hospital to suspend its outpatient department operations.
Meanwhile, the DOH has intensified its hospital referral system and response measures.

articles.title: PNP may form quick reaction teams vs school shootings
articles.summary: In the wake of recent shooting incidents in schools, the government is eyeing the establishment of police quick reaction forces that will respond to incidents of violence on campuses.

blocks.text: Philippine police gather at a school following a shooting in Zamboanga on August 18, 2026.
AFP / Roel Parreno

MANILA, Philippines — In the wake of recent shooting incidents in schools, the government is eyeing the establishment of police quick reaction forces that will respond to incidents of violence on campuses.

Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla and Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez are studying the formation of specialized police teams that could be deployed immediately in the event of shootings in learning institutions.

Nartatez, for his part, said they are backing proposed legislation by Sen. Bam Aquino seeking to establish a sustained and coordinated approach to protecting students from threats and emergencies in school campuses.
Aquino has filed Senate Bill 2426, or the Comprehensive School Safety Act, which would establish a nationwide system for school safety.
Nartatez said they are ready to work with the Department of Education to ensure that schools remain safe spaces for students, faculty and school employees.

articles.title: Zaldy Co, 8 DPWH execs face malversation raps
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft charges before the Sandiganbayan against former congressman Zaldy Co and eight officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways…

blocks.text: Zaldy Co.
Zaldy Co / Philstar.com's screenshot

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft charges before the Sandiganbayan against former congressman Zaldy Co and eight officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) over an allegedly anomalous P77-million flood control project in Balagtas, Bulacan.

The ombudsman said its investigators found probable cause to charge Co and DPWH officials Henry Alcantara, Brice Hernandez, Arjay Domasig, Jaypee Mendoza, Niño Lawrence Morales, Juanito Mendoza, Floralyn Simbulan and Christina Mae Pineda with graft and malversation of public funds through falsification of public documents.
Co’s staff members John Paul Estrada and Mark Tecsay were also included in the indictment.
The charges involve the construction of a riverbank protection structure along the Balagtas River in Purok 4, Barangay San Juan, Balagtas, Bulacan.
The project was awarded to SYMS Construction Trading and had a revised contract amount of approximately P77.2 million.
The ombudsman said it was found through inspection that the structure was non-existent despite documents and certifications indicating accomplishment of the project.
“The project supposedly started last February 24, 2025 and was declared to be 100% accomplished on May 2, 2025. However, upon inspection, it was non-existent,” the resolution read.

The ombudsman, in finding probable cause, said Alcantara collected kickbacks from contractors and delivered these to Co, who ensured that the projects would be “inserted” in the National Expenditure Program prepared by the executive and eventually funded in the General Appropriations Act or the national budget.
“Co’s participation was therefore necessary or indispensable in this elaborate scheme of embezzling funds intended for flood control projects,” the resolution stated.

articles.title: Pump price rollback seen next week
articles.summary: September is set to start on a good note for motorists, with diesel prices expected to drop by P3.50 to P4 per liter next week.

blocks.text: Gasoline prices are also seen rolling back, although by a much smaller P0.25 to P0.75 per liter.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — September is set to start on a good note for motorists, with diesel prices expected to drop by P3.50 to P4 per liter next week.
The projections are based on the four-day average of Mean of Platts Singapore prices and movements in foreign exchange rates.
The final adjustments, which are expected to be announced on Monday, will still depend on the outcome of the last trading day.
Jetti Petroleum president Leo Bellas said prices fell this week amid signs that talks could resume to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a key trade route for oil and gas shipments.
“Iran said it had resumed talks with Oman, although the physical supply picture reflects a still-constrained market and supply disruption risks remain,” Bellas said yesterday.
Also weighing on prices were rising regional inventories as supplies from China and India continued to increase.
However, global oil prices recently rebounded after reports that the United States was no longer interested in returning to the terms of its previous ceasefire deal with Iran.
“The potential rollback on local pump prices next week could be capped, with the risk of pushing to the lower limits of the initial estimated range,” Bellas noted.
Last Tuesday, gasoline, diesel and kerosene prices climbed by up to P1.08, P2.31 and P0.95 per liter, respectively.
The Department of Energy expects fuel price adjustments, whether rollbacks or hikes, to remain at single-digit levels in the weeks ahead.

articles.title: Missing Filipino in Nepal identified; family asks for help
articles.summary: A 30-year-old doctor has been identified as the Filipino missing in Nepal following a catastrophic flash flood that has claimed the lives of at least 489 people.
articles.byline: Andrew Ronquillo, EJ Macababbad, Michael Punongbayan, Bella Cariaso

blocks.text: A drone shot shows firefighters conducting search and rescue operations at a damaged road leading to Gyirong Port yesterday following a mudslide and flashflood in Gyirong county, Shigatse, Tibet Autonomous Region. Inset shows a Facebook image of Juan Carlos Manalo, the Filipino doctor who is currently missing after the catastrophic flash flood in Nepal.
MANILA, Philippines — A 30-year-old doctor has been identified as the Filipino missing in Nepal following a catastrophic flash flood that has claimed the lives of at least 489 people.
In a Facebook post yesterday, Chiara Manalo said her brother, physician Juan Carlos Manalo, “has been missing and out of contact since the flash flood at the Nepal border last Aug. 26, 2026.”
“Please help us look for my brother,” she appealed to the public.

Chiara said her brother’s last contact with the family was around 1 p.m. (Philippine time) on Tuesday, a day before the flash flood hit in the Bhotekoshi River, on the Nepal-China border in Rasuwa district.
In a list provided by Nepali Police, Manalo was reported to be among a group of pilgrims on their Kailashyatra tour organized by the India-based spiritual organization Isha Foundation.
“The group’s last known whereabouts was at the immigration office at Gyirong,” Chiara said, citing information from the Philippine counterpart of the pilgrimage group.
At least 77 pilgrims en route to India remain unaccounted for after the flood hit the immigration center, according to a social media post on Wednesday by Isha Foundation founder Sadhguru.
Chiara said her brother served as a volunteer medical worker at the foundation for the past couple of years and had joined the tour early this month.
“Kuya went to India in May this year for a retreat with the Sadhguru group. He mentioned that they would go to Nepal. They previously went there last year,” Chiara said.
“We humbly ask to include him in your prayers, that he may return to us safely soon,” Chiara added.
“We’re considering if we want to go (to Nepal). Realistically, we don’t know what will happen. Right now, we’re focusing on getting as much reach as possible,” Chiara said.
Juan Carlos, a general physician, is the oldest among four siblings. His interests include yoga and meditation, Chiara said.
The Department of Foreign Affairs said yesterday that the government is coordinating with the Philippine embassy in India and the honorary consulate general in Nepal to assist affected Filipinos.
Similar scenario?
Asked whether what happened to Nepal could take place in the Philippines, a disaster-prone country, Science Secretary Renato Solidum Jr. said, “not to that extent or scale.”
He, however, did not discount the possibility of another Typhoon Sendong happening in the country.
The 2011 typhoon caused up to 2,500 deaths in Mindanao as flash floods caused dams to burst.
Debris avalanches could also pose danger for people living in mountainous areas, like the tragedy that struck Saint Bernard town in Southern Leyte in 2006.
Mahar Lagmay, executive director of the University of the Philippines Resilience Institute, said many Filipinos continue to be vulnerable to debris flows.

articles.title: Monsoon to spawn weekend rains over Luzon
articles.summary: Heavy rains from the southwest monsoon or habagat are expected to affect large parts of Luzon through Monday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration said.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Heavy rains from the southwest monsoon or habagat are expected to affect large parts of Luzon through Monday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration said.

According to the impact-based warning of PAGASA yesterday, prolonged and widespread disruption to the daily routines of households and businesses is anticipated in parts of Bataan, Bulacan, Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Tarlac and Zambales.

Under the “severe” level, widespread damage to houses and buildings, crops, livestock and aquaculture may occur. Road and rail transportation may also be disrupted, while health facilities, power and water services may be affected.
The warning also noted that severe injuries, permanent disability and danger to life may be expected.

As of yesterday, two low-pressure areas were being monitored by PAGASA. The first was inside the Philippine area of responsibility, last located 560 kilometers east-northeast of Itbayat, Batanes, while the other was outside PAR, last located 1,460 kilometers east of Central Luzon.
Both had a medium chance of developing into a tropical cyclone within the next 24 hours.

From this afternoon until Monday afternoon, an orange warning is expected over Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Abra, Benguet and Zambales, while a yellow warning is expected over Batanes, Apayao, Kalinga, Ifugao, Mountain Province, Nueva Vizcaya, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija, Bataan, Pampanga, Bulacan, Metro Manila, Rizal, Cavite, Batangas and Occidental Mindoro.
Class suspensions
Malacañang suspended work in government offices and classes at all levels in public and private schools in Metro Manila and 16 provinces yesterday afternoon.
The order, contained in Memorandum Circular 132 issued by Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, took effect at 1 p.m.

Citing the expected further enhancement of the southwest monsoon, the suspension covered the National Capital Region, Abra, Benguet, Ilocos Sur, La Union, Pangasinan, Bataan, Bulacan, Nueva Ecija, Pampanga, Tarlac, Zambales, Batangas, Cavite, Rizal, Oriental Mindoro and Occidental Mindoro.
Government agencies providing basic and health services, disaster preparedness and response and other vital services were directed to continue operating.
Local chief executives were also authorized to suspend classes and/or work in government offices in their areas.
In the private sector, the suspension of work or adoption of alternative work arrangements was left to management. — Bella Cariaso, Helen Flores, Aubrey Inosante

articles.title: At least 93,000 ‘in great need’ after Nepal-Tibet flash floods, says Red Cross
articles.summary: Federation says it fears death toll of nearly 600 will continue to rise as rescuers reach cut-off areas
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies

blocks.text: The Red Cross has said at least 93,000 people may have been affected by Wednesday’s flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border, which have killed nearly 600 people, left another 1,900 missing, and triggered a huge rescue operation that is being hampered by fears of new flooding.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), the world’s largest humanitarian network, said it feared the death toll would continue to rise as some of the hardest-hit areas remained inaccessible after roads and bridges were destroyed by the torrents.
“The trauma of this event is enormous,” David Fisher, the IFRC head of delegation for Nepal, said on Friday.

“Thousands of homes have been destroyed or suffered significant damage. We believe that at least 93,000 people have been affected and are in great need. The death toll is very high and unfortunately likely to continue to rise.”

The deadly floods occurred on Wednesday morning after an enormous section ⁠of a glacier in the Himalayas broke loose and crashed on to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, unleashing a massive surge of water, mud, rock and ice that thundered down rivers and valleys. The resulting floods obliterated villages and destroyed power stations, roads and bridges.

Nepal’s steep slopes and the lush valleys below are especially vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events, such as intense monsoons, and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.

“The damage is just incredible,” Lila Pieters Yahia, the UN resident coordinator for Nepal, said on Friday, adding that more than 40 bridges had been destroyed or badly damaged and “over 40km of road completely destroyed”.

By Friday afternoon, the death toll stood at 584 people: 579 in Nepal and five across the border in Tibet, China. Authorities in Nepal said 1,942 people were still missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals who were in the area to work, trek with guides or make a pilgrimage.

blocks.caption: On the ground in Nepal after deadly flash floods - video

blocks.text: Rescue teams have reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Indian border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.

Rescuers were forced to suspend operations on Friday morning after a dam of debris overflowed on Friday, increasing the risk of further flooding. Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses.

blocks.caption: Relatives display photos of missing people outside a hospital in Kathmandu, where they have travelled from Rasuwa to seek information about family members. Photograph: Subaas Shrestha/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the border overflowed.
Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

blocks.caption: People surveying the aftermath of the flooding in Bidur. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.
Nearby, people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

blocks.caption: A woman among the ruins of Bidur. Photograph: Ahmer Khan/The Guardian

blocks.text: Most areas battered by the flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, from where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned in a matter of minutes.
The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.
Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search and rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of bridges and roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search and rescue teams to assist in the operation.

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with Tibet.
“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.
But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only five deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.

blocks.caption: Excavators clear debris to restore a road damaged by the flash floods on the Tibet side of the border. Photograph: China News Service/Getty

blocks.text: With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Norway’s King Harald dies aged 89
articles.summary:
Norwegians gather to remember monarch whose death comes amid scandal over links between crown princess and Jeffrey Epstein

Norwegians have gathered in their thousands to pay their respects…

blocks.text: Norwegians have gathered in their thousands to pay their respects to King Harald V, Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, who has died, aged 89, in Oslo. He was succeeded immediately by his son, King Haakon VIII.

The new king thanked “the government and Norwegian people for their support and sympathy for the royal family at this time”. A period of national mourning was announced as crowds left wreaths and messages outside the royal palace in Oslo.

Flags around the country were lowered to half mast and church bells rang out at midday. “An era has ended. A new one begins. The king is dead. Long live the king,” the prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said after meeting Haakon.

The new king, whose wife, Mette-Marit, has recently come under scrutiny over scandals including a much-criticised association with the late US child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, formally notified the government of his father’s death on Friday morning.

blocks.caption: People gather outside the royal palace in Oslo after the death of King Harald. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

blocks.text: Haakon, 53, told the cabinet at an extraordinary council of state that he would take the name Haakon VIII, as expected. He also chose as his personal motto: “Everything for Norway.”

The new king will swear an oath of accession in parliament within the next few days. Coronation ceremonies were abolished in Norway more than a century ago, but Haakon could choose to have his reign blessed at a consecration ceremony.

The palace had said on Thursday that Harald’s health had deteriorated and that the king, who was seen as a unifying figure and a force for stability amid a string of recent family scandals, was in an “extremely serious” condition.

blocks.caption: King Harald during a welcoming ceremony for the Danish king and queen in Oslo in May 2024. Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty Images

blocks.text: Støre said earlier that he had received the news “with deep sadness”, adding: “A whole nation is in mourning, and ⁠the people of Norway are left with a ​deep sense of ‌gratitude for a ‌long life in the service of Norway.”

Royalty around Europe sent their condolences, with Spain’s royal family hailing Harald’s “responsibility, dignity, humility and tireless dedication”, and Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary saying he was “loved like few others”.

King Carl XVI Gustaf, of Sweden, said: “Throughout the years, King Harald has been a good friend to me, my family, and to Sweden … I ​wish ​my dear godson Haakon, ​who now succeeds his father as head ​of state, ‌success and ​good ​fortune.”

Belgium’s royal family recalled Harald’s “humour, humanity and sincerity”, while Britain’s King Charles mourned the loss of his “dear cousin”, paying tribute to a “towering figure” who guided his country with “warmth and humility”.

blocks.caption: People gather at Palace Square in Oslo to pay their respects to King Harald. Photograph: Rune Hellestad/Getty

blocks.text: Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Norway had “lost a great figure who stood for prudence and unity”, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, expressed “deep sadness”.

Norway’s ceremonial head of state since 1991, Harald was being treated in Oslo’s University hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of the body’s red blood cells.

He had had numerous health problems – an operation for bladder cancer in 2003 and a pacemaker fitted in 2024 – but always ruled out abdicating, saying he had taken a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament.

His death comes amid a turbulent period for Norway’s royal family. Documents published in the US in January showed that Mette-Marit corresponded with Epstein between 2011 and 2014, long after he was convicted.

blocks.caption: Haakon had taken on additional royal duties while his father was ill. Photograph: Per Ole Hagen/Getty

blocks.text: The files appeared to contain almost 1,000 mentions of Mette-Marit, including intimate exchanges. They drew fierce public criticism, with Støre accusing her in unprecedented comments of “poor judgment”.
after newsletter promotion

Mette-Marit subsequently released a statement via the royal household expressing her “deepest regret for my friendship with Jeffrey Epstein” and apologising for “the situation that I have put the royal family in, especially the king and queen”.

blocks.caption: Mette-Marit had a successful lung transplant in July. Photograph: Lise Åserud/NTB Scanpix/AP

blocks.text: Marius Borg Høiby, 29, Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship, has also been in the spotlight after being sentenced in June to four years in prison for two rapes and 32 other charges, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed against the decision.

The scandals have affected public support for Norway’s monarchy, with a poll in February finding support down to 54% from 72% in 2024. Several polls found nearly half of the population felt Mette-Marit could not become queen.

blocks.caption: The royal family pictured in 2022. Front, left to right: King Harald, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Queen Sonja. Back, left to right: Marit Tjessem, the mother of Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Crown Prince Haakon, Prince Sverre Magnus and Marius Borg Høiby. Photograph: Lise Åserud/NTB/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Harald was seen as the Norwegian monarchy’s great moderniser, revamping the crown estates and changing the way the court is run. He married Sonja, a commoner, in 1968 and welcomed two others, Mette-Marit and Ari Behn, as the spouses of his children.

A great-great-grandchild ‌of Britain’s Queen Victoria, he succeeded his father, Olav V, at the age of 54 after studying at Oxford and representing his country in sailing events at the Tokyo, Mexico City and Munich Olympics. He was widely appreciated in Norway for his unassuming lifestyle and commitment to national unity.

In an emotional speech in 2011 after the far-right extremist Anders Behring Breivik killed 77 in two terror attacks, he told his subjects that “freedom is stronger than fear” and as “a father, grandfather and spouse, I can only begin to sense some of the pain you feel. As king of the nation, I feel for every one of you.”

In a widely praised 2016 speech, he lauded diversity, tolerance and LGBTQ+ rights, saying Norwegians came from Afghanistan and Pakistan, believed “in God, in Allah and in nothing”, and included “girls who love girls, boys who love boys and girls and boys who love each other”.

blocks.caption: King Harald and Queen Sonja at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan, Italy. Photograph: Heiko Junge/Reuters

blocks.text: Mette-Marit, 53, who has a serious lung disease and had a transplant in July, was a single mother to Høiby, who was four years old when her engagement to Norway’s crown prince was announced in late 2000.

The marriage, which marked the first time in modern European history that a direct heir to a throne had brought a stepson into a royal family, caused huge controversy in Norway but was strongly backed by King Harald and Queen Sonja.

Mette-Marit acknowledged having what she described as a rebellious youth and prior drug use, holding an emotional press conference a week before the wedding in which she expressed regret for her choices and strongly condemned drug use.
