The king was "at the prime of his life", she said in a video shared on social media, "as young as he was, he had an impact on his kingdom".
Muhanga said they would be planting a million trees in his honour during the mourning period, and wants to ask the neighbouring districts in Tooro to do the same.
Uganadan musician Juliana Kanyomozi called it a "very dark day for Tooro", in an Instagram post. "Gone too soon. What a loss!!!!"
Meanwhile, pop star-turned-politician Bobi Wine, called for King Oyo's "soul to rest in eternal peace".

items: Image source, The Denver Post via Getty ImagesImage caption, When he was 10, King Oyo was pictured on a trip to the US with Queen Mother Best Kemigisa (L) and Mayor of the city of Denver Wellington Webb (R). He was there on a humanitarian mission for Aids orphans in Uganda.

articles.title: Detroit despairs as ‘insanity’ of Trump’s Canada trade war punishes city
articles.summary:
Unpopular new policy comes as midterms loom and control of Congress could be decided by several Michigan races

Every day $1bn worth of…

blocks.text: Every day $1bn worth of goods crosses the river dividing Detroit, Michigan, and Windsor, Ontario, two largely blue-collar US and Canadian cities that have come to act as one in the creation of North America’s auto industry.

News this week of Donald Trump’s escalating trade spat with Canada has everyone worried. Political and economic leaders and observers labeled the move an act of “hubris” , blamed Trump’s “ego”, and called the escalation “insanity”.
“We don’t need Canada, they need us,” Trump declared.
But many are hoping that Trump’s imposition of 50% tariffs on Canadian goods this week will not last long, with the upcoming midterm elections as a pivotal reason the plan may be scrapped.

Control of the US Congress hangs in the balance and will almost certainly be decided by several close Michigan races. It also comes just two months after polling highlighted Michiganders’ fatigue with and opposition to the president’s unprecedented tariff program.

By a 63%-31% margin, residents here oppose tariffs on Canadian goods, according to a June Epic-MRA poll, including 35% of Republicans. Meanwhile, nearly 75% of Michiganders said the tariffs are fueling high prices.

Trump doubling down on an unpopular policy deep into election season is viewed by many observers as a gift to Democrats, and there is a real possibility that it contributes to a midterm loss for the Republicans. Meanwhile, there seems to be little upside for Trump.
“I don’t understand what Trump is thinking,” the Epic-MRA pollster Bernie Porn said.

Regardless, Michiganders have already suffered disproportionately as they pay on average over $3,200 annually for tariffs, or about 142% more than the rest of the country, because of the state’s shared border with Canada.
The Canadian economy would also take a major hit if the tariffs are imposed, said Patrick Anderson, a Michigan-based economist with the Anderson Economic Group.

blocks.caption: The Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters at Renaissance high school in Detroit, Michigan, on 7 August.  Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Both will suffer – there are no two ways about it,” Anderson added.

This critical upper midwest swing state has picked the presidential winner in five consecutive elections, going from Barack Obama to Trump to Joe Biden and back to Trump. Democrats’ chances to retake the Senate rest heavily on the Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed beating Trump ally Mike Rogers in the 3 November general election race. Rogers has supported the tariffs, but so far has been silent on the latest escalation.

The tariffs and the unpopular Iran war’s contribution to inflation represent a “double hit” for Republicans, Porn said, and Trump is handing ammo to a particularly adept candidate in El-Sayed. He has energized people with his anti-establishment, populist political vision, and a no-holds-barred delivery.

“El-Sayed has proven to be very, very articulate on a number of issues,” Porn added. “I think that he is going to try and just throw bombs at Rogers [in an upcoming debate] because Rogers supports these tariffs and trade war. Trump’s low popularity is an anchor around Rogers’ neck.”
In a statement, El-Sayed hammered Trump and Rogers, saying that the president “cares more about his ego and saber-rattling than addressing the affordability crisis.

“Donald Trump is launching this trade war for his own vanity, and he’s asking Michigan families to pay the price,” El-Sayed said. “Trump has been failing Michigan through these chaotic tariffs and bad trade deals for far too long, and Mike Rogers won’t do anything but rubber-stamp them.”
El-Sayed said he would push for “real, fair trade deals that create good-paying jobs”. Rogers’ campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

The United Auto Workers (UAW), which has 350,000 members in Michigan and is often a political kingmaker here, has supported some of Trump’s targeted tariffs, but said in a statement it “rejects” the latest escalation.

“If we’re going to increase tariffs anywhere, it should be on countries where automakers continue to offshore jobs because they can pay workers $3 an hour, force them to work in unsafe conditions, and crack down on independent unions,” the UAW president, Shawn Fain, said. Canada has strong unions, and the UAW supports those.

“Tariffs work, but only if they are deployed intentionally to protect workers and grow our manufacturing communities, and it’s time to permanently end offshoring and the race to the bottom,” Fain added.

Mexico and Canada currently face 25% US tariffs on autos, though partial exemptions in the nations’ free trade agreement make the effective rate much lower, overall. Anderson estimated tariffs cost US auto companies about $12.5bn in 2025.

The Canadian government has announced it will impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of goods starting 8 September. The actions leading to the latest blow-up have been “rife with miscalculations, overreactions, and hubris”, Anderson said. He read through the list of goods on which tariffs would be imposed – feathers, sweaters, girls’ dresses, lobster.
“This is not a trade war. This is an annoyance list. Chest pounding,” Anderson said.

The North American auto industry over the last 60 years has integrated across the continent, and auto parts cross a border an average of six times before they land in a final product. That means there would be shared pain, Anderson said, and it would reverberate across the upper midwest, where bigger manufacturing cities are typically powered by industries that are often reliant on international trade.

But the Canadian economy is smaller, and Ontario’s economy is so concentrated that it would hit harder north of the border, Anderson added. Ultimately, the real threat is that “these two countries go pell-mell into it” and impose tariffs on oil, energy and commodities that hit harder than lobster.

The dialogue has devolved into the usual petty antagonism that is a hallmark of Trump’s beefs. Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario “Lake America” on Thursday, and Vice-President JD Vance referred to Canada as the 51st state.
“Let me say with great understatement that this is not helpful,” Anderson added.

blocks.caption: The American and Canadian flags fly at the midway point on the Gordie Howe International Bridge, that connects Windsor, Ontario, and Detroit, Michigan. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Indeed, the Windsor mayor, Drew Dilkens, took exception to that particular comment. In an interview, he expressed deep frustration over Trump’s moves, and labeled justifications Trump has used for issuing tariffs, including framing them as a response to illegal immigration on the northern border, “nonsense”.

The latest escalation “is an aggressive move, one that could not be ignored by our country”, added Dilkens, who leads the city of 230,000 people. “It’s just offensive that he launches these attacks at Canada, who is your largest trading partner, your closest ally, and your neighbor.”

The chaos has cooled investment in Windsor, and prices remain high on both sides of the border. He pointed out how much more US consumers are paying not just for automobiles, but for beef, which in part stems from tariffs on Canadian beef.
“What is really crazy is that he is willing to throw his own citizens under the bus to pursue his tariff agenda,” Dilkens said. “They have Donald Trump to thank.”

Highlighting the tension among the president and some in his base, the Michigan chamber of commerce, a trade organization that lobbies on behalf of the state’s largest corporations, normally vocally supports the president on economic issues. It has not made a public statement, and did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian.
However, the typically pro-Trump Detroit chamber of commerce did not mince words.

“Escalating tensions and tariffs will only cause economic pain on both sides of the border, especially in Michigan and the binational Detroit-Windsor region,” the chamber said in a press statement, adding that global competitors like China benefited most.
“Our economies are intertwined, interconnected, and stronger together; the sooner normalcy is restored the better.”

articles.title: 555 stranded tourists evacuated from Tibet after mudslide
articles.summary: BEIJING, China – Rescuers have evacuated 555 stranded tourists from Tibet after a devastating mudslide on the China-Nepal border, Chinese state media reported Friday. State broadcaster CCTV said that…

blocks.text: BEIJING, China – Rescuers have evacuated 555 stranded tourists from Tibet after a devastating mudslide on the China-Nepal border, Chinese state media reported Friday.
State broadcaster CCTV said that 499 local residents, as well as 555 tourists, had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday morning. It did not specify the tourists’ nationalities./dp

articles.title: How Trump’s lumber tariffs made a bad situation worse in B.C.
articles.summary: Donald Trump is hardly the first U.S. president whose government has imposed steep duties on Canadian lumber. The tariffs are the latest chapter in a dispute that's been going on for more than four…

image.caption: Logs are seen piled up at West Fraser Timber in Quesnel, B.C., in April 2009. Over a dozen forestry facilities have closed in B.C. in recent years — but steep U.S. tariffs on Canadian lumber are an issue that have persisted for decades. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: More than 20 lumber mills closed across B.C. over the last three years. Billions in wood products affected by U.S. tariffs. Tens of thousands of jobs lost in Canada.
The state of B.C.'s forestry industry is, by most accounts, dire.
While there are many factors driving the decline, recent U.S. tariffs haven't helped.

But Donald Trump is hardly the first U.S. president whose government has imposed steep duties on Canadian lumber. The tariffs are the latest chapter in a dispute that's been going on for more than four decades.
Here's how we got here.

items: 'Absolutely worst situation': B.C. forestry sector fears it will be hardest-hit by U.S. tariffs

blocks.text: What is softwood lumber and why is it important?
Softwood lumber is manufactured from coniferous trees. In Canada, this is mostly spruce, pine and fir.

It's used in residential and non-residential construction, repair and remodelling and furniture manufacturing, according to Natural Resources Canada. The byproducts supply industries including pulp and paper, wood-based panels and bioenergy.
In 2024, softwood lumber made up 98 per cent of Canada's wood production, according to Statistics Canada.
That year, Canada exported just over half — 58 per cent — of its softwood lumber to the U.S.
Almost a third of that – 32 per cent – came from the B.C. Interior, which was the country's leading producer, according to Statistics Canada.
In 2024, nearly half of American wood product imports — worth about $11 billion US — came from Canada, according to the U.S. Congress.
Why is it a trade issue?
It boils down to differences in how much Canadian and American producers have to pay for access to wood, according to Export Development Canada (EDC).
In Canada, 94 per cent of forested lands are publicly owned, EDC says. Governments charge companies a fee, known as stumpage, for logging access to Crown land.
In the U.S., more than half of forested land (58 per cent) is privately-owned, according to the U.S Congress. Access prices are generally determined by the market, rather than government.
The U.S. has long argued that the low stumpage fees charged by Canadian governments amount to a subsidy that allows Canadian lumber to be sold in the U.S. at below-market value.

But Zoltan van Heyningen, the executive director of the U.S. Lumber Coalition, says these differences account for "one tiny, small aspect of Canadian subsidies," arguing the Canadian government has spent billions in taxpayer dollars in the last year supporting the industry.
In his view, the problem is one of chronic excess supply on the Canadian side, which ends up in the U.S. and drives down prices, harming American producers.
How long has the dispute been going on?

The American lumber industry first made this argument to the U.S. Commerce Department in 1982, out of concern over Canada's growing share of the U.S. market. The request was for tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber to level the playing field.

The first bilateral negotiations began in 1986. The two countries signed an agreement later that year, under which Canada agreed to impose a 15 per cent tax on its own exports of some softwood lumber to the U.S.

Over the next three decades, the dispute generally involved the U.S. imposing tariffs on Canadian softwood lumber, and Canada increasing stumpage fees or accepting export caps to minimize or avoid these duties.
Forestry sector hit with new tariffs, adding to industry woes, says analyst
Canada has regularly appealed U.S. duties, including at panels set up under the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and its predecessor, as well as the World Trade Organization.
It has been generally successful in arguing the U.S. duties were unfairly high.
There were also periods when trade was governed by various softwood lumber agreements, the most recent of which expired in 2015.
How is it affected by the U.S.-Canada trade war?
In 2017, the U.S. Commerce Department again concluded Canada's softwood imports were unfairly subsidized, and imposed duties.

These duties, which were amended in the summer of 2025, are known as anti-dumping duties — tariffs placed on imported goods when they are sold below market value — and countervailing duties, intended to cancel out tax breaks or subsidies a foreign government gives its own producers.
Taken together, they added 35 per cent to the cost of most Canadian softwood lumber in the U.S., according to Global Affairs Canada.
Separating fact from fiction in the U.S.-Canada softwood lumber trade war

Later that year, in October 2025, the Trump administration imposed an additional 10 per cent tariff on softwood lumber following a Section 232 national security investigation into imports of timber, lumber and their derivative products.

This was in response to a report by the U.S. commerce secretary, which found wood product imports are "resulting in the persistent threats of closures of wood mills and disruptions of wood product supply chains, among other things," Trump said in a September 2025 proclamation announcing the tariffs.

The October 2025 duties brought the total tariff level on most softwood lumber imported from Canada to 45 per cent. They also added 25 per cent duties to imports of upholstered furniture and kitchen cabinets and vanities.
Most recently, the Trump administration imposed another round of tariffs under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which took effect last week.

These 50 per cent tariffs are in response to what U.S. President Donald Trump called discriminatory Canadian treatment of U.S. motor vehicle, alcohol and dairy exports and apply to a wide range of products.

items: How 50% U.S. tariffs will impact the average British Columbian
Fact-checking the White House statement of facts about Canada

blocks.text: They don't apply to products, including those from softwood lumber, already subject to the Section 232 tariffs.

But they do hit a wide range of value-added wood products worth about $4 billion, including plywood, wood mouldings and particle board, according to Forest Products Association of Canada president and CEO Derek Nighbor.
What is the reaction?
U.S. reaction is divided, with the lumber industry largely supportive, and those forced to pay higher prices for building materials — such as the National Association of Homebuilders — opposed.
"Building material tariffs heighten market uncertainty, strain supply chains and increase construction costs," the association said in a statement.
"As the president continues to advance his tariff agenda, NAHB is urging the administration to exempt building materials in light of the ongoing housing affordability crisis."
The U.S. Lumber Coalition's van Heyningen applauded the tariffs.

"Our industry is not able to produce to their full capacity, and they're not able to expand, when Canada takes up an artificially high market share because they're dumping their excess lumber capacity into the U.S. market," he said in an interview.
"So it's very much a jobs issue for us as well."

The Forest Products Association of Canada's Nighbor argued the shortfall in Canadian lumber has been made up with imports from the European Union, which faces a much lower U.S. tariff rate of 15 per cent.
"Americans cannot meet their domestic needs," he said. "And right now, even though the Canadian numbers are down, it's the Europeans who have primarily benefited from that."

articles.title: King Haakon begins reign after turbulent year for Norwegian monarchy
articles.summary: Haakon becomes the king at a turbulent time for Norway's monarchy.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
King Haakon VIII has adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway"
ByJames Gregory and Mallory Moench
King Haakon VIII has inherited the Norwegian throne after the death of his father, Harald V. Many in Norway believe he has big shoes to fill.
King Harald was immensely popular with ordinary Norwegians, as shown by his consistent high polling and the outpouring of emotion in the lead-up to his death.
Haakon is the fourth king to head Norway's modern monarchy, since it was restored in 1905 after the country gained independence from Sweden.
Among his first duties as monarch, he led an extraordinary cabinet meeting where he announced his royal title and adopted his father's motto "Everything for Norway".
Many commentators believe he is well-placed to follow in his predecessors' footsteps.

As crown prince, Haakon worked closely with his father as he carried out his royal duties and in recent years was handed more responsibility, increasingly acting as regent while Harald was ill or absent.
"I am so lucky that Crown Prince Haakon is the one who will carry this forward," King Harald wrote of his son in his biography The King Tells.
Historian Trond Norén Isaksen tells the BBC that Haakon will be a different type of king to his father, but no less respected.
"King Harald... [was] very charismatic, he [had] a great sense of humour, which everyone appreciates, and Haakon is a bit more reserved, a bit more like his mother.

"But in recent years he has also become a bit more relaxed and opened up a bit and showed a bit more of his sense of humour... he has been pulling enormous weight for many years given his parents have become older and his wife has been ill."
Haakon is a great-great-great-grandson of Britain's Queen Victoria.
His daughter Ingrid Alexandra, 22, now becomes the crown princess and heir to the Norwegian throne.

blocks.caption: Image caption, At the age of 22, Ingrid Alexandra becomes Norway's crown princess

blocks.text: At the age of 22, Ingrid Alexandra becomes Norway's crown princess
Haakon was ahead of his older sister, Princess Märtha Louise, in the line of succession.
The constitution was changed in 1990 to give women the right to inherit the throne, so Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra is in line to be Norway's first female head of state since the 15th Century.
Haakon has become the king at a turbulent time for Norway's royal family.
The monarchy remains broadly popular among Norwegians and has been long praised for its modern outlook.
But in recent years it has been beset by scandal.

Only this year, Haakon's wife Mette-Marit, now Queen of Norway, has apologised for several years of ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and her son has been convicted of rape in a high-profile trial. Marius Borg Høiby, who was born from an earlier relationship, is appealing against the conviction.
Born in 1973, King Haakon is the youngest child of the late king and Queen Sonja.
By Haakon's own admission, he struggled at times to accept his royal status in his early years.
"Yes, I was a royal, but I did not want to talk about it... ​At school it made me anxious," he wrote in his 2023 autobiography, recalling his days in a state primary school in the 1980s.
He became crown prince in 1991 at the tender age of 17, following the death of his grandfather King Olav V.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Three generations of monarch at the family's Skaugum estate in 1982 - King Olav V, with the young Prince Haakon and then-Crown Prince Harald

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Three generations of monarch at the family's Skaugum estate in 1982 - King Olav V, with the young Prince Haakon and then-Crown Prince Harald
Unusually for a royal, he was educated at local state schools before embarking upon a four-year-long naval career, graduating from the Norwegian Naval Academy in 1995.
He decided not to follow his father and grandfather to Oxford University, instead flying to California to enrol at the University of Berkeley, where he studied political science.
Soon after his return to Norway, Haakon met his now-wife Mette-Marit at a music festival in her home city of Kristiansand in 1999.
She was dubbed by the press as the Cinderella of Kristiansand - a reference to her humble beginnings.
"What we two found together was so strong that I could not let it go," the then-Crown Prince Haakon said of Mette-Marit ahead of their wedding in 2001.
But their relationship was not without controversy and there was a fierce public debate in Norway from the moment Haakon first announced they were dating.

Some commentators even warned at the time that their relationship could spell the end of the Norwegian monarchy, with comparisons being made to the infamous union between American divorcee Wallis Simpson and British King Edward VIII which led to his abdication in 1936.
Queen Mette-Marit was not the first commoner to marry into the Norwegian royal family - the late King Harald had already broken with tradition by marrying Queen Sonja three decades earlier.
She was, however, a single mother to a four-year-old child whose father had served time for a conviction of cocaine possession.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Crown Princess Sonja, Princess Märtha Louise, Prince Haakon and Crown Prince Harald at Skaugum in 1987

blocks.text: Crown Princess Sonja, Princess Märtha Louise, Prince Haakon and Crown Prince Harald at Skaugum in 1987

The royal couple's co-habitation in an Oslo flat had also drawn criticism from the conservative Lutheran Church of Norway - though polls from the time showed most ordinary Norwegians did not care about either.
What many Norwegians did question, though, was whether her former party lifestyle was one compatible with that of someone married to the future king.

In an emotional interview three days before their marriage, Mette-Marit publicly apologised for her "wild past" and condemned drug use after reports that drugs were taken at parties she attended in Oslo during the 1990s.
She did not say whether she had taken them herself.
It was seen as something of a turning point. She won the affection of ordinary Norwegians and for years has been seen as the embodiment of a modern monarchy capable of shaking up convention.
The couple have two children together, Ingrid and Prince Sverre Magnus.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Haakon and Mette-Marit married in August 2001

blocks.text: Haakon and Mette-Marit married in August 2001
In her new role as crown princess, she took up popular causes including support for people with HIV and promoting literacy.
Her diagnosis with pulmonary fibrosis in 2018 also led to widespread public sympathy.

Haakon has said Mette-Marit helped him come out of his shell and described her as an emotional counterweight to his analytical mind. "I am not very good socially," he wrote. "Mette is a natural talent. She can go into a room and get along with everyone."
But in recent times, Haakon's family has come under increasingly heavy public scrutiny and criticism.
Marius Borg Høiby's rape conviction hangs over the family. One of women was raped on Haakon's estate at Skaugum outside Oslo.
Høiby has always been treated as one of the family, although the royal house has repeatedly stressed he is not a royal.
Days before his trial began, documents were released revealing Mette-Marit's frequent contact with late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She later apologised to King Harald and Queen Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement", adding in a national TV interview that she wished she had never met him.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Haakon's family affairs have been the subject of media and public scrutiny in recent times

blocks.text: Haakon's family affairs have been the subject of media and public scrutiny in recent times
Several polls conducted earlier this year found nearly half of Norway's population felt the crown princess could not become queen, even though it was always bound to happen.
Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant, eight years after her initial diagnosis.
Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and the new king will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.

Caroline Vagle, royal correspondent for Se og Hør magazine, says in regards to Epstein the most important thing the royal family can do is be "completely open about what actually happened, and not allow public speculation to take on a life of its own".
"But I also don't think we should overestimate the impact of one or two difficult cases," she says.
"What will ultimately matter is how the royal family handles them, and how Haakon and the next generation manage to build on the trust that Harald has earned over a lifetime."
Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, believes the scandals will be challenging but Haakon is "very much ready for the task".
"I'm sure that in the future he will be respected and loved, similar to King Haakon VII, King Olav V and also King Harald V."
Haakon's reign begins in the backdrop of these scandals, and how he navigates them might come to define his monarchy.

articles.title: Watch: Why rescuers fear new barrier lake could cause another Nepal-Tibet flood
articles.summary: Laura Bicker explains how a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border is raising fears of a second flood.

blocks.text: China has warned there is a "high risk" that a lake which formed after the recent landslide near the Nepal-Tibet border may breach its banks, causing a second flood downstream.
The warning comes after Wednesday's deadly flash flood in the same area which scientists say was triggered by the collapse of a mountain glacier into a river.
China correspondent Laura Bicker explains.

articles.title: Nepal-Tibet flood rescue efforts resume after being halted by overflowing lake
articles.summary: Risk of fresh flooding had forced rescue teams to withdraw as residents rushed up hills to escape possible river surge
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Bidur, Sam Jones and agencies

blocks.text: Rescuers searching for survivors of deadly flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have resumed their efforts after suspending operations when a debris dam burst its bank on Friday, increasing the risk of fresh flooding.

Residents in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, on the border with Tibet, were seen rushing up hillsides ⁠on Friday to escape a possible surge in the river, ⁠according to witnesses. Fears of another flood came as authorities in Nepal and China said that at least 543 people had been killed in the disaster.

blocks.caption: Barrier lake forms at base of mountains near Nepal border

blocks.text: More than 500 foreign citizens were among 826 people missing in Nepal, police and tourism ⁠officials said, including 177 from India, 90 from the US, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 25 from Canada. Chinese state media said at least 558 were missing on the Tibet side of the border, of whom at least 260 were foreign nationals.
The flood on Wednesday had destroyed power stations, roads and bridges along a route that links Kathmandu with Lhasa in Tibet and is ⁠popular with trekkers and pilgrims.

The Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported that a lake formed by piles of debris from the mudslide had begun overflowing on Friday, sending water towards the area where rescue teams were headed, and forcing a brief pause in operations.

Rescue efforts in Bidur, the capital of the Nuwakot district in Bagmati province, Nepal, were disrupted on Friday morning as the the Trishuli River began to rise again after the lake near the China border burst its banks.
Rescue workers were moved from the area and people who had tried to return to what remained of their homes were told to evacuate again immediately.

Bidur, once a bustling town on the banks of the Trishuli, now lies in ruins. Most homes were washed away when a tide of mud, rocks and debris surged down the river valley early on Wednesday. Survivors described clinging to buildings and trees as the water rushed over them.

The mangled concrete remains of a bank, a government office and an ATM booth were among the few structures left standing, although they were submerged in mud. Officials said there were still bodies inside the buildings but it was too dangerous to recover them.
Nearby, local people gathered along the muddy road, calling out for lost relatives and trying to dig out what was left of their belongings.

Most areas battered by flash floods remained accessible only by army helicopter. At the Bidur army camp, where much of the rescue effort was being coordinated, rescue and military helicopters flew in and out every five minutes, bringing in dozens of traumatised victims. Many said that in a matter of minutes, the floods had taken their loved ones, their homes and everything they owned.
The international community is scrambling to get aid to flood-stricken parts of Nepal and Tibet.

blocks.caption: Sludge inundates homes after flash floods in Nuwakot district. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Nepal has said it does not yet need foreign assistance as the search-and-rescue operation – complicated by the destruction of dozens of bridges and miles of roads across the mountainous region – continues.

“The offer for help is natural,” Lok Bahadur Chhetri, a spokesperson for Nepal’s foreign ministry, said on Friday. “Our security agencies ‌are doing the search and rescue operation. For now we don’t require such help.”

The Kathmandu Post reported that India, China, the US, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh had asked the government to allow their search-and-rescue teams to assist in the operation.
after newsletter promotion

Dinesh Bhattarai, a former Nepali ⁠ambassador to the UN in Geneva, said the government’s reluctance to ​accept foreign assistance may ​be linked to sensitivities over ​Rasuwa district and its border with China’s Tibet region.
“They may have thought about ​the locational sensitivity ‌of the region and ​decided not to ​accept foreign teams,” Bhattarai told Reuters.
But Chhetri said Nepal’s own rescue teams were handling the operation and the decision to refuse foreign assistance had nothing to do with sensitivities involving China.

Scant information has emerged from Chinese authorities about the scale of the destruction in Tibet, the most tightly controlled part of China even under normal circumstances. Only brief, state-controlled media reports about the floods have been allowed to circulate in China and the authorities have confirmed only three deaths there. Chinese reports have focused on rescue efforts.
In Nepal earlier on Friday, army helicopter rescue teams were working to free about 100 people trapped in a tunnel at a flooded hydropower project.
“Our focus is in search and rescue of people … some people are trapped in the tunnel of Trishuli 3A hydropower project,” said the Nepal army spokesperson, Raja Ram Basnet.

“Two helicopters have been dispatched but it is challenging because it is tough to even locate the entry points of the tunnel. Relief efforts are also under way to provide the rescued people what they need.”
The prime minister’s office said the army was working in challenging conditions and had rescued 350 workers and local people who were trapped in the tunnel.

Rescue teams reported finding bodies hundreds of miles downstream from the disaster zone in the Chitwan district of Nepal, near the Tibetan border. Dozens of injured people were transported to Kathmandu for advanced medical care and more than 100 people were rescued by Nepali army personnel in helicopters.
CCTV said 499 Chinese nationals and 555 foreigners had been transported out of the disaster zone as of Friday.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: Why Germany's military is betting on gamers
articles.summary: For the past 10 years, the German armed forces — the Bundeswehr — have been represented at Gamescom, Cologne's video game trade fair. They've been criticized for trying to draw more young people into…

image.caption: The Bundeswehr will once again be represented at the Gamescom video game trade fair in Cologne in 2026Image: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: Gamescom, which runs from August 26-30 in Cologne, is promoted as the world's largest video game trade show.

Last year, two-thirds of its non-industry visitors were male, with over 40% of them between the ages of 16 and 25. Those are precisely the young people the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, is trying to reach as it urgently seeks to expand its ranks.

Germany's military aims to have 260,000 active-duty soldiers by 2035. The German government has supplied hundreds of billions of euros to modernize the country's armed forces. Defense has become a priority for Germany in the face of the current global security situation.
Career advice in camouflage
The Bundeswehr set up shop at Gamescom for the first time in 2016. It's been back every year since.

A brand-new, olive-green Caracal off-road vehicle is one of the main attractions. Alongside it are laptops belonging to the Bundeswehr's Center for Cyber Operations — tasked with cyber defense, among other responsibilities.
Under a watchful eye, visitors can try their hand at hacking.

blocks.caption: The Caracal off-road vehicle is a popular photo opportunity at the Bundeswehr boothImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: At another station, visitors can put on VR headsets to get a glimpse into the working life of a soldier aboard a naval vessel. Pilots, aircraft mechanics and air traffic controllers present their professions in a 3D experience. Elsewhere, several fit mountain infantry soldiers stand beside a pull-up bar, where visitors are invited to test their strength.

New this year is a career lounge where interested visitors can have what the Bundeswehr is calling "career counseling sessions." The atmosphere is positive, with soldiers promoting their jobs without being pushy, taking time to answer questions from visitors — who have primarily come to Gamescom to have fun, meet friends and play the latest games.
Do gamers make good soldiers?

A representative study by Germany's Bitkom digital association found that one in five people found it likely that video and computer games teach skills that could be useful in wartime — training reaction speed and problem-solving, for instance. However, being a good gamer doesn't necessarily make for a good soldier.

blocks.caption: Lieutenant General Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel ManagementImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: "We need people who are comfortable with technology," Lt. Gen. Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel Management, told DW. "What we don't want are people who think we're playing an ego shooter or some kind of shooting game. That doesn't do justice to the seriousness of the situation at all. War isn't a game. As a soldier and a general, it is important to me that people understand the seriousness of what we do."

For Sieger, educating people about the Bundeswehr and the range of careers it offers is a central reason for having a booth at Gamescom. "We're an integral part of our country's safety net. We have to simply be here and show what it means to stand up for the freedom of our country, be that as a soldier or a civilian."
Criticism of Bundeswehr presence
The Bundeswehr is represented alongside many other employers in the gaming trade show's Job Area, including Germany's federal police, retailer Edeka and software company DATEV.

Gamescom is, however, still a video game trade show — and not everyone is comfortable with the Bundeswehr getting close to the gaming world. The German Peace Society — United War Resisters has criticized the Bundeswehr presence at Gamescom, along with booths operated by Germany's foreign intelligence service and defense companies such as Airbus and Rheinmetall.

blocks.caption: 'Level Up for Your Career': Peace activists criticize the Bundeswehr's use of gaming jargonImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: Peace campaigner Marius Pletsch says the Bundeswehr uses inappropriate slogans, designed to appeal specifically to gamers, and distorts the image of military service.

"We think it's wrong to lure young people to the booth by appealing to their sense of adventure. We don't think the Bundeswehr should be represented at a trade show that is primarily about video games and leisure to boost its personnel numbers," he told DW.
For two days, the peace organization will have a booth outside the trade show exhibition halls, providing information about conscientious objection to military service.
Bundeswehr: Not just any job
"Being a soldier isn't a normal job," the peace initiative said in a statement.
Lt. Gen. Sieger uses similar terms, but puts it somewhat differently: "Being a soldier isn't a job like any other. We put our lives on the line for the security of our people."

He reaches a different conclusion than the peace advocates, though. "It would be downright negligent for an organization responsible for our country's security not to be an inherent part of society," Sieger said. "As an inherent part of society and a modern employer, of course we have our rightful spot here in the Job Area, just as we have over recent years."
What do young Gamescom visitors make of the Bundeswehr's presence?

"Morally questionable, but a good employer," said Dennis, a 22-year-old computer science student, although he said the Bundeswehr wasn't for him. Dominik, 26, said he was pleased that the German military was represented at Gamescom. "You can actually have a pretty good conversation with them. They're all very nice," he said. He said he may even consider working for the Bundeswehr's cyber defense division.
This article was originally written in German.
Hooked on video gaming

articles.title: China warns of high flood risk from lake formed by mudslide: state media
articles.summary: BEIING, China – Chinese authorities warned that an artificial lake formed after a mudslide hit the China-Nepal border faces a “high risk of breaching and sending floodwaters downstream,”…

blocks.text: BEIING, China – Chinese authorities warned that an artificial lake formed after a mudslide hit the China-Nepal border faces a “high risk of breaching and sending floodwaters downstream,” according to state media.

“According to forecasts, inflows into the lake could reach about 3 million cubic meters over the next three days amid continued rainfall, increasing the risk of a breach that could send floodwaters downstream and potentially cause further damage in areas including Gyirong Port and elsewhere downstream,” state news agency Xinhua reported late Thursday./dp

articles.title: Norway's King Harald dies aged 89: A beloved monarch buffeted by family crises
articles.summary: The late king, who reigned for 35 years, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and was widely loved by Norwegians.

blocks.text: Watch: A look back at the King who broke with tradition
Norway's King Harald V has died at the age of 89, after he was taken to hospital last week for treatment for a rare blood condition.
The palace in Oslo said he passed away peacefully at 06:35 local time (04:35 GMT) on Friday at the national hospital in Oslo.

The royal flag on the roof of the palace has been lowered to half-mast and a period of national mourning has been declared leading up to the day of his funeral. Crowds of mourners have streamed to the royal palace to lay flowers and flags.
Harald was the nation's first king born there since the 14th Century. He has been succeeded by his son Haakon, 53, who will hold an extraordinary council of state with the government later on Friday.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Harald was Norway's first king born in Norway since the 14th Century

blocks.text: Image source, Anwar Hussein/Getty Images
Harald was Norway's first king born in Norway since the 14th Century

King Charles III sent his "most heartfelt condolences" at the death of his "dear cousin" - who was a second cousin to Queen Elizabeth II - while King Carl XVI Gustaf of Sweden remembered "a good friend to me, my family and to Sweden", wishing his godson Haakon "success and good fortune".

After 35 years on the throne, Harald will be remembered as a popular and reforming figure who modernised the monarchy, broke with tradition by marrying a commoner and served as a unifying figure at Norway's most difficult moments.
Royal observers say he was down-to-earth, respected and beloved, describing him as a "grandfather" of the nation and the "People's king" - a title also used by his father King Olav V.

During his reign, the Norwegian monarchy became more egalitarian and transparent about the royal family's finances and health matters, Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen, historian and TV2 royal correspondent, told the BBC.

Tove Taalesen, royal correspondent for Nettavisen, described the late king as "one of us", while Caroline Vagle, royal expert for Se og Hør magazine, said he had "always been very close to the people".
"He has never been afraid to show emotion, humour or vulnerability, and that has made him very human."

blocks.caption: People and children gather in a row alongside flowers and flags on the ground.

blocks.text: Image source, REUTERS/Dylan Martinez
In the wake of the 2011 bomb and gun attacks on Oslo and the island of Utøya, Harald appealed to Norwegians to support each other and not "let fear take over".

More recently, Harald and his family faced health challenges and scandal, especially over his daughter-in-law Mette-Marit's association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and her son Marius Borg Høiby's conviction for rape.
He is survived by his wife of almost 58 years, Queen Sonja, their daughter Princess Märtha Louise, their son, the new King Haakon, and six grandchildren.

blocks.caption: Image caption, King Harald and Queen Elizabeth II were second cousins

blocks.text: Image source, Dominic Lipinski/PA Wire
King Harald and Queen Elizabeth II were second cousins
Harald was born on 21 February 1937 on the Skaugum estate near Oslo. He was three when dictator Adolf Hitler ordered the Nazi German invasion of Norway early in World War Two.
Harald's mother fled with her children across the border to Sweden, and they travelled to the US on the invitation of President Franklin D Roosevelt.

Prince Harald returned with his family to Norway at the end of the war and completed his school and compulsory military service. He became crown prince in 1957, studying social science, history and economics at Balliol College in Oxford from 1960 to 1962.

He met Sonja Haraldsen, the daughter of a businessman, at a party, but the crown prince had to wait nine years before he was allowed to marry her. Eventually he told his father that if he could not marry Sonja, he would stay single, King Harald once told Norway's public broadcaster, external.
His father finally gave his consent and the couple wed in Oslo Cathedral on 29 August 1968.
Harald's choice paved the way for his own two children to marry commoners too, and for Vagle, that "helped bring an end to a very male-dominated royal family".

blocks.caption: Image caption, (L-R) Prince Sverre Magnus, the new King Haakon, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Queen Sonja and King Harald of Norway attend Norwegian Constitution Day at the Royal Palace in Oslo in May

blocks.text: Image source, Per Ole Hagen/Getty Images
(L-R) Prince Sverre Magnus, the new King Haakon, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, Queen Sonja and King Harald of Norway attend Norwegian Constitution Day at the Royal Palace in Oslo in May
When his father became ill in 1990, the then-crown prince became regent. Harald then ascended to the throne when Olav died on 17 January 1991.
The new king came into his own around 2000, according to historian Trond Norén Isaksen, growing from a shy man into someone much more open and empathetic.

In July 2011, Harald faced his greatest challenge yet as king, when neo-Nazi Anders Breivik murdered eight people with a car bomb in Oslo before moving onto a youth camp on the island of Utøya, where he shot dead 69 others, most of them teenagers.

He gave a televised address the next day, and weeks later he delivered a speech, empathising with the victims and their families as a father, grandfather, husband and king. On the verge of tears, his voice quivered and broke.
"I can only imagine the depth of your pain. As king of this nation, I feel for each and every one of you," he said.
Looking back, historian Ole-Jørgen Schulsrud-Hansen said: "I think that moment has been burned into our minds of what a monarchy should be."

blocks.caption: A picture taken on August 29, 1968 shows Norway's Crown Prince Harald and Sonja Haraldsen waving as they leave in their car the Oslo Cathedral during their wedding ceremony.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
In 2016, the king made headlines again by giving a, external speech, external supporting diversity of religion, ethnicity and sexual orientation.

He said Norwegians were from "Afghanistan, Pakistan and Poland, from Sweden, Somalia and Syria", that they "believe in God, Allah, the Universe and nothing", and that they "are girls who love girls, boys who love boys, and girls and boys who love each other".

The king was also a keen athlete and environmentalist - one of the initiators of the Norwegian branch of the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), who served as president of the Norwegian chapter for 20 years.
He was such an accomplished sailor, he represented Norway three times at the Olympics.

When Crown Prince Haakon married Mette-Marit in 2001, the king and queen welcomed her four-year-old son from a previous relationship. Høiby was treated as one of the family, but the royal house later stressed that he was never a royal.

The king's daughter Princess Märtha Louise initially married a Norwegian writer before controversially remarrying an American self-styled shaman in 2024. The couple's business activities eventually led to her halting her royal duties.

blocks.caption: Image caption, King Harald welcomed the Norwegian national football team to the palace after they made it to the quarter-finals of the World Cup for the first time this year

blocks.text: Image source, NTB/AFP via Getty Images
King Harald welcomed the Norwegian national football team to the palace after they made it to the quarter-finals of the World Cup for the first time this year

While some Norwegians may have felt Harald was too lenient with his family's controversial life decisions, Vagle believes he had "shown himself to be someone who puts talking things through ahead of issuing harsh instructions".
As the king's health declined, he permanently reduced his public engagements in April 2024.

More recently, he was treated with cortisone for a rare blood condition, haemolytic anaemia, which causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced. He entered hospital on 17 August and his son became regent, assuming his activities.
This year alone the Norwegian royal family has faced compounded personal health challenges and scandals.

The rape trial of Høiby, convicted of multiple offences in June, hung over the royal family for many months. He has now appealed against a four-year jail term and appeared at Harald's bedside shortly before he died.
Days before the trial began, documents were released revealing his mother Mette-Marit's frequent contact with the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Harald and Sonja regularly supported Norway's teams at the Olympics

blocks.text: Harald and Sonja regularly supported Norway's teams at the Olympics
She later apologised to Harald and Sonja for her three-year friendship with Epstein and admitted to "poor judgement".
Two days after her son's trial came to an end, Mette-Marit received a lung transplant. She had been diagnosed with a rare form of pulmonary fibrosis eight years prior.
Her doctors will not declare her stable until a year after the transplant, and King Haakon will face a difficult period of succession as he continues to support her.
The crises surrounding the monarchy have had an effect on its popularity. One poll for newspaper Aftenposten found that support had dropped from 72% in 2024 to 54%.

blocks.caption: Family tree of King Haakon's family

blocks.text: Other polls suggested almost half of Norwegians believed Mette-Marit could no longer become queen, although Haakon is now highly likely to say she will.
However, Vagle said criticism was rarely directed at the late king personally, leaving her with the impression that "everyone has loved King Harald".
"When things go wrong in the royal family, people tend to blame anyone but the king," Isaksen remarked.

Haakon has faced questions about the turbulence surrounding his own household that will "follow him into his position as a king", according to Taalesen, however she believes he has shown leadership and dealt with recent events well.
The royal family's main strategy has been to separate itself from Høiby's trial, and Schulsrud-Hansen believes that has largely succeeded.
Although there may be further scrutiny over the Epstein files, the focus for Norwegians now will be on remembering a "greatly beloved king" and supporting his son.

articles.title: Norway's King Harald dies at 89
articles.summary: King Harald is succeeded by his son, who has taken the name King Haakon VIII, with Crown Princess Mette-Marit now queen.

image.caption: Prince Harald was born on 21 February 1937Image: Fredrik Varfjell/NTB/AFP

blocks.text: Norway's King Harald, Europe's oldest living monarch, has died at 89, the royal court said on Friday.
The monarch had been receiving treatment for a rare blood condition, hemolytic anemia, at Oslo University Hospital since mid-August.
His son, Prince Haakon automatically becomes King Haakon VIII, with the Norwegian Royal Court also confirming on Thursday that his wife, Mette-Marit, will become queen.
The Norwegian monarch is head of state, but has a largely ceremonial and representative role.
What the palace said about King Harald's death

"It is with deep sadness that we announce that His Majesty King Harald passed away today. King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday, August 28 at 6:35 a.m.," the palace said in a statement.
Harald's condition worsened over the last few days, and his wife, Queen Sonja, and son, Haakon, canceled all their engagements to be at his bedside.

Harald, who had been king since 1991, suffered a series of health problems in recent years and had increasingly scaled back his official duties. However, he repeatedly ruled out abdicating, saying the oath he had taken on becoming king "lasts for life."

blocks.caption: People gathered for a night vigil at the Palace Square in OsloImage: Odd Andersen/AFP

blocks.text: Hundreds of well-wishers gathered outside the royal palace in Oslo overnight, holding a vigil as the king's condition deteriorated.
King's body moves from hospital to palace
A motor procession carrying King Harald's casket left Oslo University Hospital for the royal palace, as per television images.
Thousands of people have gathered outside the palace to pay their respects to the late king and bid him farewell. They laid down flowers, cards, cuddly toys and Norwegian flags.
"He was the king of the people," mourner Kristoffer Hamre told AFP.
The government has announced a period of national mourning, and flags were flown at half mast on Friday.
"I think he has been such a down-to-earth king who has cared about all of us, and the words he always uses when he gives a speech are so wise and so valuable," Vigdis Haug, 65, told AFP.

blocks.caption: Despite the rain, people queued the streets in wait of King Harald's funeral cortegeImage: Dylan Martinez/REUTERS

blocks.text: Will King Haakon VIII be crowned?

Haakon VIII will take his oath of allegiance to the constitution in a ceremony scheduled for next Tuesday. He is due to deliver a short address that will be broadcast on TV, with parliament saying the address will focus on the monarch's limited power.
Norway no longer stages a traditional coronation.
"King Haakon will promise and swear to govern Norway in accordance with the Constitution and law of the land," President of the Storting [Norway's Parliament], Masud Gharahkhani, said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Representatives of different faiths made their way to the Royal Palace in Oslo to pay their respectsImage: Björn Larsson Rosvall/TT/IMAGO

blocks.text: World leaders, royals pay tribute
Britain's King Charles expressed his condolences for Harald's death, paying tribute to a "towering figure" who guided his country with "warmth and humility."
Norway's prime minister, Jonas Gahr Stoere, said Harald demonstrated an "unwavering faith in the Norwegian people" and "helped us to see the best in ourselves – and in one another."
Swedish King Carl XVI Gustaf said the late king had "been a good friend" and would be "mourned by many in our country."
"I wish my dear Godson Haakon, who now succeeds his father as head of state, success and good fortune in the important role that lies ahead of ‌him," he added.

King Frederik and Queen Mary of Denmark praised Harald's "warm personality and rock-solid calm," saying he "combined duty and responsibility with presence and humanity. He was loved like few others and will be missed by many."

blocks.caption: Flags were flown at half mast at Amalienborg Palace in Denmark following King Harald's deathImage: Ida Marie Odgaard/Ritzau Scanpix/REUTERS

blocks.text: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described him as "a true European and a lifelong servant of his people."
"In moments of joy and sorrow, he brought Norwegians together," she said.
NATO chief Mark Rutte said Harald "showed himself to be a dedicated leader. His own military roots made him a champion of the Norwegian military and a long-time friend of NATO."
How will King Harald be remembered?

Born in 1937, Harald became Norway's first prince to be born in the country in more than 500 years. As a child, he fled Norway with his mother and sisters following the Nazi invasion in 1940, spending much of World War II in the United States.

Harald succeeded his father, King Olav V, in January 1991 and went on to modernize the Norwegian monarchy during more than 35 years on the throne. He was widely praised for his response to the 2011 far-right terrorist attacks that killed 77 people and later drew attention for speeches stressing tolerance, diversity and LGBTQ+ equality.
The king's death comes after a turbulent period for Norway's royal family.

blocks.caption: King Harald V waves during a 1991 coronation tour after his accession to the throneImage: Lise Åserud/NTB/picture alliance

blocks.text: Crown Princess [nonw Queen] Mette-Marit has faced scrutiny over her past correspondence with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced in June to four years in prison after being convicted of two rapes and dozens of other offenses, including violence against a former partner. He has appealed the verdict.

articles.title: Norway holds its breath as King Harald’s health deteriorates
articles.summary: OSLO, Norway – Norway’s royal family gathered Thursday at King Harald V’s bedside in hospital, while hundreds paid respects outside the palace, after the court announced that the…

blocks.text: OSLO, Norway – Norway’s royal family gathered Thursday at King Harald V’s bedside in hospital, while hundreds paid respects outside the palace, after the court announced that the 89-year-old monarch’s health condition was “extremely serious”.

Queen Sonja and Harald’s 53-year-old son Crown Prince Haakon, who is acting as regent, have cancelled all royal engagements and spent much of Thursday at his side at Oslo University Hospital along with other family members.
The palace said late Thursday afternoon the king’s condition was “unchanged”, shortly after Haakon, his wife Mette-Marit and their two adult children were seen leaving the hospital.
Norwegian broadcaster NRK then on Thursday evening reported that Haakon and Mette-Marit had returned to the hospital a second time.

Europe’s oldest reigning monarch has been in hospital in Oslo since August 17 suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
“His Majesty the King’s health condition is extremely serious,” the palace said, providing no specific details.

Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle bracelet after a rape conviction in June that he has appealed, was also seen leaving the hospital after a more than four-hour visit, as was the king’s sister.
Hundreds of people gathered outside the palace in central Oslo, with many laying down bouquets of flowers for the broadly popular king in front while staying for hours.
“He is Norway’s grandfather,” 57-year-old Trine Bakke Jord told AFP, adding that she appreciated that he was so “down-to-earth” while wiping away tears.
Kaspara Bolstad, 24, told AFP Harald had been “a very steady and warm king”.

“I think the entire Norwegian people see him as a role model and as someone who brings people together. Whether you’re for or against the monarchy, I think he’s well-liked across the board,” she said.
Magnus Skaugseth, 27, agreed, lauding the king’s “inclusive” side.
“When there is so much division and polarization, he was a pillar pointing in the opposite direction.”

Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, who cancelled a work trip to Germany on Thursday following the update on the king’s health, told AFP he was “deeply affected” by the news of the king’s health condition.
“I stand together with the entire country as we now send our warmest thoughts to the king and the rest of the royal family,” he said.
Church of Norway bishops also cut short a study visit to Rome where they had met Pope Leo and were to return to Norway Thursday, according to Christian newspaper Vart Land.

Caroline Vagle, a royal reporter for the Se og Hor magazine, called Thursday’s statement from the palace “dramatic”, noting that it was usually “very restrained in its communication about the King’s health, even when he has been hospitalised or undergone treatment.”
“There is also an entire nation that is deeply concerned and saddened. King Harald is a much-loved king,” she told AFP.
The monarch was admitted to Oslo University Hospital due to fluid retention from cortisone treatment he was receiving.
The palace said on Sunday that he was receiving antibiotics for a bacterial infection in his blood and that he had responded to the treatment./dp

articles.title: FM says ‘difficult’ to locate missing Australians in Nepal
articles.summary: SYDNEY, Australia – Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong acknowledged Friday it was “difficult” to locate citizens out of contact in Nepal following deadly flooding. The number…

blocks.text: SYDNEY, Australia – Australia’s Foreign Minister Penny Wong acknowledged Friday it was “difficult” to locate citizens out of contact in Nepal following deadly flooding.
The number of Australian nationals missing following the floods has risen to 39, Wong told the Today Show.
“We know many people have been killed, many people are missing and the scale of the disaster is quite horrific,” Wong said.
Australia’s foreign ministry has about 20 people on the ground in Nepal, she said, and will “build on that over the coming days”.
The country will spend Aus$5 million ($3.6 million) on humanitarian assistance for flood relief, she added. /dp

articles.title: Trump orders Lake Ontario to be renamed ‘Lake America’
articles.summary: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump stepped up an escalating feud with Canada on Thursday, ordering that Lake Ontario — a body of water shared by both countries — be renamed…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON, United States — US President Donald Trump stepped up an escalating feud with Canada on Thursday, ordering that Lake Ontario — a body of water shared by both countries — be renamed “Lake America.”
Trump signed an executive order on the name change at the White House, further trolling Canada as the North American neighbors plunge deeper into a trade war.
“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.
Behind Trump’s desk were two maps of the US-Canada border — one with the words “Lake America” in red over the lake, and the other with the header “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater.”
Asked why he was targeting an ally for punishment instead of America’s adversaries, Trump replied: “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people.”
“People, oftentimes, they’ll ask me who’s the worst to deal with on trade? And I said that’s easy. Canada. They are the worst to trade with,” the 80-year-old Republican added.

Canada did not immediately comment but is unlikely to accept the renaming of Lake Ontario, the smallest of the five Great Lakes by surface area, which borders Canada’s Ontario province and New York state.
US-Canada trade talks collapsed at the eleventh hour last week, with Trump’s tariffs taking effect on Saturday.
Canada responded with tit-for-tat tariffs on Tuesday, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying: “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.”
The same day, Trump announced that he was giving “serious consideration” to changing the name to Lake America.
He then posted a TikTok video late Wednesday saying that he intended to do so after all.
‘Now all we need is an ocean’
The name change mirrors Trump’s unilateral altering of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America on his first day back in office in January 2025.
That change obliged the US federal government to refer to the gulf by the new designation, although Mexico has rejected any move to rename it and it lacks international recognition.

Trump said the name change was “something I’ve been thinking about for a long time, actually. As you know, we took something called the Gulf of Mexico, we changed it, and now it’s very routinely the Gulf of America.”
Trump also hinted at renaming oceans that border the United States.

“So, if you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean. So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both,” he said.

While Lake Ontario shares its name with the Canadian province, the name itself is derived from the indigenous Huron word “Ontari’io,” which means “great lake” or “beautiful water,” according to the National Museum of the Great Lakes.
Toronto, Canada’s largest city, sits on its northwestern shore.
During his second presidential term, Trump has irked a series of allies with his outlandish territorial claims, including that Canada should become the 51st US state.
Trump has also laid claim to Greenland, an autonomous territory of NATO ally Denmark, and talked about making Venezuela a state following the US capture of its leader Nicolas Maduro.
In recent days, he has also said that he will make the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman a US territory, despite the fact that the war with Tehran remains ongoing.

articles.title: Himalayan ‘tsunami’: Over 350 dead, 1,400 missing
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A Filipino was reported to be among the more than a thousand people missing in the flash floods and landslides that occurred on the Nepal-Tibet border, where the confirmed death…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A Filipino was reported to be among the more than a thousand people missing in the flash floods and landslides that occurred on the Nepal-Tibet border, where the confirmed death toll had reached at least 359 people as of Thursday.
The lone Filipino was on the initial record cited by the Nepal Tourism Board, though it was yet to be confirmed by the Philippine government at press time.
The tsunami-like rumble of water and mud struck villages and towns on the path of two rivers—Bhote Koshi and Trishuli—on Wednesday night.

A terrifying clip of surveillance video from the Chinese side of the frontier shows a massive wall of mud and debris crashing over a building several stories high on Wednesday morning, engulfing it as dozens of people ran for their lives below.
The surge swept away buses and cars like they were toys.
The US Geological Survey believes the disaster was caused by a glacial collapse that sent a flow of debris engulfing homes along the way.

blocks.caption: SWAMPED Local residents watch as a helicopter flies above houses lying deluged in sludge after flash floods at Devighat, Bidur municipality in Nepal’s Nuwakot district on Aug. 27 —AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: According to the Nepal Tourism Board, its preliminary record as of 2:45 p.m. on Thursday (Philippine time) showed 644 travelers reported missing in the affected areas, including one Filipino.
The agency gave no further details about the missing Filipino, saying the information was still being verified and crosschecked with travel agencies and other local authorities.

In Manila, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (Owwa) have started coordinating with officials in Nepal, as well as with the Filipino community, to determine the extent of the disaster’s impact on Filipinos, Palace press officer Claire Castro said.
Based on information from the DFA and Owwa, there are 128 Filipinos in Nepal, mostly women married to Nepalis. Among them are 18 overseas workers.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the disaster.
“The Philippines extends its deepest condolences to our friends in Nepal and to all those affected by the deadly flash flood yesterday,” Mr. Marcos said in a social media post.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to those who lost family, loved ones, and friends. Please accept our most heartfelt prayers for strength in this difficult time,” he added.
Wall of mud, debris

blocks.caption: Aerial views show houses inundated by mud and water in Nuwakot district—AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: The Nepali police on Thursday said they had recovered 162 bodies, as rescue teams rushed to find more than 1,400 people still missing.
Another 823 people, including 579 Nepali and foreign tourists, remained out of contact in Nepal, according to the country’s disaster agency.
Across the border, Chinese state media said the “mudslide disaster” at the Gyirong Port in Tibet claimed three lives while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, were still missing.
Raju Bhadel, 56, a businessman in Nepal’s Nuwakot district, recounted receiving a call from his brother-in-law in distress.
“They were crying and said their entire house had been swept away. Three family members were rescued, but his brother is still missing,” he said.
Also at Nuwakot, teacher Manok Mishra witnessed “nine trucks being swept away by the floods, including people.”

blocks.caption: Aerial views show houses inundated by mud and water in Nuwakot district—AFP PHOTOS

blocks.text: ‘Inland tsunami’
Rescuers waded through mud and sludge to look for survivors after floodwaters buried the lower floors of multistory buildings.
The foreigners out of contact included Indians, and others from Australia, Britain, Malaysia, the Netherlands, Portugal, South Africa, South Korea, and the United States, Nepal’s tourism board said.
Hiking company Himalayan Glacier told Agence France-Presse (AFP) 47 people from a group including two children were missing in Nepal.

The sudden rush of mud and debris was “like an inland tsunami, traveling nearly 170 kilometers down the Bhote Koshi valley into Central Nepal,” said environmental historian Ruth Gamble of La Trobe University in Australia.
“It is a popular route for international tourists traveling from Kathmandu to Lhasa,” she added.

blocks.caption: GRIEF A girl cries as she waits for news of relatives missing after flash floods in Bidur, Nepal, on Aug. 27. —AP

blocks.text: Rasuwa, in the north of Nepal, was the first district to be affected. But deaths have been reported from seven Nepali districts in total as the floodwaters raged through to Chitwan in the south, on the border with India.
The Nepali Army was carrying out flights and had rescued scores of people, while others living near the river in danger zones had been told to relocate.
Tibet government officials mobilized nearly 800 emergency workers and 150 vehicles as well as sniffer dogs and speed boats to help the rescue efforts, China’s state-run news agency Xinhua said.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said it was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers, and body bags.
Seismic event

blocks.caption: Himalayan ‘tsunami’: Over 350 dead, 1.4K missing

blocks.text: The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear in the hours after it occurred early Wednesday, but the US Geological Survey said it was a glacial collapse that caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
“This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake,” it said.

“Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.”
Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, increasing the risks of glacial lake floods and glacial collapses.
Qianggong Zhang, head of climate and environmental risks at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, warned of the potential for a second flood.
“With a blockage still lodged upstream on the Nepal-China border river, authorities warn a second flood may occur,” he told AFP. —With a report from AFP

articles.title: UN body calls for release of Cumpio, activists from arbitrary detention
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Human rights group Karapatan on Wednesday welcomed the findings of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (UN WGAD), which declared as arbitrary the detention…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Human rights group Karapatan on Wednesday welcomed the findings of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (UN WGAD), which declared as arbitrary the detention of Tacloban community journalist Frenchie Mae Cumpio, humanitarian worker Marielle Domequil and human rights worker Alexander Abinguña.
The UN WGAD stated its findings in its opinion report, which was released only recently and first adopted during its 105th session held from March 23 to April 1.

“The UN WGAD opinions reaffirm our position that the charges against Cumpio, Domequil and Abinguña are baseless and trumped-up, that their rights under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights were violated, and that their release from prison is long overdue,” Karapatan secretary general Cristina Palabay said in a statement.
The rights groups called for the release of the three, noting that they have been detained for more than six years following their arrest on Feb. 7, 2020.
Terrorism financing

Cumpio and Domequil were convicted in January by the Tacloban City Regional Trial Court for “terrorism financing” and sentenced to 12 to 18 years in prison. From the Tacloban City Jail, they were transferred in April to the Correctional Institute for Women in Mandaluyong City where they remain detained after their petition for bail was denied by the court. They have appealed their conviction before the Court of Appeals.

“The inordinate delay of the court proceedings that has prolonged their detention is an additional layer of injustice against the three. Their release should immediately be given due course,” Palabay said.
The UN WGAD found a lack of factual and legal basis for the criminal charges against the three, concluding that their deprivation of liberty was arbitrary.
It also determined that their detention stemmed from the exercise of their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association.
Based on the UN body’s report, the three have been targets of Red-tagging and accused of associating with the Communist Party of the Philippines and its armed wing, the New People’s Army.
It said the appropriate remedy would be the immediate release of Cumpio, Domequil and Abinguña, along with an enforceable right to compensation and other forms of reparation under international law.
Probe pushed

The UN WGAD also called for a full and independent investigation into the circumstances surrounding their arbitrary detention as it urged authorities to hold accountable those responsible for violating their rights.

In June, United Nations Special Rapporteur Irene Khan cautioned that freedom of expression is “under attack in multiple ways,” citing the case of Cumpio in her final report to the UN Human Rights Council. —WITH A REPORT FROM SHERIDAN DELFINO

articles.title: Iran, Qatar hold Hormuz talks as US blockade chokes Iran’s oil imports
articles.summary: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran’s top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a…

blocks.text: TEHRAN, Iran — Iran’s top diplomat met his Qatari counterpart on Thursday in Tehran for talks on the strategic Strait of Hormuz, as a US naval blockade squeezes oil supplies to Iran amid a domestic shortfall.

The visit by Qatar’s Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani follows a week of intense diplomacy in Iran involving separate meetings with Oman’s top diplomat and senior Pakistani officials seeking ways to end the Middle East war and reopen Hormuz.

It also comes as Washington threatens wider secondary sanctions against countries, banks and companies that continue doing business with Iran, part of a broader campaign it has called “economic asphyxiation.”
Iranian state television said Al Thani, who is also Qatar’s prime minister, had met with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without providing details.
In a statement after the talks, Al Thani said they focused on efforts to de-escalate tensions and boost security in the region.
“Qatar believes that dialogue and diplomacy remain the best way to overcome crises,” he wrote on X.
Qatar’s foreign ministry said they discussed the proposed framework for Hormuz between Iran and Oman.
“Talks stressed the importance of respecting freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law,” Al Thani added.
Alongside mediator Pakistan, Qatar had played a key role in securing an April ceasefire and June deal between Iran and the United States, but those deals have since collapsed.
Fuel shortage

Since war with the United States broke out on February 28, Iran has maintained tight control over Hormuz, a vital global energy conduit, with Washington imposing a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
On Wednesday, Iran’s Vice President Mohammad Jafar Ghaempanah said the blockade had prevented his country from importing enough gasoline to cover a shortfall in domestic production.
“Gasoline production is insufficient, and because of the US naval blockade, we cannot import it,” he was quoted by the official IRNA news agency as saying.
In recent days, many Iranians have been seen queuing outside gas stations. Presidential chief of staff Mohsen Haji-Mirzaei said gasoline quotas would be reviewed, without elaborating.
Iran, a major oil producer with some of the world’s cheapest fuel, has for years heavily subsidized gasoline, making changes to pricing politically sensitive.
As the US seeks to strangle Iran’s economy, Iranian officials have dismissed the measures as “failed policies” that will not force Tehran to change course.
“The country is in an all-out economic war,” said Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf in a statement carried by local media.
“We will see that the government … will defeat the enemy on this ground as well,” he added.
Even before the war, Iran’s economy was battered by decades of international sanctions and has long suffered from chronic inflation and a weakening currency.
Talks on Hormuz

Iran has for weeks been in talks with Oman, which also overlooks the Strait of Hormuz, over a framework agreement that would establish a “temporary corridor” for shipping and provide for clearing mines Tehran says were laid during the war.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Wednesday said the two countries had agreed on each country’s share of the waters and any revenues collected from managing the waterway.

Tehran has nonetheless insisted that the strait will not be reopened unless Washington meets its demands, including lifting its naval blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad and removing oil sanctions.
Since the war broke out, Iranian forces have required vessels to obtain permission to transit the waterway and struck ships that failed to comply.
Tehran has also sought to impose service fees on ships using the strait — a move strongly opposed by Washington and regional countries.
