The boat reportedly encountered strong winds and rough lake conditions while returning from a vaccination program and a meeting under the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps).

Six passengers died in the incident: Elvis Tiglao Pabalan, 33; Joanavie Mae Tiglao Pabalan (age not listed); Sally Serrano Dela Cruz, 29; Prince Lenard Serrano Dela Cruz, 1; Evelyn Yurik Lagman, 45; and Cedric Serrano Liwanag, 2.
Four survivors were identified as Rebecca Paana Sulit, 39; Palit Liwanag, 32; and Julian Pabalan Balario and Marqie Paanan Balario, whose ages were also not listed at press time.

The passengers are members of the Aeta community in Sitio Lumibao, an area across Mapanuepe Lake from the main part of Barangay Buhawen. Residents have to cross the lake by boat to reach the barangay proper./coa

articles.title: ‘Archival not a micromanager,’ says chief of staff Siasar
articles.summary: CEBU CITY, Philippines – Mayor Nestor Archival is not a micromanager but a hands-on leader who wants to know what is happening around Cebu City, his chief of staff Kenneth Siasar said Thursday, as he…

blocks.text: CEBU CITY, Philippines – Mayor Nestor Archival is not a micromanager but a hands-on leader who wants to know what is happening around Cebu City, his chief of staff Kenneth Siasar said Thursday, as he defended the mayor’s close involvement in a recent flood control cleanup.
This amid online criticism describing Archival as a “micromanager,” which he said partly stemmed from a photo showing the mayor personally sweeping during a cleanup operation.
“I do not know how to describe that one, because he is a kind of person man jud who wants to know what’s going on sa iyang surroundings,” Siasar said.
(He’s just the kind of person who really wants to know what’s going on in his surroundings.)

Siasar said Archival’s involvement in the cleanup should not automatically count as micromanagement, particularly because the operation addressed a drainage problem that had persisted for nearly two decades.
“May not be considered nga micromanagement at all kay nagpa-update man ka unsay going on. Tanan,” Siasar said.
(It may not be considered micromanagement at all because he is simply asking for updates on what is going on.)
Siasar cited a drainage cleanup conducted the previous Sunday as an example of Archival’s hands-on approach.
The mayor instructed the team to document the operation so residents could understand why flooding occurred in the area, Siasar said.
“Ang instruction sa mayor lang is, ‘Kenneth, ato ning videohan aron makahibaw ang mga tawo sa reason why nag-flood’,” he said.
(The mayor’s instruction was simply, ‘Let’s record this so people will know the reason why it floods’)
According to Siasar, the team found a drainage canal that had accumulated debris and had severely restricted water flow.
The canal, which measured about 2 meters deep, had narrowed to only about an inch of water passage in some portions, he said.
The cleanup crew used six tankers to remove about 30,000 units of accumulated material and hauled away three dump truckloads of garbage, Siasar said.
“Micro[management] ang perception sa public, but that was a long-term solution already for the people residing in that area,” he said.
(The public’s perception is that it is micromanagement, but that was already a long-term solution for the people residing in that area.)

articles.title: Nurse killed as waiting shed collapses in Catbalogan
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — A 35-year-old nurse died after a concrete slab from a waiting shed collapsed on him while he was waiting for a boat ride home in Sierra Island, Barangay Canhawan Gote, Catbalogan…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — A 35-year-old nurse died after a concrete slab from a waiting shed collapsed on him while he was waiting for a boat ride home in Sierra Island, Barangay Canhawan Gote, Catbalogan City, Samar, on Thursday afternoon.
The victim was identified as Kelvin Castro, 35, a Department of Health nurse assigned to the Catbalogan City Health Office and a resident of Purok 3, Barangay Canlapwas, Catbalogan City.
Police said Castro and his colleague, also a nurse at the City Health Office, had just completed a measles-rubella supplemental immunization activity in Barangay Canhawan Gote.
After the activity, the two went to the docking area for motorboats to wait for their ride back to Catbalogan City.
While waiting, Castro sat under a waiting shed when the structure suddenly collapsed, causing a concrete slab to fall directly on him.
Castro sustained multiple injuries to different parts of his body, particularly to his head.
Cañete, along with several residents in the area and daycare teachers from the City Social Welfare and Development Office, helped pull Castro from underneath the collapsed structure.
They immediately brought him to Samar Provincial Hospital for emergency medical treatment.
Doctors and other medical personnel performed resuscitation procedures upon his arrival, but despite their efforts, Castro was declared dead on arrival./coa

articles.title: Protesters set fire to migrant camp in Ceuta
articles.summary: The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish exclave in North Africa.

image.caption: Police had to intervene when protesters began setting fire to the parts of the campImage: Marcos Moreno/EUROPA PRES/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Protesters in Ceuta set fire to a migrant camp and clashed with police on Thursday. The unrest comes one month after a mass influx of migrants from Morocco to the Spanish enclave in North Africa.
Footage on Spanish television showed a group of demonstrators on a beach, throwing objects into the fire. Police pushed the protesters back while the migrants retreated to a pier.
Earlier on Thursday, a military vehicle was attacked with stones and other objects by about 70 people, a police spokesman in Ceuta told the AFP news agency.
Local protesters tried to stop Red Cross vehicles from reaching the beach to distribute food to migrants. People waving Spanish flags shouted "They should leave" and "Out with the Red Cross."

blocks.caption: Locals in Ceuta accuse the government of mishandling the situationImage: Marcos Moreno/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: How many migrants are still in Ceuta?
In July, more than 70,000 migrants entered Ceuta irregularly in the hope of reaching the European mainland.
While the vast majority of them have since returned to Morocco, several thousand remain in Ceuta, living on the streets or on the beach.
Spain's government in Madrid puts the number at below 7,000 while Ceuta officials say it's at least 10,000. Ceuta's population is about 84,000 people.
Growing pressure on Madrid

The Spanish government is under growing pressure over the situation in Ceuta. The conservative opposition is accusing left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez of failing to act and abandoning Ceuta's residents.

Madrid has recently moved to speed up efforts to identify the migrants and decide who will be sent back to Morocco. The government also approved extra funding to help unaccompanied minors entitled to special protection.
The crisis comes ahead of general elections next year and has deepened political divisions in Spain. The conservative opposition is calling for a tougher stance on migration.
The mass influx in July had also led to tension within the EU over how to respond to the situation in Ceuta.

articles.title: Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic dead
articles.summary: BELGRADE, Serbia — Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military chief who was convicted of war crimes for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, died in a hospital on Thursday, according to a…

blocks.text: BELGRADE, Serbia — Ratko Mladic, the former Bosnian Serb military chief who was convicted of war crimes for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, died in a hospital on Thursday, according to a United Nations international tribunal.

Mladic, who had suffered several strokes in recent months, was serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity after overseeing the Srebrenica slaughter, Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.
His conviction for wartime killings as the former Yugoslavia descended into carnage following the fall of communism led the media to dub him the “Butcher of Bosnia.”
The 1992-1995 war left around 100,000 people dead and 2.2 million displaced.
Mladic was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by former Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic.
Serbian state officials and Mladic’s family had appealed for his release due to his failing health, but those calls were rejected by the Hague tribunal.
A representative of the Mothers of Srebrenica victims’ association, reacting to Mladic’s death, told AFP that his name would always “symbolize genocide.”
“That will never be erased from his name,” said Sehida Abdurahmanovic, who believes her missing brother was among those killed in Srebrenica.
Srebrenica
In the war’s most infamous atrocity, Serb forces under Mladic’s command executed 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys who had sought shelter in Srebrenica, which was meant to be a UN-protected enclave.
Their bodies were dumped in mass graves, many of which were dug up and reburied in an attempt to hide the evidence.
The few who escaped told harrowing stories of murder, torture and rape by Bosnian Serb forces.
In November 1995, the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia (ICTY) indicted Mladic, who was dismissed from his post but evaded capture for another 16 years.
At first, he led a life of luxury, pampered by the military in Serbia, where some to this day see him as a hero.
But the pressure mounted on him after Milosevic fell from power in 2000. Mladic was finally arrested in May 2011 and transferred to The Hague.
He was convicted in 2017, with the life sentence upheld on appeal in 2021.
On the streets of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo, Hava Suljic told AFP she welcomed the news.
“I’m delighted to know there is one less war criminal walking around in this world,” Suljic, a Bosnian Muslim from Srebrenica, said.
But reactions in the Serb entity of divided Bosnia were in stark contrast.
Former Bosnian Serb leader Milorad Dodik said Mladic’s death had “hit hard” and that the Republika Srpska “will not forget his role,” the Serb statelet’s public broadcaster reported.
Locals who spoke with AFP in the Republika Srpska’s capital, Banja Luka, called Mladic the “greatest.”
“The greatest man has died, the greatest general of the Serbian people,” pensioner Dragan Beric said.
‘Epitome of evil’
Mladic was also found guilty of orchestrating a wider campaign of ethnic cleansing to drive Muslims and Bosnians out of key areas to create a so-called Greater Serbia.
The tribunal said at the time that the crimes committed were “among the most heinous known to humankind.” Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra’ad al Hussein described him as “the epitome of evil.”
But many Serbs continued to revere a military commander who portrayed himself as a “simple man” whom fate had chosen to protect his people.
His age has always been a matter of dispute. He claimed to have been born in March 1943, but the tribunal listed his birth year as 1942. Local media widely reported that he had died at age 84.

articles.title: PH may be caught in US rivals’ ‘crosshairs’ – Tinio
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday warned that the growing US presence in the country’s military and economic assets could put the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Deputy Minority Leader and ACT Teachers Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday warned that the growing US presence in the country’s military and economic assets could put the Philippines in the “crosshairs” of its rivals.

“In the event of a war between the US and China over the Taiwan issue, we can infer that China would target US facilities—both military and commercial—located in the Philippines. Our concern is that the US presence in the country is situated within our strategic and critical economic infrastructure,” Tinio said in a statement released on Thursday.

Tinio’s statement followed his heated exchange with Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro during the House committee on appropriations’ hearing on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of National Defense last Tuesday, Aug. 25.

During the hearing, Tinio raised reports that US soldiers had attempted to enter the Philippine Veterans Investment Development Corporation Industrial Authority in Tagoloan, Misamis Oriental, where the new Philippine Navy dry dock is set to be established.
Teodoro dismissed claims about US interest in the dry dock, saying the presence of foreign troops was for the Balikatan loading exercise.
For Tinio, however, the incident was part of a broader pattern of Washington’s agenda in the country.
He cited the US-led Pax Silica, the US Navy’s use of Subic Bay for repairs and plans for an oil depot in Davao Gulf.

Tinio said the growing US presence in strategic military and economic facilities was particularly concerning because the Philippines lacks the capacity to defend these assets should geopolitical tensions escalate.
“How is the Philippines? The Gulf states are rich countries. They can afford high-tech missile defenses. How are we? What is the capability of the Armed Forces to defend these facilities?” he asked.
Tinio called on the public to remain vigilant against “foreign manipulation and intervention.”
“We must oppose all efforts to sell us out,” he added. /mcm

articles.title: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Mark Carney rejects attempt to rename lake as did several US governors, with Tony Evers mocking the move

blocks.text: Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday directing the federal government to rename Lake Ontario, making it Lake America, amid his escalating trade war with Canada.

The order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases. But Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.
The move follows a similar action the president took on the first day of his second term in office, when he signed an order renaming the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America”.

“We have a gulf and we have a lake – now all we need is an ocean. Maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific,” he told reporters, sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. “Maybe we’ll change them both.”
Propped behind the US president was a large map of the Great Lakes region, with “Lake America” printed in red lettering above Lake Ontario.

Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, rejected the US’s attempt to rename the body of water, explaining in a post on social media that its name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

“We know that America is changing. Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms,” he wrote on X. “Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”
Tim Houston, the premier of Nova Scotia, responded: “We’re into some real foolishness now. It’s Lake Ontario, buddy.”
Several US governors in the Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change.
“New York won’t be calling it that,” the state’s governor, Democrat Kathy Hochul replied. New York borders the lake.

Michigan’s governor, Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat, recalled that schoolchildren learn the acronym H-O-M-E-S for the names of the five great lakes: Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior. And the Wisconsin governor, Democrat Tony Evers, mocked the move by sharing a video of himself changing the name of Lake Michigan to Lake Wisconsin, signed on a restaurant napkin.

The latest tweak of Canada’s nose by the US president comes as tensions increase between the US and its northern neighbor. Over the weekend, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed and the US imposed a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports, with Trump threatening another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney hit back with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods.

“They want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Trump said, a nod to his previous suggestions that Canada should become the “51st state” in the union, a prospect that has enraged Canadians. “But they want to be treated like they’re a state, and so we just can’t do that any more.”

Trump complained about a $60bn US trade deficit with Canada, which economists note is attributable almost entirely to US imports of oil; without that exchange, the US runs a sizable trade surplus. Trump claimed that American farmers were being charged a 400% tariff; about 97% of US agricultural exports to Canada enter duty-free under the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement, though over-quota eggs, milk and dairy have Canadian tariffs of up to 300%.

“As you know, Canada has been ripping us off for a long time on trade. Sad,” Trump said after signing the executive order updating the Department of Interior’s naming conventions. “Even the military: we defend Canada for nothing. We don’t get anything. They don’t pay us to defend Canada. But we defend Canada.”
Both Canada and the United States are Nato members and have treaty obligations of mutual defense under the North Atlantic Treaty, the Ogdensburg Agreement and numerous other treaties.
Trump claimed the name change was something he had been considering for “a long time”.
“We’ve notified all the various people we have to notify,” he said after signing the order … This is official effective immediately.”
An administration official noted that the lake bordering Canada and the state of New York has most of its volume in the United States and that the deepest part of the lake is in US territory.

articles.title: Marcos confers Order of Sikatuna on outgoing Japanese envoy Endo Kazuya
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Thursday honored Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya during a farewell call at Malacañang and conferred him with the Order of…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. on Thursday honored Japanese Ambassador to the Philippines Endo Kazuya during a farewell call at Malacañang and conferred him with the Order of Sikatuna, Rank of Datu (Grand Cross), Gold Distinction.
During their meeting, Marcos thanked the Japanese envoy for his contributions to strengthening the Philippines’ relationship with Japan, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said.
The President recognized Endo for promoting bilateral exchanges and deepening cooperation between the Philippines and Japan in areas of defense, security, and development cooperation.

Meanwhile, the award cited the envoy’s support for initiatives aligned with the Philippines’ priorities in infrastructure, education, transportation, maritime domain awareness, and human resource development.

“Endo was likewise recognized for advancing Japan’s longstanding commitment to peace and development in Mindanao, including its support for the peace process, grassroots development and the transition of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao,” the PCO said.

“The citation also highlighted the ambassador’s efforts to mobilize humanitarian and development assistance from the Japanese government during natural disasters and recent regional crises,” it added.
Additionally, Marcos acknowledged Endo’s initiatives that fostered friendship, mutual understanding, and goodwill between the Filipino and Japanese peoples.
The Order of Sikatuna is conferred upon individuals who have rendered exceptional and meritorious service to the Philippines.
The Philippines and Japan are celebrating 70 years of normalized relations this year and 11 years of strengthened strategic partnership since 2015. /gsg

articles.title: Spain: Thieves steal Bronze Age gold in lightning raid on Villena Museum
articles.summary: One of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections has been swiped, almost in its entirety, from Villena Museum. A highly professional group of thieves were in and out in four minutes flat…

image.caption: The Bronze age collection's historical value is incalculable, but even the gold is worth a pretty penny if melted down and therefore lost forever [FILE: Nov 10, 2016]Image: Lanmas/Visually/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thieves on Thursday raided one of the world's greatest Bronze Age gold collections in the latest of a series of high-profile heists on European museums in recent months.
The early morning raid on Villena Museum in eastern Spain lasted just a few minutes.
A group of thieves described by one official as "super-fast and super-professional" made off with almost the entire Treasure of Villena collection, leaving behind only a few items.
What happened in the heist?

"The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20 a.m.," said a spokesman for the town council, adding that within four minutes, they had all left the building again in an extremely rapid and professional operation.
The collection of Bronze Age gold, some of which we now know hailed from a meteorite, was a centerpiece at the small museum in the Alicante province.

"They've taken most of the treasure," the mayor of Villena, Fulgencio Cerdan told journalists. "We are absolutely devastated, I'm even trembling. The truth is that for those of us from Villena, this destroys us. It's part of our heritage, our wealth."
The thieves arrived in several vehicles and apparently entered the museum "through a window," according to the Spanish government's deputy representative in Alicante, Manuel Pineda.

Mayor Cerdan said that only three silver vessels, a bracelet, an earring and one of four crowns in the collection — which the thieves appeared to have "dropped" while making their exit — remained behind.
"All security systems were activated," according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been "no failure" by the museum.

blocks.caption: The collection was discovered more than 60 years ago and is thought to be a little more than 3,000 years oldImage: Museo de Villena

blocks.text: What is the Treasure of Villena?
The Treasure of Villena is a collection of more than 50 mainly gold objects, discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a sunken vessel in a dried out riverbed.
They are dated to between 1300 and 1000 BCE.
The gold pieces include 11 bowls, three bottles and 28 bracelets.

The collection has been exhibited beyond Villena in cities including Madrid, Alicante, Tokyo and Kyoto, and two sets of replicas were later made to showcase the collection without taking it away from the armored display at the Villena Archaeological Museum.

The relics' historical value is incalculable, although thieves might struggle to sell them even on the black market after having famously lifted them from a well-known display. The mayor said the gold alone would be worth around €1.7 million or $2 million.

According to the museum's website, specialist researchers consider it the most important collection of gold tableware from the Bronze Age. It also represents the earliest known example of iron use in Western Europe, two pieces crafted from a metal that recent studies showed hailed from a meteor.

blocks.caption: The collection includes some of the oldest known iron metalwork, seemingly thanks to the raw materials landing as part of a meteoriteImage: Museo de Villena

blocks.text: Several slick heists on European museums recently, most famously the Louvre
Thursday's lightning dawn raid is the latest in a series on European museums in the last year.

Most famously, the Louvre Museum was hit in broad daylight last October, escaping in less than 10 minutes with jewelry worth millions. This led to the director's eventual resignation and a protracted political scandal, as well as forcing part of the museum to close for an extended period.
Italy's Culture Ministry announced on Sunday that four works of "extraordinary value" by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily.

Shortly before that, Italian police said they had recovered three paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse stolen from a museum near Parma. Again this involved a highly-organized group of thieves who were in and out in a matter of minutes.
Louvre heist inspires freight lift ad campaign

articles.title: The man behind Srebrenica: Ratko Mladic dies at 84
articles.summary: For many, Ratko Mladic represented the horrors of the Bosnian War. He was convicted of genocide for the Srebrenica massacre and of other war crimes. Now he has died in detention at The Hague.

image.caption: Ratko Mladic in the courtroom in The Hague on June 8, 2021Image: Jerry Lampen/REUTERS

blocks.text: More than 30 years after the end of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992-1995), Srebrenica remains emblematic of its brutality. And no one is more closely linked to the genocide that took place in the small town in eastern Bosnia than Ratko Mladic, the former commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb army.

Although the United Nations had declared Srebrenica a "safe area," Bosnian Serb forces attacked the town. Within just a few days in July 1995, they expelled women and children, then killed more than 8,300 unarmed Muslim boys and men in the nearby village of Potocari — on Mladic's direct orders, according to the verdict handed down by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) in The Hague 22 years later.

At the time, Srebrenica was the largest massacre in Europe since World War II. The ICTY classified it as genocide. Mladic was also held responsible for other war crimes beyond the Srebrenica genocide. Under his command, the years-long siege of Sarajevo began at the start of the war. The city was shelled for more than 40 months, killing around 11,000 people, including more than 1,600 children.

Mladic always claimed that he targeted only military objectives. But numerous reports and intercepted radio communications indicate that civilian facilities and residential areas were also deliberately attacked. Around 100,000 people were killed during the four-year war in Bosnia, while some 2.2 million were driven from their homes in cities and villages across the country, half of its total population at the time.
Former Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead
'The butcher of the Balkans'
In 2017, Mladic was sentenced to life in prison by the tribunal in The Hague.
International media dubbed him "the Butcher of the Balkans."
He was found responsible for some of the most serious war crimes and the genocide committed during the Bosnian War.

Mladic consistently denied any responsibility. He saw himself as an avenger of the Serbs for centuries of Ottoman rule in the Balkans, and viewed Bosnia's Muslims, who today call themselves Bosniaks, as direct descendants of the Turks. In front of his soldiers, he referred to them simply as "the Turks" and showed no empathy.
"Borders are always drawn with blood, and states are marked with graves," he is quoted as saying.
Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre
Career in the Yugoslav army

At the beginning of the Croatian War in June 1991, when Serbs living in Croatia rose up against the independence of the former Yugoslav republic with active support from Serbia, Mladic's role fundamentally changed. As a colonel in the Yugoslav army, he became commander of the 9th Corps in the Croatian city of Knin. His task was to organize Serb militias and support them in their fight against Croatian independence.

Under Mladic's command, the Croatian cities of Sibenik and Zadar were bombarded, and Croatian civilians were driven from surrounding towns and villages. In May 1992, he took on the same role in Bosnia. By then promoted to general, Mladic became commander-in-chief of the Bosnian Serb forces, seeking to establish a territorial link between Serb-held areas in the east and west of the former Yugoslav republic.

blocks.caption: Ratko Mladic (left) and Radovan Karadzic, the political leader of the Bosnian Serbs during the Bosnian War, on August 5, 1993.Image: picture-alliance/ dpa

blocks.text: Flight, arrest and final verdict

At the height of his career, Colonel General Ratko Mladic was a fervent Serbian nationalist. But he began his career as a committed communist. Born in eastern Bosnia in 1943, Mladic was just two years old when his father, one of Tito's Partisans, was killed by fascist Croatian Ustasha militia. The loss is often described as a formative influence, shaping his later worldview.

As a young man, Mladic embarked on a military career, attending the Military Academy in Belgrade. He later graduated at the top of his class. He quickly rose through the ranks of the Yugoslav army, which for many years was regarded as one of the most stable institutions in the multiethnic state.
Serbian nationalist

Before the end of the Bosnian War in late 1995, Mladic was indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. But he evaded arrest for years. Supported by networks within the Serbian military and political establishment, he lived largely undisturbed underground and was even seen in public. He was finally arrested in 2011, after 16 years on the run and mounting international pressure.

The subsequent trial in The Hague lasted a total of 523 days. Nearly 600 witnesses testified, while numerous documents and other pieces of evidence were examined. Mladic was ultimately sentenced to life in prison at trial, among other charges for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. In 2021, an appeals chamber upheld the verdict, making it final. Legally, this established his responsibility as one of the principal figures behind the crimes committed during the Bosnian War.
Ratko Mladic life sentence upheld
A war criminal who saw himself as a hero

Internationally, the verdict was hailed as historic. United Nations officials saw it as a signal that accountability can still be pursued decades after crimes are committed. For many survivors and relatives of the victims, the verdict was a long-overdue but important acknowledgment of their suffering.
Mladic himself, however, remained defiant to the end. Throughout the trial, he maintained that he was innocent, calling the charges against him "disgusting" and the tribunal "satanic."

Many of his supporters in Serbia and among Bosnian Serbs still see him as a hero. While he is regarded internationally as a war criminal, his admirers continue to portray him as a defender of Serbian interests and a hero — even painting his likeness on walls.

While he was still on the run, Mladic threatened his pursuers, claiming he always carried a poison pill and that he would never be captured alive. But he never swallowed the pill during his decades in hiding. He survived several strokes while in prison.
Ratko Mladic died on August 27, 2026, at the prison hospital in The Hague at the age of 84.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Climate crisis could be destabilising mountain areas like Nepal, experts warn
articles.summary: Unusual heat this year may have melted ice and thawed bonds that hold glaciers in place – leading to catastrophe

blocks.text: The devastating flash flood that has ripped through the border communities of Nepal and Tibet has heightened fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions, threatening millions of people.

Satellite imagery suggests a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the deadly torrent of mud, water and ice that tore along the Bhotekoshi River on Wednesday. It swept away buildings and roads and left at least 360 dead and 1,400 missing.

A magnitude 4.4 earthquake was initially blamed for the collapse. However, it is now thought to have been caused by the huge wall of ice that crashed down on to the north slope of Langtang Lirung, a 7,000-metre (23,000ft) mountain, the impact of which registered a magnitude of 5.2.
“Additional analysis of long-period seismic waves indicates that the seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow,” the US Geological Survey said.

The ice-rock avalanche pushed boulders and other debris into the Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River. Water levels in rivers downstream rose by between 7 and 9 metres within 30 minutes, according to the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development, an intergovernmental scientific institution.

Scientists are still examining the precise mechanics of the Himalayan disaster, but many observe that glaciers and permafrost around the world are being weakened by global heating, caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal.

blocks.caption: Flooding in the Bhotekoshi River has affected low-lying areas along the riverbanks and nearby homes in Nuwakot, Nepal.  Photograph: Ap Tolang/Nexpher/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The detachment of a chunk of the glacier wall came amid unusual heat that was likely to have melted the ice that bound the splintered bedrock together.

Two days before the collapse, the ground temperature hit its highest point in the last two years, according to Dr Hamish Pritchard, a glaciologist with the British Antarctic Survey, whose team had sensors 6 miles (10km) away from the site.
“These high temperatures would have weakened the snowpack, filled crevasses with water and thawed the bonds between ice and rock that hold these glaciers in place,” he told the Science Media Centre.

A series of intense heatwaves has hit the region since early this year and affected countries around the world. Another factor here was the monsoon season, which saturated the soil and swelled rivers.

Disasters like this were foretold. In 2023 the UN’s top scientific advisory body warned that previously ice-bound landmasses – from permafrost tundra to mountain glaciers – would become increasingly unstable as temperatures rose.

“Every increment of warming will multiply and intensify future hazards from cryosphere regions,” observed the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change in its sixth synthesis report. “Floods, landslides and freshwater shortages from glacier retreat and snow loss pose a serious threat to mountain regions across the world.”

Average global temperatures are nudging closer to 1.5C above preindustrial levels. Even faster warming is occurring in alpine and polar regions because the loss of snow and ice is removing the thermal insulation of the land.

Dr Richard Waller, a senior lecturer in physical geography at Keele University, said: “The progressive loss of snow and glacier ice results in the surface being less reflective, so it absorbs more solar energy and heats up. In combination with atmospheric warming, this is leading to the melting of mountain permafrost.

“Think of the high mountains like this as shattered bedrock glued together by ice-filled joints. As the permafrost and the ice-filled joints melt, then there’s the potential for these types of catastrophic failure.”

blocks.caption: A destroyed building in Devighat, Nuwakot. Photograph: Niranjan Shrestha/AP

blocks.text: The thaw is altering the shape, colour and solidity of the landscape, creating or expanding glacial meltwater lakes and, in the long term, threatening the origin of many rivers and the drinking supplies of populations downstream. In many parts of Asia, hundreds of millions of people depend on the rivers such as the Ganges and the Brahmaputra that descend from the glaciers.

Scientists have high confidence that glacier retreat is caused by human-driven global heating. This has caused glacier collapses from the Alps to the Andes. In the Langtang catchment area in Nepal, glacier loss rates have increased more than fourfold since 1964, a study has shown.

This has contributed to a loss of life on multiple occasions. A smaller flood hit the Bhotekoshi River in July 2025 and in 2015, the Langtang Lirung mountain was hit by an earthquake-induced avalanche that destroyed Langtang village.

As emergency services look for bodies and humanitarian relief groups mobilise for survivors, others are asking where next. Waller said any high mountain areas with glaciers and permafrost could be vulnerable, including the European Alps, Caucasus, Himalayas, Andes and beyond.

As glacier weakening accelerates, Pritchard called for greater disaster preparedness. “More avalanches and more floods are inevitable, particularly as lakes grow in front of the retreating glaciers,” he said. “Early warning systems are urgently needed to protect the people living in these valleys.”

articles.title: Marcos sends condolences, offers prayers to Nepal flash floods victims
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the major floods and landslides that struck the Nepal-Tibet border. He also offered…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Thursday expressed his condolences to the victims of the major floods and landslides that struck the Nepal-Tibet border.
He also offered prayers for strength of the calamity victims.
“The Philippines extends its deepest condolences to our friends in Nepal and to all those affected by the deadly flashflood yesterday,” Marcos said in his social media post.
“Our deepest sympathies go out to those who lost family, loved ones and friends. Please accept our most heartfelt prayers for strength in this difficult time,” he added.
The Nepal Tourism Board reported that one Filipino traveler was missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal.
According to the tourism board, as of 2:45 p.m. Philippine time, preliminary records showed that 644 travelers had been reported missing in the affected area, including one Filipino.

Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said in a briefing earlier that the Department of Foreign Affairs and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration were coordinating with officials in Nepal, as well as with the Filipino community, to determine the extent of the disaster’s impact on Filipinos. /apl

articles.title: How a glacier collapse may have caused Nepal-Tibet disaster
articles.summary: BANGKOK — A huge piece of ice that fell thousands of meters from a glacier into a river below may have unleashed the disaster in Nepal and Tibet that killed at least 180 people. Here is what…

blocks.text: BANGKOK — A huge piece of ice that fell thousands of meters from a glacier into a river below may have unleashed the disaster in Nepal and Tibet that killed at least 180 people.
Here is what experts believe happened so far:
Glacier collapse
A glacier collapse in Nepal’s mountains near Tibet appears to have triggered the disaster.
“A large chunk of glacier fell from about 5,200 meters (about 17,000 feet)… into a valley,” said Simon Cox, principal scientist at New Zealand’s GNS Science.
It “transformed into this raging mass of debris… where it picks up rocks and sediment and trees and anything in the way and fires it on down through the canyon,” he told AFP.
The wall of water first impacted a border post, as documented in terrifying CCTV footage showing mud and debris engulfing the area as people fled before it.
It then travelled downstream into Nepal, flooding villages and bringing down bridges and buildings.
Seismic activity
The glacier collapse was large enough to register as a seismic event, initially mistaken for an earthquake.
But after further analysis, the US Geological Survey determined “that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.
The collapse registered as a 5.2-magnitude “seismic event”, which took place at 8:37 am local time (0252 GMT).
Estimating just how much of the glacier collapsed will take time, Cox said, but it could range from “half a million cubic metres to tens of million cubic metres.”
Detective work
With the affected area largely inaccesible, experts are using satellite imagery and any available measurements on the ground to reconstruct the disaster.

“We can look at satellite imagery taken before and after the event, and try and see what has changed, essentially looking for what is missing from the mountains in the ‘after’ imagery,” said Lauren Vargo, a glaciologist at New Zealand’s Victoria University of Wellington.
Soon after the seismic activity was recorded, a nearby water monitoring station stopped transmitting, Nepali authorities said.
Stations downstream began going offline one by one, though water was registered reaching up to 12.3 metres high in Kalikhola, near the Tibet border at 2:14 pm, they added.
GLOFs
Early speculation suggested a glacial lake outburst flood, or GLOF, a growing risk as glaciers melt due to climate change.
A GLOF occurs when a fragile debris wall holding back a lake of glacier melt suddenly collapses, unleashing the water behind it.
Some experts suggested a GLOF might have been involved.
“Water does flow within glaciers and flows beneath glaciers,” said Adrian McCallum, a glaciologist at the University of the Sunshine Coast.
“But to my mind, the only reason why a large volume of water should all of a sudden flow down a valley is because it has been released,” he told AFP.

Other experts said they did not detect existing glacial lakes near the site of the glacier collapse, and theorised that water collected under the glacier might have cascaded down with the falling chunk.
The falling glacier ice could also have briefly dammed the river, collecting water behind it that was released when it dislodged.

Summer glacier melt upstream and monsoon rains would mean the rivers were already high, and the volume of water was also swelled by debris and mud picked up as it travelled kilometres from the initial collapse, added Cox.
Warnings
Nepali authorities first received word of a flood around 9:00 am local time, and began alerting areas along the Bhote Khoshi river to “stay on high alert and stay in safe areas”.
But is is unclear how many people received the warning, or how much time they would have had to respond.
“The reality is, if you are in a community underneath a large glacier and potentially a glacier lake where a GLOF could occur, then to some extent, it’s a ticking time bomb,” said McCallum.
And even for those receiving a warning, options would be limited, said Hatim Sharif, a hydrologist at the University of Texas San Antonio.
“Running will not help,” nor will trying to flee by vehicle, he told AFP, because the mud and water moving at high speed form a lethal combination “like liquid concrete.”
The only solution is to climb up a hill, at least 20 feet (six meters), he estimated.
Climate change
While it is hard to immediately attribute any individual glacial event to climate change, the warming planet is a constant background stress on these ancient ice rivers, expert say.
Glaciers are retreating globally, creating disaster risks but also depriving downstream communities of vital water sources.
“The biggest way to mitigate the risk would be to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions to limit warming,” said Vargo. /dl

articles.title: Filipino traveler among hundreds missing in Nepal flash floods
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – A Filipino traveler remains missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal on Wednesday evening, the Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – A Filipino traveler remains missing following a flash flood in the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers in Nepal on Wednesday evening, the Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday.
According to the tourism board, as of 2:45 p.m. Philippine time, its preliminary records showed that 644 travelers were reported missing in the affected area, including one Filipino.
Earlier, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro reported that there were no Filipino casualties in the flash flood as of Thursday morning, citing the Department of Foreign Affairs.
The board has yet to disclose any details about the Filipino tourist but noted that the information is still being verified and crosschecked with travel agencies and other local authorities.

“Following the devastating flash flood… Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation Government of Nepal, Nepal Tourism Board, Tourist Police and tourism stakeholders are working to verify the whereabouts and safety status of tourists or travelers who were at or travelling through the affected areas,” the Nepal Tourism Board said in a statement.
At least 165 deaths were reported after the flash flooding, and the riversides of the four affected districts were left severely damaged. /dl

articles.title: Nepali PM Balendra Shah heads to flood-hit Nuwakot to assess damage
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah left early Thursday for a field inspection of flood-hit areas in Bidur, Nuwakot. Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal is…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah left early Thursday for a field inspection of flood-hit areas in Bidur, Nuwakot.
Minister for Infrastructure Development Sunil Lamsal is accompanying Shah on the visit.
According to the Prime Minister’s Secretariat, the team left Kathmandu by road at 9:30am for Bidur, one of the areas worst affected by the flooding.

During the visit, Shah and Lamsal will assess the physical damage firsthand and meet local officials, security agencies and elected representatives to discuss relief, rehabilitation and the restoration of disrupted infrastructure.
They are also expected to issue instructions to speed up the delivery of relief to affected communities and accelerate infrastructure reconstruction, the secretariat said.
Shah has been closely involved in the rescue and relief efforts since the flood entered the Bhotekoshi river from Tibet and caused damage downstream on Wednesday. /dl

articles.title: Deadly floods in Nepal, China: UN’s Guterres offers condolences
articles.summary: UN Secretary-General António Guterres has expressed condolences over the loss of life and widespread destruction caused by severe flooding in Nepal and China on Wednesday. Guterres was saddened by…

blocks.text: UN Secretary-General António Guterres has expressed condolences over the loss of life and widespread destruction caused by severe flooding in Nepal and China on Wednesday.
Guterres was saddened by reports of deaths and people still missing, as well as extensive damage caused by the floods, his spokesperson said in a statement.
He offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a speedy recovery. He also expressed solidarity with all those affected.
In Nepal, the United Nations is supporting the government-led response, including efforts to assess the extent of the disaster and deliver immediate assistance, the statement said.
UN agencies and humanitarian partners are mobilising supplies and personnel to support affected communities.
Guterres praised emergency responders working to save lives and reaffirmed the UN’s readiness to provide further assistance. /dl

articles.title: How the Nepal flood unfolded over 10 hours
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — An initial technical assessment has found that the devastating flood that hit the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa on Wednesday entered Nepal as a major surge from Tibet. The flood then…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — An initial technical assessment has found that the devastating flood that hit the Bhotekoshi river in Rasuwa on Wednesday entered Nepal as a major surge from Tibet. The flood then traveled downstream through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers before reaching the Narayani river.

According to a technical report prepared by the Flood Forecasting Division of the Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research, authorities received information at 9:05am on that day that a major flood had entered the Bhotekoshi from the Tibetan side. The surge then moved downstream through the Bhotekoshi into the Trishuli river and gradually spread to downstream areas.

The division said it issued early warnings and alerts to people in the affected districts, river corridors and other high-risk settlements based on available river-level data, the flood’s movement and information received as the event unfolded.

The report says a magnitude 4.4 earthquake was recorded at 8:37am. About 13 minutes later, at 8:50am, the water-level monitoring station in Syabrubesi, Rasuwa, stopped transmitting data. Its last reading showed the river at 1.62 metres at 8:40am. The station’s warning level is 6 metres and its danger level is 9 meters, according to the report.

About 15 minutes later, authorities received information that a major flood had entered the Bhotekoshi river from Tibet. Between 9:15am and 9:16am, SMS alerts were sent to residents in riverbank areas of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and Chitwan, urging them to remain on high alert. More than 600,000 messages were sent.
At 9:20am, the Betrawati water-level monitoring station also stopped transmitting data. Its last recorded river level was 3.55 metres.

By 10:28am, the flood was expected to reach the Dhading-Galchhi area and pass Muglin within a few hours. Authorities then sent further warnings to people along the Prithvi Highway, the Muglin-Narayanghat road and settlements along the Trishuli river.

At 11:26am, the river level at the Phurke (Malekhu) monitoring station had risen above the danger mark. Seventeen minutes later, at 11:43am, the flood swept away the Phurke river bridge and other structures. By 11:50am, floodwaters had reached the Malekhu area.

At 1pm, authorities received confirmation that the flood had already passed Muglin and urged people living along the river as far as Devghat to move to safer areas. The river level at Devghat reached 4.76 meters at 1:30pm. The initial estimate was that the main flood surge would reach Devghat at about 3:30pm, with the river level potentially rising to around 8 meters.
At 2:14pm, the water level at the Kalikhola monitoring station rose above the danger mark. The station recorded a peak level of 12.3 metres, according to the report.
By 3:20pm, the flood had reached the Narayani-Devghat area and the river level was still rising. At 4pm, the water level at Devghat peaked at 6.57 metres before beginning to fall.

By 6:30pm, the water level at Devghat had fallen back to about 4 meters. The initial technical assessment estimates that the flood brought an additional volume of about 20 million cubic meters of water, the report said.

From the earthquake recorded at 8:37am until the river level at Devghat began to recede at 6:30pm, the flood traveled from the Bhotekoshi through the Trishuli to Muglin, Malekhu and Devghat in roughly 10 hours.

The report shows that data transmission from several river-monitoring stations was disrupted as the flood moved downstream, while authorities continued issuing advance warnings and alerts to people living along the river corridors. /dl

articles.title: French Alps cable car accident leaves 23 injured
articles.summary: LYON, France — A cable car hit a crane in the French resort of Alpe d’Huez leaving 23 injured, three critically, officials said Thursday. There were about 50 people in the cabin of the…

blocks.text: LYON, France — A cable car hit a crane in the French resort of Alpe d’Huez leaving 23 injured, three critically, officials said Thursday.
There were about 50 people in the cabin of the cable car when the accident happened Wednesday morning at at altitude of 2,300 meters (7,500 feet), Alpe d’Huez mayor Jean-Yves Noyrey told AFP.
“There are mainly people in shock and cases of concussion,” Noyrey said, adding that he believed most of the injured had left hospital.
Cable cars are designed to stabilize themselves if they brake suddenly, but “on hitting the crane, the car tilted, and the people inside slid”, the mayor said.
“They thought they were going to die,” he added, “but the operator reacted well by reversing to level the cabin.”
The regional prefecture said there were 23 injured, with three in critical condition and 13 with severe injuries. /dl

articles.title: Norway’s King Harald, 89, in ‘extremely serious’ condition – palace
articles.summary: OSLO — The health of Norway’s 89-year-old King Harald, hospitalized with a blood disease, has deteriorated and he is in an “extremely serious” condition, the palace said…

blocks.text: OSLO — The health of Norway’s 89-year-old King Harald, hospitalized with a blood disease, has deteriorated and he is in an “extremely serious” condition, the palace said Thursday.

Queen Sonja and Crown Prince Haakon, who is acting as regent during his father’s illness, have cancelled all royal engagements, said a palace statement. Norwegian media said they were at the king’s bedside.

Europe’s oldest reigning monarch has been in hospital in Oslo since August 17 suffering from hemolytic anemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells which leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
“His Majesty the King’s health condition is extremely serious,” it said, providing no other details.
The queen, Haakon and his wife Mette-Marit were all at the king’s bedside, with media showing them arriving at the hospital.
The monarch was admitted to Oslo University Hospital due to fluid retention from the cortisone treatment he was receiving.
Harald, who ascended the Norwegian throne in 1991, has had multiple health problems in recent years, forcing him to have a pacemaker fitted and to scale back his official schedule.
But he has always ruled out abdicating, arguing that he took a lifelong oath before the Norwegian parliament. /dl

articles.title: INQToday: Deadly Nepal floods, LPA watch, Romualdez plea
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Here is INQToday’s lineup at this hour: From a deadly disaster along the Nepal-Tibet border to a developing weather disturbance closer to home, authorities are racing…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Here is INQToday’s lineup at this hour:From a deadly disaster along the Nepal-Tibet border to a developing weather disturbance closer to home, authorities are racing against time as threats mount.

More than 1,000 people remain missing after flash floods and landslides left at least 165 dead, while the Philippine weather bureau monitors a low-pressure area that could develop into a tropical depression within the next 24 hours.
Meanwhile, former House Speaker Martin Romualdez is asking the Ombudsman to consider the recantations of witnesses in the cases filed against him. /dp

articles.title: Desperate families search for missing after Nepal floods
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — Anxious relatives crowded the corridors of a Kathmandu hospital Thursday as they searched for missing family after devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 165…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — Anxious relatives crowded the corridors of a Kathmandu hospital Thursday as they searched for missing family after devastating floods on the Nepal-Tibet border killed at least 165 people.
Among them was Subash Khatani, scanning lists and speaking to officials in the hope of finding news of his elder brother, one of the hundreds unaccounted for after the disaster.
“My elder brother Ram Sharan Rasaili is among those missing in Rasuwa. That’s why we are out searching for him,” Khatani told AFP at the government-run Bir hospital in the capital.
On Wednesday, a tsunami-like wall of water and mud swept through villages and towns along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers, with Nepali police saying they had recovered 162 bodies.
Rasuwa in northern Nepal was the first district hit. But deaths were reported in seven districts as floodwaters surged more than 160 kilometres (100 miles) south to Chitwan, near the Indian border.

The cause of the disaster was not immediately clear, but the US Geological Survey said it was a glacial collapse that caused seismic activity and the “catastrophic” downstream impacts in Nepal and Tibet.
Chitra Bahadur Nepali was looking for his nephew Yubraj Sewak, a driver who had been travelling towards the worst-affected Rasuwa district before contact was lost.
“My nephew was on his way to Rasuwa and was in contact with my sister until about 8:00 am yesterday,” Nepali, 52, said, showing his photograph on his phone.
“We have not heard from him since the flood. His name is not on any of the lists we have seen, and another member of our family is also missing.”
As rescue teams scoured for survivors in the flood-ravaged districts, families moved between hospitals and police helpdesks, desperately hoping for word on those missing.
The Bir hospital said it would treat all victims for free and was “fully prepared” to handle the surge in patients, local media reported.
In Nepal, 823 people — including 579 tourists from both Nepal and abroad — remained out of contact, according to the country’s disaster agency.
In Tibet, Chinese state media said that the “mudslide disaster” had killed three people, while 558 people, including 260 foreigners, were missing. /dl

articles.title: From romantic getaway to hotbed of crime? Rumor mill fans Jeju fears
articles.summary: Jeju Island, South Korea’s traditional honeymoon destination, is facing an image crisis as a police scandal over allegedly mishandled missing-person cases fuels broader fears about safety on the…

blocks.text: Jeju Island, South Korea’s traditional honeymoon destination, is facing an image crisis as a police scandal over allegedly mishandled missing-person cases fuels broader fears about safety on the island.
In just three days through Monday, four people who had been reported missing on Jeju were found dead, according to police.

Authorities have not linked the deaths or found evidence of widespread foul play. But the discoveries, which followed a large-scale search prompted by revelations that a police officer had falsely closed at least two missing-person cases, have shaken public confidence and fueled anxiety online.

At the center of the scandal is the case of Jang Mi-ran, a 37-year-old woman who disappeared after leaving her home in Hallim-eup, Jeju City, sometime between late May 12 and early May 13. Nearly three months later, a body believed to be hers was discovered Monday among palm trees less than a 10-minute walk from where she stayed.

blocks.caption: A police officer accused of falsely closing missing-person cases on Jeju Island is escorted out of Jeju Dongbu Police Station on Sunday. (Yonhap)

blocks.text: Jang’s case drew national attention after the police officer in charge allegedly closed it in May, falsely claiming that he had spoken with her.

Authorities found a man in his 60s who had been reported missing dead in Gujwa-eup on Saturday after a delayed search. His case, like Jang’s, had been falsely closed by the same police officer, news reports said.

The same day Jang’s remains were discovered, another person previously reported missing was discovered dead near a valley in Aewol-eup. The following day, a fisherman spotted the body of a man in his 70s in waters off Sinheung-ri, Jocheon-eup, and alerted emergency authorities.
Growing Jeju phobia

blocks.caption: A guesthouse on Jeju Island listed on accommodation booking platform Stayfolio (Stayfolio)

blocks.text: The concentration of cases, and the local police’s failures surrounding some of them, has unsettled residents and visitors alike.

“Many people come to Jeju to stay for several months at a time. I’ve heard that some tenants are canceling their leases following the recent incidents,” a Jeju resident surnamed Cho, who runs a short-term rental business, wrote on Instagram.

A recent Instagram post by Hong Hye-geol, a doctor specializing in preventive medicine and a television personality who has lived on the island for seven years, read, “When I cycle around Jeju, I often come across deserted roads in villages without even venturing deep into Hallasan. Stray just a little from a trail, and you can find yourself somewhere no one would hear you scream. I wouldn’t recommend either women or men going around here alone, even in broad daylight or on paved roads.”
Some even spoke of canceling trips to the resort island.

One Threads user wrote, “I was going to take my wedding photos in Gujwa because I’d heard it was quieter and had prettier fields than central Jeju, but I canceled. With everything that’s happened recently, I don’t think I’m overreacting.”

Another user called for a boycott, writing “We shouldn’t travel to Jeju until they get to the bottom of what the police officer did in Jang’s case and someone takes responsibility for the other missing-person cases.”
Although no clear drop in tourist numbers has emerged, tourism operators are growing concerned.

Bang, 52, who has run a women-only guesthouse in Jocheon-eup for eight years, said she has been receiving frequent calls from guests concerned about safety. Just two days ago, a group of three guests canceled their reservation, though it was unclear whether the recent missing-person cases had prompted the cancellation.

“The neighborhood is well lit, with streetlights and additional lights every 20 to 30 meters. We’ve always felt safe enough to leave the front gate unlocked while guests hang out in the common area before bed,” Bang told The Korea Herald.

“Catering exclusively to women used to be what set us apart, but now it seems to be making guests even more nervous. The police and local authorities need to step in before the baseless crime-related rumors surrounding the island create even more unnecessary fear.”
Tourism businesses in Jeju are particularly on edge as the island is already grappling with a decline in domestic visitors.

According to the Jeju Tourism Organization, 963,401 domestic travelers visited the island in July, down 12.4 percent, or 136,620, from 1,100,021 a year earlier. It marked the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic began in 2020 that Jeju’s monthly domestic visitor count fell below 1 million.
The downward trend continued into August. From Aug. 1-23, Jeju received an average of 35,295 domestic visitors per day, about 300 fewer than the 35,575 recorded during the same period last year.

According to data from the Korean National Police Agency, the island recorded the country’s highest crime rate in 2024, at 4,539.6 crimes per 100,000 people. The rate is calculated based on Jeju’s resident population of around 663,000, while the island receives millions of visitors each year. /dl

articles.title: Tragedy in Nepal: How do flash floods happen?
articles.summary: When flash floods sweep through the Himalayas, there is often little time to react. Scientists are working to understand the risks and improve early warning systems.

image.caption: Flash floods are a recurring threat in the Himalayas. Climate change contributes to the problemImage: Sunil Pradhan/ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The disaster in the border region between China and Nepal was as sudden as it was unexpected: Within just 10 minutes, enormous volumes of water and debris swept 20 kilometers downstream on Wednesday, with devastating consequences for thousands of people in the region.

Flash floods are a frequent occurrence in the Himalayas. "They are more the rule than the exception," says Niels Hovius, head of the Geomorphology Section at the GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam. He has worked in the Himalayas and other mountainous regions for many years and is an expert on early warning systems.
What triggered the flash flood?

Scientific data indicate that the disaster began with a glacier collapse in the northern part of the Langtang massif: a large amount of ice broke away and turned into a massive ice avalanche. The Langtang massif is located in central Nepal near the border with China.
Devastating flash floods hit northern Nepal

"This glacier collapse sent huge amounts of ice rapidly downhill," says Hovius. The heat generated by friction melted the ice into water, which then swept up debris and mud. The resulting mudflow moved downhill at speeds "reached by passenger cars on German highways."

Seismological instruments recorded an earthquake measuring 4.4 on the Richter scale at the time of the glacier collapse. However, Hovius says, it was not a "classic" or tectonic earthquake. Instead, the instruments measured the force of the falling glacier.
Why can flash floods in the Himalayas be so devastating?
Flash floods in high mountain regions can be triggered in different ways — by glacier collapses or by so-called glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs, or Glacier Lake Outburst Floods).

In such cases, the topography around a glacial lake suddenly changes, for example when a slope collapses into the lake. The large volume of water that suddenly spills over the lake's banks can then turn into torrents rushing downstream. In this particular case, however, it is clear that this was not a GLOF, says Hovius.

Landslides can also cause deadly mudflows without any glaciers or glacial lakes being involved. In the Himalayas, all three types of events are possible, and historical data show that all three occur regularly, Hovius says.
Compared with the Alps, the valleys of the Himalayas are relatively narrow. The water and mud cannot spread out but are instead forced into a confined space, increasing their depth and speed.
Alps warming fast: Europe’s water lifeline is running dry
In addition to the speed of the water and debris, the extent of the devastation caused by a flash flood depends on how far local populations are from the source.
How can people be protected from flash floods?

Nepal faces two major challenges. Many people have settled along rivers in the valleys of the Himalayas — in precisely the areas that are vulnerable to flash floods. Secondly, there are very few early warning systems in the country, which is one of the poorest in Asia.

Even with a timely warning, the particularly devastating flash flood would have given people only a few minutes to reach safety. Hovius describes a flood that occurred in the same region last year. It was smaller, and therefore less severe. At the time, it took the water an hour to reach a settlement — enough time for people to escape if they had received a timely warning.

"There are initiatives in Nepal to establish local acoustic early warning systems," says Hovius. However, these systems are available only on a very limited scale. At most, they cover one percent of areas at risk. The GFZ researcher adds that mobile phones should be used to send people warnings via push notifications. Hovius is researching how the data needed for such a system could be generated.

Checks should also be made on how settlements are planned, Hovius says. At present, the bulk of a community's infrastructure is concentrated along rivers. "People have moved down from the mountains and settled in the valleys over the past few decades. Perhaps it would make sense to move back to higher ground."
Are flash floods in mountainous areas more frequent amid climate change?

"Attributing individual events to climate change is always difficult," Hovius says. But it is clear that glaciers in high mountain regions become less stable as temperatures rise. Larger volumes of water are also accumulating in glacial lakes, making GLOFs more likely.

As for the current flash flood, it is too early to say whether climbing temperatures caused the glacier to collapse. Flash floods have long been a regular occurrence in the Himalayas. "But I think it is likely that we will see more and more of these events," Hovius says, warning that future disasters could be even more serious.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Andre Rankel named Germany's new men's ice hockey coach
articles.summary: Germany's men's ice hockey team has appointed a new head coach following a string of dissappointing tournaments. He's two decades younger than the man he's replacing but he has no previous experience…

image.caption: Former Germany player Andre Rankel spent the past three seasons as assistant coach in BerlinImage: Franz Feiner/HMB Media/IMAGO

blocks.text: The German Ice Hockey Association (DEB) presented former Germany player Andre Rankel as the new coach of the men's national team at a press conference in Munich on Thursday.

Rankel, who spent the past three seasons as an assistant coach with Eisbären Berlin, champions of Germany's top division (the DEL), has never served as a head coach. DEB sport director Christian Künast stressed that he does not see this as a problem.
"Andre is here today because he was the best [of the candidates interviewed for the job]. That's the main point," Künast said.

"I simply don't see Andre as a rookie coach. I've known him for a long time and I have had a lot of conversations with him about how you lead a team. He is ready to take over the national team and that's the most important thing."
Rankel said he was "incredibly proud" to be named Germany coach.

"What I learned as a player and captain over all these years, what constitutes team cohesion and commitment, I now want to pass on as head coach. My goal is to develop a clear idea together with the players and the coaching staff of how we want to play, and to grow step by step based on that.

Although this will be his first job as a head coach, he is highly respected in German hockey having played 17 seasons in the DEL for Berlin. In the capital, he was captain for many years, won seven titles as a player and three more as assistant coach. He also made 46 appearances as a winger for Germany, including at the 2010 Olympic Games in Vancouver.
DEB CEO Frank Lutz said Rankel had been given a four-year contract, a reflection of the fact that the organization is looking to him to help further develop the national team in the longer term.
A generational change for German hockey

The appointment of Rankel, who turned 41 on Thursday, marks a generational change for Germany. Rankel replaces Canadian-born Harold Kreis, 67, who after leading the national team to a silver medal at the 2023 World Championship had a disappointing series of tournaments. Perhaps the most damaging was the 2026 Winter Olympics. The Germany team that entered the tournament was considered the greatest ever and was led by NHL superstar Leon Draisaitl, but it crashed out against Slovakia in the quarterfinals.

While appointing someone with no head coaching experience may seem like a risky move, the DEB have been down this road before. Marco Sturm also had no head coaching experience when he was appointed in 2015. He went on to lead Germany to a silver medal at the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeonchang – their greatest achievement and which marked an upward turn in the national team's fortunes.
With this progress having stalled in recent years, the DEB are betting that Rankel is the man to get Germany's men back on the right track.

Rankel's first tournament behind the bench will be the Deutschland Cup in Düsseldorf, a four-team invitational held annually during the November international break. His first major test will come next May, when Germany host the World Championship in Düsseldorf, Mannheim and Gelsenkirchen.

articles.title: New study shows German football remains male-dominated
articles.summary: The top leagues of German football remain a largely male environment. A new study reveals that only seven clubs have women in upper management levels.

image.caption: Christina Rühl-Hamers is just one of nine women in management positions in German footballImage: Wolf von Dewitz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The nonprofit organization "Fussball kann mehr" (FKM –– Football Can Do More) has released its third report on diversity in professional German football. This time, all 36 teams in the top two divisions took part, and the results reveal a familiar tale of dominance. A revealing 29 of the 36 clubs have an all-male management team.

There was a noticeable increase in women in top management positions in the 2025-26 season though, with four of the 18 new appointments to top management positions being women. The previous season, only one of the 19 open positions at the time were filled by a woman. RB Leipzig's Tatjana Haenni, who became the first female CEO in the Bundesliga in late 2025, is one of them. Nicole Kumpis of Eintracht Braunschweig remains the only female president of a club in the top two flights. Kathleen Krüger's appointment at HSV came after the study's cutoff, boosting the original numbers.
Only nine of the 94 positions at the highest management level are now held by women. The nine women are:

items: Tatjana Haenni, CEO at RB Leipzig
Luise Gottberg, vice president at St. Pauli
Hanna Obersteller vice president at St. Pauli
Petra Saretz, executive board member at Heidenheim
Jennifer Zietz, managing director of women's football at Union Berlin
Katharina Kienemann, executive committee member at Union Berlin
Svenja Schlenker, managing director of HR at Borussia Dortmund
Christina Rühl-Hamers, board member for finance, HR, and legal at Schalke
Anne-Kathrin Laufmann, managing director of sports & sustainability at Werder Bremen

blocks.text: Seen through a comparative lens, this is three more than the previous season. The only number lower than the number of women in management roles is the international diversification on supervisory boards – fewer than 3% of members are not German.

"We would love to report that the spirit of renewal exuded by these top executives is permeating German professional football and that the necessary transformation is in full swing," Katja Kraus, co-chair of the FKM advisory board, said in a press release.

"But progress remains slow; spectacular isolated cases and stagnation at the grassroots level are not mutually exclusive, but rather explain each other. Visible exceptions create an impression of progress that reduces the pressure on what is actually a sluggish structure."

blocks.caption: Katja Kraus believes football's approach to diversity has a lot to learn from the business worldImage: Martin Hoffmann/Imago Images

blocks.text: Women's football has untapped potential

Also addressed in the survey was women's football. The Women's Bundesliga's decision to move away from the DFB and operate independently opens up new doors, especially for women looking to move into management positions. Currently though, men still dominate in the women's game too, with only four of the 14 Women's Bundesliga teams coached by women (Cologne, Union Berlin, Werder Bremen and Hoffenheim).

In the face of structural barriers for women in elite sport, the challenges remain in both men's and women's football. The hope is that in the years ahead, particularly with Euro 2029 being held in Germany, that German clubs will look to implement change when it comes to the diversity of their management.

articles.title: Ex-Bosnian Serb military leader Ratko Mladic dead at 84
articles.summary: The former Bosnian Serb general was convicted of genocide committed during the bloody 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

image.caption: Mladic was dubbed the 'Butcher of Bosnia' for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre [FILE: June 8, 2021]Image: Jerry Lampen/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bosnian Serb general Ratko Mladic, who was serving a life sentence for war crimes committed during Bosnia and Herzegovina's 1992-95 war has died, a United Nations official said.
Serbian state broadcaster RTS reported on Thursday that he died in a prison hospital in the Hague, after suffering several strokes.

A family member of Mladic, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the situation, confirmed the reports to the Associated Press and said Mladic's son, Darko Mladic, was on the way to the Hague.

The International Criminal Court for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY) convicted Mladic of charges including crimes against humanity and genocide in 2017, handing him a life sentence. The verdict was confirmed on appeal in 2021.
30 years on: The Srebrenica genocide explained
Commenting on Mladic's death on Thursday, United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres expressed his support for the war criminal's victims.
"The secretary-general stands in solidarity with the victims, survivors and their families who suffered the crimes for which Mr Mladic was found guilty," spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters.
'The butcher of Bosnia'
Mladic was held responsible for his role in the 1992 to 1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including July 1995 massacre of some 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica.
The slaughter, the worst single atrocity in Europe since World War II, saw him named the "Butcher of Bosnia."
Under Mladic's command, Bosnian Serb forces besieged Sarajevo and other towns, operated detention camps for non-Serbs and enemy soldiers, and systematically killed prisoners.
Did foreigners pay to shoot civilians during Sarajevo siege?
Former UN rights chief Zeid Ra'ad al Hussein described him as "the epitome of evil" after his conviction.
"This is all lies, you are all liars," he shouted when he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017.
On Monday, Serbia's justice minister, Nenad Vujic, asked for Mladic to be transferred to a Belgrade military hospital, warning that his death "could come at any time."
Srebrenica massacre discredited international community
Born in Bosnia in 1942, Mladic was a former Yugoslav army officer who rose to command the Bosnian Serb army during the 1992-95 war.
A hardline nationalist, he portrayed the conflict as a historic struggle against Ottoman rule and celebrated the 1995 capture of Srebrenica.
After the capture of the city, Mladic ordered the evacuation of women, children and the elderly but said all men of fighting age are taken prisoner.
In the following days more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys are systematically butchered by the Bosnian Serb forces and their bodies dumped in mass graves.

blocks.caption: Mladic was the military face of a brutal trio, led on the political side by ex-Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic and former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic [August 5, 1993]Image: Str/epa/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: In 2022 The Netherlands apologized for the Dutch peacekeepers' failure to prevent the killings.
Mladic himself has never repented.

articles.title: Venus' US Open invitation raises questions about wild cards
articles.summary: Although her current world ranking wouldn't allow it, Venus Williams is set to play singles in the US Open – thanks to a wild card. Who gets these coveted spots—and how?

image.caption: Venus Williams is back at the US OpenImage: Zou Zheng/Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: Venus Williams hasn't won a singles tennis match since July 2025. The seven-time Grand Slam champion and former women's No. 1 is currently 611th in the WTA rankings and 46 year's old, but she is in the main draw of the 2026 US Open, thanks to a wild card.
"I get a lot of joy out of being different or unexpected or bucking the system,” she told Vogue earlier this year. "I find that thrilling."
Nevertheless, her invitation to play in the women's singles of the US Open raises a fundamental question: How do wild cards work?
The power of the organizers
