A wild card allows a player to participate in a tournament even if their current ranking doesn't warrant it. Organizers can use wild cards to promote young players, facilitate comebacks—or bring in big names.
Williams' case is supported by her extraordinary career. She won two of her seven Grand Slam titles at the US Open and her name alone still sells tickets.
'The most effective tool for developing young talent'
In a statement to DW, the German Tennis Federation (DTB) described wild cards as "one of the most effective tools for developing young talent."
It was something that offered youngsters with "experience at the highest international level—experience that cannot be fully replicated through training or competing at lower-tier tournaments."

blocks.caption: Venus and Serena Williams won the women's doubles at Wimbledon in 2008Image: Corinne Dubreuil/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

blocks.text: However, the DTB also noted: "In our view, there is no automatic priority given to either 'big names' or up-and-coming players. The deciding factors are the specific situation and the tournament's objectives."

In addition to sporting criteria, factors such as "a tournament's appeal or marketing potential could also play a role," the DTB explained. However, there must "always be clearly added value for the tournament and the sport."
Mixed reactions from the tennis world
After Venus received a wild card for the Miami Open in March despite being on a losing streak, former world No. 1 Yevgeny Kafelnikov was critical.

"I have incredible respect for Venus Williams' achievements. Multiple Grand Slam singles champion, world No.1, but it's time," he told the Hard Court podcast. He also argued that wild cards would be better used to help younger players in their development.
Andy Roddick, former US Open winner and world No. 1, disagreed.

"You can save all of your 'she shouldn't get a wild card.' If you won five Wimbledons, seven majors, you're part of the most iconic tennis family in history, this is a win for the tournament at Washington DC, the city of Washington DC," Roddick said on his Served podcast ahead of last year's DC Open.

Andy Murray also pushed back against criticism regarding his wild cards back in 2021. After everything he had been through and contributed to the sport, he "shouldn't have to justify why I should get wild cards," said the three-time Grand Slam winner.

Venus' sister, Serena, received a wild card for Wimbledon this year at the age of 44. The 23-time Grand Slam champion had not played a singles match in nearly four years prior to that. She lost in the first round. (Both Venus and Serena have also been granted a wild card to compete in the US Open women's doubles.)
Wawrinka' frown turned upside down

Stanislas Wawrinka, who is retiring after this season had hoped for one final appearance at the US Open – but was initially denied a wild card. It was bitterly disappointing for the now 41-year-old Swiss, who is ranked 127th in the men's rankings but won the tournament in 2016 – one of his three career Grand Slam titles. However, after the slightly higher ranked American, Patrick Kypson, withdrew due to injury, the organizers extended an invitation to a delighted Wawrinka.
"I'm incredibly excited to accept the wild card for the 2026 US Open and look forward to competing in front of the fans in New York once again," he said in a statement.

blocks.caption: Stan Wawrinka had originally been passed over for a wild card for the US OpenImage: Matthieu Mirville/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Tatjana Maria has also experienced just how unpredictable wild card decisions can be. The German won the WTA 500 tournament at London's Queen's Club in 2025, defeating four top-20 players along the way. A year later, the defending champion didn't receive a wild card, with all four invitations going to British players.
"I was pretty sure I'd get a wild card—or at least I hoped so, since I won here last year," Maria said.
She wound up having to go through the qualifying rounds—and won both of her matches to make it into the main draw.
Two bagels and 20 double faults

There was also a bizarre case in Kenya earlier this year. At the International Tennis Federation (ITF) World Tennis Tour W35 tournament in Nairobi, 21-year-old Egyptian player Hajar Abdelkader received a wild card. The World Tennis Tour is a developmental series for the WTA Tour.
Abdelkader lost to Germany's Lorena Schaedel 0–6, 0–6 in a match that lasted just 37 minutes. She won just three points and committed 20 double faults.

The ITF described her performance level as "unacceptable." Tennis Kenya admitted that she shouldn't have been granted a wild card. The ITF announced plans to review its procedures and consider establishing a minimum sporting standard for wild cards.
A better solution?

The US Open itself has found a way to tie wild cards more directly to sporting criteria. In the US Tennis Association's "Wild Card Challenge," players accumulate world ranking points over several weeks; the leader at the end secures a spot in the main draw. Carol Young Suh Lee clinched a main-draw women's singles wild card for this year's tournament, while J.J. Wolf did the same on the men's side.
This article was adapted from German.

articles.title: DW users on life in Russia: 'People are mad as hell'
articles.summary: Official polling suggests public sentiment in Russia is deteriorating as economic pressure builds. DW asked its users to share their experiences.

image.caption: Many DW social media users paint a bleak picture of life in RussiaImage: Pavel Bednyakov/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fuel shortages are disrupting daily routines. Discontent over pay is rising as job prospects weaken. Planning for the future has given way to short-term coping as anxiety spreads in Russia.

Even Russia's major pollsters, including state-run VCIOM and FOM, as well as the independent Levada Center, report a clear decline in public sentiment. The Kremlin, however, insists that conditions remain stable. DW invited its social media users to share their stories. All responses have been anonymized for safety reasons.
'If there is gas at all, there are massive queues of 50 to 100 cars'
A DW subscriber in Moscow's Pechatniki district described a recent attempt to refuel late at night, covering around 40 kilometers (24 miles) in search of stations with supply.

"If there is gas anywhere at all, there's a massive queue of 50 to 100 cars," he said. "We decided that waiting until 3 or 4 a.m. only to head straight to work was a terrible idea, so we went home to sleep. We're on half a tank for now, but by the end of the week we'll either have to hunt for fuel or stand still. Lately, we use the car almost exclusively for trips to the dacha to see our elderly parents."
"Now you have to hunt for gas at night. You don't always get lucky. Often there's no gas at all. If there is, it's a two-to-three-hour wait," said another subscriber.

blocks.caption: Fuel shortage in Russia: Drivers wait in line for gas at a gas station in MoscowImage: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Fuel shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have become a leading public grievance. Data from BenZinMap, a fuel tracking portal, show severe sales restrictions across 66 regions as of August 27, with another 16 reporting localized disruptions or sharp price increases.

Alexander Shokhin, head of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP), told news portal RBC that refining capacity has fallen by nearly a third, a view echoed by independent analysts. Government measures — including export bans, increased imports, and relaxed fuel-quality standards — have failed to close the gap.

The data provided by Russia's state statistics service Rosstat show average retail gasoline prices are up 7.4% this year, outpacing overall inflation of 4.19%. But the averages conceal sharp regional variation. Stations owned by major oil companies have kept price increases relatively modest, drawing long queues. Independent stations are charging significantly more, adding pressure on household budgets.

There are few signs of outright panic, though. Drivers appear to be adapting to intermittent supply. "Gas is tight, but St. Petersburg is still holding up for now," said one user. "There were disruptions with gas, but the situation is better now, though it's not available everywhere," said another.
Putin faces falling popularity as Russian economy slows
'Getting a new job is becoming harder'

Official statistics point to exceptionally low unemployment in Russia, with Rosstat reporting a record-low rate of 2.2%. But the figure is misleading. Recruitment platforms hh.ru and SuperJob report a sharp rise in CVs alongside a decline in job postings, suggesting growing dissatisfaction among workers but limited alternatives.

Wage growth has also slowed. Companies in struggling sectors such as automaking and coal mining are increasingly shifting staff to reduced hours or mandatory leave. Some DW readers also describe a labor market under strain.
"Getting a new job is becoming harder and harder: There are no new openings, and the ones available are either low-paying or involve grueling 12-hour shifts," wrote one subscriber.

"Wage delays make it hard to keep up with loan payments," said another. "I've been working for two-thirds of my salary all summer. It covers food and gym, and that's about it," noted a third. "Layoffs have hit many industries," added a fourth. "The race of inflated salaries is over. And life has gotten monstrously more expensive than before 2022."

This grim sentiment has spread even to prestigious white-collar roles. An IT professional from St. Petersburg described the shift: "There are no sudden economic shocks, just a gradual decline that has been dragging on for the last 10 years. Job prospects are tight, and finding a new role will be extremely difficult."

A 54-year-old Moscow entrepreneur recalled running a service firm for Western clothing brands before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine. After major clients pulled out, he was forced to close the business. He later launched a new venture manufacturing apparel in Central Asia and Bangladesh for sale on Russian online marketplaces. Early on, rising consumer incomes drove rapid growth. But as economic pressure mounted, conditions worsened.

blocks.caption: DW users complain about rising prices across RussiaImage: Erik Romanenko/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "At first, sales grew faster than we expected. But this business too got caught in the fallout of current policies, isolation, and economic instability," the businessman explained. "Revenues are collapsing catastrophically. And it's not just us. People are cutting back on almost everything."
'People plan nothing, withdraw cash, and buy dollars'

The dominant theme in responses received by DW is the absence of a positive vision of the future. Respondents, judging from their comments, are not preparing for a single shock, but for a prolonged period of stagnation or decline.

"In our region, the changes are not yet significant," wrote a woman from Sakhalin, an island in Russia's Far East. "Prices are rising, of course, but overall, it feels like people live just as they did before. Personally, the changes in daily life I feel most are with internet service. It has gotten slower, and the VPN is on almost constantly to bypass censorship. A huge number of people from my personal bubble left Russia, though that has been happening since 2022. We sent our son to another country, too."

When planning becomes difficult, day-to-day coping dominates. "Fuel shortages, drone attacks... Basic trips to Turkey have become unaffordable," said another subscriber. "People plan nothing, withdraw cash, and buy dollars. There are no hopes for a bright future or a change of power. Everyone lives for today. Drinking has increased significantly — even in Moscow."
Beyond anxiety and apathy, a notable number of responses point to growing social fragmentation, with people withdrawing into narrower circles and avoiding broader discussion.

"People are mad as hell and blame the West for all their troubles. Life has become far poorer, duller, and more dangerous than before the war," noted one subscriber. "People either shut down or cut off any conversation about life and the war immediately. Almost no one is left putting on a brave face or posturing."

"The issue isn't just fuel or the internet — it's the change in people, even quite decent ones," wrote another subscriber, a woman working in healthcare. "There's internal fear, deep irritation — even among those who understand nothing and want to know nothing. But everyone sees the prices. It frightens people. Internal social taboos are vanishing... The intelligentsia suddenly lost its dust, its cultural veneer — especially military-industrial engineers."
Putin admits Ukraine's drones are hurting Russia's economy

articles.title: Nepal flash flood death toll climbs to 579, with 32 Canadians, permanent residents among missing

image.caption: Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home Friday following flash floods in Devighat, Nepal. A sudden flood swept through the Bhote Koshi River basin in northern Rasuwa on Wednesday. (Ezra Acayan/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Thirty-two Canadian citizens and permanent residents are among the nearly 2,000 people missing after the catastrophic flash flood along the Himalayan border between Nepal and Tibet, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand confirmed Friday.
Anand confirmed during a media conference that 579 bodies had been recovered in the area so far and 1,924 people were still unaccounted for. Of those, 517 are foreign nationals, she said.
No Canadians are among those confirmed dead, Anand added.
"Nepal is facing a devastating humanitarian emergency with catastrophic damage," she said.
Canada also announced it was providing $5 million to support emergency relief funds to Nepal.
Meanwhile, rescuers worked through mud and debris Friday in areas devastated by the flood, continuing the search for those still missing.

Nepalese and Chinese authorities also warned of further flooding from a lake that formed upstream after Wednesday's disaster and was already overflowing. They urged people in potentially affected areas to move to safer ground.
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority says 3,742 people have been rescued.

The missing include tourists from several countries. Nepalese army spokesperson Brig.-Gen. Raja Ram Basnet told The Associated Press that a team had been deployed Friday to the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project near the Nepal-China border following reports that people were trapped inside a tunnel.
"It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud," Basnet said. "Our first priority is rescuing the stranded people."

The rescue effort has been challenging, and it's difficult to access some of the communities that have been most affected, Santosh Pandey, Oxfam's humanitarian lead in Nepal, told CBC's As it Happens from Kathmandu.
"Entire villages, entire communities, have been swept away. There is no one actually in the community to help each other," Pandey said.
"A lot of public infrastructure has been damaged, a lot of hospitals and health facilities have been completely swept away.
"It's a very chaotic situation right now."
Rescue workers climb through mud to free people trapped in tunnels
'We have to find him'

As rescuers work to reach remaining survivors, desperate families have crowded around hospitals trying to see if their loved ones can be identified among the hundreds of bodies that have been recovered.
At the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital, relatives peer at grim images lining a wall outside the forensic identification unit.
The photos show the badly battered bodies of victims, including young children who had been pulled from the mud.
“I came here because I hope I find [my brother]. I will search until my last breath is gone,” said Nirmala Sapkota Koholi, 49, who lives in the city of Lalitpur, south of Kathmandu.
“I have to go everywhere, we have to find him.”

Koholi told CBC News that her younger brother, Pradip Kumar Sapkota, was working as a driver with a group of pilgrims, including some from the United States and India. He had been on his phone with his daughter at 8:45 a.m. Wednesday. His daughter heard a loud boom and then the call suddenly cut off. They haven’t been able to reach him since.
Koholi has been to three hospitals and believes one of the victim photos could be her brother.
“He was a very good person. That is why God took him away.”
Lake formed from glacial debris poses new flood threat at Nepal-Tibet border
Red Cross raises alarm about secondary flood

Red Cross officials, at a news conference in Switzerland, expressed concern about a secondary flood and said that the organization's rescue operations were temporarily halted after trucks with relief supplies were were blocked ⁠by further flooding.

"We believe that at ​least 93,000 people have been ​affected and are in great need," said David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation ​of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies ⁠in Nepal.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry said on Friday that it appreciated the offers of help from several countries ‌with nationals missing amid the disaster but that it was able to manage the rescue efforts at present.

items: 10 Toronto residents on a trek in Nepal unaccounted for after deadly flash floods: non-profit group

blocks.text: Flood survivors, including injured people, were taken to Kathmandu and other locations.
The affected areas are popular with hikers and for pilgrimages to religious sites.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry and said that he last spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash on Wednesday morning at 9 a.m.
"This was the first time they had gone on this pilgrimage and it was something my mother always wanted to do," he said.
Survivor sees 'black storm'
Customs officer Karbir Gaire is among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with Tibet.
Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. on Wednesday and was busy working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

"Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us," he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. "We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us."
The disaster started with a glacier collapse that sent ice and rock flowing downstream, and which registered as a magnitude-5.2 seismic event at the U.S. Geological Survey.
The science behind Nepal's catastrophic flash floods
Gaire doesn't remember exactly how many people were in the office when the disaster struck, but his 15 colleagues have gone missing.
"It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don't call it a flood, it was a tsunami," he said.
Gaire described Timure as a vibrant place filled with government offices, hotels, cafes, banks, primary schools, tea shops and residential buildings, where more than 1,500 people were living.

articles.title: The great lake divide: Collapse vs. comeback
articles.summary: As some of the world’s biggest lakes are vanishing in real time, others are proving that recovery is still within reach.

image.caption: The Caspian Sea is under enormous pressureImage: Hossein Beris/Middle East Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Some of the world's largest lakes could shrink substantially within this century, with far-reaching consequences for ecosystems and roughly a quarter of the global population living in affected regions.
Although restoration efforts have proved successful in some cases, many inland bodies of water face extreme challenges.
Caspian Sea: A shrinking giant

Despite its name, the Caspian Sea is actually a lake. Bordered by Iran, Russia, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan, it is the largest inland water body on Earth. But its surface area has been rapidly receding since the 1990s.

This shift is partly due to the use of dams and water-management practices in the Volga River basin. But hotter conditions driven by burning fossil fuels to power societies is also a contributing factor. Rising temperatures increase evaporation rates.

Scientific models project that water levels could fall up to 21 meters (68 feet) by 2100. Even a decline of 10 meters could leave large parts of the shallow northern basin dry, eliminating nearly one-third of the lake's current surface area.

The consequences are already becoming apparent. Ports require increasingly extensive dredging, fish stocks and wetlands are coming under growing pressure and habitats used by the endangered Caspian seal are drying out.
Scientists also warn that exposed lakebeds could release dust and pollutants. Joint conservation efforts among the five coastal states remain politically challenging.

blocks.caption: The water quality in Lake Constance has improved considerably, but evaporation driven by high temperatures poses a threatImage: Markus Keller/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Lake Constance: A pollution turnaround

Like much of Europe, Lake Constance has been impacted by high temperatures this summer. Bordered by Germany, Austria and Switzerland, the 63-kilometer-long (39-mile-long) lake has experienced high evaporation rates that have caused water levels to fall significantly in some places.

In the late 1970s, however, low water levels were not the main concern. At the time, the lake was suffering from severe nutrient pollution and was at risk of ecological collapse. Massive algal blooms and oxygen depletion in deeper waters threatened fish populations and led to swimming bans.

The expansion of wastewater treatment facilities and removal of phosphorus from sewage significantly reduced nutrient concentrations, led to the stabilization of lake trout, which had been at risk of disappearing.
#DailyDrone: Lake Constance
Local communities also benefited. Around 4 million people in the southern German state of Baden-Württemberg rely on Lake Constance for their drinking water.

Yet the ecosystem is far from fully restored. Shoreline development, invasive species and climate change continue to pose major challenges. Restoring more of the lake's natural shoreline could help strengthen its resilience.
Aral Sea: A disaster with glimmers of hope

The Aral Sea in Central Asia has become one of the defining examples of how water extraction can devastate even the world's largest lakes. Only a few decades ago, it was the fourth-largest lake on Earth.

During the Soviet era, vast amounts of water were diverted to irrigate cotton and rice fields, creating an environmental catastrophe whose effects continue today. By 2010, the surface area had shrunk by more than 50,000 square kilometers.

blocks.caption: Where once there was water, vegetation has taken over. Water was already being diverted for agriculture and industry back in the Soviet eraImage: Ekaterina Venkina/DW

blocks.text: Thirty fish species that once supported commercial operations have disappeared, and entire communities along the former shoreline have vanished with them. The Aralkum Desert has emerged where the water once shimmered, covering roughly 62,000 square kilometers.
Today, dust and sandstorms carry salt and toxic residues from the former lakebed across surrounding regions, posing serious risks to human health.

blocks.caption: Land that was previously submerged has been given over to desert shrubs that trap dust and toxins and retain moisture in the soilImage: Ekaterina Venkina/DW

blocks.text: But the North Aral Sea has benefited from the Kok-Aral Dam, which raised water levels. Where a return of the lake is considered unrealistic, saxaul shrubs are being planted to stabilize the sand and contaminated dust. According to the Kazakh government, more than 1.8 million hectares have been planted since 2018.
Muskegon Lake: The big clean up
For decades, Muskegon Lake in the US state of Michigan was polluted by industrial waste and contaminated sediments.

Extensive clean-up efforts by local environmental authorities removed contaminated soil and more than 110,000 tons of historic sawmill waste. As a result, 54 hectares of habitat along the shoreline and in surrounding areas were restored.

blocks.caption: Muskegon is an example of how ecosystems and the economy can benefit from sustainable policies and clean-upsImage: Wirestock/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: In 2025, authorities finally removed Muskegon from the list of severely degraded lakes.

According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the restoration efforts now generate an estimated $28 million (€23 million) in additional recreational value annually and attract roughly 500,000 extra visitors each year.
However, the lake is not entirely free of pollution. Authorities continue to warn against eating certain fish species because contaminant levels remain too high.

blocks.caption: Today the lake is a hotspot for tourists and has become important for recreational timeout in the regionImage: Wirestock/IMAGO

blocks.text: Lake Chad: A region fighting for survival

The vast Sahel forms the transition zone between the Sahara Desert to the north and the African savannas to the south. Stretching across the continent from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea, it is home to one of Africa's most distinctive ecosystems: Lake Chad.
Shaped by sand, wind and harsh environmental conditions, the wetland ecosystem is a critical source of water for people and wildlife and supports livelihoods across the region.

blocks.caption: Water levels in the Lake Chad wetlands fluctuate significantly Image: Joris Bolomey/AFP

blocks.text: In the 1960s, during periods of high water, Lake Chad covered up to around 25,000 square kilometers, slightly more than the area of New Jersey. During severe droughts in the 1970s and 1980s, it temporarily lost more than 90% of that area.
Since then, the lake has partially recovered. Its size now fluctuates considerably depending on rainfall and the season — ranging from roughly 12,000 to 20,000 square kilometers.

Climate change, irrigation and deforestation continue to put pressure on the lake. According to aid organizations, its decline has contributed to a wider ecological crisis across the region and threatens the food security of millions of people.

blocks.caption: Lake Chad is the lifeline for many millions of people in the region. It has recovered to some degree, but still faces challengesImage: Michael Runkel/robertharding/IMAGO

blocks.text: Some 30 million people depend on the resources of the Lake Chad basin. Hundreds of bird species migrate from Europe and Asia to Africa each winter, and many use Lake Chad as an important stopover site.

Some waterways previously blocked by dams have been reopened. In May, the African Development Bank, the Lake Chad Basin Commission and five neighboring countries launched investment projects worth $10 million. The funding is intended to help preserve the lake both as a habitat and an economic lifeline for the region.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Why social media addiction is so hard to regulate
articles.summary: Meta and other social media platforms face lawsuits alleging they foster addictive use among young people. Now regulators are struggling to rein in their engagement-driven business models.

image.caption: Social media giants like Meta are facing multiple lawsuits over alleged harmsImage: Ismail Kaplan/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

blocks.text: Addiction, self-harm, suicide: Social media's engagement-driven strategy is under intense scrutiny for allegedly engineering compulsive use and severe psychological harm, especially in children.
Platforms like Facebook, YouTube and TikTok make huge profits by keeping users hooked via nonstop scrolling, recommendations and constant notifications.
Facebook owner Meta, for example, generated a record $196.2 billion (€168.3 billion) in advertising revenue last year, driven by its ability to keep people glued to their screens.

That business model is now facing major legal and regulatory roadblocks, with social media bans for people younger than 16 spreading globally and a growing wave of lawsuits, mainly in the United States.
In the latest major case, 29 states, including California, Colorado and New Jersey, sued Meta earlier this month, alleging that the social media giant designed its platforms to addict young users.

In a settlement announced on Wednesday, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion to 47 states, the District of Columbia and US territories — including a separate $1 billion settlement with Texas. The platform also agreed to implement usage limits and to block teens from using its apps at night.
Social media growth outpaced regulation
Governments around the world have spent the past decade tightening rules, yet policymakers struggle to keep up with the rapidly changing technology.

Several major studies link social media use in teenagers to increased anxiety, depression and body dissatisfaction. Meanwhile, leaked documents from Meta in 2021 indicated that company researchers had identified links between Instagram use and body-image and mental health concerns among some teenage girls.
Meta faces key trial that could reshape Facebook, Instagram

According to market intelligence firm Sensor Tower, US teens in 2025 spent about 90 minutes a day glued to TikTok. Tests by groups like Amnesty International in 2023 showed that the platform's algorithm can recommend videos related to depression and self-harm to users who engage with mental health content.

"Companies operating at this scale, with so much influence over people's lives, have to meet basic safety standards," Camille Carlton, senior director of strategy and impact at the Center for Humane Technology, told DW.
"This isn't a radical idea," she said. "This is the same standard we apply to other products such as cars, medications and children's toys."
US move toward tighter child safety
After years of gridlock, bipartisan support in the US is growing for tougher rules to protect children from social media harms, through the Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA).
The plans include the strongest safety settings by default for minors and will give parents more tools to control their children's accounts.

blocks.caption: Australia, Indonesia, Brazil and Malaysia have banned social media for childrenImage: Marcus Brandt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The technology is advancing so fast, and the evidence of harm is mounting so fast, that I'm really optimistic that we're going to get major legislation passed in the next session of Congress," social psychologist Jonathan Haidt, author of the bestselling book "The Anxious Generation," told Politico's The Conversation podcast last week.

While KOSA could impose a clear duty of care on tech giants to anticipate foreseeable harm and design features to prevent them, Carlton is pushing lawmakers to place social media products under US consumer-protection and product-liability rules.
Support for alternative models — in theory
In Germany, Cornelia Sindermann, a psychology professor at Charlotte Fresenius Hochschule in Heidelberg, has been studying users' attitudes to alternative social media models.
These include pure subscription plans to avoid ads, which Meta has been testing on Facebook and Instagram in the 27-member EU and the United Kingdom.

Sindermann's 2024 research also found that more than half of adults and two-thirds of adolescents would be willing to pay for a public-service version of, say, Facebook, with much stronger guardrails.

While social media platforms will likely "reinvent aspects of their business models and test additional revenue streams," Sindermann told DW she is "doubtful" that these alternatives will replace the most popular social platforms.
AI investment complicates regulation
Another issue for policymakers is that the same social media platforms used by billions are the ones pouring hundreds of billions into top-tier artificial intelligence (AI) projects.
Some analysts argue that social-media data provides valuable real-world behavioral data for AI development.

As these tech giants grow ever more powerful, their new AI businesses are proving just as difficult to regulate. Experts are increasingly concerned that the same flawed practices that shaped social media are now being built into far more powerful AI products.
So, while social media fights for our attention, AI is now positioned to influence human thought, behavior and relationships in ways that are difficult to imagine, noted Carlton.
"When the incentives driving a product are misaligned with human well-being, we can't expect companies to consistently prioritize the public interest on their own," warned Carlton.

articles.title: CDU's Volkmann: Ukraine aid is not charity
articles.summary: Former German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's grandson Johannes Volkmann spoke to DW about why Germany must continue to support Ukraine.

image.caption: Johannes Volkmann is the grandson of late German Chancellor Helmut KohlImage: Ievgen Shylko/DW

blocks.text: At 29, Johannes Volkmann is one of the youngest members of Germany's parliament — and one of the most dedicated supporters of Ukraine. When he was head of the council of the Lahn-Dill district in the state of Hessen, he launched a municipal partnership with the Ukrainian city of Brovary near the capital Kyiv to deliver supplies to those in need.

As a member of the Bundestag's Committee on Foreign Affairs and the United4Ukraine group, an international network of lawmakers, he continues to advocate for Ukraine. During his latest trip to the country, he spoke with DW about why he thinks aid to Ukraine is so important.
DW: Mr. Volkmann, you were last in Ukraine exactly a year ago. What has changed since then?

Johannes Volkmann: The number of airstrikes — and thus the threat to the civilian population — has increased significantly again. And at the same time, there is a sense that the Ukrainian people still want to stand their ground. I have utmost respect for that. Ukraine is demonstrating that freedom and democracy can defend themselves and fight back. That is a very important message of hope.

German support is particularly important for Ukraine's defense capabilities — Germany is the largest bilateral donor to Ukraine in Europe. At the same time, political forces in Germany oppose this support. The voters of these parties share this view and consider aid to Ukraine a waste of money. What would you say to them?

Everyone needs to understand that Ukraine today is not only defending itself, but also protecting Europe. Russian imperialism is not only a threat to Ukraine's borders, but also to those of our allies in the Baltic states and in Poland. That is why every euro we invest in Ukraine today is a good investment in our own security.

On top of that, Ukraine is able to help us more and more in Europe by sharing its experience on the battlefield with European armies — with regard to modern technologies, drones, the training of soldiers and modern tactics.
When it comes to experience, Ukraine has a tremendous lead in these areas. That is why Ukraine is now effectively a provider of security in Europe and no longer merely in need of security.
Germany pledges €50m to repair Chernobyl nuclear shelter

The Alternative for Germany (AfD), which currently leads the polls, has called for an end to German support for Ukraine. Many in Ukraine are wondering: What will happen if the AfD performs even better in the next German election and becomes part of the government?

I can understand this fear. The Bundestag was elected to serve until 2029. For me personally, as well as for my parliamentary group, the CDU/CSU, it is clear that Ukraine must be supported militarily because it is in our own interest in terms of security. For me, the AfD's position on Ukraine is an important reason why my party has ruled out any cooperation with them.

There is also a humanitarian responsibility: If millions of Ukrainians flee their homeland because Russia's war of aggression succeeds — and, of course, they won't want to live under Russian colonial rule — then that will destabilize our countries. That would place a much greater financial burden on us than supporting Ukrainians today in their defense of their homeland.
Drone warfare: German startup draws on Ukraine's experience
Do you view Russia as a military threat to Europe and Germany? Some are asking: If Russia has struggled so much in Ukraine militarily, what threat can it pose to NATO?

It is important to understand that Russia's hybrid attacks on Europe are not primarily aimed at military conquest but rather at achieving certain political objectives. These include the destruction of EU and NATO cohesion.

So, it is entirely possible that Russia, perhaps with threats involving nuclear weapons, could attempt to occupy specific areas in the Baltic region to test the significance of NATO's Article 5 — the solidarity clause. This is why it is all the more important that we remain vigilant about this issue and develop the capacity to defend ourselves in order to deter Russia from any such aggression. We can only protect peace through our own strength; weakness will be seen as an invitation to attack.
Made in Germany — Rebuilding Ukraine

Germany was one of the countries particularly hesitant and cautious regarding Ukraine's possible accession to NATO. At the 2008 NATO summit in the Romanian capital Bucharest, it was against granting Ukraine a Membership Action Plan (MAP). Many in Ukraine believe that their country's rapid admission into NATO — or at least the granting of an MAP — could have prevented Russia's hybrid war in 2014 and the full-scale invasion in 2022. Was Germany's policy at the time a mistake?

It is clear that the hypothesis put forward by the German government at the time has turned out to have been wrong — the assumption that trade, for example in gas via the Nord Stream pipeline, would create mutual dependencies and thus prevent violence from occurring. The same applies to the assumption that neutrality would protect other countries.

It was a big mistake for Germany to not listen to the insights of our neighbors to the east, who, because of their own experiences with Moscow, historically have a much better understanding of what Russia actually wants.

Apart from accession to NATO, many Ukrainians view membership of the European Union as the best guarantee of security. But German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has ruled out Ukraine's accelerated admission to the bloc. Could Germany be making the same mistake again?

NATO membership and EU membership are two very different matters. The EU is a very comprehensive community based on the rule of law. There are 35 negotiating chapters necessary for accession. To rush through the process despite Ukraine not being ready in certain areas would do neither it nor the EU any favors.

At the same time — as the chancellor has also made clear — the idea is not to hold Ukraine back. It has to be clear that once certain milestones are met, the process of European integration will move forward.

Ukraine is fighting to be a European country. That is why I think it goes without saying that Ukraine, too, can be a full member of the European family with free self-determination. We should do everything in our power to support Ukraine on this path.

One issue many in Ukraine are concerned about is corruption and scandals — including those in President Zelenskyy's inner circle. How dangerous are such cases for the international support for Ukraine?

Personally, I am very worried about this. It would be even worse if corruption scandals were not exposed. It is good when corruption cases are thoroughly investigated and there are no false compromises when dealing with them. That is why we will be closely following the verdicts and consequences that result.

I can only encourage Ukrainian civil society, journalists, the public, members of parliament and the opposition to continue keeping a close eye on the situation and to ensure that Ukrainian and European funds are used properly.

Today, there aren't even any serious discussions about peace negotiations with Russia. The Kremlin insists on its maximum demands, which essentially amount to Ukraine's surrender. At the same time, there are forces in Germany, such as the AfD and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), that have called for talks with Russia. Do you currently envisage any possibilities for diplomatic initiatives?

There have, of course, been numerous attempts by the Ukrainian president and Western states to start peace talks. At the same time, there are no serious signs that the Kremlin has any desire for peace. Such a desire for peace will only emerge when Putin recognizes the futility of his efforts for military conquest.

This requires an increase in military, financial and civil support for Ukraine. And above all, it requires a clear message that the Kremlin cannot hope that Europe will stop supporting Ukraine in 2027 or 2028. We stand with Ukraine — today and tomorrow.
This interview with Johannes Volkmann was conducted by Mykola Berdnyk.

articles.title: UK urged to help free British-Egyptian ‘arrested in Cairo over sister’s activism’
articles.summary:
Lawyers claim Eman el-Shazly, from Birmingham, was detained in effort to silence her sister, a critic of Sisi regime

The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release…

blocks.text: The UK Foreign Office has been asked to intervene to secure the release of a British-Egyptian woman who it is claimed has been arrested in Cairo because of her sister’s political activism.

Eman el-Shazly, a 45-year-old based in Birmingham, was arrested on 16 August while visiting Egypt. Her lawyers say she has been detained in an attempt to silence her sister Mona, a relentless and harsh critic of the Egyptian government on her UK-based YouTube channel.

Her two brothers have already spent three years in jail and, in May, were rearrested. They were previously held in pre-trial detention, facing charges of “promoting the ideas of a terrorist organisation on social media, as well as broadcasting false news harmful to state security”.

The UK Foreign Office has confirmed to the husband of Eman that she is being held in the Ramadan rehabilitation centre and her case has been given the same file number as that of her two brothers, Hassan and Eid.

The government of President Abdel Fatah al-Sisi has faced allegations that it frequently arrests relatives of political critics to put indirect pressure on the dissidents to end their overseas criticism of his rule or of state corruption. Much of Mona’s activism focuses on alleged cases of corruption inside the security services or public utilities, a highly sensitive subject in Egypt.

Arfan Rashid, the lawyer acting for Eman’s husband with whom she has four children, says that unlike Mona his wife has never been involved in politics, and had gone to Cairo two months ago to look after her ill mother after the arrest of her two brothers.

“There is ample evidence that Eman has been arrested to silence Mona,” Rashid said. He added that Eman had told the security officials she was no longer in contact with her sister, and that many family members had repeatedly asked her to stop her political activism in the UK, but to no effect.
Mona confirmed to the Guardian that she had been asked to halt her activism by other family members, including to take down her YouTube videos.

But she added: “I have done nothing wrong nor broken any law … I am a very strong woman, but it is very traumatic for me since 11 or 12 children are without their parents. It is a horrible situation, but the Egyptian government will not stop if I appear weak. The government is close to collapsing.”

Rashid said the UK government had recognised the practice of “punishment by proxy” in Egypt in its country profile policy and information note published in March 2026. Human Rights Watch and the House of Commons library warned in 2021 of an escalating pattern in which Egyptian family members of critics living abroad were being targeted.
Mona runs a YouTube channel in the UK that has 130,000 subscribers. She is also active on X, making specific and controversial claims about government officials.
The UK’s Foreign Office representation in Cairo has asked for access to see Eman but has not yet received a positive reply.

Eman’s husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, has said Egyptian police and security officers attended the family home where she was staying a few days before the arrest, and demanded that Eman tell Mona to stop publishing material against the Egyptian government.

On X, Mona has claimed as many as five members of her family have been detained or harassed by the Egyptian authorities. She wrote: “Kinship is something beyond my family’s will, and I invite them to disown me to save themselves from this despicable, illegitimate dictator. I am the one opposing Sisi, not five individuals from my family. This is a crime against humanity that does not lapse with time.” She has lived in the UK for 18 years.

Eman became a British citizen through marriage. Her lawyer has asked whether Alistair Burt, the UK’s new envoy on complex consular cases, should be asked to intervene by the Foreign Office. Burt was appointed a month ago and has been tasked with working to secure the release of British citizens held abroad.
Burt has already met Gurpreet Singh Johal, the brother of Jagtar Singh Johal, who has been detained by the Indian authorities for nearly nine years without a conviction.
The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Bundesliga season 2026-27: All you need to know
articles.summary: From key dates to rising football stars and changes, DW has the latest on the new Bundesliga season.

image.caption: Bayern Munich are the defending Bundesliga champions yet againImage: Matthias Schrader/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: When does the new Bundesliga season start?

The 2026-27 Bundesliga season starts on August 28 with defending champions Bayern Munich at home against Stuttgart. Borussia Dortmund host Hamburg, while newcomers Elversberg start at home against Bayer Leverkusen.

The Women's Bundesliga began on August 21, as Bayern Munich defeated Union Berlin in the capital. Both Stuttgart and Mainz are new to the league this year, replacing Carl Zeiss Jena and Essen who were relegated.

As is custom in Germany, the domestic men's season truly begins for Bundesliga sides with the first round of the German Cup, which started the week before the league season. The biggest upset in the opening round was Heidenheim, who were in the Bundesliga last season, losing to fourth-division team Jeddeloh. Both Bayern and Dortmund will have to wait a bit longer to play their first round game because the two faced off in the German Super Cup (the game between the league and cup winners of the previous season) - where Bayern ran out winners.
The first 'Klassiker' of the new Bundesliga season is at the end of October and will be played in Munich.
The winter break starts after the 14th game of the season on December 20. The Bundesliga will resume play on the weekend of January 8 and has midweek games immediately afterwards.

blocks.caption: Bayern vs. Dortmund remains the biggest game in GermanyImage: Ina Fassbender/AFP

blocks.text: Are there any new rules in the Bundesliga season?
Some of the new rules we saw at the World Cup will be applied in the Bundesliga too.

Measures are being introduced to improve time management, with the referees able to use the five-second countdown that was on show at the World Cup for goal kicks and throw ins. Although rarely seen, if the limit is exceeded a goal kick becomes a corner for the opposition and a throw in changes hands.
Substitutes will have 10 seconds to leave the pitch, otherwise the new player will have to wait until a break in play – at least a minute later – before he can return to the field.

VAR will also be allowed to have a say in second yellow cards and corner kicks. If a player covers his mouth during a dispute with an opponent, he may be punished with a yellow card. At the World Cup, this was punishable by a red card. Scheduled hydration breaks, regardless of the temperature, will not be introduced in the Bundesliga.

There will also be a new longer international break this season, which sees September's and October's breaks merge into one three-week break starting on September 24 and ending on October 4. This means Bundesliga action will pause for 16 days. The November international break will remain a nine-day interruption.

blocks.caption: Nathaniel Brown was one of the few bright sparks for Germany at the 2026 World Cup in the USA, Canada and MexicoImage: David Ballering Ii/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Have there been any major Bundesliga transfers?
There have been a few signings of real note this summer, perhaps most famously and unsurprisingly at Bayern Munich.
Breakout Germany wingback Nathaniel Brown signed from Frankfurt, while Moroccan striker Ismael Saibari also joins as a strong back-up to Harry Kane.

Elsewhere in the league, Dortmund signed Konstantinos Karetsas for a reported €30 million ($34.6 million) from KRC Genk. Gladbach's German midfield starlet Rocco Reitz left for RB Leipzig, while Hoffenheim are excited by the arrival of 18-year-old holding midfielder Nathan De Cat. Leverkusen reportedly spent €32 million on Afonso Moreira. The Portuguese left winger hopes to continue the form he showed at Lyon.
Freiburg have a new goalkeeper – Mio Backhaus signed from Werder Bremen. Noah Atubolu is expected to join Frankfurt.
The son of former England striker Emile Heskey, Reigan has signed for Cologne, and Robin Gosens returns to Germany to play for newly promoted Schalke.

There have also been a few departures from the league this season. After leaving Bayern Munich at the end of his contract earlier in the summer, Leon Goretzka is reportedly on the verge of joining Aston Villa in the Premier League. Former Borussia Dortmund defender Niklas Süle has retired, opting to play for fun in the lower leagues. Former Dortmund teammate Julian Brandt has moved to Ajax on a Bosman.

Bazoumana Toure leaves Hoffenheim after just a year at the club. The 20-year-old Ivorian winger left the Bundesliga for the Premier League, signing for Newcastle for reportedly a whopping €50 million.
Leverkusen moved on from Alejandro Grimaldo and Matej Kovar, while Freiburg's exciting Swiss midfielder Johan Manzambi moved to Aston Villa for a reported €60 million.

blocks.caption: Martin Demichelis, pictured here in 2008 playing for Bayern Munich, returns to the Bundesliga as coach of RB LeipzigImage: AP

blocks.text: Who are the new teams and coaches in the Bundesliga?

For the first time since 2012, there will be three new teams in the Bundesliga. Elversberg become the 59th club in the history of the Bundesliga, while giants Schalke return after three years away. Paderborn won the playoff to also return, having been in the second division for six years. Wolfsburg lost that game, which saw them relegated for the first time in their history. St. Pauli and Heidenheim were the other two teams relegated.

There have been four coaching changes for the new season. Marie-Louise Eta, who was only in a caretaker role, is replaced full time by the Swiss Mauro Lustrinelli at Union Berlin. Albert Riera's disastrous run at Eintracht Frankfurt was unsurprisingly ended, as Adi Hütter returns to a club he last managed in 2021. Bayer Leverkusen removed Kasper Hjulmand from his position, opting for Spaniard Carles Martinez Novell who last coached at Toulouse. Perhaps the biggest coaching news is former Bayern Munich player Martin Demichelis taking over at RB Leipzig for Ole Werner, who was dismissed despite leading the club to third last season. Hamburg don't have a new coach, but in Kathleen Krüger they welcome a new Head of Sport who is not only breaking the glass ceiling but will give the club a new strategic vision moving forward.
Who are the new, exciting players to watch?

Dortmund’s Karetsas is an exciting, very talented player who was on the wish list of many clubs across Europe. The 18-year-old, who can play in attacking midfield and on the wing, joined Dortmund from KRC Genk this summer.
Nathan De Cat is one of the most exciting young Belgian players. The 18-year-old defensive midfielder joined Hoffenheim this summer, leaving Anderlecht.

A duo of young German prospects at newly promoted Elversberg is worth keeping an eye on: Francis Onyeka (on loan from Leverkusen) and Noah Darvich (on loan from Stuttgart) are considered two of the most exciting 19-year-old players in the country. They are expected to play a major role in Elversberg's debut Bundesliga season, and take big strides in their development in the process.

Germany’s arguably most sought-after talent, Kennet Eichhorn, who left Hertha Berlin for Bayer Leverkusen this summer, must first recover from an injury. The 16-year-old is currently battling a metabolic disorder that led to significant weight loss and physical weakness during preseason. His Bundesliga debut is most likely to come in 2027 as a result.

articles.title: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama dies at 97
articles.summary: From works of "self-obliteration" to polka dotted nudes, the pioneering artist developed a unique body of work likely to be relevant for years to come.

image.caption: Yayoi Kusama died at the age of 97Image: Kirsty Wigglesworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yayoi Kusama gained fame in recent years for her Instagramable "Infinity Rooms" — immersive installations using mirrors, lights and reflective surfaces to create the illusion of endless space — as well as her large-scale polka dot sculptures. While her works often appear playful, behind them lies the story of a woman who has faced major social and mental health challenges.

Around the age of 10, Yayoi Kusama began experiencing hallucinations, seeing dots and net patterns enveloping everything in her mind's eye. She attributed these early visions to the psychological strain of growing up with an unloving mother, who forbade her from painting and tried to impose traditional expectations on her behavior. Although she continued to experience hallucinations until late in life, Kusama learned to live with them and channel them into her art. "My artwork is an expression of my life, particularly of my mental disease," Kusama once told US arts publication Bomb Magazine.
Yayoi Kusama: Dots, mirrors, infinity

After attending the Kyoto School of Arts and Crafts, Kusama held her first exhibitions in her hometown of Matsumoto. She was unusually open about her mental health at a time when such topics were heavily stigmatized.
"It was extraordinary that she addressed it so openly," said Stephan Diederich, curator of the Kusama retrospective at Cologne's Museum Ludwig which took place in 2026.
"For her, art was a survival strategy and a form of therapy, which she always made clear without making it the main focus," Diederich told DW.

blocks.caption: Stephan Diederich in front of Yayoi Kusama's "My eternal soul" at the Museum LudwigImage: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kusama's escape to New York
For Kusama, who was born on March 22, 1929, life in Japan soon became too stifling.

"[My parents] were always trying to rope me into arranged marriages with men I'd never met who came from very particular families," Yayoi once told writer Andrew Solomon, referring to her early 20s as "my era of mental breakdown." She increasingly felt like "a prisoner surrounded by a curtain of depersonalization."

Finally, she broke free from the conventions and expectations of postwar Japan and moved to New York in 1958. "She was exceptionally self-confident and determined to go her own way and pursue a career," said Diederich. Kusama's mother provided her with financial support to get started — on the condition that she never return to Japan. Fellow artist Georgia O'Keeffe, to whom Kusama had previously sent a selection of her works, helped her gain a foothold in the United States.

Kusama often spent entire days working and produced a vast body of art. She became part of the New York avant-garde scene, where her meticulous "Infinity Net" paintings drew attention for their hypnotic, repetitive patterns.

blocks.caption: Kusama's work drew attention for their hypnotic, repetitive patternsImage: Debbie Hill/UPI Photo/newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: Her works, including soft, often phallic fabric sculptures, paralleled some of the approaches of contemporaries like Andy Warhol and Claes Oldenburg.

"She was very confident in saying that she set the benchmarks that her male colleagues later drew on," explained Diederich. However, he added, it's impossible to determine definitively who was first. In any case, her male fellow artists were more commercially successful than the young Asian woman, contributing to her attempted suicide, which she fortunately survived. Kusama made a statement about the gender pay gap with her sculpture "Traveling Life" (1964), which features a ladder covered in phallic shapes with women's shoes on the steps.

Phalluses are another recurring motif Kusama used to process her "fear of sex as something dirty," as she wrote in her 2022 autobiography. Returning to the universe through self-obliteration in the 1960s, Kusama held "happenings" as protests against the Vietnam War. They were often provocative, sometimes involving nudity and sexual activity, although Kusama often noted that she didn't personally participate in the sexual aspects of these events.
"Why should people who share pleasure with each other go to war and kill others? Through free sex, the wall between me and others can be torn down," Kusama wrote in her autobiography.

She was known for painting nude female and male bodies with dots, with the aim of erasing the individuality of those painted. She calls this "self-obliteration," and it runs through her entire body of work. "By obliterating one's self, you return to the infinite universe," Kusama once said.

blocks.caption: Kusama once told an interviewer she wanted 'to become more famous, even more famous'Image: Dagmara Jakubczak/DW

blocks.text: In 1966, Kusama staged her work "Narcissus Garden" at the Venice Biennale. She placed 1,500 mirrored spheres on the lawn outside the entrance of the Venice Biennale, which she hadn't been invited to, and attempted to sell them for $2 each. Biennale officials eventually intervened and stopped the sale, but the work still served as a pointed critique of the commercialization of the art world and the role of artists in it.
Fame later in life
In 1993, Kusama returned to the Venice Biennale as an officially invited artist, representing Japan.

She later told the Financial Times that she wanted "to become more famous, even more famous," a remark that reflects how important recognition had become in her career and one that some commentators critiqued as overly focused on fame.

Over the past decade she reached a level of fame any artist would be envious of. In 2018, The Broad museum in Los Angeles quickly sold 90,000 advance tickets for a Kusama exhibition. A yearlong show at London's Tate Modern in 2022 sold out in no time, as did the one-year extension. Her artworks went on to fetch millions at auction.

Yayoi Kusama returned to Japan in 1973 and chose to live in a psychiatric clinic in Tokyo, where she received treatment for her mental health. She remained highly productive, creating paintings, sculptures, installations and other works that are exhibited around the world until her last days.

"I will continue to create artwork as long as my passion keeps me doing so. I am deeply moved that so many people have been my fans," she said in a previous interview. "I suppose I would not be able to know how people would evaluate my art until after I die. I create art for the healing of all mankind."

blocks.caption: Image: John Angelillo/IMAGO/UPI Photo

blocks.text: This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Trump downplays Moscow visit by CIA director as ‘semi-routine’
articles.summary:
President denies visit was to gain support for Iran sanctions or due to fears that Putin plans to ‘test Nato resolve’

Donald…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has downplayed a visit to Moscow by the CIA director, John Ratcliffe, as “semi-routine” after he turned up in the Russian capital unannounced, triggering a wave of speculation about the reasons for his trip.
Ratcliffe was reported to have flown to Moscow on a government transport plane on Tuesday in a rare visit after taking off from the Andrews air force base in Maryland.
The White House, CIA, Pentagon and the US air force all declined to comment on the visit, which was confirmed on Wednesday by the Kremlin spokesperson, Dimitry Peskov.

Interviewed by the conservative radio host Glenn Beck, Trump poured cold water on speculation that Ratcliffe had travelled in response to fears that Vladimir Putin, the Russian president, was planning to “test Nato resolve” or to win Moscow’s cooperation for intensified US sanctions on Iran.
“None of the above,” the US president said in response to Beck, who referred to the speculation as “crazy”.
“He’s there, you know, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end,” Trump said.

“John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy. He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things that you said. Now something may come … out of it. We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point.”
On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the visit, that the reason for the spy chief’s surprise visit was to warn Russia not to attack Nato countries.
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first from a CIA director since his predecessor Bill Burns travelled to Moscow in November 2021 to warn Putin of the consequences of attacking Ukraine.

The Russian leader went ahead with the attack regardless in February of the following year. Trump’s efforts to end the war – which he once vowed to bring to a conclusion on “day one” of his second presidency – have proven unsuccessful, despite his friendly personal relations with Putin.
Peskov, the Kremlin spokesperson, said Ratcliffe did not meet Putin during his visit.
after newsletter promotion

Washington and Moscow have found themselves on opposite sides following Trump’s decision last February to go to war with Iran, with Russian satellite technology said to have been used to help Iranian forces with precise targeting of US and allied bases in the Gulf and beyond.

With military hostilities at an impasse, the US treasury department this week unveiled a new program of economic warfare against the Tehran regime involving secondary sanctions against countries that trade with it. To be effective, it would need the cooperation of allies of Iran such as Russia and China, experts say.
Peskov did not give a reason for Ratcliffe’s visit, but described forecasts that it would lead to an upturn in US-Russian relations as “premature”, the Washington Post reported.

“Contacts through intelligence-service channels are in themselves a positive phenomenon, a positive process. These contacts often continue even in the most difficult moments of bilateral relations,” Peskov told reporters. “But whether this will affect, on the whole, the process of bringing our bilateral relations out of the deep crisis they are in – it’s premature to say at this point.”
In recent days, Ukraine has targeted Russia’s energy infrastructure and online retail facilities in long-distance strikes, while Russia has intensified drone and missile attacks on Kyiv.

articles.title: Was the heat of this summer really 'normal?'
articles.summary: Some political messaging denies the role of human-caused climate change in this summer's extreme heat. The science tells a different story.

image.caption: As temperatures climbed past 40 degrees Celsius across southern Europe this summer, scientists say such extreme heat is increasing due to human-caused climate changeImage: Tiziana Fabi/AFP

blocks.text: As a summer of European extreme heat draws to a close, politicians are looking back at the toll. Germany recordedaround 14,000 heat-related deaths, almost two-thirds in one scorching week of June alone. A Dutch bank estimated summer heat will cost the EU €180 billion ($209 billion) in lost GDP. And in June, European farmers lost approximately 9 million tons in grain crops.

Climate change, long a politically charged topic, has become a daily reality for people around the world. These effects and more are making it increasingly difficult to challenge what people are seeing with their own eyes.

Yet that hasn't stopped the global populist right from trying. Richard Tice, deputy leader of the UK's far-right Reform Party said "climate change has always happened, it always will," adding that it was arrogant to try to stop it. He encouraged the British public to enjoy the heat.

In the United States, Harriet Hageman, a Republican politician and potentially Wyoming's next senator, told far-right channel Real America's Voice that Europe’s heatwave was business as usual. "It's called summer. Some years are hotter than others and some years are colder than others," she said. "But that's just the cyclical nature of weather."
And Tino Chrupalla, co-leader of Germany’s far-right AfD party
a journalist in recent days that it's been a "completely normal summer." He dismissed climate change as "hype."
But claims like these don't stand up to scientific scrutiny.

blocks.caption: A pharmacy thermometer in Cologne hit a record-breaking 42.2°C as last month ranked among the two warmest ever recorded globally.Image: teutopress/picture alliance

blocks.text: As NASA statesplainly: "Scientific evidence continues to show that human activities (primarily the human burning of fossil fuels) have warmed Earth's surface and its ocean basins, which in turn have continued to impact Earth’s climate."
This was not 'a completely normal summer'

This summer has been historically hot. Independent climate monitoring bodies, including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) in the US, the Copernicus Climate Change Service in the European Union and the Japan Meterological Agency, all called last month either the joint-warmest or joint-second warmest month on record.

The conditions have led energy plants to halt production, outdated concrete motorways blowing up, and older buildings overheating during the day and barely cooling down at night — threatening inhabitants with exposure to heat stress.
The extreme heat was felt almost everywhere on the globe. According to NOAA's data, it was the warmest July ever for North America, Africa and Asia.

The continental United States just surpassedits warmest July records. They were previously set in 1936, during the infamous Dust Bowl that scorched the US Great Plains with extreme temperatures, and in 2012, when North America suffered an extreme heatwave.

And the daily average sea surface temperature hitits highest level since records began in 1979 — reaching 21.1 degrees Celsius (70 degrees Fahrenheit) this month. That's a result of both human-driven warming as well as El Nino, a climate cycle that weakens trade winds and warms tropical Pacific surface temperatures.
How climate change supercharged this summer's fires
In Spain, the far-right Vox party saidfires — which burned more than 254,000 hectares of land across the country this season — were not connected to climate change.

Yet experts agree rising global temperatures played a major role in the intense wildfire season that also scorched large parts of France and Canada. That's because extreme heat creates ideal conditions for wildfires to start and spread.

blocks.caption: Scientists have established a clear connection between hotter temperatures and the likelihood of wildfires Image: Umit Bektas/REUTERS

blocks.text: A field of climate research called attribution science explores the extent to which climate change exacerbates extreme weather events like this summer's wildfires. Using models, researchers compare the likelihood and intensity of an event in today's climate with a simulated world in which there is no human-caused warming.
Analyses done this summer showthat hotter global temperatures created conditions that made the wildfires in Spain 20 times more likely to happen, and twice as probable in France.
This is due to a phenomenon known as weather whiplash, where ecosystems swing dramatically between wet and dry conditions.

When the planet warms, the atmosphere holds more moisture, rainfall is intensified, and plants grow. Then, in summer, that same warm atmosphere draws water from soil and plants, worsening drought and drying out vegetation, turning it into the perfect fuel for fires.

"We know — and this is mathematically proven — that the probability of having fire weather that can sustain and create this kind of event has been altered by climate change," Francesca Di Giuseppe, a fire forecast project coordinator at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, told DW about this summer's fires in Spain and France.
Climate change's ripple effects
Overall, this summer has left its mark in numerous ways that are impossible to ignore.

Bodies of water across Europe are drying out under the intense heat. Parts of the Rhine, Danube and Po rivers have fallen to historically low levels, making it impossible for ships to pass through in some spots.

blocks.caption: Drought and heat have pushed the Rhine to historic lows, forcing cargo ships to carry lighter loadsImage: Martin Meissner/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: This has a number of knock-on effects. Drinking water costs could rise dramatically as much of Germany's clean water first passes through reed-filled riverbanks that are crucial for filtration.
Supply chains are also be disrupted, as vessels can't carry as much cargo when water levels are lower, increasing prices across the economy in products like steel or petroleum.

In America, drought conditions are wreaking havoc on crops and livestock. In June, the US Department of Agriculture said the 10-month stretch from August 2025 to May 2026 was the nation's driest period since 1976-77.

Now, 59% of the country's sorghum is being grown in areas experiencing drought. More than half the nation's cattle production and almost two-thirds of spring wheat production is happening under water scarcity.
Such conditions can put direct strain on the country's food supply, increase prices and threaten rural livelihoods.
By any measurement — thermometers, drought maps, or death tolls — and in much of the world, this summer has been historically extreme.
Why Europe's extreme summers are getting worse

articles.title: Tim Curry, of 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show,' dies at 80
articles.summary: The gender-bending role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter put Curry on the map in 1975. He then went on to play a number of villainous roles like Gomez Addams, Pennywise and Bill Sikes, but also Mozart and…

image.caption: Tim Curry had a stroke around 10 years ago and suffered severe health issues ever since [FILE: August 2016]Image: Richard Shotwell/Invision/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Actor Tim Curry died at the age of 80, Variety, TMZ and other celebrity news outlets reported on Wednesday.

A cause of death was not immediately given but Curry had been in poor health for some time following a severe stroke that left him confined to a wheelchair and wrote in his memoir "Vagabond" last year that he was still not able to walk.
Curry won Laurence Olivier and Tony Award nominations for his work on stage in the UK and the US, as well delivering Emmy-winning TV performances later in his career.

blocks.caption: Curry was another member of the class of 1946 to feature in 'Home Alone 2,' as was the current US President Donald TrumpImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Who was Tim Curry?

Curry was born in Cheshire into a Navy family in 1946 and spent his life bouncing around an array of different homes in the UK and even Hong Kong. He ultimately went to school in Bath, impressing as a soprano singer, and university in Birmingham.
He played in London musicals in the late 60s and early 70s seeking his big break, which came in a 1973 unusual musical ultimately destined to graduate to the silver screen.

blocks.caption: One review at the time referred to Dr. Frank-N-Furter as an 'ambisextrous' character in the cult musicalImage: Collection Christophel/picture alliance

blocks.text: Curry was given the role of the lingerie-clad sweet singing transvestite Dr. Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic film "The Rocky Horror Picture Show" in 1975. Despite the very German sounding name and initial rehearsals with a German and American accent, he ultimately played the mad scientist with an exaggerated upper class Belgravia accent, in what a Guardian newspaper 1973 review referred to as a "garishly Bowiesque performance as the ambisextrous doctor."

blocks.caption: Curry played everyone's least favorite clown — at least in Derry, Maine — Pennywise in 1990Image: United Archives/Impress/picture alliance

blocks.text: He went on to play an array of other roles that involved elaborate costumes, unusual mannerisms, and often a fairly pronounced dark but also comedic side in his career.

blocks.caption: Curry was able to cross threatening Kermit the Frog with an antique pistol off his bucket list in 1996Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: These included Gomez Addams in the "Addams Family Reunion" cinema reboot, Long John Silver in "Muppet Treasure Island," the suspicious Plaza Hotel concierge in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York," Pennywise the Clown in a miniseries based on Stephen King's novel "It," and even as the voice of Chancellor Palpatine in "Star Wars: The Clone Wars."
In another Star Wars connection, Curry was even cast as the Joker for "Batman: The Animated Series," having been considered for the role in the 1989 film as well, until Mark Hamill supplanted him.

blocks.caption: Curry took up the arm-kissing role of family patriarch Gomez in "Addams Family Reunion," the 1998 movie reboot of the hit TV seriesImage: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: Curry also played some of history's most consequential figures like Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, William Shakespeare, and even King Arthur — albeit in the Monty Python musical stage show "Spamalot." He was also among the first actors to branch out into video game roles, perhaps most notably as the fictional Soviet military officer Anatoly Cherdenko in Command and Conquer: Red Alert 3.

blocks.caption: As well as Mozart and Shakespeare, Curry played the 'Red Eminence' Cardinal Richelieu in "The Three Musketeers" released in 1993Image: Everett Collection/picture alliance

blocks.text: He released several solo studio albums and also contributed to various soundtrack records throughout his career, with his musical background apparent in many of his acting roles.

articles.title: South African police arrest two Thai men for allegedly smuggling parrot eggs
articles.summary:
Bird eggs intercepted in homemade incubators at Johannesburg airport as officials try to halt wildlife trafficking

South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents…

blocks.text: South African police have arrested two Thai nationals in separate incidents for allegedly attempting to smuggle endangered parrot eggs out of the country as authorities try to stem the tide of wildlife trafficking.

A 50-year-old Thai national was arrested at OR Tambo international airport in Johannesburg on 20 August, carrying 50 bird eggs in a homemade incubator in a hand-luggage bag, South Africa’s environment ministry said in a statement.

blocks.caption: The seized parrot eggs. Photograph: Ministry of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment

blocks.text: The ministry said preliminary investigations indicated that the eggs were from parrot species listed under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (Cites), which regulates international trade in wild animals and plants to ensure species do not become extinct. It did not specify which species.

Another Thai national, a 23-year-old, was arrested at the same airport on 16 July, allegedly trying to smuggle 418 parrot eggs in two homemade incubator bags. Thailand’s embassy in South Africa did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
South Africa is battling wildlife smuggling on several fronts, from poached rhino horns and the bones of illegally farmed tigers to abalone shellfish and succulent plants.

The environment ministry said: “The illegal collection and trafficking of parrot eggs pose a serious threat to wild bird populations and animal welfare. Eggs are often concealed in improvised incubation devices and transported under conditions that significantly compromise their viability and endanger the welfare of developing embryos and hatchlings.”

Staff at the National Zoological Garden in Pretoria are incubating the seized eggs, the ministry said. “Several of the rescued eggs have successfully hatched and the chicks are receiving intensive veterinary and husbandry care to maximise their chances of survival,” the statement added.

The ministry said the arrests were carried out after a “joint intelligence-driven operation” led by its Environmental Management Inspectorate, known as the “Green Scorpions”, and police intelligence, border and endangered species units.
South Africa punishes the illegal export of Cites-listed species with a fine of 10m rand (£460,000), up to 10 years in prison or both.

articles.title: Saxony-Anhalt election: Why the AfD is so strong
articles.summary: The AfD is polling above 40% ahead of Saxony-Anhalt's election. What is driving support for the far right in this predominantly rural eastern German state?

image.caption: Magdeburg is the state capital of Saxony-AnhaltImage: Heiko Kueverling/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Saxony-Anhalt, one of Germany's 16 federal states, boasts a rich cultural and historical heritage: Many of the world-famous architects associated with the Bauhaus in Dessau lived and worked here. The towns of Eisleben and, above all, Wittenberg preserve the memory of the great reformer Martin Luther. It was in Wittenberg that he famously nailed his 95 theses to the door of the Castle Church, setting the Reformation in motion.

Saxony-Anhalt is home to the Chemical Triangle around Leuna and Bitterfeld in the eastern part of the state, which still provides around 10,000 jobs. To the west lies the Harz mountain range, while the River Elbe, one of Europe's major waterways, flows through the state from southeast to north.

The southern part of Saxony-Anhalt is being forced to reinvent itself as it undergoes structural change following the decision to phase out lignite coal. Unemployment remains slightly above the national average.
How one region in eastern Germany is getting a second chance
