Home to around 2.1 million people, it is one of Germany's more sparsely populated states. Only two cities, the state capital Magdeburg and Halle, have more than 200,000 inhabitants.

Nevertheless, in September 2026, international attention is likely to turn to this small eastern German state. For the first time in postwar German history, a candidate from a party that Germany's domestic intelligence agency classifies as "confirmed right-wing extremist" in parts could become the head of a state government. The Alternative for Germany (AfD), whose lead candidate is Ulrich Siegmund, holds a clear lead in all opinion polls.
The AfD is far ahead in the polls

Just before the election, the AfD is polling at more than 40% in Saxony-Anhalt. The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), which has been the dominant governing party in the state since its re-establishment in 1990, trails far behind, with support ranging between 23% and 26%.

The state office for the protection of the constitution classifies the AfD as a "confirmed right-wing extremist" organization, but this has done little to dent its popularity among voters. The Left Party is polling at 13%, while support for the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) stands at between 6% and 7%. It remains uncertain whether the Greens and the pro-business Free Democratic Party (FDP) will succeed in returning to the state parliament.

CDU politician Reiner Haseloff served as State Premier of Saxony-Anhalt for 15 years before stepping down in January 2026. In an interview with Der Spiegel, Haseloff said that he had often felt, while sitting in the state parliament in Magdeburg, "as though I were in the final phase of the Weimar Republic's Reichstag, or later in Berlin's Sportpalast."

The Weimar Republic, Germany's first democracy, came to an end in 1933 when the Nazis seized power. It was in Berlin's Sportpalast that Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels, a close confidant of Adolf Hitler, delivered his notorious 1943 "total war" speech.

Haseloff's successor, Sven Schulze, also of the CDU, must now take on the AfD. If he fails, the CDU's long dominance of state politics could come to an end in September. Most recently, the conservatives governed in coalition with the Social Democrats and the FDP.
Saxony-Anhalt's unusual political history

From 1994 to 2002, Saxony-Anhalt once again found itself at the center of national political attention. In July 1994, the late Social Democrat Reinhard Höppner formed a minority government with the ecologist Greens that relied on the support of the left-wing Party of Democratic Socialism (PDS), successor to East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party (SED).

Just five years after the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, cooperation with the heirs to East Germany's former ruling party was widely seen across the country, especially by conservatives, as crossing a political red line.

Support for extremist parties has long been stronger in Saxony-Anhalt than in many other parts of Germany. In 1998, the far-right German People's Union (DVU), classified as right-wing extremist, won 12.9% of the vote and entered the state parliament. However, internal divisions within the party were so deep that it chose not to contest the 2002 state election.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
What's driving AfD support in Saxony-Anhalt?

Experts attribute the AfD's strong showing in the polls largely to the widespread dissatisfaction many people in Saxony-Anhalt feel with developments in Germany. In the years following reunification, large numbers of jobs disappeared, particularly in the lignite mining and chemical industries.

Saxony-Anhalt faces pronounced demographic challenges. With an average age of 48.3 years, it had Germany's oldest population in 2024. The state also has a pronounced gender imbalance among younger age groups, with approximately 120,240 men aged 18 to 29 compared with around 103,177 women. At the end of 2025, foreign nationals accounted for about 9% of the population, compared with roughly 15% nationwide. Many young people left the state and never returned.

Many people oppose further immigration, even though the state's foreign population remains comparatively small. Nevertheless, its size has increased markedly over the past decade. According to the Statistical Office of Saxony-Anhalt, the number of people without German citizenship has more than doubled since 2015.
What would AfD rule mean for Saxony-Anhalt?

According to many observers, the DVU's success some 25 years ago demonstrates that right-wing extremist parties have long had a loyal core electorate in Saxony-Anhalt. Today, that electorate largely backs the AfD, regardless of its election manifesto or policy program.

Political scientist Benjamin Höhne of Chemnitz University of Technology told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that he believes the AfD would seek to reshape the constitutional order if it were to take power in Saxony-Anhalt. Liberal democratic and rule-of-law principles, he argued, would be systematically eroded. "I think the AfD is currently watching the United States very closely." In his view, President Donald Trump's administration in the US is pursuing a similar course.

Höhne believes, however, that such radical agendas would be difficult to implement in a single federal state. "You cannot simply pull a lever in one state and expect everything to fall into line with a far-right script."
One thing seems certain: on September 6, all eyes will be on this small state in the center of Germany.
This article was originally published in German.
Threat from the far right: Never quite German enough?

articles.title: Reports: UEFA backs off FIFA boycott threat
articles.summary: UEFA is reportedly set to withdraw a threat to boycott FIFA tournaments over a plan to partially privatize football tournaments. The Under-20 Women's World Cup is to be hosted by Poland next month.

image.caption: UEFA boss Aleksandar Ceferin (right) spearheaded opposition to FIFA boss Gianni Infantino's privatization planImage: Mark Pain/IMAGO

blocks.text: English newspapers The Times, the Guardian and news agency Reuters reported on Wednesday that UEFA, football's European governing body, was set to drop its threat to boycott all FIFA tournaments.

The decision to allow European teams to participate in next month's Under-20 Women's World Cup in Poland came after UEFA had reportedly received guarantees that football's world governing body would not revive a plan to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments to private investors. FIFA President Gianni Infantino had dropped his plan to create a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprises (FFE) in the face of widespread protest last month.

UEFA spearheaded opposition to the plan but it had also demanded that "assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again," something that until now, FIFA had declined to do. The reports suggest this demand has now been met.

The reports also said UEFA would use a meeting of its executive committee and most of the presidents of its 55 national associations in Monaco on Thursday to inform them that the U20 tournament could go ahead.
'Not a UEFA defeat'
The Guardian reported that the FIFA and UEFA officials had been in private talks for weeks intending to prevent a boycott.

"It's not a UEFA defeat, rather the reality of avoiding hurting young players during a once in a lifetime ⁠opportunity," a source familiar with the discussions told Reuters. "The actions and insistence on change will ​continue."
The Times reported that UEFA was working on other ways to try to step up the pressure on Infantino.

It cited a letter reading that "UEFA hereby gives formal notice that it is actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan proposed by FIFA and all related matters.

"You and FIFA are required to take immediate steps to identify, locate, and preserve all documents and electronically stored information described in this notice that are in your or FIFA's possession, custody, or control."
'Best possible conditions' for the tournament
Before the latest reports, the Polish FA (PZPN) told DW in a statement that it was continuing with its preparations to host the Under-20 Women's World Cup as planned.
"Our priority remains to ensure the best possible conditions for the competition and for all participating teams," the statement read.

"For many of these young players, this tournament represents an important milestone in their sporting careers, and we remain fully focused on delivering an event worthy of their talent and commitment."
The tournament kicks off with the opening match between Poland and Argentina in Katowice on September 5.

Gianni Infantino is expected to stand for re-election at the FIFA Congress in March 2027 and so far no other candidate has come forward to challenge him. UEFA President Aleksander Ceferin has already said he will not run.

articles.title: Gamescom 2026: What's next for the gaming industry?
articles.summary: As Gamescom 2026 opens in Cologne, AI, hardware costs and slowing user growth are putting pressure on the global games industry despite its current strength.

image.caption: AI is bringing significant challenges for the gaming industry, but it could also help significantly reduce costsImage: Political-Moments/IMAGO

blocks.text: Earlier this month, gaming giant Electronic Arts was sold to an investment consortium including Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund and US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, for $55 billion (€47 billion).

The deal stood out in a few ways. It is believed to be one of the largest leveraged buyouts in history, meaning a significant chunk of the $55 billion was borrowed money that the company itself will have to pay back.
It was also the second-biggest deal in gaming history, after Microsoft's purchase of Activision Blizzard, the company behind the "Call of Duty" franchise, for $69 billion in 2023.

The Electronic Arts sale additionally shone a light on the growing economic significance of the gaming industry and the increasing interest from major global investors such as Saudi Arabia, seeking to benefit from the sector's cultural and financial clout.
How big is Gamescom and the global gaming industry?
That cultural and financial clout will be on full display over the next few days in the German city of Cologne, where Gamescom, the world's largest gaming event and trade fair, takes place.
The event attracts thousands of exhibitors and games developers, close to half a million visitors and many more millions of fans connecting online from around the world.
It's the place where companies build hype for their upcoming releases, with massive rooms packed with screens, consoles and a range of gaming experiences.
Robots impress at China's World Humanoid Robot Games
"Gamescom is a very useful barometer for the health and mindset of the industry," Piers Harding-Rolls, a games industry analyst with Ampere, told DW.
That health looks fairly robust at present.

The global games market is currently valued at $213.9 billion, up 6.1% year on year, according to Newzoo, a gaming industry market analysis company. Manu Rosier, the company's director of market intelligence, says that growth is broad across the sector's three main platforms: mobile, console and PC.
It now comfortably rivals the movie and music businesses both in terms of finances and, some would argue, cultural significance and reach.
"If you add the music subscription and transactional markets together with the cinema box office, spending on games is over three times bigger," said Harding-Rolls.

blocks.caption: Gamescom 2026 takes place from August 26-30 in Cologne, Germany, and could once again bring in close to half a million visitors Image: Wolf von Dewitz/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Joost van Dreunen, an assistant professor at NYU Stern School of Business and the author of "One Up: Creativity, Competition, and the Global Business of Video Games," says gaming's communal aspects have powered its growth.

"The cultural relevance of interactive entertainment has substantially expanded in the past few years, as millions of players around the world have found a common interest in playing together online," he told DW. "That's something few other forms of entertainment have accomplished."
How AI and rising costs are shaping the gaming industry
Yet the sector faces significant challenges. Like most industries, it is grappling with artificial intelligence (AI) and an onslaught of AI-generated material.

"AI is flooding the existing digital markets with content that is generally disregarded by players," said van Dreunen. "It nevertheless makes it more difficult for audiences to find relevant content in an expanding sea of slop."

There is already clear evidence of resistance from gamers toward AI. A recent survey by Quantic Foundry, a gaming analytics company, found that 85% of respondents had a less than neutral position on generative AI.

Another challenge AI is bringing to the gaming industry is cost related. The development of AI infrastructure and data centers has led to a surge in demand for chips and memory, which has driven prices up. Nvidia recently warned some of its largest customers that semiconductor prices would increase by as much as 15%.

That has driven up component costs for the gaming sector. "It shows on every platform. PC builds and upgrades, console prices climbing mid-cycle rather than falling as they did in past generations, and rising smartphone prices," said Rosier.

He thinks the increased costs could delay the introduction of the next generation of games console in the next few years, while Piers Harding-Rolls thinks it is adding pressure to a sector grappling with other financial concerns.

"Increasing costs for games hardware components pushing up prices, hyper-competition across all areas of the market meaning a glut of content, and challenges in discovery (of new users) and user acquisition," he said.
Hooked on video gaming

Joost van Dreunen also cautions that the sector is now more dominated by the biggest players than in previous years, with major releases this year such as the latest "Grand Theft Auto" and Marvel's "Wolverine" helping boost overall revenues.
"Demand is more top-heavy than in the boom years, which makes it really strong at the top and precarious in the middle," he said.

Another challenge is keeping gamers gaming and adding new ones. Manu Rosier says there are now 3.7 billion gamers around the world, more than 40% of the global population and more than 60% of all those who use the internet. However, there are signs that new user growth is slowing, he says.
How the games industry is evolving
Yet as the industry gathers in Cologne, there is an unmistakable optimism about its prospects. Beyond the gloom around AI, there is the belief that technology could also significantly reduce costs.

"AI is being used across games companies to replace repetitive tasks that are better done by agents including preproduction work and coding. This saves time and hopefully delivers efficiency, with the aim of cutting cost," said Harding-Rolls.
As for its ability to improve gameplay, many gamers remain doubtful. That's in part because the definition of a "gamer" has shifted, which has helped the industry itself evolve.

blocks.caption: Popular titles such as 'Grand Theft Auto' and Marvel's 'Wolverine' are powering major growth for the industry in 2026Image: Rockstar/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "A generation ago, games were predominantly single-player focused and narrative-driven. Today, games are more social and less focused on story," said van Dreunen.
Yet that in turn brings its own challenge, with developers competing for the attention of billions of gamers around the world in a more crowded market.
"The market is continually evolving and reinventing itself," added Harding-Rolls. "Companies are continually challenged to innovate and bring new experiences to consumers."

articles.title: Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained?
articles.summary:
The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected

A fresh outbreak of mpox

blocks.text: A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed?

Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic.
What is mpox?

Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs.

blocks.caption: A colourised electron microscope image shows Mpox virus particles, represented in green, found within infected cultured cells, represented in blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for their differences in shape. Photograph: AP

blocks.text: It used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend changing it to mpox.

It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox was on course to become endemic in the US.
Why is it spreading to new countries?
There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”.

The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with men at the highest risk.

blocks.caption: A Red Cross worker disinfects a tent in the Don Bosco camps for internally displaced people in Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Photograph: Moise Kasereka/EPA

blocks.text: In June 2024, researchers raised the alarm about a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024.

“Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months.

“Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said.
What happened to those two big outbreaks?

The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections.

blocks.caption: A passenger passes mpox alerts at Chennai airport in India. Photograph: R Satish Babu/AFP

blocks.text: The 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency status lifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled.

If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again.
How worrying is the new outbreak?
Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four.

“The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.”

blocks.caption: Furaha Elisabeth applies medication to the skin of her child, Sagesse Hakizimana, at a health centre near Goma, in the DRC. Photograph: Arlette Bashizi/Reuters

blocks.text: However, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.”

Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.”
Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases.
Are there vaccines and treatments?

The WHO recommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available.

Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.”

A new global stockpile is due to be launched within weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand.

blocks.caption: A young mpox patient receives treatment at the Kavumu hospital in Karanrhada, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Photograph: Michael Lunanga/EPA

blocks.text: An antiviral called tecovirimat did not appear any better than a placebo when tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival.

While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak.

“Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.”

articles.title: On scraps of land and under constant threat, Gaza farmers struggle to survive
articles.summary:
Efforts to rebuild domestic food production face severe challenges and have come at deadly cost

As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the…
articles.byline: Seham Tantesh in Gaza, and Julian Borger

blocks.text: As Gaza’s population of 2.1 million has been hemmed into an ever smaller slice of the territory, farmers are using every last remaining patch of unspoiled earth, no matter how tiny, in their struggle to survive.

With severe shortages of water, fertiliser and pesticide, and with more than 80% of greenhouses ruined, it has taken inventiveness and determination to clear land of debris and coax new seedlings into life. Moreover, venturing out into the open to tend to plants can be deadly.

Saqer Abu Rabee’s eldest son and brother were killed while at work growing food for their communities on their small agricultural plots in Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza. His son Yousef was 24 when he was killed by a drone-fired missile in October 2024. Abu Rabee was working in the fields 10 metres from his son when it happened.

“The missile was aimed directly at him and I have no doubt that he was the intended target,” Abu Rabee said. Yousef was well known locally as the driving force behind a collective first called We’ll Plant It and now simply Our Land, which brought together volunteers and encouraged farmers to go back to the land to restore agriculture in the area.

blocks.caption: Yousef at work in 2024. He was killed by a drone-fired missile that year aged 24. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: “They decided to target him directly,” said Abu Rabee, who stressed his son had no political affiliations. “Before his death, we received daily threats from the Israeli army. They shelled our area every day three or four times while I was working alongside the labourers.”

Abu Rabee’s brother Bilal was killed on 2 July after he went to retrieve some agricultural supplies from a destroyed building. His death came nine months into a partial ceasefire during which Israeli forces have killed more than 1,200 Palestinians. Abu Rabee is convinced farmers have become prime targets because of their role in sustaining Palestinian communities among Gaza’s ruins.
The Israel Defense Forces deny targeting farmers or any civilians, saying they have only responded to imminent threats from Hamas since the October ceasefire.

Despite the risks, Abu Rabee, 48, is still at work every day cultivating a 1.4-hectare (3.4-acre) plot in Beit Lahiya that was an orchard of orange trees before the war. He said the orchard was bulldozed by the Israeli army.
“We cleared it and rehabilitated it using only basic tools, manual labour and tremendous human effort. It took a great deal of time and hard work before it was ready for cultivation again,” he said.

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee works on his plants nursery in Gaza

blocks.text: Out of that scrap of land, Abu Rabee says his family have produced hundreds of thousands of aubergine, tomato and pepper seedlings. They raise cash by growing their own aubergines to sell to wholesale traders, while most of the seedlings are distributed to other farmers or to individual households to plant in patches of earth around their homes and tents.

He says the supply has transformed the local food market. Aubergines now cost less than two shekels a kilogram, compared with 40 shekels a few months ago. Peppers and mulukhiyah, a dark green leafy vegetable, are now selling at a tenth of their market price earlier this year.

“What has happened is that Beit Lahiya has regained a degree of self-sufficiency,” Abu Rabee said. “In my view, without Beit Lahiya, Gaza would face famine. Before the war, it was considered the food basket of Gaza Strip because of its fertile soil, fresh groundwater and light, productive land.”

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee checks the state of crops grown for the production of seeds. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Increased aid and commercial deliveries under the ceasefire have brought Gaza back from the abyss of last year’s famine conditions, but according to UN agencies there are still 1.4 million people – 67% of Gaza’s population – facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity or worse.

Much of the commercial inflows of food are of poor nutritional quality. The director general of the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), Qu Dongyu, has said the limited recovery will remain fragile without domestic food production.
“Food security in Gaza cannot recover unless local food production starts again and farmers, herders, fishers and other producers can rebuild their livelihoods,” Qu said in July.

blocks.caption: Saqer Abu Rabee harvesting aubergines. Photograph: Amjed Tantesh/The Guardian

blocks.text: Based on satellite data, the FAO estimates that little more than a quarter of Gaza’s total prewar cropland, 4,100 hectares, remains accessible, and only about 3%, 450 hectares, is undamaged, free of debris and ready for immediate cultivation.
Most of Gaza’s prewar farmland is under Israeli military occupation, and the proportion has grown as the army has pushed the “yellow line” steadily forward over the course of the ceasefire.

Using specialised satellite imagery, the human rights advocacy group Forensic Architecture carried out a survey of flora across Gaza as a measurable proxy for cultivable land. It found that nearly 68% of the territory’s flora was on the Israeli side of the yellow line and another 5% was inside a buffer zone declared by the army, delineated on maps with an orange line, where it is extremely dangerous for Palestinians to venture.

Bilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, was shot dead along with another man when they came within range of Israeli sniper positions. Their bodies were left out in the open for two days because it was too dangerous for their relatives to retrieve them.

The family’s old farm is now under Israeli control, so after the ceasefire was declared they came to Beit Lahiya to try to start again from scratch on leased land. Since last October the army has pushed the yellow line forward, swallowing up nearby farms in west Beit Lahiya.

“The expansion has had a devastating impact on the agricultural sector,” Abu Rabee said. “Fertile farmland that farmers had worked tirelessly to cultivate after spending everything they had or even borrowing money, simply it was seized just as it was ready for harvest, leaving them with nothing.”

blocks.caption: Bilal Abu Rabee, Saqer’s brother, who was shot dead in July. Photograph: Handout

blocks.text: On the remaining land, the challenges appear endless. With hardly any livestock left, there is little homegrown dung-based fertiliser, so the family are improvising by piling decaying vegetation under tarpaulins. Meanwhile, they are battling nematodes and other soil infestations and a chronic lack of water, all the time under the constant, unpredictable threat of death.

Abu Rabee said: “Stray bullets frequently reach this area and strike many places around us. Many people have also been wounded in the streets as a result of indiscriminate attacks. I fear for my own life simply because I’m a farmer.”

articles.title: Iran seeks to criminalise all contact with foreign media in ‘chilling’ crackdown
articles.summary:
As photojournalist sentenced to 15 years, rights groups warn law would turn civic engagement into security crime

Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign…

blocks.text: Iran has taken the first step towards criminalising contact with foreign media, in a move human rights groups have said attempts to “sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world”.

For journalists, researchers and even ordinary citizens, the proposed law being discussed by Iranian lawmakers this month could make speaking to international audiences and groups a potential criminal act and restrict coverage of events such as January’s mass anti-regime protests.

Even social media platforms that the regime considers to be “financed” by another country, such as Instagram and X, would fall under the bill, said Moein Khazaeli, an Iranian human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists.

“It means any kind of interview, contact, or sending photographs to them [foreign media or organisations] could lead to six months to two years’ imprisonment. Not just the US and Israel, but any contact with foreign media in any country could be considered a crime if one doesn’t inform the intelligence ministry beforehand,” said Khazaeli.

Among the recent examples of the risks facing Iranian journalists is the case of Yalda Moaiery, an acclaimed photographerwho was sentenced this month to 15 years in prison in Tehran for documenting the US-Israeli war on Iran.

blocks.caption: The Iranian photojournalist Yalda Moaiery, who was sentenced in absentia to 15 years in prison for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran.  Photograph: Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle/Polaris/eyevine

blocks.text: Although Moaiery was charged under the espionage law introduced after last year’s 12-day war between Iran and Israel, Khazaeli said the new bill signalled a broader effort to regulate and punish contact between Iranians and foreign media and institutions. “It could move [Iran] to a North Korea kind of situation,” he said.

Moaiery, 44, has spent two decades covering the harsh realities faced by people in Iran, including the nationwide Woman, Life, Freedom protests in 2022 and the anti-regime protests that led to thousands being killed in January.

She came to international prominence in 2019 after criticising Trump’s use of one of her photos of a woman at a demonstration near Tehran University, saying Trump’s sanctions were damaging Iranian lives, including those of her friends and family. “This image shows my people and is for my people, and shouldn’t be abused by these men in Washington,” she wrote.
Now, in a cruel irony, Moaiery said she had been sentenced in absentia for her work covering the US-Israeli war in Iran and accused of media activity deemed to strengthen and aid Israel and the US.

“I have been a critic of Israel and its policies all my life. I am not an Israel supporter, never, ever. And I have always been a critic of American politics. It was like something that you are against, and they want to stick it to you. So it’s hard. It’s super hard,” she told the Guardian.
Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), said the new law on media contact risked turning Iran into an “isolated black hole”.

“It is not simply an attack on journalists and citizen journalists; it is an attempt to sever the entire Iranian society from the rest of the world by criminalising the free flow of information itself.
“It sends a chilling message and threatens to turn ordinary academic, professional and civic engagement into a potential national security crime,” she said.

blocks.caption: Casualties in Tehran of an airstrike during the 40-day US-Israeli war on Iran, taken by Yalda Moaiery on 15 March. Photograph: Yalda Moaiery/Reuters

blocks.text: Moaiery was arrested and sentenced to eight years in prison in 2022, but later received an amnesty. This time, however, she fears her sentence could be upheld and she might be jailed.
“Of course, I am scared,” she said. “The only thing that I’m worried about is wasting my life if I have to be there for 15 years. When I get out, I’ll be 60 years old.”
She also criticised foreign journalists who travelled to Tehran to cover the funeral in July of the late supreme leader, Ali Khamenei.

“I have one word for them: shameful. They just want to say, ‘We were in Tehran.’ OK, but what did you do? They didn’t go and ask people about the economic situation or talk to the families of the thousands who died in January. Why were you here? To participate in their propaganda?”

articles.title: Iran faces strait of Hormuz paradox as strategic value of chokehold erodes
articles.summary:
Internal calls to end war get louder as Gulf neighbours plan alternative pipelines to cut reliance on waterway

Is the strait of Hormuz, recently cited by the office of the Iranian supreme…

blocks.text: Is the strait of Hormuz, recently cited by the office of the Iranian supreme leader as “the pillar of Iran’s new security order”, and as transformative as possessing a nuclear weapon, in reality becoming a fast-diminishing asset, leaving Iran increasingly vulnerable to the new planned US wave of economic sanctions?

It is the key debate that is raging inside Iran, with many different conclusions being drawn for Tehran’s negotiating strategy. Those who warn the strait’s value as a chokehold on the world economy will erode, leaving the country without foreign exchange reserves, argue that Iran’s negotiators should seek a deal soon.

One analysis written by Hamid Paktinat, the founder of the Forum of Economic Activists, suggests the construction of alternative pipelines and export routes by Iran’s Gulf neighbours will halve the strait’s strategic value within three years.

Those who worry about wasting assets inevitably set store by the separate visits this week to Tehran of Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, and Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir. These two men are critical to renegotiating the terms for the reopening of the strait and the revival of the discarded memorandum of understanding agreed by the US and Iran in June.

The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, have both recently made unusually blunt comments about the need to end the war – and the economic consequence of continuing it. Ghalibaf said that regardless of how much military power Iran possessed, “if people are hungry” and there was no economic growth, the country could not endure. Security, he argued, could not be sustained without a functioning economy. He added that, as someone with a military background, “we know the value of peace better than those who talk about peace”.

Pezeshkian was even more blunt: “The war must end at some point,” he said. His argument was that Iran should end the conflict now, while Tehran still believes it is negotiating from a position of strength, rather than wait until its position weakens.

The Iranian central bank governor, Abdolnaser Hemmati, also recently went on TV to warn about the economic pressures. “We are facing four or five major challenges simultaneously, including maximum sanctions, blockade, cutting off oil exports, and a budget imbalance, each of which puts pressure on the economy,” he said. “One of the neighbouring countries told me that if one-fifth of what happened in your country happened in our country, we would not be able to govern the country.”
What is driving these remarks is the pressure on ordinary people in Iran, and an acceptance that the strait cannot become a permanent security doctrine in itself.

Hamid Asefi, a Tehran-based journalist specialising in geo-economics, is one of many warning that if Hormuz is to be played as Iran’s final card every time a crisis arises, this card will gradually lose its value. “A threat that is constantly repeated turns from ‘deterrence’ into a political habit; and a political habit, if not accompanied by concrete achievements, sooner or later leads to an inflation of threats,” he said.
The main question is no longer: can Iran close the strait, he wrote, but if Iran closes Hormuz to the world, does it open the door to power for itself or lock part of its power behind that door?

“This is the Hormuz paradox. In international politics, a lever that is constantly flaunted can become its own enemy because it forces others to plan to reduce their vulnerability […] the main question of Iranian policy in Hormuz must change from: ‘How can we make the passage difficult?’ to ‘How can we make the passage so safe and stable that everyone needs Iran to maintain this order?’”
That does not imply the lever is valueless. Far from it.

According to data compiled by the ship tracker Kpler, only 112 oil and gas tankers went through the strait between 1 and 19 August. Almost 79% used unconfirmed routes, 19% used Iran’s preferred northern route and 2% used the Omani route. In reality many of the ships that used the unknown routes probably turned off their transponders and used US protection along the Oman route.

It also appears that aided by the US government, Saudi, Emirati, Qatari and Kuwaiti oil companies have chartered a small group of oil tankers to take cargo through the southern route to the Gulf of Oman, where they then offload the oil to waiting tankers owned by their customers. Much of the risk is therefore transferred from shipping companies and oil customers to the more highly motivated state oil producers and to the US government. Iran has drawn up a blacklist of about 48 ships that it will try to ban or fine.

But the US government is probably exaggerating the impact of these workarounds. Chris Wright, the US secretary of energy, claimed on 18 August the US navy had assisted in the transfer of more than 15m barrels of oil and other products. He also claimed the average daily transfer of oil through the strait was now more than 8m barrels, but even this figure is less than half the prewar average and is anyway seen as inflated. Most ship data trackers estimate the daily figure at closer to 6m barrels a day.

Arsenio Dominguez, the secretary general of the International Maritime Organization, furthermore dismissed Donald Trump’s outlandish claim that the US navy had all but opened the strait, telling Bloomberg: “Given the very small number of ships that transit the strait of Hormuz, it is clear that this strait is, in practice, not open.” The US president has countered that all mines in the strait have been removed, leaving Iranian drone and naval attacks as the chief threat.

But the fact that before the war the strait accounted for 20% of oil and oil-related products is serving as a catalyst for the restructuring of the global energy infrastructure. Countries in the Gulf are rapidly building a network of alternative pipelines, with the aim of protecting more than half of their prewar exports from the impact of Hormuz by the end of this decade.

Paktinat has looked through the region at the capacity, length and cost of pipelines being prepared in six countries over the next one to four years. He concluded Saudi Arabia’s reliance on the strait of Hormuz would decrease from 70% to 15%. The UAE’s reliance would decrease from 50% to 15%, and Iraq’s dependence would fall from 100% to 30%.

Kuwait and Qatar’s reliance would decrease from 100% to less than half. Bahrain’s reliance would fall from 100% to 15%, he assessed. Finally, Oman’s reliance would change from 0% to becoming a major coastal oil transfer hub for the entire region.

Overall, he says, the strategic value of the strait of Hormuz will be halved within three years and almost lost within six years with the implementation of these projects. The narrow horseshoe waterway will remain, but its strategic importance – the centre of Iranian gravity – will have evaporated.

In the meantime, the US will try to turn Trump’s premature boast that the Iranian economy has completely collapsed into reality. It will try once again to block the vital arteries of the Iranian government across five key sectors: gold, cryptocurrency, technology, shipping and aviation.

Success is by no means guaranteed, as Trump must know from the failure to defeat Iran in his first term. But slowly chipping away at Iran’s economic resilience until the strait finally becomes an irrelevance may be Trump’s only remaining option.

articles.title: Remembering Dolly Parton: 8 facts about the icon
articles.summary: Dolly Parton, one of the world's most successful artists, has died at the age of 80. Here are some important and extraordinary facts about the country music superstar.

image.caption: Dolly Parton, seen here in 1977, had a career that spanned seven decadesImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: More than 100 million records sold, 25 No. 1 hits on the US country charts, 11 Grammys and three Emmys — country star Dolly Parton was one of the most successful singers in the world. On Tuesday, her nephew Bryan Seaver announced in a video shared on Parton's social media channels that his aunt had died.

"Dolly... opened doors for generations of singers, songwriters, musicians and dreamers from every walk of life and across every continent," Seaver said in the video. "She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."
Here are eight facts from eight decades of Dolly Parton.
1. Cornmeal for the doctor
Dolly Parton came from humble beginnings, growing up with 11 siblings in Sevier County, Tennessee.
Born on January 19, 1946, her parents paid the doctor who assisted at her birth with a sack of cornmeal — though some sources claim it was oats.
Parton was born into a musical family and learned to play the guitar when she was 7. She gave her first performance on television at age of 10.
2. No 'Dumb Blonde'

Multiple sources have reported Parton's IQ to be at least 140. Her first song, which entered the US country charts on January 21, 1967, was "Dumb Blonde." In it, she sings "this dumb blonde ain't nobody's fool." It was a bold start for her entry into 1960s show business, at the time dominated by men.
"I'm not offended by all the dumb blonde jokes because I know I'm not dumb… and I also know that I'm not blonde," she said of the stereotype.
3. Impressive parade of wigs
Across her seven-decade career, Parton loved following fashion trends — especially when it comes to hairstyles.

But her trademark platinum blonde hair was never truly her own. Rather than spoil her hair with bleaching, she began wearing wigs from early on. It's said her collection numbered over 350 different wigs.

blocks.caption: Even wigs need styling: Parton, who appeared in the film 'Steel Magnolias,' visited the Broadway show in 1988Image: Mark Lenihan/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Parton never made a secret of her cosmetic surgeries. Over time, she used it to change her face and figure — but she always remained the friendly superstar with a big heart.

In 2025, Forbes magazine valued Parton's fortune at around $450 million (€387 million). She shared her wealth with people in need for decades — in particular in her home state of Tennessee, but also around the globe.
4. Promoting reading for kids

Since 1995, Parton's The Dollywood Foundation has been sponsoring books for children as part of her Imagination Library program. From the day a child is born, parents can apply to receive a book every month up until the age of 5. More than 300 million books have already been distributed in five English-speaking countries: the US, Canada, Australia, UK and Ireland.

blocks.caption: Parton donated her royalties to good causesImage: Mark Humphrey/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The program is funded by the foundation itself, government support and private donors. Recently, however, some Republican-governed states in the US have announced plans to scrap financial support for the Imagination Library. Parton, who didn't have children of her own, founded the library program in honor of her father Robert Lee Parton — who was unable to read.

Each year, the foundation also awards five university scholarships to high school graduates from Sevier County. The Dolly Parton Scholarships of $15,000 are aimed at "students who have a dream they wish to pursue and who can successfully communicate their plan and commitment to realize their dreams," as stated on the foundation's website.
5. A million dollars during COVID
In 2020, Parton donated $1 million to the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville, Tennessee, where the biotechnology company Moderna was working on a COVID-19 vaccine.

On the BBC's "The One Show" in November 2020, she said of her donation: "I'm a very proud girl today to know I had anything at all to do with something that's going to help us through this crazy pandemic."
A few months later, she received the vaccine on camera and rewrote her hit song "Jolene" to "Vaccine" for the occasion.
6. Hundreds of 'Jolene' covers

"Jolene" is one of the most frequently covered songs in pop music history. The web portal cover.info notes over 80 official cover versions — from famous artists to indie musicians. Countless other versions can be heard on YouTube and other platforms.

One of the most popular covers was the raw and gritty 2004 interpretation by US duo The White Stripes. Parton herself has recorded several versions of her famous hit — accompanied by a cappella group Pentatonix, for instance, or alongside her famous godchild, pop star Miley Cyrus. In 2016, all of them got together to perform it live together on TV talent show "The Voice."
7. Two world hits in one day
Parton wrote both "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You" on the same day in 1972. When Whitney Houston covered the latter two decades later, it became an instant global hit.

You might be surprised to know that "I Will Always Love You" was never meant to be a romantic song. In fact, it was about Parton ending her professional collaboration with her mentor, country star Porter Wagoner.
Speaking with radio host Howard Stern in 2023, Parton recalled the conflicted emotions she felt when writing the song.
"How am I going to make him understand how much I appreciate everything, but that I have to go? I thought, well, what do you do best? You write songs. So I sat down and I wrote this song."

blocks.caption: Dolly Parton at an event to celebrate the expansion of the Imagination Library of Kentucky in 2024Image: Timothy D. Easley/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Houston's '90s cover version earned Parton another $10 million in royalties. Speaking in 2021 on "Watch What Happens Live," Parton revealed that she invested the money into an office complex in a Black neighborhood in Nashville, Tennessee.
"I just thought, 'This was great. I'm going to be down here with her people, who are my people as well… I think, 'This is the house that Whitney built,'" she said.
8. Not the best doppelganger
Last but not least: Parton said she once took part in a Dolly Parton drag queen lookalike contest — and lost.

On "The Ellen DeGeneres Show," Parton revealed that she had overdone her styling to avoid being recognized: She made her beauty mark bigger, her breasts larger and her hair bigger. All the contestants had to walk across the stage at a gay bar, and whoever received the most applause was declared the winner. In the end, it wasn't Parton who won.
This article was originally written in German. It was first published on January 18, 2026 and was updated upon news of Parton's death on August 25, 2026.

articles.title: US country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80
articles.summary: Representatives of the country music legend told US media that Dolly Parton died after a "brief battle with cancer." Parton's career spans more than half a century and includes a wide array of smash…

image.caption: Dolly Parton consistently churned out hits ever since her debut album 'Hello, I'm Dolly' in 1967Image: George Walker IV/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US country music singer Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80.
Her nephew Brian Seaver announced the news in a video posted to Parton's Instagram page.

"After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her Earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center surrounded by loved ones," Parton's team later said in a statement to CBS News.

Earlier in the year, Parton canceled a series of shows in Las Vegas citing ongoing treatment for health problems. Late last year, she had rebuffed rumors about her health with typical good humor, declaring in a short video, "I ain't dead yet!"

The 80-year-old singer spent almost all of her life making music and is known all over the world for a series of major hits like "Jolene," "9 to 5" and "I Will Always Love You." Her career earned her 10 Grammys and 13 Academy of Country Music (ACM) awards.
Country music icon Dolly Parton dies
What did Parton's nephew say announcing her passing?

Parton's nephew and longstanding head of security Seaver said it was an "honor that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness," to issue this announcement on her behalf, saying she had asked him to do so long ago.
He hailed her influence both on his life and his family's but also on the wider world's.
"By her example, we believed anything was possible," he said of Parton. "She never saw a door she couldn't open, and the doors she opened made and changed history."

"My family and I have shared a lifetime of beautiful memories with Dolly Parton, but so have you," he said. "She has always been on your television, your record player, your CD and on your phone playlist, becoming an extended part of your family whether you liked it or not."
Trump pays tribute, says flags will fly at half-staff for a week
US President Donald Trump said he had called for flags around the country to be "lowered" for one week starting on Tuesday night in memory of Parton.
"Rest in Peace, Dolly!" Trump wrote on social media, describing her as "one of the greatest Country singers, and far beyond, EVER."
"This is a true loss for millions of people. There has never been anyone like her, and never will," he wrote of a fellow famous member of the class of 1946.
Democratic Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer wrote simply: "Rest in peace, Dolly Parton — a true legend and force for good. May her memory be a blessing."
Dolly Parton: musical tributes

The Academy of Country Music hailed Parton's "unmistakable voice, unforgettable songs, generosity and larger-than-life spirit," saying: "Her music will live on, carrying her voice and her story forward for generations to come."
Beatle Paul McCartney said Parton's "songwriting, her singing and her philanthropy were unrivaled in the world of country music" and said it is "hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly."

"There was no greater honour for me than to have her sing my song 'Let It Be' and, even though I only made a small contribution to it, I am so honored that she did it. I am so proud to have known her and admire her unique talents."
Mick Jagger of The Rolling Stones said: "What a wonderful songwriter and singer Dolly was. She brought so many people together, we will all miss her so much."

"It's hard for me to imagine the world without Dolly," said singer-songwriter Cyndi Lauper. "Dolly's heart was as big as her talent. She used her art, her fame and her money to help so many people. She was a great role model for all of us."
Who was Dolly Parton?
Dolly Rebecca Parton was born on January 19, 1946 in Sevierville into what she called a "dirt poor" Tennessee family in the US south.
She was the fourth of 12 children, growing up in the family's small shack in the Great Smoky Mountains.
From singing her first songs to chickens, Parton graduated to performing in a church, where her grandfather was a preacher.
Her debut album, appropriately titled "Hello, I'm Dolly," was released in 1967 with Parton having barely entered her 20s.

She was prolific in her output. By 1974, Parton was already releasing her 13th studio album. Entitled "Jolene," it included what would become two of Parton's most famous songs, the eponymous first track and the opening track of side two, "I Will Always Love You."
She released a staggering 49 solo studio albums in a career spanning well over half a century, concluding in 2023 with "Rockstar."

Parton was known not only for her voice, stage presence, provocative costumes and ample bust, but also as a rapier wit and a stellar storyteller on stage when she had the mic in her hand between her songs.

Sometimes this would also spill over into her creative process. On a visit to the 2014 Glastonbury music festival in the UK, performing in front of an estimated 180,000 sodden fans braving horrendous weather, she said she had composed a special rap just for them earlier that morning, called "Mud."
Catchier lines included rhymes like "Up to our bums in all this crud," while the crowd soon caught on to the chorus by the second go around — chanting "mud, mud, mud!" on her behalf.
You can read more about the country music legend here: Remembering Dolly Parton: 8 facts about the icon

articles.title: Grain exports stall as Ukraine steps up attacks on Russia's Black Sea ports
articles.summary: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian infrastructure on the Black Sea are disrupting grain and oil exports from the port of Novorossiysk and other key hubs.

image.caption: Novorossiysk has been one of Russia's most important ports since the 19th centuryImage: Alexander Strela/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: When Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke in 2014 about Russia's motives for annexing the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and thus violating international law, he justified it by saying: "We could not allow NATO forces to eventually come to the land of Crimea and Sevastopol, the land of Russian military glory, and cardinally change the balance of forces in the Black Sea area."

What now? Intensified Ukrainian attacks on Novorossiysk, Russia's largest commercial Black Sea port, have caused significant disruptions to oil and grain shipments in recent weeks. The Russian navy no longer dominates the region. And exporting goods via the Black Sea is becoming increasingly difficult for Russia because of Ukraine's drone strikes. It is only possible to reorganize logistics partially.
If the attacks continue at such intensity, the consequences for Russian exporters and the national budget could be significant, experts told DW.

blocks.caption: Container ships and other vessels have also come under attackImage: Igor Onuchin/TASS/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Novorossiysk major Russian hub for exports

Novorossiysk has been a major hub for Russian exports since the 19th century and even today it remains Russia's largest port in terms of cargo volume, as well as one of the largest in Europe. Up to a third of Russia's grain exports are handled through the hub, which is located close to the country's major agricultural regions. Crude oil, metals and containerized goods also pass through the port.

Recent Ukrainian maritime and aerial drone attacks have severely disrupted shipments, particularly of grain. Andrei Sisov, the head of SovEcon, a research and consulting firm specialized in agriculture, uses Telegram to follow the developments. On August 12, he posted that the Novorossiysk Bread Products Plant (NKHP ) — one of Russia's largest grain export terminals — and the Novorossiysk grain terminal had ceased operations. A day later, KSK, one of Russia's largest deep-water grain terminals, also halted its operations. Operations at a major grain terminal in Taman had already come to a standstill at the end of July. Prior to that, Ukraine paralyzed operations at the shallow-water ports of the Sea of Azov.

At the time of publication, only Tuapse, the smallest of Russia's deep-water grain terminals, was still in operation. "This means that virtually all Russian grain exports via the Azov-Black Sea basin are blocked," Sisov said.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian drone attacks are doing consistent damage to Russian infrastructureImage: Vantor/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Oil exports also affected

The situation regarding oil exports is not quite as dramatic but while they have not come to a complete standstill, they are frequently disrupted. According to the British news agency Reuters, the Sheskharis terminal — Russia's main oil export facility on the Black Sea, handling some 700,000 barrels of crude oil per day — halted loadings on August 14, which resumed only two days later.

According to London-based Argus Media, a global energy and commodity price reporting agency, Russia could have 45 million metric tons of wheat — Russia's main agricultural export good — for export in 2026 to 2027. However, the situation in the Black Sea, through which about 90% of shipments are usually routed, will make it almost impossible to supply the global market.
Sisov of SovEcon estimated that "many Russian producers will not survive this season, especially after several years of deteriorating financial conditions."

Because exports have come to a standstill, surplus grain will have to be sold on the domestic market, which is already putting downward pressure on prices. Even if exports were to recover over time, there will still be problems. August is usually when shipments peak and it will be difficult to deliver anything no sent this month because terminals tend to operate at full capacity during the autumn anyway.
Ukraine's desperate search for farm labor
Ukrainian grain exports also decrease
The escalation of hostilities in the Azov and Black Sea regions will also be felt on the global market since Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter.
Ukrainian grain exports have also fallen sharply since there are attacks on both sides. In the past month, Russia too has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian ports and ships that are docked there.

"The disruptions have blocked out good wheat harvests in Ukraine and Russia from accessing global market," Xiaoyi Deng from Argus Media told DW. "Both have struggled to work with alternative infrastructure, such as Baltic ports (via rail) or Danube River ports but the alternatives would not be up for full replacement."

According to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Helsinki-based think tank, the port of Novorossiysk "loaded 30% less oil than during the same period last year" in the first two weeks of August. The decline was preceded by a Ukrainian strike on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) marine terminal on July 19.
How Ukraine fights in the Black Sea without a navy

Isaac Levi, an energy analyst at CREA, pointed out that damage to infrastructure was not the only reason for shipments to fall. He said that "strikes on vessels have discouraged ships from calling at ports considered major targets." According to US business news channel Bloomberg, a Greek tanker believed to be carrying Russian oil came under attack on August 17.

"If these constraints persist through August, Russia will find it increasingly difficult to simply defer shipments and make up the lost volumes later," Levi said. "Russia can reroute barrels, but it cannot reroute infrastructure. The most plausible alternatives include the Baltic ports of Primorsk and Ust-Luga.

"But rerouting oil through the Baltic Sea ports would significantly increase transportation times and costs compared with Black Sea exports, while available capacity remains too small to replace significant volumes from Novorossiysk."
This article was originally published in Russian.

articles.title: Schalke coach looks to Bosnia bond in Bundesliga return
articles.summary: After three seasons in the second division, Schalke are back in the Bundesliga. Just a year ago, few would have guessed that their revival would largely be 'Made in Bosnia.'

image.caption: Miron Muslic's goal is to establish Schalke in the Bundesliga beyond this first season back in the topflightImage: Kroeger/RHR-Foto/IMAGO

blocks.text: "A year ago, I told my team that we need to step things up by two gears, and we did that," Schalke's second-year coach, Miron Muslic, told the club's website ahead of this season's return to the Bundesliga.

"Now we need to step things up by two gears all over again. At first glance it may sound like a threat, too dramatic, but this is what we will need to meet this challenge. The lads know this and we are confident that we have a higher gear in us."
The challenge for Muslic is not simply to avoid relegation in year one after three seasons in the second division, but to "establish ourselves in the Bundesliga."
It will also be Muslic's first season in the Bundesliga after he succeeded where several of his predecessors failed – guiding the Royal Blues back to the topflight.
'Where did this guy come from?'

It's something few would have predicted just over a year ago, when he was unveiled as Schalke's new head coach. Many, if not most, of the club's supporters will have been left scrolling on their phones to try to figure out just who he was. It's a point not lost on the Austrian coach, who fled the Bosnian War with his parents at the age of nine.

"Many were wondering; 'Who is this guy, where did he come from?'" Muslic, who joined from lower league English club Plymouth Argyle, told German football magazine "kicker" last October, after Schalke had climbed to the top of the standings for the first time in the campaign.

That's where they finished the first half of the season. But during the January transfer window, Muslic and sporting director Frank Baumann still weren't sure the squad had what it would take to guarantee a top-two finish – and automatic promotion – at the end of the campaign.
Proven goal scorer looking for playing time

Then the final piece to the promotion puzzle fell into Muslic's lap. Bosnia captain Edin Dzeko, a striker who has been prolific virtually everywhere he has played, was largely languishing on the bench at Italian club Fiorentina, and looking for playing time. He let it be known that he was prepared to take a major pay cut to help Schalke achieve promotion. By the time they'd done just that, he had contributed six goals to the cause – and just turned 40.

Many expected Dzeko to hang up his boots after he captained Bosnia in just their second appearance at the World Cup this past summer. However, a couple of weeks before the start of the season, Dzeko confirmed that he would make his return to the Bundesliga – 15 seasons after he last played in the league with Wolfsburg. After signing a one-year, bonus-heavy contract, Dzeko said that while he had "three other options" he made up his mind that if he was to continue playing, it would only be at Schalke.

blocks.caption: Edin Dzeko captained Bosnia at this summer's World Cup in North AmericaImage: Mutsu Kawamori/AFLOSPORT/IMAGO

blocks.text: Dzeko 'still hungry' at 40
"Winning promotion to the Bundesliga is one of the highlights of my career," Dzeko told the club's website.
"I'm still hungry. And I want to help our team in the Bundesliga, too."

Just how much action Dzeko will see in the Bundesliga is unclear. However, Muslic, who is understood to have pushed hard to bring his countryman back for another year, believes he can still be a difference maker in key situations.

Still, he isn't expected to see as much playing time as the third member of Schalke's Bosnian triumvirate, central defender Nikola Katic, whose winding road to Gelsenkirchen saw him work with Muslic a few years ago at Plymouth. Even before Dzeko arrived in Gelsenkirchen last winter, he and Katic already knew each other from the national team.
'Once Schalke, always Schalke,' but...

Now all three are committed to ensuring that Schalke's return to the Bundesliga is more than a one-season excursion, and Muslic, whose contract runs through the end of the 2027-28 season, hopes he will remain in charge for years to come.
"I will remain a member of Schalke 04 forever — 100 percent. No matter how our paths might part one day," the coach told "kicker" last October.

blocks.caption: Nikola Katic (right) has established himself as a stallwart in Schalke's central defenseImage: Kroeger/RHR-Foto/IMAGO

blocks.text: At the same time, he's realistic enough to know that as a coach, he won't be in Gelsenkirchen forever. While his current focus is all about Schalke, he already knows where he would like to wind up somewhere down the road.
"I would like to be the national team coach of Bosnia-Herzegovina one day," he said.
"And I believe it will happen. The fundamental prerequisites are simply a perfect fit — my background, my connection, and the love for my home country."

For now though, the focus is on the new season; Schalke were left licking their wounds after fourth-tier Halle took them to extra time in their first-round German Cup match on Monday – before emerging with a 5-2 win. Dzeko, who had come on in the 64th minute expecting to play only half an hour, scored two of Schalke's goals.
Ever the optimist, Muslic said afterwards that the hard-fought result not only proved that "we'll need Edin" in the Bundesliga season, but that Schalke had also demonstrated their "resilience."
Next comes the first real test of whether Schalke can indeed kick it up a couple of gears, when they make their Bundsliga return in Augsburg on Sunday.

articles.title: Can Germany defend itself against drone attacks?
articles.summary: Explosive-laden drones at Leipzig/Halle airport have exposed gaps in Germany's defenses. DW looks at how prepared the country is for future drone attacks.

image.caption: One defense method involves interceptor drones, which chase drones and capture them with a netImage: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: On August 25, German media reported on a third drone allegedly found near Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. A drone and a substance — which initial assessments suggest could be around 50 grams of Hexogen, a highly explosive military-grade explosive — were reportedly discovered in a field outside the airport grounds. Consequently, public broadcasters NDR and WDR, and the daily broadsheet Süddeutsche Zeitung are speculating about a plot that may be far more extensive than what has been publicly disclosed so far.
Speaking on the sidelines of a federal government retreat in the state of Brandenburg, Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) stated: "Germany has increasingly come into the crosshairs of hybrid attackers."

Merz also pointed to measures aimed at better protecting the public. Just a few days ago, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) inaugurated a drone security research center in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, not far from Leipzig and Halle in Saxony.

How could drones laden with explosives fly unhindered near or into Leipzig/Halle airport and remain unnoticed for at least several hours? Interior Minister Dobrindt had immediately spoken of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers."
Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because one drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation.

However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights.
Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, security expert Nico Lange warned.
"We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW.
Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany
The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense.
"That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident.

The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible.
Why coordinating Germany's drone defense is difficult
Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions.

In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted.

Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in.
Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin
Will Germany's federal police lead on drone defense?
Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities.
"The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer.

Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport.

Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry.
Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany?

As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country.

A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added.

In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster."
German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses
Why German airports and train stations still lack protection
There is also a lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones.

"There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place."

The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said.
The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year.
This article was originally written in German. It was first published on August 14, 2026, and updated on August 25 to reflect news developments.

articles.title: Why Germany's Volkswagen could cut 100,000 jobs
articles.summary: Europe's biggest automaker, Volkswagen, faces Chinese competition, high costs and US tariffs. What could its restructuring mean for the German car industry?

image.caption: VW's management is meeting workers at the carmaker's headquarters in Wolfsburg where they could announce big changes for the companyImage: Moritz Frankenberg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 1. Why is Volkswagen holding crunch talks with workers?

Volkswagen's management is holding extraordinary meetings with workers this week amid an unprecedented cost-cutting drive, including reports of up to 100,000 job losses and the possible closure of several German car factories.
Germany's auto industry faces a deep structural crisis due to intense pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to electric vehicles (EVs), higher production costs and other challenges.
As Europe's biggest carmaker by volume, VW has the heaviest exposure to overcapacity in its German plants, high fixed costs and its reliance on China.
Workers have been particularly concerned by how the restructuring was communicated so far, which representatives have described as "disastrous."
Nine separate meetings will be held, starting on Tuesday at VW's headquarters in Wolfsburg, with talks at other sites including Emden, Zwickau, Braunschweig and Hanover before the end of the week.
Workers had already agreed to around 50,000 job cuts, mainly through voluntary redundancy schemes. But management now thinks a further 50,000 jobs will have to be lost.
2. Why does Volkswagen need to make such drastic cuts?
CEO Oliver Blume has stressed that VW is in a "more than critical state" and that the measures adopted so far are not enough to restore competitiveness.
"We are oversized. That often makes us too slow and too complicated," he told staff in an interview on the company's intranet last week.

With nearly 630,000 workers, VW has grown more bloated than its peers over decades after choosing to control more stages of production — including components and software — while mopping up rivals such as Skoda, Porsche, SEAT and Bugatti.
The automaker was also slow to transition to EVs just as Chinese competitors gained ground, causing a large sales drop in its former number one market — China.
Blume warned that VW is currently over-producing around half a million vehicles in Europe every year.
While closing German factories would be a last resort, Blume said management "cannot currently see any way of them remaining profitable in the 2030s."
Other automakers have criticized Germany's high operating costs, including Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Källenius, who last month spoke of a 70% cost gap between the firm's Hungarian and German operations.
3. What reaction is expected from workers?
Blume is expected to face an angry reaction from VW employees, who rank as some of the best-paid auto workers in the world thanks to the power and influence of unions and the works council.
After already accepting VW's earlier restructuring plans, Christiane Benner, the head of the IG Metall union, said workers "are getting another slap in the face."
During the meeting with workers in Wolfsburg on Tuesday, VW works council chair ‌Daniela Cavallo said "trust" in Blume and the executive board "has been ‌damaged," but "not yet beyond repair."
Last month, VW's supervisory board — which includes shareholders and worker representatives — rejected the second round of cost-cutting proposals.
