The move is further complicated as VW is part-owned by the state of Lower Saxony, which holds 20% of the voting rights. The state has refused to sign off on the plans, according to German media reports.
"Lower Saxony is automotive country ... and this must remain so," said Olaf Lies, the state's premier on Monday. "Now it is important to me that we find joint ​solutions."

blocks.caption: Volkswagen workers in Germany could face big layoffs due to red tape, US tariffs and rising competition from China, says managementImage: Moritz Frankenberg/picture alliance/dpa

blocks.text: 4. How is Volkswagen planning on getting back on track?
Blume told the Bild am Sonntag newspaper last weekend that he had drawn up "the largest transformation plan in the history of the Volkswagen Group."

His Target Vision 2030 plan aims to cut VW's model lineup by half and lower overheads, particularly in Germany. The automaker will also reduce its global production target, which peaked at about 11 million vehicles in 2018, to 9 million a year in the future.
Faced with rising competition from China, along with US tariffs, geopolitics and red tape, Blume warned that VW management has to "assume the risks will get worse, worldwide."

Most global automakers are struggling to react to Chinese EVs flooding global markets, increasingly unpredictable markets and the mounting pressure of EU net-zero rules, which include fines for not hitting emissions targets.
Blume told the newspaper that the next few years would be "decisive" in determining which carmakers remain viable.
He said although VW achieved a solid 3.8% operating margin, the profits are not enough to invest in new technologies, products and maintain the company's sites.

articles.title: Can new US sanctions cripple Iran's shadow economy?
articles.summary: The US is expanding sanctions on Iran's financial networks, targeting crypto, gold, aviation and shipping. DW spoke with analysts about what could change.

image.caption: Women shop for produce at a market in Tehran in August 2026Image: AFP

blocks.text: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has unveiled a new phase of Washington's economic campaign against Iran, this time aimed not only at sanctioned Iranian institutions but at the international networks Tehran has used to keep money and goods moving.

Speaking on August 24, Bessent said the United States would target what he called five economic lifelines: digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. He also warned foreign entities that help the country illicitly move money around.
"Any entity that facilitates money laundering for Iran will be removed from the US dollar-based financial system," Bessent said. "The countdown starts now."

The approach represents an effort to tighten secondary sanctions, putting pressure on companies, financial intermediaries and trading partners outside Iran rather than simply adding restrictions on an economy already heavily sanctioned.

The US announced measures against around 60 individuals, entities and vessels. But it stopped short of targeting major Chinese banks, highlighting the limits of how far the US may be willing to push enforcement against Iran's biggest remaining trading partner.
How Iran has been evading US sanctions
For years, Iran has relied on networks outside the formal banking system to move money.
Exchange houses, gold, cryptocurrency, front companies and opaque shipping networks have helped Iran bypass sanctions.
The latest US strategy appears designed to make those methods more difficult by increasing the cost for foreign intermediaries and comes at a vulnerable moment for Iran.

blocks.caption: Though many big-ticket items are priced and sold in US dollars, it would be a stretch to say that Iran's domestic economy has become dollarizedImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Oil exports have fallen sharply amid US efforts to disrupt Iranian oil shipments. Shipments to China, Iran's main oil customer, dropped to about 534,000 barrels per day in August from 823,000 in July and from a peak of around 1.58 million barrels earlier this year.
At home, food prices rose around 128% year on year in July, according to official data cited by Reuters news agency.
Iran's currency has lost so much value that many transactions, including property and car sales, are now conducted in US dollars. Advertisements are sometimes even priced in dollars.
Rising inflation hits Iranian businesses
The pressure is increasingly visible in ordinary businesses.
A building materials seller in the capital, Tehran, told DW that inflation has become so severe that simply holding goods can sometimes be more profitable than selling them.
"If I keep something in my warehouse for a month, its price may rise by more than the profit I would make by selling it today," he said.

He also owns a stone-cutting business and said fulfilling older contracts has become increasingly painful because replacement materials may cost considerably more a few weeks later. And raising prices offers no easy solution.
"If I increase the price beyond a certain point, nobody can afford to buy it," he said.
US troops feel strain of Iran war deployment
The restrictions also disrupt how private companies pay suppliers, import raw materials and maintain employment.
Another Iranian who works at a trading company told DW that more than 70% of its employees had been laid off during the past six months.
The company imported raw materials for various personal products and previously transferred payments through exchange houses in the United Arab Emirates.
"Now no exchange house is willing to work with us," the employee said.
How sanctions affect Iranian businesses abroad
The effects are also spreading to Iranian businesspeople outside the country.

An Iranian businessman who moved to Dubai told DW that he had previously owned several cosmetics and hygiene brands in Iran. Restrictions on imports and difficulties obtaining raw materials eventually pushed him to relocate.
In Dubai things were more manageable. But since the war, that has changed, he said.
"These days, having an Iranian passport makes almost every transaction more difficult," he told DW.
He said Iranian entrepreneurs are increasingly uncertain whether banks will maintain their accounts or whether residency rules could be tightened.
"In an environment where there is no stability and the outlook is unclear, you cannot really run a business," he said.
Can more sanctions change Tehran's behavior?
Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, is skeptical that the new US measures will produce a fundamental strategic shift.

Iran is already sanctioned across most major sectors, he told DW. Further restrictions may involve expanding enforcement of existing networks rather than creating entirely new forms of economic pressure.
"Their principal effects are likely to be psychological, intensifying inflationary expectations," Salavati said.
What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz?
Salavati also warns that economic pressure could weaken the remaining middle-income and professional groups that traditionally provide space for more moderate politics.
Rather than producing rapid political change, he believes the pressure could deepen polarization and encourage the state to reduce already limited subsidies and social assistance.
Could US sanctions strengthen Iran's shadow economy?
There is another paradox. The more Washington restricts formal financial channels, the stronger the incentive becomes to develop informal ones.
Iran's sanctions economy has already created complex networks of intermediaries, cryptocurrency transfers, front companies, cash transactions and unofficial currency markets.
Closing one route may make transactions more expensive without necessarily stopping them.
"The broader consequence is likely to be corrosive rather than transformative," Salavati said, warning that the result could be an even larger and less controlled underground economy.

The new sanctions may make it harder for Tehran to finance trade, obtain foreign currency and sustain its existing economic networks. But the immediate burden is falling on companies, workers and households already dealing with wartime disruption and extreme inflation.
Whether US pressure changes the behavior of Iran's leadership remains uncertain.

articles.title: Trees are vital for cooler cities, but they need help too
articles.summary: Record-breaking heat and drought are putting urban trees at risk. Experts explain how to protect these essential assets and build city forests that can withstand the climate challenges ahead.

image.caption: Different ages of trees require different volumes of water to keep healthyImage: Claus Völker/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Walking beneath the trees this historically hot summer, sometimes felt like autumn had already arrived: dry, dead leaves crunching underfoot, and crowns tinged yellow or completely bare.

That's a problem because large leafy trees help make our cities more livable. They block sunlight, reduce pollution, store carbon, provide habitats for biodiversity to thrive, soak up otherwise harmful stormwater runoff and even boost the mental and physical health of residents.
"When trees go away, those things go away as well," Nina Bassuk, who runs the Urban Horticulture Institute at the US-based Cornell University, told DW.
That's why cities and scientists are racing to figure out how to save trees and choose smarter ones for the future.
Why cities need trees
As humans have burned fossil fuels to power industry and heat homes, the planet has become hotter, making the role of urban trees ever more vital.

Why? Because they essentially act like giant air conditioners, which makes a big difference in hot cities. Inside a tree's canopy, temperatures can be up to three degrees cooler than the surrounding area. This is down to evapotranspiration, the process of trees absorbing water and releasing water vapor through their leaves.
In addition, trees cast shade, which keeps their surroundings from heating up in the first place.

"When we stand under a tree, the temperature we perceive can be 10 to 12 degrees Celsius (18 to 22 degrees Fahrenheit) lower than right next to it," said Matthias Beyer, a hydrologist at the Institute of Geoecology at TU Braunschweig.
And it's not just cooling. There have been numerous studies correlating all sorts of other positive effects of robust trees.

One showed that cities with more tree canopy had lower rates of cardiovascular disease. Another concluded that greener school surroundings were associated with better grades in high schools. And further research suggested that more greenspace exposure during pregnancy can lead to healthier outcomes for newborns.
How much water do trees need to survive drought?
Though a warmer climate makes trees more necessary, it also makes it harder for them to thrive.
Healthy trees need a minimum of 10 to 15 liters of water a day, but mature ones with full foliage require up to four times that.
While there may be a temptation for cities to focus on planting new, less water-hungry trees, experts agree that the priority should be protecting older, struggling ones.

Research shows it would take around 400 saplings to replace the benefits of an old tree with a crown circumference of 20 meters. Once trees reach maturation, their benefits can be exponential, but this takes time and lots of maintenance.
"A lot of trees can't deliver the full function until 40, 50 years from the day they were planted," said Henrik Sjoman, a researcher at the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences.
The best way to water trees
It's better to give trees a large amount of water over a short period so it can soak down deep, rather than letting it stay in the upper soil layers, where much of it evaporates.

For newly planted trees, a ring of metal or sturdy plastic is often fixed into the ground around the trunk. Where that's not available, a shallow depression around the tree can be created, allowing the water to pool. What matters is not damaging any surface roots in the process.

When the soil is extremely hardened, so-called irrigation bags or cushions can help. Water drips slowly but steadily into the soil through small holes on their underside. The water mustn't sit on the surface for long periods, since that can cause rot, which damages the tree.

blocks.caption: If they don't have the right growing conditions, trees can struggle to put down roots in cities Image: IMAGO/viennaslide

blocks.text: But sometimes the soil has been heavily compacted to support sidewalks above, meaning water can't get through at all. Thirty years ago, Bassuk helped pioneer a method that mixes specially sized gravel in with the soil. It lets the stones bear the load of the sidewalk, while leaving more space for roots to stretch across dense urban ground.
"As long as you get the soil and the stone proportions right, you can compact it and yet trees can access that and grow for long distances," Bassuk said.
How to choose the right trees for cities
When it comes to climate adaptation, there's also the question of which trees to plant in the first place.

Historically, Sjoman says urban tree selection was often driven by aesthetics and design, which led to the over-planting of single species that were vulnerable to threats like pests or disease. Horror stories of Dutch elm disease wiping out entire populations in the 20th century helped to transform urban forestry planning, placing the focus far more on diversity and climate adaptation.

blocks.caption: It can take a long time for trees to reach their full potential in terms of how much they can cool their surroundingsImage: Philipp Böhme/DW

blocks.text: The 10-20-30 rule of thumb was coined in 1990 by the late Frank Santamour, who worked as a research geneticist at the US National Arboretum. It states that urban forest populations should include no more than 10% of any one species, 20% of a single genus or 30% of any family.

In Germany, there are several tools and databases that offer planting guidance, and several cities are taking part in an official street tree test. The idea is that 45 species are tested at more than 220 locations to gather knowledge of how they thrive.

Another resource is the CITREE database, which categorizes almost 400 species of woody plants, sortable by more than 50 different features, including leaf density, fruit color, allergy potential, limb breakage and more.

The key feature cities need to select is drought tolerance — considering the immense biological strain urban trees are facing in an ever-warming world. But knowing the benefits trees offer a city means that is not the only factor.
"The demands of trees today — it's so much bigger, so much deeper than it was just a couple of decades ago," Sjoman said.
This article was adapted from German, with additional reporting.

articles.title: The new Bundesliga season is here, but has the glow gone?
articles.summary: Another Bundesliga season arrives, but are the golden years of Germany's top football league already over, and what can it do to change its course?

image.caption: Without Harry Kane, the Bundesliga may have struggled to gain attention in recent yearsImage: RONALD WITTEK/EPA

blocks.text: The 64th season of the Bundesliga is here. The tiny team from Elversberg will become the 59th club to play in the league, Ismael Saibari is Harry Kane's new back-up at Bayern Munich, Schalke return after three years away, and Kathleen Krüger is Head of Sport at Hamburg.

Coming off an XXL World Cup and a new broadcasting deal in the US, the Bundesliga is looking to step forward into a new era. But beyond the loyal support of club fans both domestic and abroad, has the international appeal of the league, particularly in the key US market, worn off?

"It would be hard to argue that the Bundesliga has not suffered some backsliding in their standing. When Bayern and Dortmund met in the Champions League final [in 2013], I believed it was just the league announcing its superiority with intent to stay at the pinnacle of club football in Europe. I couldn't have imagined that might have been the brief apex," Randall, a US-based Cologne fan who has been watching the league for 16 years, told DW.
"Frankly, the Bundesliga has likely already seen its popularity at its peak. It is only downward from here."
Dominik Schreyer, a professor of sports economics at Germany's Otto Beisheim School of Management, doesn't believe that is the case though.
"I would be cautious about declaring the Bundesliga's golden era over," Schreyer told DW.
"The league still has full stadiums, strong clubs, excellent players and coaches, and a distinctive football culture."

Schreyer does admit though, despite the league's great reputation of player and coach development, failing to retain players like Erling Haaland or Florian Wirtz makes it more difficult to increase the reach of the league.

"Bayern's prolonged dominance has reduced uncertainty at the top, while the Premier League has developed a major financial and distribution advantage. The problem is therefore not simply a lack of talent or stories, but the Bundesliga’s limited success in turning those strengths into regular international viewing habits."
Club support strong, but league lacking luster

Robin Austermann, Bundesliga Americas executive vice president, said in the statement about the new Bundesliga broadcasting deal in the US that Bundesliga fans in America had grown by "43% over the past five years."
This is obviously a positive, although it would be intriguing to know how much growth had been made per year. For some fans though, beyond supporting their team, the league is lacking.
"Honestly, for pure viewing I prefer the Premier League since in their league at least three or four teams can win the title," Dave, a US-based Schalke fan since 1974, told DW.

"There is no doubt that both the Bundesliga and the second division are the envy of other countries from the attendance and management perspectives, but I feel that the overall competitive sporting quality has declined. I absolutely believe that the Bundesliga has lost some of its luster and reputation."
Cologne fan Randall agrees.

"You get a little drama around the border between the last Champions League slot and Europa League, but that doesn't really get the blood pumping how, does it? I still love watching the league, but I still have days on which I wonder if a Super League would really have been such a bad thing if it returned some competitive balance to the Bundesliga."

blocks.caption: Borussia Dortmund fans are one of the most famous groups of fans in both the Bundesliga and EuropeImage: Piroschka Van De Wouw/REUTERS

blocks.text: How can the Bundesliga change its course?

Much of the desire for change has to do with the lack of competition at the top. Bayern have won 13 of the last 14 titles. Some believe a more equitable distribution of TV revenue is a possible way forward.
"The market has become more fragmented, abundant, and competitive," Schreyer said.

"Availability no longer guarantees attention. Viewers increasingly encounter football through individual players, creators, highlights, short-form content, and major tournaments before deciding whether to watch full matches. The Bundesliga therefore needs a clear path from initial discovery to repeated viewing and, eventually, fandom."

Whatever the choice, the change needs to be made without losing what sets the league apart, namely the competitive ticket prices and passionate fan base. German football fans offered a vision for football in the country back in 2020 after the COVID-19 pandemic, but the gap between the rich and the poor in European football continues to widen.
"I think throwing out what makes German club football great in pursuit of competing in the market with the Premier League would be folly," Randall said.
Schreyer believes the major clubs and established stars are the strongest way to capture audiences' attention.
"Once viewers are engaged, the league's wider strengths, including supporter culture, historic clubs, player development, Schalke's return, and Elversberg's rise, can deepen that interest," he said.
This Bundesliga season a pivotal moment for the league

Clearly, the US view is only one slice of the Bundesliga's market. Fan numbers doubled in Brazil between 2018 and 2024 to 24 million, and community initiatives through Bundesliga Common Ground have helped build interest in countries all over the world such as Thailand and Vietnam.
But the new deal in the US is perhaps revealing when it comes to the challenge the Bundesliga currently faces to position itself globally.
"A lot of fans were disappointed by the league's move to go with Fandango this next season," said Jody, who has been watching German football since 2006.

"If the Bundesliga wants to grow in the US, they need to look at what NBC did when it won Premier League broadcast rights. It needs a more mainstream distribution in the US and more publicity of the league to draw new viewers in."
Schreyer argues that this is not the entire story.
"The new deal should ultimately be judged by whether it helps rebuild demand, not by potential reach alone," he said.

Criticism is something the Bundesliga has become familiar with in recent years. But off the back of a World Cup in the US, a key target country where a new broadcast deal was recently agreed, this feels like a pivotal moment for the league's development.

articles.title: Star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter: 50 years on stage
articles.summary: Anne-Sophie Mutter constantly reinvents herself. For her 50th onstage anniversary, the star violinist is surprising audiences with sounds from around the world and never-before-recorded commissions.

image.caption: On the world's great stages: Anne-Sophie Mutter performing with the Munich PhilharmonicImage: Matthias Balk/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The list of international composers who have written for star violinist Anne-Sophie Mutter is a long one. It features names like Krzysztof Penderecki and Sofia Gubaidulina, along with Andre Previn and Jörg Widmann. In recent years, women like Iranian-Dutch composer Aftab Darvishi and South Korean composer Unsuk Chin have also written works for Mutter.

On the occasion of the violinist's 50th stage anniversary, she's now recorded over 30 works either dedicated to her or commissioned by her — all part of her "ASM Forte Forward" project on the Alpha Classics label.

blocks.caption: Anne-Sophie Mutter is deeply committed to social causesImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The first album in the series, "East Meets West," reflects not just the artist's musical passions but also her social engagement. The opening "Likoo for Solo Violin," composed by Aftab Darvishi for Mutter in 2024, leaves a powerful impression. "Likoo" is a lament about loss, written at a time when especially women in Iran were fighting repression by the regime.
Giving women a voice

"I wanted to create a musical tribute to the people in Iran and to those fighting for freedom, coexistence, empathy and equality, in the hope that these atrocities would never be repeated," Mutter told DW. "War is raging on our wonderful planet even as I'm playing, but I won't give up hope for love and empathy." Mutter's performance of it is deeply moving — one can almost hear the women's cries in the violin, fading into silence.

With the situation in Iran deteriorating, Mutter says it's especially important to her to keep "Likoo" in her repertoire. "I have great admiration for Persian culture and for the female composers who still live in Iran — such as Golfam Khayam, who managed to send me her score by email during a pause in the shelling. I still hear from her from time to time," Mutter says.

"These female composers in Iran fascinate me, and the piece 'Likoo' in particular. That's why — also sadly because of the current situation — it's very important to me to perform 'Likoo' at the anniversary concert." The concert is being held on August 25 at the Lucerne Festival.
Her 1976 stage debut in Lucerne

On August 23, 1976, a 13-year-old Anne-Sophie Mutter took the stage at a young artists' concert in Lucerne. It was there that conductor Herbert von Karajan first encountered the young talent. A year later, he hired her for a concert with the Berlin Philharmonic at the Salzburg Easter Festival. So began Mutter's long collaboration with Karajan and his Berlin orchestra.

blocks.caption: Anne-Sophie Mutter at the International Music Festival in Lucerne in September 1976Image: ZUMA/Keystone/IMAGO

blocks.text: Another figure who shaped her musical life on stage in the 1980s was Swiss conductor and patron Paul Sacher. "He was a major influence on my interest in contemporary music," Mutter says. She cherishes the undogmatic learning experience she gained from Sacher and her other mentors. Sacher always afforded her the freedom to decide how she would approach an assignment. He passed a motto on to her: "What I can't do, I can learn. What I can't learn today, I can learn later."
The Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation

A four-time Grammy winner and recipient of Japan's Praemium Imperiale, she's now supporting highly gifted young musicians through the Anne-Sophie Mutter Foundation. She encourages her scholarship recipients to embrace social engagement alongside contemporary music. She's herself a supporter of humanitarian organizations such as Save the Children and Doctors Without Borders, and from 2021 to 2025 served as German Cancer Aid's chairwoman.

blocks.caption: In 2019, Mutter received the Praemium Imperiale, sometimes referred to as the Nobel Prize of the arts. On the right is Klaus-Dieter Lehmann, the prize's representative for GermanyImage: Jörg Carstensen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: It's difficult for young musicians to build an audience and make money with contemporary music, Mutter says. "All the same, I want to keep them grounded and show them it's not just about getting rich and famous; they have a role to play in society — in social environments. Playing at a nursing home, for example, or teaching, supporting charitable organizations with benefit concerts."
A platform for composers

As well, Mutter uses the work she commissions — including from former and current scholarship recipients — to help advance their careers. "I want to give these pieces a platform, along with a recorded presence. Without that, these wonderful works couldn't be heard all over the world."

The next album in the "ASM Forte Forward" series being released for the anniversary is "American Tunes #1." It includes works by Andre Previn, whom Mutter was married to for four years, as well as US composer Sebastian Currier, who has written several pieces for Mutter.

blocks.caption: Fellows from the Mutter's Virtuosi ensemble accompany her on international performancesImage: JANEK SKARZYNSKI/AFP

blocks.text: "It gives me particular pleasure that many works by colleagues from my foundation, as well as by former and current scholarship recipients, have actually been recorded," Mutter says. "I have managed to put many of my young musicians at the center of this new 'Forte Forward' series, and that makes me very happy."
Albums of memories

To further mark her onstage milestone, Mutter has planned several projects with her longtime label, Deutsche Grammophon. Among them is the release of seven location-centered albums featuring selected works — pieces that, as in the case of the city of Lucerne, were premiered there or hold special significance in Mutter's musical life.

So far, "My Berlin," "My London" and, in connection with the anniversary concert in Lucerne, "My Lucerne" have been released digitally. The seven planned albums will follow the artist around the globe, from Berlin, London and Lucerne to Tokyo and New York.

blocks.caption: As early as age 17, Anne-Sophie Mutter was playing a Stradivarius violinImage: Karl Staedele/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Anne-Sophie Mutter's constant companion is her Stradivarius violin. "The violin is the coolest instrument in the universe. For 50 years I've tried again and again to show that," she says.

The instrument is her voice, too, she adds: "I find it fascinating how music becomes so expressive precisely where language ends, and how in this cosmos of creativity we can connect, discover ourselves, give ourselves over to expression, and truly experience life."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Scientists discover new 'immune hubs' in skull bone marrow
articles.summary: "Immune hubs" that actively defend the brain have been discovered in mouse skull marrow. Similar cells exist in human skulls, but their role remains unclear.

image.caption: Researchers at WashU Medicine discovered lymph node-like structures (shown cyan) in the skull bone marrow of miceImage: Jang Hyun Park/WashU Medicine

blocks.text: The skull has traditionally been regarded largely as armor for the brain. New research from the United States suggests it may have another role: proactively helping to defend what lies beneath it.
Researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis identified previously unknown immune "security stations" in the bone marrow of mouse skulls.
What the mouse experiments revealed

The lymph node-like structures responded to brain tumors before more distant lymph nodes in the neck did. When researchers disrupted the structures in mice with glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, the tumors grew faster and the animals died sooner.
"The skull should no longer be viewed simply as a protective shell around the brain," senior study author Jonathan Kipnis told DW.
"It contains specialized immune environments that appear capable of responding locally to changes within the brain."
The discovery, published in the journal "Nature," comes with an important caveat: The researchers have so far only demonstrated how the structures function in mice, not humans.

blocks.caption: The newly discovered immune structures have so far only been shown to function in miceImage: Imago/CTK Photo

blocks.text: Kipnis cautioned that the human evidence remains preliminary: "We found similar immune cells in human skull marrow, suggesting that related structures may exist, but we have not yet demonstrated that they are organized or function in the same way as those in mice," he said.
How scientists' view of brain immunity changed
For much of the 20th century, the brain was described as "immune privileged" — unusually protected from immune activity because inflammation that is useful elsewhere can damage delicate brain tissue.

The blood-brain barrier, which tightly controls what can pass from the bloodstream into brain tissue, reinforced the idea that the brain was largely isolated from the body's conventional immune system.
That picture has changed dramatically.
Researchers now know that the brain communicates continuously with the immune system, particularly through tissues surrounding the brain.

Kipnis' lab helped drive that rethink in previous work, first by identifying lymphatic vessels in the membranes surrounding the brain and later by showing tiny channels connecting those membranes to the skull's bone marrow.
Why sleep is so important for your immune system

"The traditional concept of immune privilege has already changed substantially," Kipnis said. "Our findings add another layer by showing that specialized immune structures exist within the skull bone marrow, immediately adjacent to the brain."
How the skull's immune hubs are organized
The researchers tracked proteins moving from mouse brains through microscopic skull channels and into the bone marrow.
There they found organized clusters of so-called B cells and T-cells. T cells help B cells in "creating large amounts of powerful antibodies that help fight disease and infection."

Finding immune cells in bone marrow was not unusual. The surprise was their organization into structures resembling lymph nodes elsewhere in the body. These immune hubs are where immune cells work together to respond to threats.
Being so close to the brain could allow the immune hubs a faster, more specialized immune response.

blocks.caption: Microscopy image clearly shows  B cells (blue) and T cells (red) organized together in the marrow Image: Jang Hyun Park/WashU Medicine

blocks.text: "The lymph nodes in the neck are 'shared' with tissues such as the mouth, throat and skin," Kipnis said.
"The skull structures may provide the brain with something resembling its own dedicated lymph nodes, allowing immune responses to be coordinated locally."
Why the skull immune hubs are significant

"We have never seen such structures in healthy bone marrow before," study co-author Jang Hyun Park said. "It is an exciting discovery that points out that a complex brain requires its own specialized immune structures to defend it."
Marco Prinz, a neuroimmunologist at the University of Freiburg who was not involved in the study, described the discovery as a "milestone finding."
Prinz said what made the finding significant was the unexpected organization of the immune cells.
"I think nobody expected to find these lymph node-like structures in the skull," he told DW.
But Prinz stressed that researchers have yet to demonstrate that the hubs themselves exist and function in humans.

"The major challenge, however, will be to see them in the human skull as well and to show that they are functional there. This would then indeed change how we view the central nervous system's immune response in humans," Prinz said.
How the immune hubs affected brain tumors

After finding that disrupting the skull immune hubs made brain tumors grow faster, the researchers tested whether strengthening the response could help. They stimulated the skull marrow with immune-boosting proteins. The treated animals rejected tumors more effectively and survived longer.

blocks.caption: Researchers want to know whether the newly discovered immune structures could also play a role in diseases such as Alzheimer'sImage: Frank Gunn/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: The experiment raises the possibility of one day targeting the skull's bone marrow to influence the brain's immune defenses, without delivering treatment directly into the brain.
Any such treatment in humans remains a distant prospect.

"We first need to confirm their organization and function in humans, understand how they change across different diseases, and determine how to manipulate them without causing harmful inflammation," Kipnis said.
What this could mean for other brain diseases
The potential implications extend beyond cancer.

Prinz said the structures may be especially important in brain tumors and infections, where the protective blood-brain barrier can become leaky. Their importance in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, where changes to that barrier are generally less pronounced, "has to be shown," he said.
Kipnis expects that, if similar functioning structures are found in humans, their role could be much broader.
"If I had to bet, I would bet that these structures play a role in any brain disease that has an immune component to it," he said.

articles.title: Spiraling health costs force Iranians to delay care
articles.summary: A single chemotherapy session in Iran can cost six times the monthly minimum wage. As drug prices soar and medicine is in short supply, doctors say more patients are delaying or abandoning treatment.

image.caption: Iranian patients are paying the price as war, sanctions, rising costs and a depreciating currency burden the country's health care systemImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 70-year-old woman with advanced breast cancer was supposed to undergo chemotherapy every two weeks. Doctors had scheduled six treatment sessions, each costing around 100 million Iranian tomans (about $530 or €450).
Iran's minimum monthly wage for workers covered by the country's labor law is 16.6 million tomans, meaning that just one of her chemotherapy sessions costs roughly six times the monthly minimum wage.

The woman's children asked her doctor to postpone the next round of treatment while they searched for a loan or any other source of financial support, according to colleagues of Hamid Hemmatpour, an Iranian physician based in Austria and a member of the executive board of the Association of Healthcare Professionals for Human Rights-Austria.

Her story is far from unique. Across Iran, rising prices, persistent shortages, disruptions in foreign currency transfers and growing pressure on the health care system are making access to treatment increasingly difficult, according to Hemmatpour and another Iranian physician based in Austria, Hassan Nayeb Hashem.
Drug prices rise sharply in Iran
In one example, an Iranian pharmaceutical company recently announced price increases for 82 products.

The average price of those medicines rose from roughly 180,000 tomans to 390,000 tomans, an increase of around 120%, according to figures published by Tasnim News Agency, which is affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

The list shows particularly steep increases for a number of medicines. Donepezil rose by about 543%, clarithromycin by roughly 308%, and amoxicillin by around 115%. The prices for some acetaminophen and diphenhydramine syrups increased by about 135%.
The figures relate to a single manufacturer, but they illustrate the scale of the financial pressure many patients face.

Insulin users are among those hardest hit. Hemmatpour said the cost of a monthly prescription of four NovoRapid insulin pens has risen from about 280,000 tomans after insurance reimbursement to roughly 1.1 million tomans.
German medical network helps Iran's injured protesters
When patients delay treatment
Hassan Nayeb Hashem warns that shrinking access to vital treatments could have tragic consequences.
"If the medicine becomes inaccessible, patients can develop complications much sooner," he told DW. "The most serious risk is premature death."
In many cases, switching medications is not a practical solution.
"For many specific diseases, there is effectively no substitute," he added.
Cancer patients are particularly vulnerable because treatment schedules are often tightly structured. Delays can reduce the effectiveness of therapy and affect outcomes.
Hamid Hemmatpour says some patients ask physicians abroad to obtain cancer medicines, while others postpone or abandon treatment after learning the cost.

The cancer drug Keytruda (pembrolizumab) is one example. An Iranian-produced version can cost around 70 million tomans, more than four times the monthly minimum wage, according to Hemmatpour. Imported Indian versions may sell for around 300 million tomans, European versions can cost even more.
Not surprisingly, experts report rising demand for medicines obtained through unofficial cross-border channels.

"The question is under what conditions these medicines were transported," Hemmatpour said. "Some of these drugs require refrigerated transport. Patients often have no way of knowing whether proper storage conditions were maintained during the journey."
Hemmatpour and Nayeb Hashem also warn that imported drugs may be counterfeit or expired, potentially reducing their effectiveness and posing additional health risks.

blocks.caption: Numerous Iranian medical facilities have been damaged according to authorities since the start of the joint US-Israel military campaign earlier this yearImage: Mahsa/MEI/SIPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Why medicine shortages persist in Iran

Many of the country's health challenges predate the current war. Iran's pharmaceutical industry had already been struggling with a weakening currency, rising production costs and delayed payments from insurers.

US sanctions added another layer of difficulty. Medicines and humanitarian goods are generally exempt from sanctions, but restrictions on banking transactions and international payments can complicate pharmaceutical trade.
Iranian officials have attributed part of the current shortage to a disruption of supply chains and difficulties in transferring foreign currency.

Mehdi Pirsalehi, head of Iran's Food and Drug Administration, has said money transfers slowed dramatically after the war began, nearly coming to a standstill for one to two months and continuing at a reduced pace for several months afterward.

At the same time, Abdolnaser Hemmati, governor of the Central Bank of Iran, says the amount of foreign currency allocated for medicines and medical equipment during the first five months of the current Iranian year was 30% higher than the same period a year earlier.
The statements suggest the problem extends beyond the amount of foreign currency allocated. Delays in payments, imports, manufacturing or distribution can all contribute to shortages.
Why Iran faces a deeper medicine crisis

Medicine shortages are not unique to Iran. In recent years, countries including Germany and the United States have also faced shortages of antibiotics, cancer therapies and other essential medicines, partly because of manufacturing problems and vulnerabilities within global supply chains made especially clear by the COVID-19 pandemic.
Iran's situation is particularly difficult as it finds itself facing the brunt of several pressures at the same time.

Currency depreciation, rising production costs, pressure on insurers, sanctions-related obstacles and the economic consequences of war have all converged on a health care system that was already weak.

Salman Eshaghi, spokesman for the Health and Treatment Committee of Iran's parliament, says around 43 medicines are currently classified as being in "critical shortage," while nearly 1,000 pharmaceutical products face some degree of shortage.
He says higher prices for medicines used to treat cancer, hemophilia and thalassemia have already caused some patients to reduce treatment or stop it altogether.

Originally, patients were expected to pay about 30% of health care costs, with insurers and the government covering the rest, according to Eshaghi. But now patients are paying more than 70% out of pocket.
For the 70-year-old woman with breast cancer, however, the broader debates and international wrangling do not alter her predicament.

Her doctor recommended treatment and her family wanted her to continue, but they simply could not afford the next chemotherapy session. It remains postponed while her children hunt for a way to pay for it.

articles.title: Could Russia's growing fuel crisis help end the Ukraine war?
articles.summary: Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries have deepened Russia's fuel crisis, with shortages reaching Moscow. Could growing public anger put Putin under pressure?

image.caption: Cars waiting in line to refuel at a Rosneft gas station in Moscow on August 17Image: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries have triggered a new fuel crisis in Russia.

Reuters news agency reports that at least 30 regions are now affected. Unlike the previous wave of shortages, which began in late May and lasted until mid-July, the current crisis is particularly affecting Moscow and the surrounding area, as is apparent from posts on social media. The gas station chains Gazprom Neft and Tatneft have already restricted the sale of fuel in the capital.

"You can't say there isn't any fuel. But it's obvious there's a crisis," says Oleg Grigorenko, editor-in-chief of the Russian independent media portal 7x7, which Russia has branded a "foreign agent." "It's not just a personal problem if you leave the city and don't know whether you can get back again, for example. It's also an economic problem,"

Grigorenko reports that in several regions taxi drivers, courier services and the construction industry are already losing business, as many of their supply chains are fuel dependent. "The logistics of private construction companies is heavily reliant on gasoline," Grigorenko explains.

People are also having to queue for hours at gas stations in the southern Russian region of Krasnodar, according to local media. The authorities are blaming this on a supposed increase in demand during the holiday period.

But many locals are saying that this summer season is a disaster. Real estate agent Igor Zakharchenko, from Sochi on the Black Sea coast, wrote on Instagram: "With its quiet atmosphere and leisurely pace of life, Sochi today is reminiscent of the time before the Olympic Games, when there were still not many cars on the roads and the city had far fewer holidaymakers and inhabitants. But the thing is: There's no gas in Sochi."
A two-fold fuel crisis: Poor quality and shortages

Speaking on the Russian broadcaster RTVI, Igor Ananskikh, first deputy chairman of the energy committee in the Russian parliament, said he expected the gas supply situation to normalize within two to three weeks.

blocks.caption: After waiting hours to fill up, many drivers have found their cars won't start as poor quality fuel has damaged the engineImage: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Economist Nikolai Korzhenevsky says this is unlikely. He left Russia in protest at Moscow's war against Ukraine and now lives abroad. In an interview with DW, he highlighted the worsening quality of fuel in Russia. Acquaintances had sent him photos of their cars displaying error messages that indicate engine damage caused by impurities in the fuel.

"The car won't start and has to go to the garage. The same people are telling me garages have waitlists of several months, even in Moscow," Korzhenevsky says. "And then you have to wait again for months for replacement parts. Obviously, some vehicles can't handle the gasoline that's being put in their tanks."
He sees the ongoing problems in the oil and gas industry as harbingers of a much larger and lasting crisis.
Russia's oil exports have fallen more sharply during the war than ever before, Bloomberg news has reported. Oil production has also dropped.

"In 2019, Russia produced 11.5 million barrels per day," says Korzhenevsky. "Today it's less than 9 million. If this trend continues, and the problems with oil refining get worse, production may fall to 8 million barrels. That would create the conditions for a complete economic and systemic crisis."
He doesn't see any quick solution to these problems. In fact he sees Russia going down a similar route to Venezuela, an economy with national income in chronic decline.
Could India and China ease Russia's fuel shortages?

The Russian authorities propose to remedy the fuel shortages with imports from India, China or other countries. But Vyacheslav Shiryaev, a Russian business journalist who also now lives abroad, says this is not viable.

blocks.caption: Fuel distribution is being restricted due to the lack of supplyImage: Anastasia Barashkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Given Russia's current isolation, it's impossible to ensure a daily supply of 200,000 tons of fuel, which is the approximate amount of gasoline and diesel Russia needs every day, he told DW. Shiryaev, who publicly opposed the war in Ukraine, is also on the Russian authorities' list of so-called "foreign agents."
Another Russian economist on that list is Igor Lipsits. He told DW that the damaged refineries cannot quickly be restored and will be vulnerable to further air attacks.

This, he says, is why the authorities are already restricting fuel consumption. Municipal services vehicles — medical and rescue workers, police, firefighters — are allowed to jump the line and fill up and so are security personnel and the authorities.

"This is happening in front of people who've waited for hours and it's causing a lot of resentment," says Lipsits, a Kremlin critic who left his teaching post at the Higher School of Economics in Moscow because of increasing political pressure. He too now lives in exile in Europe.
To Lipsits, the current developments in Russia are strongly reminiscent of the collapse of the Soviet Union.

"There were special supply systems for the elite, their own shops and warehouses where they could buy everything they wanted without much difficulty, without waiting in line, and at relatively low prices. That made Russians very angry," he recounts. "When Boris Yeltsin announced that he was going to abolish these closed distribution centers, the people enthusiastically supported him. We are now in a similar situation."
Lipsits says a closed system for fuel distribution is evolving in Russia that will make it a luxury to be able to drive a car.
A threat to Putin's Ukraine war plans?

The economist Shiryaev believes Ukrainian attacks on Russian targets that serve both a military and a civilian purpose could cripple the Russian economy and hasten the end of the war. He believes it would end in just a few weeks if the West supported Ukraine in doubling or tripling the intensity of its attacks.
"Ukraine could bring about disorganization and chaos in the Russian interior, resulting in a total loss of control," Shiryaev says.
Russia’s oil empire under pressure
To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio
He also thinks the fuel shortage could have a decisive role in undermining the stability of Vladimir Putin's regime.

"If there's no diesel, thousands of kilometers of Russia's railway come to a halt," he says. "It could also cripple hundreds of factories and businesses. Without diesel, tens of thousands of trucks would be unable to run, food wouldn't get to the stores, and farmers wouldn't be able to harvest their crops."
Shiryaev says all this could result in curtailing Putin's plans to continue the war.

"If Ukraine destroys the whole oil refining infrastructure, Putin will find that, when he gives an order, it isn't implemented," the economist predicts. Everything will grind to a halt for lack of fuel.
This article was originally published in Russian.
Editor's note: We adjusted information about Russia's railway network on August 25, 2026.

articles.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy rejects wartime elections
articles.summary: The Ukrainian president says wartime elections, as called for by the ex-defense minister, could "split Ukraine." He also said Russia was planning to mobilize hundreds of thousands of troops after…

image.caption: Zelenskyy has warned against holding elections in wartimeImage: Thomas Trutschel/IMAGO

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that holding elections in his country amid the full-scale Russian invasion would be highly dangerous, in remarks made in response to a call from the former defense minister to organize a vote.
"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in remarks released on Sunday.
Under martial law, elections are currently suspended in the country as it fights the invading Russian forces. The measure has wide public support.
What did Zelenskyy say about the proposed election?

"If we want to destroy the country, then we can move in the direction of elections during these times of war," Zelenskyy said in the firm rejection of the proposal by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Fedorov made the call a month after being fired by Zelenskyy as defense minister.

Fedorov enjoys significant support among younger Ukrainians, thousands of whom have been calling for his reinstatement, with some saying he could seek to challenge Zelenskyy if an election did take place.
However, a recent poll showed that Zelenskyy would still be more popular as a presidential candidate.
Zelenskyy was critical of Fedorov in his remarks, saying: "I believe he is going himself — or is being pushed — toward wrong things."
Ukraine protests erupt over ouster of defense minister
Russia planning mass mobilization — Zelenskyy
Zelenskyy also said that Kyiv believed Russia was planning to mobilize 300,000 more troops for its invasion after parliamentary elections take place in September.
He added that Moscow might draft hundreds of thousands more in 2027 as it seeks to capture the rest of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, one of its main strategic goals.
Unwilling soldiers: A stealth mass draft starting in Russia?
Agreement on missile interceptors from Germany

As Ukraine continues to come under intense missile attacks from its neighbor, Zelenskyy also spoke of having struck an agreement with Germany on the supply of 600 Patriot PAC-2 missile interceptors for 2027-28.
The announcement comes after German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visited Ukraine on Saturday.
The US Patriots are the only weapon in Kyiv's arsenal that can take on Russia's Iskander-M and Kinzhal ballistic missiles, but ammunition for the system is running short.
France on Saturday also promised to deliver new interceptor missiles.

As Europe seeks to fill the gap left by a US that, under Donald Trump, has shown ever more reluctance to help Ukraine, Norway has also said it plans to ‌give ⁠another ⁠85 billion Norwegian ​crowns ($9.2 billion; €7.8 billion) in ​financial ​support ‌to Kyiv in the 2027 ‌fiscal year.

articles.title: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
articles.summary: Germany's centrist parties reject any cooperation with the Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are classified as right-wing extremist. However, this policy is coming under increasing…

image.caption: After a CDU motion passed with AfD votes in early 2025, shortly before the general election, there were street demonstrations against any cooperation with the AfDImage: Christian Mang/Reuters

blocks.text: A firewall is a wall designed to prevent a fire from spreading from one building to another. In German politics, the term "firewall" serves as a metaphor for a strict boundary drawn against parties regarded as extremist. Just as a firewall is intended to protect buildings from fire, the "political firewall" is intended to safeguard democracy.

Whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is in fact a party that is hostile to democracy has not yet been determined by the courts. While Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, has classified individual AfD state associations as "confirmed right-wing extremist," the question of whether the party as a whole is acting against the German constitution would have to be decided by the Federal Constitutional Court in proceedings to ban the party.
Calls for an AfD ban have been made repeatedly, but no formal application has been filed to date.
How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD?
Chancellor Merz is growing tired of the term 'firewall'
The term "political firewall" cannot be clearly attributed to any single originator. However, its widespread use is due in large part to Friedrich Merz.

Upon becoming leader of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in December 2021, for example, he told the German news magazine Der Spiegel: "Under my leadership, there will be a firewall against the AfD."
In 2018, the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility" at its party conference, rejecting "coalitions and similar forms of cooperation" with both the AfD and the socialist Left Party.

This did not apply only to formal agreements and coalitions with the AfD. At times, the CDU also deliberately sought majorities without AfD support, and CDU officeholders declined to be elected to political positions with AfD votes.

January 2025 marked a break from that path: A CDU motion in the Bundestag calling for the rejection of asylum seekers passed with AfD support. At the time, Merz was leader of the CDU and thus of the parliamentary opposition. To this day, critics continue to accuse him of breaching the firewall policy.
Now chancellor, Merz tends to avoid the term and has grown increasingly irritated by questions about it.

The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the ecologist Greens reject any cooperation with the AfD, although without formal resolutions to that effect. Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the left-wing populist Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW), takes a different stance. She explicitly opposes excluding the AfD and would even be willing to pave the way for an AfD-led government in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where elections will be held on September 6.
How Germany's Left Party is split over anti-Zionism
No firewall at the municipal level

The reliance on AfD votes by Merz's CDU in January 2025 triggered shock and outrage, but it wasn't the first time a politician who officially supports the firewall doesn't adhere to it in practice. In 2020, Thomas Kemmerich from the neoliberal FDP was elected Premier of Thuringia with AfD votes.
Angela Merkel, who was chancellor at the time, was alarmed and demanded that the election "must be reversed."
Kemmerich resigned just a few days later.

At the local level, however, the firewall is often highly permeable. In city and municipal councils, politicians from other parties have repeatedly voted alongside the AfD. Proponents of this more relaxed attitude often argue that, for example, building a daycare center does not become a bad idea simply because the AfD also supports it.

Critics, however, regularly warn of a gradual process of normalization. In their view, such cooperation makes the AfD socially acceptable, and what begins in local politics could eventually spread to state or even federal politics.
Can 40% of voters be ignored?
The firewall policy does not appear to be harming the AfD. On the contrary, its poll ratings continue to rise, despite, or perhaps even because of, the firewall.

When the AfD is particularly strong, as it is across much of eastern Germany, the other parties represented in state parliaments often have to join forces to prevent an AfD-led state government. This can come at the expense of the credibility of parties whose ideological positions are far apart.
What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt?
Political scientists also point to a democratic deficit if the political preferences of AfD voters are ignored over the long term.
Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) recently said of Saxony-Anhalt: "It is simply completely undemocratic to permanently exclude a party supported by around 40% of voters. The firewall has failed."

Some CDU politicians in eastern Germany have questioned the rationale behind the firewall. The Brandenburg branch of the Small and Medium Enterprises and Economic Union, an internal CDU interest group, recently submitted a motion calling on the party "at the federal level to work toward repealing or fundamentally revising the CDU's incompatibility resolution vis-a-vis the AfD."
Following strong criticism from the federal party leadership, the group withdrew the motion.

Saxony's CDU Premier Michael Kretschmer, who leads a minority government in Dresden, recently told the German business daily Handelsblatt: "Anyone still talking about firewalls has failed to recognize the signs of the times. We need to talk to everyone who is willing to talk."

At the federal level, the CDU would prefer to put an end to such debates altogether. Thorsten Frei, the new chair of the Bundestag's conservative parliamentary group, which includes the Christian Social Union (CSU), has made clear that he will not tolerate deviations by individual state branches.

"The ban on cooperation with the AfD is a fundamental party resolution of the CDU. It cannot be interpreted differently from one federal state to another," he told newspapers belonging to the Funke Media Group.

The chancellor, too, is holding firm now. Despite the immense pressure and the challenging political landscape in eastern Germany, and aside from the break in January 2025, he continues to uphold the resolution of incompatibility with both the AfD and the Left Party.
How governing majorities opposed to the AfD can be formed in the future therefore remains an open question.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Sydney Marathon medal wrongly shows German landmark
articles.summary: A medal minted for finishers in the Sydney Marathon features a skyline of the city — with one landmark from rather far away. Organizers say the muddle only makes the medal "a little more unique."

image.caption: Munich's Allianz-Arena is definitely the odd man out on the Sydney Marathon medalImage: Heike Feiner/HMB Media/picture alliance

blocks.text: Organizers of the 2026 Sydney Marathon are making the best of the situation after minting tens of thousands of medals engraved with depictions of landmarks from the eastern Australian city along with one that doesn't belong — the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany.
The medal should have shown Allianz Stadium in Sydney, one of the sights participants in the upcoming race will pass as they run the 42.2-kilometer (26.2-mile) course.
More than 40,000 participants are expected to earn the medal as a "badge of honor" for completing the race on August 30.
Other landmarks shown include the famous Opera House and the Sydney Harbour Bridge.
What have organizers said about the medal mix-up?
"A little too much international flavor has found its way onto the back of the finishers' medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.
"We're not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error; though it's certainly given everyone something to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humor," the spokesperson said.
"With the event a week away, this is the medal our finishers will receive."

"Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget," the spokesperson added.
"It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."

blocks.caption: Sydney's Allianz Stadium also has its own unique appearanceImage: Rafael Ben Ari/Newscom/picture alliance

blocks.text: Good-humored reaction from Munich
Munich's Allianz Arena has responded in a light-hearted manner.
"Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!" it posted on Instagram.
"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena — Sydney Opera — Unique Architecture — Both are worth a visit!"
The daily Sydney Morning Herald also came up with a gleefully teasing headline: "The medal that will put Sydney on the map. The wrong map."
The other side of the medal shows a gold-and-indigo pattern by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian that has been widely commended.
Killian has said he was not involved in the design of the side showing the landmarks.

articles.title: Could Ukraine's Mykhailo Fedorov challenge Zelenskyy?
articles.summary: An explosive video released last week by Ukraine's former defense minister spoke of corruption, a crisis of leadership and elections. What could follow?

image.caption: Mykhailo Fedorov in the video address he published on his YouTube channel on August 18Image: Mykhailo Fedorov/YouTube/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: This past week, Ukraine was rocked by a series of political scandals. A month after stepping down as defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov addressed the Ukrainian people in a nine-minute speech posted on his YouTube channel.
In his video message, he declares that Ukraine "cannot remain without a fully appointed minister of defense." But, he continues, "the main problem goes much deeper than one position or one ministry."

He says Ukraine's greatest challenge is a "systemic crisis of governance," of which corruption is only a symptom. Fedorov also criticized the fact that no national elections have been held in Ukraine since 2019.

A few hours earlier, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, had proposed Yevhenii Khmara to parliament as the new defense minister. Khmara had been made acting minister of defense on July 20, and parliament confirmed him in the position on August 19.

blocks.caption: Yevhenii Khmara attends a session of the Ukrainian parliament on August 19, when he was appointed minister of defenseImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukraine corruption scandal involves high-ranking officials

When Fedorov spoke of corruption in government authorities, he may not have known about the scandal that would break the very day after he published his speech. On August 19, Ukrainian anti-corruption investigators searched the premises of several high-ranking officials, including a presidential deputy chief of staff, Iryna Mudra, and a member of parliament, Vadym Stolar.

Ukraine's National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) stated that it was "conducting a special operation to expose a criminal organization" in conjunction with the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office.

According to the investigating authorities, this organization was led by a current and a former Ukrainian lawmaker and involved senior officials from the president's office. Volodymyr Zelenskyy dismissed Mudra from her post as presidential deputy chief of staff the same day.

In his video, Mykhailo Fedorov warns that "it is especially dangerous when society feels that the main criterion for appointing a person is not their professionalism, results, or ability […] but their personal loyalty to the system." He says that a "legal, safe, and realistic mechanism" needs to be found to make it possible to hold elections, even if Russia's war against Ukraine continues for a long time.
Why is Fedorov's support growing in Ukraine?

The president dismissed Fedorov from his post as defense minister on July 15. Protests calling for his reinstatement began the following day in Kyiv, Lviv, Dnipro, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, and other cities. According to polls conducted by the Rating opinion research institute on July 20 and 21, trust in the ex-minister rose from 35% to 65% in the first week of the protests. Of the respondents, 72% thought Fedorov should not have been sacked.

blocks.caption: Thousands demonstrated in cities around Ukraine to protest the dismissal of Fedorov as defense ministerImage: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: A poll conducted on August 5 and 6 showed Fedorov in third place in the presidential ratings, on 12.5%. Volodymyr Zelenskyy led with 25.2%, followed by Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian army, on 16.7%.

Ihor Chalenko, a political scientist from the Center for Analysis and Strategies in Kyiv, says Fedorov's address was an attempt to consolidate the political capital he won during the protests. Even though Fedorov does not present a full election program in his video, Chalenko thinks he is calculating on positioning himself as an independent political player who could stand against Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"For 35 days, people were out on the street. The demonstrations started with the demand that Fedorov be reinstated as minister of defense. But the fear is that the spotlight has moved on from Fedorov, because the protest campaign became increasingly focused on the fight against corruption and protecting the anti-corruption authorities. So the former minister has decided to position himself politically and secure the status he attained," Chalenko said in an interview with DW.
Is Fedorov positioning himself against Zelenskyy?

However, Chalenko doesn't believe that Fedorov has shifted to "irreconcilable opposition" to Zelenskyy. While there is clearly a conflict between Fedorov and the president's inner circle, Chalenko doesn't see this as a permanent rift with the government, and he doesn't rule out a return for Fedorov were he to be offered a position.

blocks.caption: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not yet been directly challenged as the constitution forbids elections in wartimeImage: Ukrainian Presidentia/Planet Pix via ZUMA Press Wire/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Oleksiy Haran, a professor of political science at the Kyiv Mohyla Academy, thinks Fedorov's remarks about elections and a renewal of the power of state send an important signal. However, he too says he sees no decisive change in opposition to the president. "We haven't heard any criticism at all of Zelenskyy," he told DW.
What would Ukraine need to hold wartime elections?

Haran says Fedorov's speech expresses what the people want. Polls show that Ukrainians do indeed want a change of government. However, the political scientist emphasizes that there is a problem: "We agree that Russia cannot dictate to us when and how we should hold elections. But the question is: how should we hold elections if Russia continues the war?"
He believes that in order to hold full elections a stable ceasefire is needed, at the very least, and this is precisely what Fedorov does not mention in his remarks.

Vadym Denysenko, a political analyst at the Ukrainian thinktank Business Capital, believes Fedorov's speech is not an election campaign by one former minister but the start of a bigger political game. In a Facebook post, Denysenko describes two developments he is observing one month after Fedorov's dismissal. First, the social milieu he refers to as "Self-Help 3.0", which includes the anti-corruption movement, has found a political leader in Fedorov. Secondly, some of Zelenskyy's former followers have switched allegiance to Fedorov, and these, the analyst says, are now his strongest supporters.

Denysenko appreciates Fedorov's comments as a contribution to the discussion about renewing the power of state. He points out that these are the same ideas Zelenskyy campaigned on in 2019. Even though Fedorov doesn't directly say in his video that he would stand in an election, the analyst is sure this is what Fedorov's inner circle is working toward.

And, in his view, they have nothing to lose. "If elections were to be held soon, Fedorov stands a good chance of doing well," Denysenko says. "If there are no elections, they can strengthen his grassroots support and further weaken Zelenskyy."
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Spain battles forest fire a short drive from flash flood
articles.summary: The blaze, near Valencia, forced more than 1,000 people from their homes. In nearby Catalonia, civil defense teams carried out 200 rescue operations after floods trapped residents in cars and homes.

image.caption: According to EU data, wildfires have torched more than 297,000 hectares in Spain aloneImage: Nacho Doce/REUTERS

blocks.text: A forest fire in eastern Spain sparked the evacuation of around 1,000 people on Saturday, authorities said.
The blaze is one of hundreds that firefighters across Europe have been battling this summer amid record high temperatures along the Mediterranean and elsewhere.
Barely 150 kilometers (93 miles) away on the Costa Dorada, flash floods trapped people in cars, toppled walls and forced the evacuation of a campsite.
What do we know about the fire?
The fire is burning close to Gatova, an inland village with a population of 450, northwest of Valencia.
TV footage showed the flames were moving close to built-up areas.
Spain's Military Emergency Unit UME posted a video to X showing its firefighters working in the darkness to douse the flames.
Several firefighting helicopters and aircraft were also deployed.
Local media reported that the blaze is thought to have been started by a lightning strike late Thursday.
By Friday evening, more than 400 hectares of land had been burnt.
Juan Carlos Valderrama, Valencia autonomous community's civil protection minister, said buses were on standby to help residents without their own vehicles to leave their homes.
Can Germany teach Europe how to prevent wildfires?
What's the latest on the floods?
Further north, along Spain's Costa Dorada, heavy rain overnight flooded streets and caused the collapse of two walls, injuring at least seven people, officials said.
According to local media, roads in the coastal towns El Vendrell, Coma-ruga and Torredembarra in the Cataloniaregion were partially submerged.
The Meteorological Service of Catalonia said several towns recorded nearly 200 liters per square meter in just a few hours.
On Saturday morning, the agency warned of more heavy rainfall for the coastal region.
Local media reported that several people got trapped in their vehicles during the flooding.
A regional emergency official said firefighters had carried out more than 200 missions to rescue people from vehicles and flooded buildings.
Three people were injured when a wall collapsed at the port of Roda de Bera, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) southwest of Barcelona, emergency services said.
Another wall collapse at a nearby campsite injured two others.
Around 300 people staying at the campsite were evacuated, with many sheltering at a nearby sports center, officials said.
Has Europe lost control of its wildfires?

articles.title: Small German airplane crashes in Croatia, killing 2
articles.summary: The two-seater motor glider went down in the Velebit mountains, near Zadar, killing both passengers.

image.caption: The plane went down in the Velebit mountains, Croatia's largest mountain rangeImage: Dalibor Brlek/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two people were killed when a small aircraft registered in Germany crashed near Croatia's coastal city of Zadar, local media reported on Saturday.
Croatian police said the two-seater motor glider, which can fly with a small engine or glide without one, went down in the Velebit mountains on Friday.
The long, rugged mountain range runs parallel to the Adriatic coast.
Authorities said the Diamond HK36 Super Dimona was en route from the Czech Republic to Zadar when it crashed.
According to media reports, contact with the aircraft was lost just after 4 p.m. local time (1400 GMT/UTC).

blocks.caption: Thick fog in the crash area prevented the use of search drones, officials saidImage: Dalibor Brlek/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the plane crash in Croatia?
Police said the wreckage, along with the bodies of two passengers, was found after a lengthy search.
Challenging terrain, along with heavy rain, wind and fog, meant it took nearly six hours to reach the location.
Croatian media outlet Jutarnji list cited the mountain rescue agency as describing the conditions as "extremely difficult."
The fog, which reduced visibility to around 2 meters, also prevented the deployment of search drones, Jutarnji list reported.
The agency sent a 35-person rescue team to the crash site, local media said.
Officials have not announced the victims' identities or nationalities
German news agency DPA cited the Czech Foreign Ministry as saying the victims were not Czech citizens.

articles.title: Industry and residents clash over water near Berlin
articles.summary: The state surrounding Berlin is drying out, but local Tesla and Red Bull plants are looking to expand. Is Brandenburg running out of water to share?

image.caption: Once considered a water-rich state, Brandenburg is now facing challenges on several frontsImage: Patrick Pleul/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For years, Petra Liesenfeld has witnessed falling groundwater levels in her hometown of Baruth. She has to water her garden far more often than she used to, and has seen some local trees completely dry out. At the same time, two beverage companies are looking to expand production in the area.

Mineral water has been bottled in the small town of Baruth, which lies around 60 kilometers (37 miles) south of Berlin, since the 1990s. The site is now run by Red Bull and Austrian beverage producer Rauch, who are planning a new canning factory and additional facilities. All in the middle of a water protection area.

The Baruth waterworks are licensed to extract a fixed amount of groundwater each year, just 8% of which goes to supply the town's roughly 4,300 residents with drinking water. The remaining 92% is reserved for Red Bull and Rauch, and is enough to cover the drinking water needs of 57,000 people. But exactly how much water the companies currently use is not made public.

blocks.caption: How much Red Bull and Rauch pay for the daily 7 million liters of permitted groundwater is confidentialImage: DW

blocks.text: This is legal under the existing contracts, said Peter Ilk, who until recently was the town's mayor and is considered a driving force behind the region's industrialization. He sees no problem with the way water is managed.

"We have always given priority to supplying the population. That is also written into all the contracts," he said, adding that it stands to reason that the companies need more than the town's residents. "That's how you end up with this ratio of around one to 10 in terms of consumption."
Old data informing current decisions

Hydrogeologist Irina Engelhardt from the Technical University in Berlin takes a more critical view, pointing out that the contracts, which are around 30 years old, are based on outdated information. Since then, groundwater levels, groundwater recharge and the way land is used have all changed significantly.

"I am concerned at how the water situation is developing in the state of Brandenburg," she said. "The volume that is actually available is currently being overestimated by the Brandenburg authorities."

blocks.caption: Members of the local initiative reached out to the authorities to get an idea of the situation, but many of the documents they received had been heavily redactedImage: DW

blocks.text: Together with a citizens' initiative made up of local residents, she is calling for new, independent assessments — and for clear and open communication. Though the authorities granted them access to some groundwater monitoring documents, large parts were redacted, which some residents believe is a move to conceal information about changes in levels.
"We ask ourselves why there can't be more transparency if everything is aboveboard. Why isn't the public allowed to know?" said Petra Liesenfeld.
Exactly how much Red Bull and Rauch pay for their daily extraction of up to 7 million liters of groundwater is not public information.
DW approached both companies for comment, but by the time of publication, neither had responded.
For drought researcher Andreas Marx, this lack of transparency is problematic.
"By law, water is a public commodity. It cannot be privately owned. So, in my view, every decision made and every contract signed over its use should be open to the public," he said.
How dry is Brandenburg?

Germany — and Brandenburg — are still water-rich regions. Marx, who heads the Drought Monitor at the Helmholtz Centre for Environmental Research, said "the challenge isn't adapting to permanent water scarcity but learning how to cope with dry periods that can last two or even three years."

Nevertheless, the water balance in the state, as elsewhere in Germany, is definitely changing. Since the 2018 drought, groundwater has not been sufficiently replenished in many places and higher temperatures and increasing evaporation are making it harder for reserves in deeper soil layers to recover.
This could cause even more problems in the future, as 95% of Brandenburg's drinking water comes from groundwater.
How much water does the energy transition need?

In Grünheide, in the eastern part of the state of Brandenburg, Tesla's Gigafactory has a permit to extract up to 1.4 million cubic meters of water per year and is planning to expand production to as many as 7,500 vehicles per week. Meanwhile, in recent years, residents have repeatedly been urged to save water.
