blocks.caption: Since the construction of Tesla's Gigafactory was announced in 2019, the project has faced strong criticism from local residentsImage: DW

blocks.text: "Many projects, including new schools and kindergartens, were put on hold because there simply wasn't enough water," said local resident Manu Hoyer.

Marx said when water resources are scarce, residents are generally the first to face restrictions because they're the easiest to limit. "Industrial companies are rarely restricted, because the economic consequences are much harder to assess," he said.
Copper for the energy transition — a risk to groundwater?

The potential for an additional water problem is brewing further south in Spremberg, where a large mine is planned. Over the coming decades, copper — which is essential for power grids, electric vehicles and the transition to clean energy — is set to be extracted from depths of up to 1,200 meters (about 4,000 feet).

blocks.caption: Lignite mining has a long history in parts of BrandenburgImage: DW

blocks.text: Geotechnical engineer Michael Pfeifer said mine water from such depths is highly saline and sulfurous and requires extensive treatment.

"But the treatment plant proposed so far is nowhere near capable of doing what's actually required to clean the water to a standard where it could be safely discharged into the Spree," Pfeiffer said of the river that flows north toward Berlin.

The river water is already affected by decades of lignite mining in the region, and it is facing additional pressures. With lignite extraction set to end by 2038, the groundwater currently pumped into the Spree from the mines will no longer be available. As a result, dry summers could see the river carrying up to 75% less water, with far-reaching consequences for water resources all the way to Berlin.
Could rainfall be stored for future use?

One possible solution to the water problems facing the state around the German capital is artificial groundwater recharge, where excess water from periods of high rainfall is stored underground and used later.

blocks.caption: In these basins in Brandenburg, treated wastewater is already deliberately allowed to seep into the ground, storing it for dry periodsImage: DW

blocks.text: Hydrogeologist Engelhardt is researching where this could be possible in the region.
"There are areas in Brandenburg — such as where Tesla is now located — where artificial groundwater recharge could meet almost the entire demand of the local drinking water supplier," she said.
However, enough available water is necessary for this solution to work.
For drought researcher Marx, one question remains crucial: What rules should determine how water is distributed between the population, agriculture, nature and industry during prolonged dry periods?
As the global temperature continues to rise, it's not just an issue reserved for Brandenburg — or even Germany.
This article was originally published in German.
Correction, August 19, 2026: An earlier version of this article misspelled the name of geotechnical engineer Michael Pfeifer. DW apologizes for the error.
German residents near Berlin fight for their drinking water

articles.title: Germany investigates arms cache found in woods near Berlin
articles.summary: Handguns and ammunition were found in a forest near Berlin last year. Reports say German authorities suspect they were to be used for assassinations on behalf of Russian intelligence.

image.caption: Without naming Russia, the German interior minister said authorities could not rule out the involvement of foreign powersImage: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Security authorities in Germany uncovered a cache of handguns in a forest near the capital, Berlin, last year, which they believe was intended to be used to carry out assassinations on behalf of Russia, according to reports on Friday.
The daily Süddeutsche Zeitung and public broadcasters NDR and WDR reported that one suspect was arrested in Romania.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said German authorities were in touch with their Romanian counterparts about the suspect's potential extradition.
"This case demonstrates that we are ​operating under a high threat level," ​Dobrindt told reporters.
What else did Dobrindt say about the weapons stash?
Dobrindt confirmed the media reports that the suspect, who was detained in Romania last year, was being investigated on suspicion of espionage and planning a violent attack that endangers the state.

But Dobrindt did not comment on the media reports' claims that the weapons were meant to be used for targeted killings on behalf of Russian intelligence. The minister only said that authorities could not rule out foreign powers being involved.
The interior minister also did not disclose the suspect's identity but said the suspect was being held in connection with planned parcel bomb attacks in Romania.
"We will then determine, in the course of the investigation, what measures ​can be ⁠taken against this person," Dobrindt added.

Dobrindt said the suspect was a "low-level agent" and unaware of the line of command above him. The minister added that other operatives, including a Kazakh citizen, had been detained this year who were similarly uninformed of the network they were part of.

blocks.caption: Interior Minister Dobrindt refused to confirm reports that Russia was involved in the arms cacheImage: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the weapons that were found?

The stash found near Berlin contained two pistols, which had signs that they had been placed there on behalf of Russia's intelligence services, German news agency dpa reported. The stash also contained ammunition.
Police disabled the two handguns but left them intact at the site before placing the location under surveillance.

Dobrindt said officers watched the stash for months after discovering it, but no one was seen approaching it. It is presumed the alleged perpetrators were aware that police had uncovered the weapons and avoided the site.
What do we know about Russia's alleged involvement?
While Dobrindt refused to be drawn into whether Russia was directly involved, the minister said this month that Germany was a "daily target of hybrid warfare."
"Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality," Dobrindt said at the time.
Those remarks came in response to the discovery of an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig Airport.
Some German lawmakers have pointed to Russia, and US media reports said American intelligence services suspected that Russia was behind the drone incident.
Russia has rejected allegations that it was involved as a ⁠"hastily fabricated provocation" that is part of a "new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany."
The Russian embassy in Berlin added that the incident "only serves the interests of Kyiv and the militarist wing of the European political class."
“Was it Russia?” Is the Leipzig drone attack part of a hybrid war?

articles.title: 'Masha and the Bear': Ukraine sanctions Russian cartoon
articles.summary: Ukraine has imposed sanctions on the hit Russian children's cartoon "Masha and the Bear," a step towards banning it. The culture minister called the show propaganda. Russia said the move showed…

image.caption: Some signs of the show's popularity in Ukraine could even be seen in the ruins of homes damaged by the 2022 Russian invasion [FILE: March 2022] Image: Rodrigo Abd/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian Culture Minister Tetyana Berezhna on Friday said Kyiv had imposed sanctions on the "producers and distributors" of the Russian children's cartoon series "Masha and the Bear," or "Masha i Medved" in the original language.
The step will enable Kyiv to seek to remove and demonentize the series on websites like YouTube or streaming services like Netflix in the country.

The cartoon about a mischievous young girl's unlikely friendship and adventures with a retired circus bear, loosely based on a Russian oral fairytale of the same name, launched in 2009 and quickly became one of Russia's most successful televisual exports.

blocks.caption: Masha and the Bear or Masha i Medved's YouTube channel is among the 50 most-watched in the world, with more than 54 billion views worldwide as of June 2026Image: Ivan Sekretarev/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did the government in Kyiv say about the sanctions?

"Ukraine has imposed sanctions against the producers and distributors of the Russian animated series Masha and the Bear," Berezhna said on social media. "This creates legal grounds to block the content in Ukraine and engage international platforms to restrict its monetization and distribution."
The show has also faced criticism from allies of Ukraine like Estonia and the UK for allegedly painting Russia in a positive light or for military or Soviet symbols sometimes appearing in the show.
"Russian propaganda has no place on children's screens — in Ukraine or anywhere in the world," Berezhna said.

In further comments on Facebook, Berezhna said the Ukrainian language channel for the show had 800 million views in 2025 alone. The Ukrainian language channel currently has roughly 18 million subscribers.
Worldwide, as of June 2026, the show had more than 54 billion combined views on YouTube, making it one of the 50 most popular feeds on the entire site.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree imposing sanctions on the creators of the show for spreading "pro-Russia narratives" and for posing a threat to Ukrainian national security. They target the studio, the show's founder, and the series' scriptwriter and director.
Ukraine said it would seek to have its sanctions mirrored by international partners, potentially widening the restrictions.

blocks.caption: The story revolves around a curious and sometimes mischievous girl's unlikely friendship with a protective former circus bearImage: Ivan Sekretarev/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: How did the show's makers and the Russian government respond?

The company behind the show, Animaccord Animation Studios, has called past allegations that the show contains Russian propaganda "false and defamatory," saying that it operates independently and receives no funding from the government in Moscow.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked about the sanctions on Friday and said that the cartoon series had "conquered the world" by promoting "the finest human qualities."
"The fact that Ukraine has launched a war against cartoons, too, likely serves as yet another illustration of the ugly nature" of the authorities in Kyiv, he said.

blocks.caption: The show has a following across much of Europe — in this case as demonstrated in hay-bale form in Croatia — and even further afieldImage: Davor Javorovic/PIXSELL/picture alliance

blocks.text: Is 'Masha and the Bear' controversial, and why?

The show has been on the radar of Ukrainian authorities for almost a decade. The first complaint by the State Film Agency dates back to 2017, amid the illegal annexation of Crimea and the lower-level war in Ukraine waged by separatists supported by Russia. Since the 2022 full-scale invasion the issue has come into sharper focus still.
In June, Kyiv protested against streaming giant Netflix's move to acquire the rights to stream new seasons of "Masha and the Bear."

A group of more than 50 British parliamentarians this year appealed to Culture Minister Lisa Nandy to urge streaming platforms to remove the cartoon. They argued that some episodes exposed children to Russian and Soviet military imagery.
Several Estonian politicians have also argued that "Masha and the Bear" is an instrument of Russian soft power, not least because of the several amiable bears in its cast.

Some Western analysts have warned against exaggerating these fears, though — for instance UK academic Mark Galeotti, who wrote an article objecting to the British lawmakers' appeal in July, saying the show was not "the most elevated of television," but "it is cute and it has a big heart."

In its earlier days, "Masha i Medved" was also a topic of some controversy in Russia. It sometimes drew critical comparisons to Western children's shows and prompted debate on whether it was contradicting traditional values about the roles of girls and fathers in Russian society, given Masha's mischievous nature and her paternal bear's gentle use of positive reinforcement rather than correctional discipline.

articles.title: German army helps Poland protect itself against Russia
articles.summary: Poland is building a defense system along its northern and eastern borders to protect itself from Russia. Since June, German sappers have been assisting their NATO ally with the construction of the…

image.caption: The German army is helping Poland strengthen the East Shield, for example by installing anti-tank obstaclesImage: Polnische Streitkräfte/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Poland started to construct a defensive barrier along its border with Russia and Belarus in 2024. The East Shield defense system will eventually be around 800 kilometers long, and is intended to protect this country on NATO's eastern flank against attack from the east.

When the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, inspected the first completed section in November 2024, he declared that the project was meant to "deter and discourage a potential aggressor" and was "truly an investment in peace."

The Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 was a profound shock to Poland's sense of security. The Tusk government has increased defense spending in 2026 to 200 billion zlotys (around 46 billion euros, or 54 billion dollars) ― almost 5% of Poland's GDP. This means that, in relative terms, Poland has the highest defense spending of all the members of NATO. The government has also bought the most advanced weapons available, particularly from the US, and is proceeding with the construction of the East Shield, a complex defense system along its eastern border.
A shield against Russia

Since June, around 40 German sappers, or combat engineers, have been helping to establish the defenses. The German army's combat engineer unit is specially trained in blocking the movement of enemy troops. The sappers are currently deployed near Budry in Masuria, close to the border with Russia. The fence marking the border is visible from where they are working, partially obscured by a row of trees on the Polish side.

The German soldiers are installing anti-tank obstacles to impede battle tanks in the event of an attack. A yellow backhoe loader lifts the spiky concrete blocks, known as Czech hedgehogs, off a truck and places them on the muddy ground.

This installation, around 200 meters back from the border, consists of three rows of these concrete blocks. A deep ditch and another line of hedgehogs run along the border itself. A Polish officer explains that mines can quickly be laid in the zone between the two lines of Czech hedgehogs.

"The German sappers have done an excellent job," the Polish general Stanislaw Czosnek said when he inspected the works on Thursday. He added that he was "very impressed" by his German colleagues' performance.
In the six weeks since their deployment, the German engineers have laid more than a kilometer of blocks.

"We stand ready to fight for democracy and freedom," stressed the German general Tito Gante, who accompanied Czosnek on the inspection. He praised the comradely atmosphere between the German and the Polish soldiers.
The Bundeswehr has declared its support for the East Shield an official mission: "We want to maintain peace with a credible deterrent," Gante said.
The German contingent will stay until October, but the sappers will soon be deployed at other sections of the East Shield. The work near Budry is due to be completed over the coming week.

blocks.caption: The anti-tank obstacles can only be moved by a backhoe loaderImage: Jacek Lepiarz/DW

blocks.text: Politically symbolic

"Above all, the participation of German sappers has politically symbolic significance," Lukasz Jasinski, an analyst at the Polish Institute for International Affairs, told DW. "Poland wants to convince Germany and other partners that Poland's eastern border is also the external border of the EU and NATO. Our Western partners should treat this border a bit like their own."

Poland and Germany were quick to establish military cooperation after the end of the Cold War. Later, when Poland joined NATO in 1999, this created the necessary political and institutional conditions for close collaboration. Since then, NATO's Multinational Corps Northeast, in which Poland and Germany both have leading roles, has been headquartered in the Polish city of Szczecin.

In 2003, Germany sold the MiG-29 fighter jets it inherited from the former East German Air Force to Poland for the symbolic price of one euro each. Joint military exercises and exchange programs for both officers and soldiers are now standard practice.

When Russia attacked Ukraine in February 2022, there were initial tensions between Germany and Poland on account of the cautious response from Berlin. Overall, though, the attack has further strengthened cooperation between the two. The Bundeswehr has supported Polish air defense by supplying several units of the Patriot air defense system, with their German crews. German fighter jets are helping to protect Polish air space, most recently as part of the NATO mission Enhanced Air Policing North (eAPN) in Malbork.

blocks.caption: A German air force Eurofighter Typhoon taking off in December 2025 from the Polish military airbase in MalborkImage: Adam Warøawa/PAP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Questions of military cooperation were also prioritized in the closing statement that followed German-Polish intergovernmental consultations on December 1, 2025. The process culminated in the signing of the German-Polish defense agreement on June 17, 2026.

On August 15 this year, three German planes, two Eurofighters and an A400M transport aircraft, participated in the celebration of Polish Armed Forces Day. The head of the German air force, Holger Neumann, was one of the guests of honor. Some American GIs marched in the military parade ― but no German soldiers.
Kaczynski: No German soldiers in Poland

However, not all the political forces in Poland are happy about this new Polish-German brotherhood-in-arms. Memories of the trauma of World War II are still very much alive in Polish society and are regularly instrumentalized by the right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) to stir up anti-German feeling.
Back in 2014, PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski said he didn't want any German soldiers in Poland.
"It will be at least seven generations before that is acceptable," he said.

blocks.caption: The line of anti-tank obstacles forming part of the East Shield near Budry in PolandImage: Jacek Lepiarz/DW

blocks.text: In the fall of 2022, when the German government offered to relocate two German Patriot batteries to Poland after an incident involving a Ukrainian rocket gone astray, the PiS government blocked the move.
"Germany's previous behavior gives us no reason to believe that it will decide to fire on the Russian rockets," Kaczynski declared.

Just last March, Poland's president Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by the PiS, vetoed legislation that would have allowed Poland to access almost 44 billion euros (55 billion dollars) in EU defense loans because German armaments companies could also have benefited.

Poland sees the US as the most important guarantor of its security, and is trying to establish a special relationship with Washington. Around 10,000 US soldiers are currently stationed in various places around the country. Warsaw is keen to establish a permanent military base on its territory: Until now, a significant number of the US soldiers are in Poland on rotation.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: France issues warning over thousands of substandard condoms
articles.summary: French anti-fraud and health agencies have issued a recall order for roughly 260,000 condoms. They advised users to consider sexually transmitted infection and pregnancy tests amid risks of bursting…

image.caption: The thought might not be uppermost in your mind when the time comes, but condoms sold in the EU and European Economic Area should always carry the CE marking on the packaging showing they have passed relevant safety and standards checksImage: Robin Utrecht/ROBIN UTRECHT/picture alliance

blocks.text: France's anti-fraud and health agencies issued a joint statement on Friday saying they were recalling more than a quarter of a million condoms that could be defective.
It said that the majority were sold online via major marketplaces by Asian vendors.
What did the government agencies say about the potentially substandard condoms?
Of the roughly 260,000 contraceptives being recalled, authorities said around 1,000 boxes, or 40,000 individual condoms, had already been sold.
"Laboratory analyses identified two non-compliant products, characterized by a risk of bursting and, in one case, the presence of perforations," authorities said.

The anti-fraud agency, the DGCCRF, and the DGS health agency said in a joint statement that the condoms lacked the required CE marking that designates a product conforms with the standards of the European Economic Area trading zone.

blocks.caption: Even novelty and seasonal condoms should carry the CE markingImage: Michael Bihlmayer/CHROMORANGE/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The identified condoms lack a CE marking, third-party conformity assessment, and — in most cases — packaging in French," the government agencies said. "Consequently, they are deemed non-compliant and potentially pose serious risks to user health and safety (such as sexually transmitted infections and unintended pregnancies)."

The statement advised people who had used the condoms to get screened for sexually transmitted infections and to take a pregnancy test if they had any reason to be suspicious such as a missed or late period.
The government said the online vendors had agreed to remove the affected listings and to send in the recalled products.
The statement listed two brands of condoms made by a Japanese company, Okamoto Industries, and the brands MyLubie and Friday Bae by Passage du Desir.
France offers people aged up to 25 free condoms via pharmacies without a prescription in a bid to prevent STIs and unwanted pregnancies.

blocks.caption: Young people in France are mostly eligible for free condoms from pharmacies without a prescription under a policy initiated during Emmanuel Macron's presidencyImage: Aurore Marechal/ABACA/picture alliance

articles.title: Ukraine's farmers struggle to sell harvest amid war, drought
articles.summary: Russian attacks on ships and ports in the Black Sea are threatening Ukraine's agricultural sector. Grain exports are severely restricted, and Kyiv is seeking solutions.

image.caption: The price of food-grade wheat has declined by 30 to 35% in UkraineImage: Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Russian attacks on civilian ships have effectively brought the ports in the greater region of Odesa to a standstill. Until recently, they handled about 90% of Ukraine's agricultural exports.
The Ukrainian government has been working on finding alternative routes via rail, road and other waterways. It is also currently in negotiations about an export corridor that would go via Moldova.

But many experts have pointed out that these temporary alternatives cannot replace the ports, and warn that the current blockade of the Black Sea is an even greater threat to the Ukrainian economy than that posed by Russia's full-scale invasion of 2022.

blocks.caption: Russian attacks have brought ships in the Black Sea to a standstillImage: Victor Sayenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: The strained security situation in the Black Sea is already having a palpable effect on Ukraine's domestic market. According to Denys Marchuk, the deputy chairman of the All-Ukrainian Agrarian Council, Ukrainian farmers have already harvested more than 28 million tons of grains and pulses.

But a large part of this harvest cannot be sold, which has led to a shortage of the cash needed to complete the harvest and to plant winter crops. Planting usually begins at the end of August in Ukraine's southern regions.

"Right now, we can barely sell our harvest. Instead, we're storing what we have harvested — that's if we find storage space. At the same time, we are wondering what to do because we need money, especially so we can plant in fall," Marchuk told DW.
He predicted that the situation would continue to worsen in the coming weeks and months when grain and oilseed crops, which are usually harvested later, compounded the crisis.
Farmers plan to leave corn in the fields

The corn harvest alone could reach about 33 million metric tons this year. Yet in the coming months, there could be a shortage of storage capacity totaling up to 10 million tons. Regions on the front, where most silos have been destroyed amid the ongoing war, are particularly affected.

"You often hear that farmers want to leave their corn in the fields to be harvested in spring. It still needs to be dried, which needs a lot of electricity that is very expensive. They don't have the money," said Marchuk. "There aren't enough places where they can sell it, nor are the prices reasonable, so for them it makes more sense to leave it in the fields as that's cheaper."
Domestic prices falling

Maksym Hopka, an analyst at the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club, estimates that Ukraine's agricultural output totaled about 3.7 million metric tons in July, of which about 2.7 million metric tons comprised grain. That was a decline of about a quarter in comparison to the previous month. He expected an additional fall of over 50% in August.
Hopka added that domestic prices were falling, with the price of food-grade wheat declining by 30 to 35%. This meant increasingly difficult economic conditions for production, he explained.
Prices have fallen so sharply because farmers cannot export all of their harvest, and can no longer cover even their production costs.

blocks.caption: Farmers in Ukraine have said it is too expensive to harvest their corn, and plan to wait until next springImage: Olena Mykhaylova/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Some farms are already operating at a loss. According to the Ukrainian Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food, annual losses from unsold agricultural produce could amount to approximately $20.5 billion (approx. €18 billion).
Ukrainian government vows to provide support

The Ukrainian government has insisted it will do everything in its power to find new ways to export Ukrainian agricultural produce by rail or road through neighboring countries or through ports on the Danube.

However, extreme heat and drought have severely reduced the Danube's transport capacity and are also hampering Ukrainian exports. There are also problems with rail and road transport. European railways are already operating at full capacity during harvest season, and transporting large quantities of grain by road is expensive.

For Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky, the top priority remains restoring safe shipping routes to the ports in the Odesa region with the help of Ukraine's military and those of its partners. He told DW that there was no comparable medium-term alternative and that rail connections and dry ports could only serve as temporary measures until the Black Sea ports reopened.
Less help from EU than in 2022

Oleg Nivievskyi from the Kyiv School of Economics said Ukraine today had fewer ways of offsetting losses in maritime trade than it did at the beginning of the full-scale invasion. In 2022, the European Union provided support to Ukraine by establishing "solidarity lanes," and import duties and quotas were temporarily suspended to ease trade.
Ukraine's desperate search for farm labor

Nivievskyi pointed out that the conditions were different now. "If we look at trade with the EU, we have gone from a free system to the pre-war trade regime with customs restrictions and quotas," he said.

He added that there were also significant shortcomings in the infrastructure, with the Ukrainian railway currently running 30% fewer trains than before 2022. Russia's constant attacks on rail infrastructure have hampered operations and necessitated regular repairs. Transport via road is also limited due to shortage of truck drivers, not least because many had been mobilized to fight in the war.
Export strategies need rethink

Nivievskyi said the current crisis could help to encourage the government to rethink Ukraine's export policies. He said the country should have developed a long-term strategy right from the beginning of the Russian invasion in order to ensure that its exports could reach global markets.

He explained it wasn't only a question of finding temporary alternatives to the ports of Odesa; the government needed to put in place logistics to ensure that the blockade of one route did not paralyze the entire sector.
Hopka has calculated that Ukraine's exports of agricultural produce will drop by about 9 million metric tons between August and October, and that losses could amount to about $1.9 billion.

In response to pressure from farmers, the government has already extended a loan program to farmers and has also applied for €220 million in aid from the European Commission. The idea is to help small and medium-sized agricultural businesses in particular to cover their payments.
This article was originally written in Ukrainian.
German farmers face harvest losses, price uncertainty

articles.title: What to do when wildfires trigger trauma
articles.summary: The wildfires this summer have broken records in Germany and are unlikely to subside in future. Psychologists say post-traumatic stress disorder caused by such disasters is serious but can be treated…

image.caption: It took almost a week to get the fire in the Hürtgen Forest under control Image: Jan Ohmen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: This year, wildfires have already burned more land than the annual average from 2006 to 2025 in Germany. North Rhine-Westphalia, the country's most populous state, has just seen the largest recorded wildfire in its history. It destroyed or damaged about 300 to 400 hectares in the Hürtgen Forest in the Eifel region.

After weeks without rain, the wildfire spread rapidly across the arid landscape with wind driving the flames in different directions. Unexploded munitions from World War II that were at risk of exploding or did explode complicated the firefighting efforts. Around 1,500 firefighters battled the flames for almost a week until the fire was stabilized, with some working 12-hour shifts.
Peter Berndgen, a spokesperson for the volunteer fire department in the Düren district in the west of the state, said that the physical and mental strain was enormous.

"Your eyes itch every night, your nose is always black and the airways and lungs are under pressure. During a 12-hour-shift, you're constantly on high alert, ready for whatever might happen," he said.
This can be trees falling or the flames changing direction, he added.

And on top of that, the constant fear that "the situation is spiraling out of my control, we won't be able to cope, you get that kind of feeling sometimes. And then you start wondering whether you'll manage to get it under control at all."
Can Germany teach Europe how to prevent wildfires?
Not everyone suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder

Despite being prepared and professional, firefighters know they are also at risk of death. "The fear, or dread, that you can have is really, where can I take refuge, how will I get out of this. I'm right in the middle of a forest."

Andreas Meyer, a psychiatrist from the Central Institute of Mental Health in Mannheim who co-authored the "Berlin Declaration on Climate Change and Mental Health," says such situations can have long-lasting effects.

"Not everyone, but several people who experience something like this end up developing what is known as post-traumatic stress disorder. They find themselves reliving the event over and over, having nightmares, and experiencing flashbacks. Post-traumatic stress disorder is three times more common among firefighters than it is in the general population."

A typical symptom of post-traumatic stress disorder is avoidance behavior. People might avoid places that resemble those where the trauma first occurred, as well as conversations about the event itself.
"This can lead to the disorder setting in," said Meyer-Lindenberg.

He explained that it was totally normal to feel shaken immediately after such a disaster; to have trouble sleeping, for example, or to feel sad, but he said that if such a state persisted for more than a month and interfered with daily life, people should seek psychological help.
"The good news is that post-traumatic stress disorder can be treated very successfully with behavioral therapy," he said, adding that it resolved the disorder in two-thirds of patients.

Apart from post-traumatic stress disorder, wildfires and other such disasters can also trigger depression, anxiety disorder or addiction. Some studies have found that people are also more likely to self-harm or even commit suicide afterward.

Meyer-Lindenberg said that the number of psychiatric diagnoses is likely to double after such a disaster. "Fortunately, for many of those affected, the symptoms subside on their own. But, unfortunately, this is not always the case. Illness might still be detected years later."
'A new normal': Unprecedented wildfires in Canada
Some population groups more likely to be affected, particularly women

Some groups of the population are more likely to be affected than others, studies have found. For example, children and adolescents, as well as people who are poor or who already had a mental illness. Women are also more likely to be affected than men.
While one in three people affected by a natural disaster is at risk of developing long-lasting post-traumatic stress disorder, this falls to one in 10 amid emergency responders.
Meyer-Lindenberg said that they were helped by experience, clear rules during an operation and working together as a team.

"So much depends on these factors when you are confronted with an emergency," he said. "Do I feel capable? Do I know what I have to do? Do I have colleagues, teammates I can rely on? Is there a structure in place or am I at the mercy of a situation?"
While ordinary people might be forced to stand by as their neighborhood goes up in flames, firefighters have the task of putting out the fire.

Peter Berndgen said that the volunteer firefighters in the Rhine region were highly motivated. "We want to protect ourselves, the population, our villages, our homes. We want to protect all of that," he said. "And I believe that gives us energy."
He added that psychological support was on hand if necessary and that talking about experiences was a routine part of operations as well as fighting the flames.
Taking action and control can be useful in fighting feeling of helplessness

Meyer-Lindenberg said that everyone affected by a natural disaster could benefit from action and taking control of their situation if possible. He said it was useful to put in place preventative measures against fires or floods, for example. However, it was not helpful to try to toughen oneself up for a disaster or to get used to them.
"Quite the contrary: if someone has already lived through such a disaster, they are more likely to suffer psychological consequences from the next one," he said

Firefighters who are able to put out a fire, as Berndgen and his colleagues did in the Hürtgen Forest, are also less likely to suffer from long-term psychological stress. "It confirms that what we did made sense," he said.

Unfortunately, he did not feel the same during the flood in the Ahr Valley five years ago, he said. "People from the Ahr region whose lives were in danger called us for help, but we knew we couldn't help them."
That is the worst possible situation for a firefighter, he said. "If I knew that I'd have to do this every six months, I would probably reach a point and ask whether I could really cope."
This article was originally published in German

articles.title: Bauhaus Manifesto: Broad alliance promoting artistic freedom
articles.summary: Weeks before Saxony-Anhalt's state election, representatives from German cultural, crafts, architecture, design and church sectors unite to promote freedom, openness and creativity.

image.caption: The Bauhaus building in DessauImage: DW

blocks.text: The "Bauhaus Manifesto 2026," published on August 20, was initiated by Germany's Minister of State for Culture, Wolfram Weimer.

"Together, we're making it clear that we want to strengthen the Bauhaus and its principles while defending them against any form of anti-democratic attack," the independent politician told the German press agency DPA.

A statement accompanying the manifesto said it was intended as a cultural and sociopolitical commitment to the principles that have made the Bauhaus art school, which operated from 1919 to 1933, a global cultural icon. Those principles include freedom of artistic thought, openness to new ideas, the connection between different disciplines, and the belief that cultural innovation can make an important contribution to a democratic society.
Revolutionary design school Bauhaus turns 100
Something to be proud of

At the publication of the manifesto, Weimer said, "The Bauhaus demonstrates the innovative power that emerges when art, craftsmanship, design and technology converge. It stands for creativity and exchange, courage and openness to new ideas." He said those values remain an important source of inspiration: "We can be proud of that."

The signatories include the German Cultural Council, the German Commission for UNESCO, the German Bishops' Conference, the Evangelical Church in Germany, the Association of German Cities, the German Museums Association, the Academy of Arts, the German Confederation of Skilled Crafts and the German Lost Art Foundation.

The Bauhaus was founded in Weimar in 1919 by architect Walter Gropius and other artists as a school of art and design. It later moved to Dessau and eventually to Berlin. When he founded the school, Gropius outlined its goals in his own "Bauhaus Manifesto." In 1933, the prestigious institution was forced to close permanently under pressure from the Nazis. The Bauhaus and its sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau have been UNESCO World Heritage Sites since 1996.

blocks.caption: Wolfram Weimer, Minister of State for Culture, initiated the 'Bauhaus Manifesto 2026'Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Bauhaus' international influence is not based solely on its modern design language and avant-garde approach, the new manifesto says. It also stems from its ethos, which remains a model today: the courage to pursue bold ideas, a belief in freedom of artistic thought and the conviction that only an open society can foster cultural renewal.

The signatories also set out to defend the Bauhaus movement itself against populist criticism: "Bauhaus institutions should be strengthened; their creative freedom and social openness recognized as exemplary and they should be defended against any anti-democratic attacks," they say.
A 'misguided aberration of modernity'?

The Alternative for Germany (AFD) party, which has described the Bauhaus as a "misguided aberration of modernity," is not named in the manifesto. But the document can be seen as a response to the far-right party's cultural agenda.

The AfD could emerge as the largest bloc in the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament after the September 6 election. The party says it wants to promote a "patriotic cultural policy," primarily supporting art that "contributes to the development of German identity."

The AfD also plans to replace Saxony-Anhalt's current image campaign, #moderndenken (think modern), with #deutschdenken (think German). In its current election manifesto, the party says the Bauhaus has always sought to avoid any hint of "national roots."
Ahead of its time: 100 years of Bauhaus in Dessau

The signatories of the "Bauhaus Manifesto 2026" take the opposite view. "We need the sociopolitical impetus of the Bauhaus pioneers precisely at a time when political fringe groups are gaining strength and advocating regression rather than progress," they state.

They also point to the Bauhaus' persecution under the Nazis. "The example of the Bauhaus and the hostility it faced from the Nazi regime reminds us that the culture of remembrance is not a nostalgic look back, but a prerequisite for democratic self-understanding."

The manifesto states that cultural institutions that preserve memory and provide spaces for constructive debate should therefore be supported. The autonomy of artists and cultural institutions, it says, is a fundamental prerequisite for a vibrant democracy.

The Bauhaus is built on the idea of bringing together creative ideas, bold experimentation, high-quality craftsmanship and technological innovation, the manifesto says. It also represents openness and renewal, exchange and networking.
"This openness is a great strength of German culture and enriches Germany," its supporters say. "We reject nationalism that is hostile to culture."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Ronaldinho to make football comeback aged 46
articles.summary: More than a decade after his last professional appearance, Brazilian superstar Ronaldinho is set for a comeback. The former world player of the year is to play in Italy’s third tier.

image.caption: Despite the smile, Ronaldinho appears unsure whether he will actually play for Ravenna FC. Image: Massimo Paolone/LaPresse/IMAGO

blocks.text: While Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo are still playing at 39 and 41 respectively, most football fans thought Ronaldinho belonged to another footballing era.
That all changed in June, when Italian Serie C club, Ravenna, announced that the former Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and AC Milan forward would play for them in the upcoming season.
On a rainy Thursday in northeastern Italy, the former Ballon d'Or winner was unveiled with a quick press conference and a sense of excitement gripping the city.
"I'm very happy to be here with friends, we have a team that can do something good," said Ronaldinho.
"I just arrived, but I have a great desire to live this experience with the whole city."
Pure PR?

The 46-year-old last played for Fluminense in his homeland in 2015 and will become a shareholder in Ravenna, owned by Ignazio Cipriani, an Italian-American businessman who has owned the club since 2024.

Despite holding up the shirt and signing a piece of paper for the cameras, the suspicion remains that this is little more than a PR stunt for an ambitious lower league club. Ronaldinho himself didn't actually dispel those rumors.

blocks.caption: Ronaldinho won 97 caps for Brazil, scoring 33 goalsImage: AP

blocks.text: "Will you see me play? I don't know, only the coach knows that," he said. "Coming back to Italy is wonderful, I'm here to help my teammates win."

Both the Brazilian and Cipriani used the same language to describe one of Ronaldinho's motivations: "Friendship and passion," they both said. Both men also referred to Ronaldinho's quest to score a 300th professional goal.
"His objective is romantic, to try to score his last goal," Cipriani said.
"His involvement is not a token gesture or a marketing stunt to get people talking about us."
How an 81-year-old sprinter chases a world record

The way in which that figure has been reached is slightly unclear, with many widely used resources saying Ronaldinho has scored far fewer than 299 goals in his career. He has, however, won the Ballon d'Or in 2005, the 2002 World Cup and topflight titles in Spain and Italy.
Ronaldinho some way off Japan's Miura

Whether he ends up playing or not, Ronaldinho's presence in the northeastern city of about 160,000 inhabitants has sparked plenty of anticipation and ticket sales. Reports suggest the club has sold 2,700 season tickets, largely off the back of the Brazilian's arrival.
Even if he does get onto the pitch at 46, Ronaldinho will be far from the oldest footballer around. That title has long belonged to Japan's Kazuyoshi Miura, 59.
The former Japan international, who also played in Italy, scored two penalties in the country's Emperor's Cup competition this week, further extending his record as the world's oldest player.

articles.title: Drought in Germany and Europe are driving up costs
articles.summary: Ongoing drought in Europe is causing rivers to dry up and crops to fail. Transport costs are rising and the price of food has exploded. Is inflation due to extreme weather?

image.caption: The Rhine is one of Europe's busiest waterways usually, but it is experiencing record low levels this year. This is the Rhine river bed near Bornheim in western GermanyImage: Robert Schmiegelt/Geisler-Fotopress/picture alliance

blocks.text: So far, research institutes have not been able to quantify the impact of extreme weather conditions on inflation in Germany, but there are clear trends.

"If ships on the Rhine can only carry a fraction of their usual cargo, transport costs per metric ton will rise significantly," Torsten Schmidt, an economist at the RWI – Leibniz Institute for Economic Research, told DW.
He added that this would drive up the cost of energy sources, such as diesel and heating oil, which are in large part transported by water. He said that higher costs would be passed on to consumers.
For its data, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) takes into account the effects of global warming, extreme weather and crop losses.
According to the FAO, food prices are currently about 30% higher than in 2020, with meat and oilseeds rising sharply since then.
Inflation driven by extreme weather and energy shocks

Recent studies also suggest that climate change and extreme weather events are affecting inflation rates, as are supply bottlenecks as well as gas and oil price shocks caused by the US-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars.

A study conducted by the European Central Bank (ECB) and five European research institutes entitled "Climate extremes, food price spikes, and their wider societal risks" that was published in July 2025, warned against escalating inflation.

"Central bank mandates for price stability may become increasingly challenging to deliver if more frequent extreme weather events make food prices less stable domestically and in global markets," the study states.
Higher coffee prices in Brazil or Vietnam can also affect inflation in the EU.
Will ECB raise interest rates again?

These challenges could become even more trying if temperature rises have a long-term effect on inflation. If inflation has to be dealt with by higher interest rates, economic growth will also be hampered.

In 2023, the ECB published a study called "The asymmetric effects of weather shocks on euro area inflation" that reached a similar conclusion after examining the four largest European Union economies.

"With a changing climate implying an increased frequency and severity of extremes in Europe, the shocks studied here can be expected to occur more frequently and could lead to persistent upward pressures on inflation, especially from extreme temperatures in summer," it read. "Given the differing impacts of shocks in different seasons and across countries, our results also suggest that climate change could enhance heterogeneity of inflation developments across euro area countries."

According to the ECB, the inflation rate in the euro area in June this year ranged from 2% in France to 5.4% in Lithuania. At 2.4%, Germany was slightly below the EU average of 2.8%. High transport costs, at 5.3%, are driving inflation.
Whether the ECB will raise key interest rates again in view of increased costs on waterways remains to be seen. On June 11, it raised the deposit rate by 0.25 percentage points to 2.25%.
Why Europe's extreme summers are getting worse
'World is unpredictable on so many fronts'

"For monetary policy, the key question is whether this is a one-time, temporary spike in costs or whether the effect is being compounded by other factors that are driving up prices, such as energy prices resulting from the war in Iran," explained Schmidt from the RWI.

He predicted that a "weather-related price spike" would probably not lead to "tighter monetary policy" but suggested the situation would be different if multiple crises coincided, resulting in "wider, more persistent inflation that the ECB could no longer ignore."

Holger Schulz, a financial expert with the German Savings Banks Association (DSGV), recommended in a statement that the "German economy should return to operating with higher inventory levels. One thing is especially important now: stock, stock, stock."
He explained that this was the lesson learned from recent supply chain crises.

"Whether the COVID-19 crisis, the war in Ukraine or the closure of the Strait of Hormuz,” he said, "higher inventory levels are a kind of insurance premium in a world that is so unpredictable on so many fronts."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Why Germany's gas storage levels are so low
articles.summary: Germany's gas storage facilities are only 50% full as traders bet that wholesale prices will fall if the Iran war ends. With around three months until winter, DW asks whether the country can refill…

image.caption: A few months ahead of winter, Germany's gas storage facilities are only half fullImage: Axel Heimken/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 1. How full are Germany's gas storage levels right now?

Germany's more than 40 gas storage facilities are barely over half full, mainly due to the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz — currently the world's most critical energy chokepoint — because of the Iran war.

According to Gas Infrastructure Europe, the industry body for the continent's gas grid operators, Germany's underground natural gas stores stood at 50.14% on Wednesday. This is the lowest level for mid-August in several years.

Gas storage is around a quarter lower than on the same date last year and more than 45 percentage points lower than in 2023 and 2024, when the country made robust contingency plans due to Russia's war in Ukraine.
That conflict forced Germany, along with the rest of Europe, to reduce its reliance on Russian energy.
The diversification came mainly through higher liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports from the United States and Qatar, as well as additional pipeline gas supplies from Norway.
In the years that followed the outbreak of war, policymakers prioritized boosting gas storage levels ahead of winter, while also cutting consumer and business demand.
2. Why are Germany's gas storage facilities so low?
Normally, traders buy gas at low prices during the summer and store it for winter, where it can be sold at a higher price. This is called the summer-winter price spread.
This year, however, operators have little incentive to fill storage facilities earlier due to higher prices for natural gas and LNG on world markets, because of Iran war disruptions.

European wholesale gas prices remain well above pre-war levels. On Thursday, the benchmark Dutch TTF stood at around €65 ($76) per megawatt-hour, roughly twice as high as during the same period last year.
Over the past two weeks, the benchmark has risen by nearly a quarter, because of renewed attacks by the US and Iran.
Can Germany refit gas pipelines to transport cleaner energy?
Unlike many other European countries where governments buy gas or use strategic reserves to fill storage facilities, Germany relies heavily on private energy trading firms.
Market players are betting on falling gas prices over the next few months if the Iran war ends, allowing them to profit from lower rates.
For LNG, however, Europe must compete with Asia for the same limited supplies, with Asian rivals often prepared to pay more.
Politicians have accused traders of speculating on Germany's energy security, including Left Party lawmaker Jörg Cezanne, who told the Rheinische Post newspaper the tactic was a "gamble."
On Wednesday, a spokesperson for Germany's Economy Ministry said it was "urging traders to increase their gas storage levels."

blocks.caption: More tankers are carrying liquefied natural gas from the United States and Qatar to GermanyImage: Stefan Sauer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 3. How do Germany's gas stores compare with the rest of Europe?
Germany isn't the only European country with lower-than-average gas supplies.
Storage facilities in the Netherlands, Belgium, Slovakia, Sweden and Latvia are all under 50% full.
As of Wednesday, the average for all European Union countries was 61%, down nearly 17% from last year and nearly a third lower than in 2023 and 2024.
Among the EU nations with the most resilient supply are Spain, Italy, Denmark and Poland.
4. Can Germany still store enough gas for winter 2026?
FNB Gas, an association of gas transmission operators in Germany, warned Wednesday that the government's target of an average gas storage level of 71% by November 1 is now "virtually unattainable."

In a LinkedIn post, it noted that storage rates are currently rising by 0.5 terawatt-hours per day and even if they reached 1.2 terawatt-hours a day, "storage levels... will be significantly below [the target]."
It also cautioned that "low LNG imports, late or prolonged cold spells and infrastructure failures could jeopardize the gas supply this coming winter."
Germany signs Canadian LNG deal to cut energy risks

While the current storage levels are not ideal, Germany's Economy Ministry has repeatedly stressed that the country's gas supply remains secure, citing new LNG sources since the 2022/23 energy crisis.
Germany has quickly built several floating and onshore LNG terminals on its North Sea and Baltic Sea coasts, allowing ship deliveries from the global market.
5. What does Germany's gas shortfall mean for winter prices?
Consumer groups are already warning of higher gas prices this winter.

"We are monitoring gas storage levels very closely and see the potential challenges for the coming winter," Ramona Pop, executive director of the Federation of German Consumer Organizations (vzbv), told the Rheinische Post on Thursday.
Pop urged consumers to "check now whether their contract includes a fixed price that extends beyond the winter," which she said could offer "initial protection against rising prices."
The price comparison site Verivox warned that new consumer gas contracts are already up sharply since early March and could now rise for existing customers.
"For a single-family home with an annual consumption of 20,000 kWh, this translates to additional costs of around €400," it said.

articles.title: Munich prosecutors close fatal 1970 antisemitic arson case
articles.summary: Prosecutors and police in Munich believe they have identified the man who set a 1970 fire at a Jewish community center and old people's home that killed seven people. But he died in 2020, so…

image.caption: The 1970 arson attack on a Jewish religious center in central Munich killed seven people [FILE: February 13, 1970]Image: Joachim Barfknecht/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Munich's Public Prosecutor's Office believes it has solved one of the worst antisemitic attacks in post-war German history.
Police and prosecutors said on Thursday that new investigations point "clearly" towards the involvement of a man who died in 2020.
Additional information came to light after his death which led to the case being reopened in April 2025.
Now, with investigators satisfied that the culprit is identified — but with no scope to prosecute the deceased and no known indications of accomplices — they are closing the file once again.

blocks.caption: West Germany's president at the time, Gustav Heinemann, attended the memorial ceremony in MunichImage: Joachim Barfknecht/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What is the case about?
On February 13, 1970, a fire broke out at the Jewish religious community for Munich and Upper Bavaria, in the area incorporating its retirement home, killing seven people.
All of them had survived the Holocaust and two were inmates in Nazi German concentration camps.
Prosecutors said the fire was set using a "gasoline mixture" that was sprinkled and lit in several different places in a stairwell, hoping to ensure that it spread.

Another 15 people were wounded in the fire, four of them seriously. The building in central Munich sustained severe damages, particularly on the upper levels as a result of the stack effect channeling the flames up the stairwell.

blocks.caption: The attack took place three days after an attack at Munich-Riem airport by Palestinian terrorists; the victim from that attack was mourned along with the seven killed in the fireImage: Joachim Barfknecht/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What led investigators to reopen the file?
Investigations were originally halted in 2017, almost 50 years after the suspected homicides.
Prosecutors and Munich's police precinct explained what led them to reopening the case in Thursday's joint statement.

"A witness provided credible information on the suspect," they said. "She said that the suspect had been in close contact with one of her close relatives in the 1970s. Shortly after the death of this relative, she revealed her knowledge on the matter."
Authorities reviewed old files and also interviewed contacts of the suspect in the renewed investigation.

blocks.caption: The fire caused considerable damage on the upper levels; a reward was offered at the time but the culprit was never caughtImage: Joachim Barfknecht/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did investigators say about the suspect?
Prosecutors did not identify the suspect, and stressed that posthumous prosecution was not possible in Germany and that the presumption of innocence still applied in death.
They identified him as a man who died in 2020 and who was 25 years old at the time of the attack. He was regularly in the area of the religious center on Reichenbachstrasse at the time, they said.

On the evening of the fire, investigators said he was alleged to have complained that "the Jews have everything" while standing in sight of the old people's home and to have expressed a desire to set them alight. Within a quarter of an hour, the building was ablaze, prosecutors said.

"These allegations are based on credible statements from the witness, who in turn was relaying what her deceased relative told her," the prosecutor's office said. "Additional relatives confirmed these statements."
What did prior background investigations reveal?
Prosecutors also said that background investigations further solidified their suspicions.
The suspect was a known member of the far-right community in Munich at the time, with witnesses describing him as an antisemite with a "Hitler obsession."

In his youth he had listened to Hitler speeches on records. He practiced shooting near Adolf Hitler's Berghof holiday home in the Bavarian Alps, the site of multiple antisemitic crimes against humanity in the Nazi era.

He had a history of using explosives and a juvenile conviction for blowing up two telephone booths in the 1960s. A headteacher also recalled a violent incident from his youth when he pulled a Hitler youth dagger which he said was a gift from his father.
Prosecutors said it was not possible to say whether the suspect acted alone or in a group with certainty, but also said the investigations had not found any indications of accomplices.

"All in all, the new investigations conducted after the reopening of the case speak clearly for the suspect's involvement," prosecutors concluded, albeit with it no longer being possible to try the case in a court of law.

articles.title: What went wrong with U.S. trade talks, according to Canada's chief negotiator
articles.byline: Benjamin Lopez Steven, Catherine Cullen, Derek Vanderwyk

image.caption: Janice Charette, Canada's chief trade negotiator to the United States, speaks at a Canadian Chamber of Commerce summit in Ottawa on April 21. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Canada's chief U.S. trade negotiator is disputing several claims made by American officials about why trade talks fell apart last week, namely that the Canadian side brought forward last-minute demands on autos and that U.S. negotiators weren't interested in French language discoverability rules.

"Canada has been resolute throughout these negotiations that we were talking about the entirety of our automotive sector," Janice Charette said in an exclusive interview with CBC's The House airing Saturday morning.

Charette's comments clash with those made by U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who told reporters Thursday that the Canadians only brought up tariff relief on medium- and heavy-duty trucks at the last minute — and further alleged the Canadians did so to kill the deal.

"The words 'medium- and heavy-duty trucks’ were raised in these negotiations on Friday at 4 o'clock," Lutnick said. Those trucks include some models of Ford's F-series pickups and the General Motors Silverado, which are made at Ontario plants.
Charette refrained from calling Lutnick wrong, but said the Canadians raised the issue on "Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday."
Charette says Canada consistently raised auto industry in U.S. trade negotiations
"Howard Lutnick was not at the negotiating table," Charette told host Catherine Cullen.
She added that the Canadians were speaking with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, and it was very clear they were seeking tariff relief for those types of autos, among other sectors.

Both countries have been trading barbs over the past week about who — and what — ultimately killed a prospective trade deal that could have granted Canada tariff relief in key sectors such as autos, steel and aluminum, and lumber.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has maintained it was late U.S. demands that prompted him to call negotiators back to Ottawa, while Lutnick and Greer argue the Canadians are at fault.
Carney outlines the last-minute changes U.S. tacked onto trade deal terms
Asked whether she views the U.S. claims on what went wrong as dishonesty or merely a question of perspective, Charette chalked it up to differing opinions.

According to Charette, the Canadians were seeking an arrangement with "the lowest rate of tariffs on the narrowest basket of goods with the best market access — so the best deal overall, and the best trade deal for each of our key strategic sectors. That's what we were working towards."

items: Trump's top trade negotiator disputes Canadian assertion that U.S. made last-minute demands

blocks.text: The Canadian government understood that a U.S. trade deal would involve some degree of tariffs on its goods and tariff-free access on American products, Charette added.
"In no case has any country been able to secure an agreement unless they agreed that U.S. goods were going to enter into their market tariff-free," Charette said.
French discoverability, Canadian free trade deals

Carney has told reporters that at the last minute, the U.S. took issue with Canadian rules that ensure French language content is easy to find on streaming platforms such as Netflix, and that the Americans tried to restrict Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries.
This week, both Greer and Lutnick pushed back on Canada's claims on French language discoverability, arguing the U.S. would not jeopardize a deal over that issue.

"If you think I ever said the word 'French' — do I care about how the Québécois speak? I mean, what could matter less to America? We don't care," Lutnick said Thursday, adding that Carney "manufactured" the issue to influence the provincial election in Quebec.

Charette pushed back on that version of events and said the Canadians were prepared to look at financial obligations imposed on streamers, but would never offer movement on measures to protect the French language.
"And it is also true that right up until the final negotiating session, Friday night, the Americans were still asking for us to remove those provisions," Charette said.

As for restrictions on Canada's future trade deals, Greer told CBC News earlier this week that there was no requirement in the text, but rather that the U.S. sought to discuss how Canada could align its tariffs so it doesn't become a backdoor for steel and aluminum from other countries.

items: LeBlanc welcomes U.S. decision 'withdrawing positions' on language, culture
What we know about how the Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart

blocks.text: Charette said the topic came up "quite late" in discussions, and it was unclear to the Canadians whether the Americans wanted a consultation on future free trade agreements, some kind of sign-off or a veto.

"But it was clear that there was an interest on the part of the United States in constraining or limiting Canada's ability to enter into future free trade agreements for important products like primary steel that would come into the Canadian market," she said.

A source has previously told CBC News that the U.S. wanted Canada to apply sectoral tariffs, primarily on steel and aluminum, to its trading partners, and countries that have a free trade deal with Canada would face tariffs on imports above 2025 levels.
Where does Canada go from here?
Charette said as it stands, Canada's "pens are down, but the door is open."
"We're prepared to go and work with the United States on a deal that would be in the economic interest of Canadians, as long as it doesn't impact Canadian sovereignty," she said.
As for whether Canada can trust the U.S. as negotiating partners, Charette said that remains to be seen.
"Trust is earned, and trust is earned through the fine print of a trade agreement that was under negotiation right up until those final moments in the night on Friday."
Canada won't accept U.S. attitude that we're a 'subsidiary,' Carney says

Greer has said there are no open channels right now, but he has a good relationship with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc. Meanwhile, Lutnick has claimed Canadian negotiators will kickstart talks again once the Quebec election and Alberta referendum are complete.

The Canadian government is bracing for a long fight. On Tuesday, it announced it will match U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods by tariffing $27.6 billion of comparable U.S. goods.

items: The art of inflicting pain: How to select targets for Canada's counter-tariffs

blocks.text: The Liberal government is also rolling out $7.5 billion to help workers and businesses weather the U.S. tariffs. Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne has said that the federal government will continue its support for "as long as it takes."
Asked how she feels about where everything stands now, Charette said she's proud of the work the Canadian team did.
"We didn't leave anything, we put it all out on the field. There was no stone unturned, we did everything we thought we could," she said.
